en: The third hexad: the Jayadratha-yāmala.
(Om, salutation to Śiva and the other gurus.

Having upraised the goad of the Vedas' outpouring, holding the excellent tooth in her hand, and bearing the head of Brahmā, she holds upon her arm the great and formidable skeleton-lute that possesses the luster of those [bones].

Sukālī, who causes this world to resound with her movements through time and form, is the sovereign of Jayadratha; she is Viṣṇu’s Rudrā, the auspicious Śivā within that Lord, and the fiercely wrathful Kālī who is exclusively devoted to the destruction of Time.
Having heard the twelve-thousand-verse [Purāṇa], she is the supreme mistress.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the Universe, she spoke again in accordance with the truth.
The Goddess said:
"O God of gods, I have heard that most excellent of all tantras and mantras."
It is accompanied by its secret teachings, greatly radiant, well-guarded, and the bestower of all accomplishments.
With the Lord of Devas, the King of Sindhu, and the Lord of Men as witnesses,
you have thus explained in detail that which was spoken to the gods.
In that regard, at the time of the *paya* sacrifice, you spoke of what is honored by the gods; how, for the sake of a Brahmin and for the benefit of those seeking Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
it was proclaimed by the Blessed One on account of Vasiṣṭha— that I shall now relate to you.
How was this *tantra* concerning Jayadratha composed for the sake of the Brahmin?
And why was it accomplished on account of Vasiṣṭha through the [intervention of] Nara and Nārāyaṇa? Furthermore, for what reason have these two names been given to this *tantra* by you?
"O Lord, instruct me in this from the beginning, together with its secret and its characteristics,
so that, becoming free from doubt, I may listen to the Tantra. Having heard this, his lotus-like eyes suddenly opened wide.
The Lord of the World, illuminating the universe with the moonlight of his smile, spoke this:
Bhairava said:
"Listen, O lady of beautiful hips; I shall tell you this wonderful secret."
Just as in the past, by the impulsion of Brahmā’s power, [the world arose];
so too, O beloved, will that which is to be, [arise] through the manifestation of the inherent power of things.

Thus, through such brief indication and detailed explanation, these things certainly exist; of this there is no doubt. This is merely a sign: Brahmā, the Lord of the Ocean, as well as you, I, and likewise other gods and the best of sages.

Indeed, the powers of the Supreme Lord manifest themselves through the perfection of various forms; this scripture has been proclaimed by the Great Lord for the sake of bestowing grace upon all individual souls.
Thus, all scriptures, following the lineage of the gurus,
are indeed of beginningless form here, having come into manifestation through the power [of Śakti].
As for the sequence of speaker and listener, it exists by virtue of the penetration of that power.
Following that impulse, it manifests in many ways as individual expressions;
the scriptures are beginningless, originating from Sadāśiva, the supreme cause.
For this reason, O Goddess, there is no one superior to the lineage of the succession of gurus.
In this matter, the wise should investigate the mere sign (nimitta).
Therefore, O beloved, by the power of immersion, this Jāyadratha-tantra belongs to Sindhu-rāja as well as to the unmanifest Brahman.
The vast, beginningless, and eternal scripture proclaimed by Śiva was brought down by Śiva himself through sentences consisting of questions and answers;
having himself cut away [doubts] from the mouth of his disciple, he repeatedly produced the sprouts of inquiry.
Having entered the mouth of the Guru, he himself answers the questions.
Thus the sequence has been fully declared; this is the primary initiation, not for any other reason.
I shall relate to you what occurred in the past concerning Brahmā himself.
Once, Brahmā, the Lord and Master of the world, residing in the realm of Brahman,
was surrounded by the gods together with the Vedas and their auxiliary branches and the Upaniṣads;
endowed with great majesty, established in knowledge, he blazed brilliantly.
O Goddess, by chance the goddess Sarasvatī herself arrived there from the world of Śiva; having heard of that supreme majesty,
O goddess of gods, she, the mistress of yoga, was strengthened by her [the former’s] power.
Seeing her with her radiant body, Brahmā, being well-pleased, said:
"From where have you come, O blessed lady, endowed with such splendor and shining so brightly?"
"Blazing with a terrible form and augmented by mantras—
tell me this, O fair-hipped one, the cause of this wonderful splendor.
Having heard this, that goddess Vāgeśī, who is skilled in speech, [replied].
I spoke loudly to Brahmā: "In the world of Śiva, I heard an incomparable secret of the Goddess by which my mind became satisfied;
through the grace of the Supreme Lord, I have arrived here fully gratified."
"O beloved, the time for the discourse of the Supreme Lord was then taking place there. Having heard this, Brahmā’s hair stood on end with joy;
he then resolved to go there, accompanied by his attendants and his powerful mounts."
Proud of his own knowledge, he quickly yoked the chariot;
having made the four great Vedas the horses and the *vasāṅgikā* his reins,
he made the *praṇava* the goad, while the Self was the driver.
In this context, one should employ *pragraha* as the *gāyatrī* and the excellent *dhvaja* as the *sāvitrī*.
Through these two, by means of the sequence of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*), one should effect the penetration of the three joints.
Having applied the *yoktra* and the fourfold net, one should conquer the two sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) that have been extended.
Established therein through the supreme transformation is the *praṇava*, possessing five deities;
likewise the subordinate elements and the rays—that which is the highest majesty.
The God of gods generated everything, and the God of gods indeed joined it all together.
Then he fashioned the Sāṃkhya-yoga, as well as the inner self (adhyātma) and the very sequence of the earth;
he then created the radiant Brahmā-ratha, belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha, among the directions of the chariot. Thus was the divine Great Chariot, auspicious by name, the Brahmaratha.
He then fashioned the out-breath and in-breath as the two arms on the chariot. Thus, being honored by all the hosts of gods and endowed with supreme splendor, he ascended that most excellent chariot.
Having thus caused that being to enter [the body], the Great-Grandfather,
employing supreme speed, proceeded to where Śaṅkara was.
And as he was then proceeding toward the world of Viṣṇu, as he advanced,
you gathered eightfold the splendor of his radiance.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu himself, composed of great illusion (mahāmāyā), [emerged] from that chariot.
Then, as Brahmā was proceeding, his supreme chariot suddenly fell from the world of Rudra; it was deprived of its horses,
its strength failed, its weapons were gone, and its goad was lost.
Seeing Brahmā thus deprived of his resolve,
they then considered themselves gentle, yet destitute of power and knowledge;
and having deemed him unfortunate, they were themselves greatly afflicted by hunger.
"Fie upon my wretched body, which is always unfortunate,
since I am not worthy for the Śakti-vijñāna that has entered the mouth of the Teacher!
Having thus reproached himself, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [reflected].
Then, having firmly resolved his mind and fashioned the divine form through *vyāna* breath,
Brahmā, the lord of the entire world, worshipped the Supreme Lord with this hymn and was immediately gratified.
Brahmā said:
Salutations to you, the God of gods, to Śiva of imperishable form,
who is most fierce and formidable, possessing the power to uplift the three worlds.
Salutations to you, the beloved of Umā, whose body is as pure as a white lotus and the moon;
salutations to the blue-throated, fierce Rudra of unmanifest splendor.
Salutations to the one whose body is Bhairava and whose abode is the cremation ground.
Salutations to you who are moving, well-concealed, and dwelling in the cave [of the heart];
salutations eternally to the one with matted hair, whose form transcends delusion, who resides within the center of the heart-lotus, and whose nature is that of the supreme swan (parahaṃsa).
Salutations to the God who is beyond the Vedas, who is the Vedānta, and who possesses great majesty;
salutations to Him who dwells within the abode [of the heart] and whose chariot is the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
To Sūrya, whose form is wisdom, who is both manifest and unmanifest,

whose body is manifested through the three qualities (guṇas), and who is the lord of Brahmā and Upendra— to you, O Lord, I am forever submerged in this worldly existence, a dense thicket of delusion and terrible peril.

O Lord of Gods, overflowing with the essence of compassion, O cloud for the forest-fire of saṃsāra, O sole extinguisher of the heat of worldly desires, please lift me up from this ocean of existence, which is difficult to cross due to the crocodiles of snakes and the like.
To the one whose very self is the sole preceptor for destroying the foremost venomous serpents that are sense-objects;
to the sun and moon for the darkness of ignorance, and the path of nectar for the destruction of death;
to the form of the Great Sun who utterly dispels the gloom of obstacles and sins.
Protect me, O Supreme Lord, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge!
Grant protection to one who has fallen, who is exceedingly wretched, terrified by the ocean of sense-objects, and whose observance of the rules of conduct has been lost— O Bull-bannered One!
"O Lord, this chariot was fashioned by me out of ignorance;
therefore, O Lord, forgive me, a foolish-minded and wicked-souled one.
Thus did the highly resplendent Brahmā utter this hymn of praise.
At that very moment, O fortunate one, a vision of the wielder of the trident was suddenly granted to him by me, as I was pleased with Brahmā’s mind. Then I spoke to that Brahmā of immense splendor.
"Arise, O Padmāsana Haimā, O wielder of the staff who has fallen into delusion!
O Lord of Gods, I am now pleased by this hymn of yours. Speak, what shall I do for you? Here I stand before you, ready to grant a boon."
Having heard this, Brahmā suddenly fell prostrate upon the earth like a staff; bowing down, he spoke to me with devotion:
"O Lord, the divine chariot fashioned for me has been destroyed."
"Because that [knowledge] was lost, I am lost along with my family and attendants.
Desiring to hear the Śākta-vijñāna, O Śiva, I have come into your presence;
I am overcome by extreme delusion and afflicted by negligence."
Therefore, let that excellent chariot seen by one such as I be granted to me.
By your grace alone, O Lord of Gods, may victory be mine in your presence.
"O Maheśvara, I possess the capacity and the fitness to hear this.
Having heard this, O slender-waisted one, I then said to him:
"By the grace of the True One, may victory now be yours through this chariot."
O Brahman, because of this extraction, I shall now myself proclaim in the world your *Jayadrathamaṇḍala-tantra* by name and in substance; furthermore,
it shall have another designation, namely "The Severing of the Head."
Thus, having consulted regarding that supreme tantra, the Gaṇa, due to the curse of Bhṛṅgin,
was born in Gandhamādana as one known by the name Jayadratha;
he will undoubtedly proclaim this most excellent tantra.
Having heard this supreme secret from my mouth by my command, come therefore to my world; there I shall teach you the Tantra,
which is Śākta, endowed with secrets, formidable, and highly honored.
Having heard this, I then went to my own world together with him.
There, the Lord of the Universe sat before me;
at that time, O Goddess of gods, the lineage of gurus was worshipped by me.
Having attained this immortal essence, that lineage of Rāviṇī was remembered;
and having bound the Rāviṇī mudrā, the goddess Karaṅkiṇī was remembered. Then the world of Malla trembled, along with the entire universe and the Hūhukas.
He rained down upon the fire from the sky in the form of a shower;
and even as he did so, the fifth head of Brahmā became filled with a terrible water, like that at the end of an eon.
Having let out a great roar, the goddess Karaṅkiṇī— possessing terrifying fangs, intent on extracting mantras,
and most formidable as she prepared to swallow the world— arrived there.
Five-faced, with terrifying fangs, and distinguished by eighteen arms;
possessing the splendor of ten million setting suns, she is the terror even of fear itself.
By the power of her immersion, that head which had emerged from Brahmā was suddenly severed; crying out with the sound of "Veda," the Goddess of gods, the wielder of the thunderbolt,
drank only the blood there.
Then, upon seeing her, with a heart terrified by fear,
I praised that slender-waisted goddess of gods with various hymns.
Thereupon, the Great Goddess, being well-pleased, vanished from sight.
Having pacified the great upheaval in this world that was so difficult to endure,
he obtained from Brahmā— who was being consoled by me with the nectar of immortality—
the subtle [power] after a hundred divine years.
Then Brahmā arose before me, he who has mastered the Vedas;
and for him, whose mind was quickened, the Goddess immediately proclaimed that unsurpassed Tantra,
beginning with a thousand syllables, which is difficult for the world to attain.
Then, having heard me endowed with the power of mantras,
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, worshipped me with devotion;
satisfied, he departed for his own celestial realm while being honored by the foremost of the gods.
From that time forth,
O Goddess, this unsurpassed tantra became known as the *Śiraścheda* and was heard [in the world] as the *Jayadratha*.
Then, at one time, O Mistress of the Gods, two [beings] were impelled by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).
The two lords of sages named Nara and Nārāyaṇa, whose souls were purified,
desiring to know the Śākta wisdom,
undertook a severe penance for a thousand divine years, subsisting on air alone and remaining without food.
Then Brahmā, his mind delighted by both of them, approached them in person.
"O Goddess of gods, by my command, the bestower of boons stands before you.
Then Brahmā chose this unsurpassed boon from the two of them.
"Tell me in brief that Goddess who is celebrated in the Vedic traditions as having a thousand syllables, just as you heard it before."
When this had been said, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
then described to them the Goddess of the gods, who is known as the Thousand-Syllabled One;
subsequently, they both arrived on earth through the lineage of teacher and disciple.
There, on the Himavat mountain, near the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha,
that best of sages was wandering about. Having then placed a living being that had come there by force into his water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) for the sake of protecting it from evil, he remained there.
He approached their presence to offer water for the hands (*argha*) and water for the feet (*pādya*).
Having honored that tiger among sages,
he was then forcibly possessed on the ground by that *apasmṛti* spirit due to his past karma.
Seeing that Bhava was thus afflicted by the sage Nārāyaṇa,
the highly fortunate one, filled with compassion,
recalled that sixty-four-fold, unassailable lore (*vidyā*) on account of that great sin.
That lord of sages gazed intently at the perfect rishi;
he [Viśvāmitra] destroyed for him his own power of sight.
Then Vasiṣṭha, freed from sin and joyful in heart, was satisfied with himself.
Having saluted them both there once again, he spoke, desiring to ask:
"By your grace, I have been liberated from a most terrible great sin;
therefore, by your favor, let that which is a secret be told to me."

"O best of sages, by the power of what mantra have I, who was scorched by the ocean of sin, been liberated by you out of compassion? Having heard this properly from Vasiṣṭha, the best of rishis," [he spoke].
He, however, truly proclaimed the Goddess-mantra that bestows great purpose:
that Goddess of a thousand syllables, augmented by the potency of mantra,
was then declared to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha by Nārāyaṇa.
Therefore, this was previously told here concerning Vasiṣṭha:
that which was formerly Śivā, now belongs to Hari and Brahmā, and today it is the destroyer of Vasiṣṭha.
In this Tantra, O slender-waisted one, that [teaching] has been declared along with its secrets.
It is threefold through the division of words for Jayadratha, the cutter of heads.
This has been fully explained to you just as I was impelled by you.

Thus, regarding the pair of feet anointed by the moonlight of the crest-jewel of the Lord of the Gods, what else need I say? Bhava’s teaching is truly the most beautiful of all and the savior from worldly existence.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction of the Questions," in the third hexad of the *Vasiṣṭha* [Saṃhitā], within the *Jayadrathayāmala*, which consists of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the *Śiraccheda* division of the *Siddhividyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairava-srotas*.
Having thus heard this secret from the Supreme Lord, the Daughter of the Mountain again questioned the Lord of Gods regarding the Great Ocean of Mantras. The Goddess said:
O God of gods, marked with the trident, compassionate toward those who have come for refuge;
O omniscient, all-pervading Lord, intent on protecting the three worlds!
Tell me, O Lord of gods, that which severed the head of Brahmā.
Terrible, the destroyer of all [defilements], garlanded with a thousand syllables—
by means of which practitioners desiring liberation no longer grieve;
she who bestows all accomplishments has been proclaimed by you in this Tantra.
Having heard these words of profound meaning, the God of gods,
his soul delighted, replied while remembering the slender-waisted Goddess.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O beloved, I shall proclaim another Vidyā that is a cow of plenty for those who desire knowledge;
it is formidable, capable of shattering the universe, and the taker of Brahmā’s head.
Within the belly of the world, there exists no other Vidyā more terrible than this.
Having attained Vāmā, practitioners free from affliction do not grieve;
she consists entirely of all heroic power, is pure, and is supreme, consisting of all mantras. (5b)

She consists of all yoga, she is subtle, and she pierces all cakras; she is the fierce crusher of all mantras and the warder-off of all obstacles. She is the bestower of all prosperity, most excellent, and the destroyer of all evil deeds.
She who generates happiness and good fortune, the destroyer of spirits and epilepsy;
she who wears the skull of Brahmā, the fierce one seated upon a great corpse;
she who possesses a beautiful lute made from the skeleton of Brahmā, striking it with the skeletal remains of Time.
O illustrious lady, listen to how the Mistress of All bestows [her grace]:
in the mother’s house, on a mountain peak, in a cremation ground, or in an excellent home, the preceptor— whose soul is perfectly serene and who is devoted to the conduct of heroes— [bestows it].
Having made the earth rubbed with skeletons and smeared with great quantities of blood,
and having strewn it with flowers and purified it with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
one who is greatly intent on the oblation there, gladdened by the joy of wine—
Well-incensed, with excellent betel, dressed in smeared garments, and with senses restrained;
one should worship the Goddess of the Gods who stands upon a thunderbolt-seat, wearing tinkling bracelets,
resting within the womb of the thunderbolt, and possessing the fivefold colors of the syllables.
Having constructed a square city divided into nine compartments,
one should eliminate the pairs situated on the left and right in successive order,
until only one remains at the throat; then, one should proceed in the same manner above that.
One should make the two ends at the tip pointed; here, there are nine squares at the extremities.
Thus, fifty-one squares are declared.
In this manner, the accomplishment of the Vajra with its sharp-pointed tip is proclaimed.
O Goddess, listen as I describe the procedure for the arrangement of syllables (*varṇavidhi*) for one who desires [success].
One should place two *praṇavas* at the front of the east; this auspicious [arrangement] is sufficient for all mantras.
Starting from the square of Īśāna up to the square of Vahni (the southeast).
The nine vowels beginning with *ā* are indeed the great [vowels].
O lady of beautiful smiles, beneath that [square] are the compartments situated in the corners.
O Goddess, having omitted the middle one,
one should write the other vowels in the four squares located in the lower corners; then, from the sixteenth [vowel] onwards, one should write the consonants beginning with *ka* in reverse order.
One should draw [the letters] in sequence within the nine squares, starting from *ja* up to the portion ending in *dhū*.
In the three upper corners and the other three surrounding [corners],
O Goddess, one should write the letters ending in *ḍha* in the middle.
Then, there are exactly five compartments arranged in nine ways.
O Goddess, one should write in sequence within them the group of five beginning with *ṇa* and ending with *dha*.
Below that, in the corner compartment situated near the letter *e*, [one should place the letter *ra*].
The letter *na* should be placed there; from the bottom of the eye, the letter *tu* is at the base.
Then, the letters beginning with *pha* and ending with *ya* should be assigned in sequence to the five central squares situated at the base.

In its southern direction, one should draw a single square. Above it, on the right side, one should inscribe the two syllables *la* and *va*. Having written the letter *sa* below that, one should write the syllable *haṃ* together with the word *granthā*.
At its base, one should always draw the nectar (amṛta) and the five-pointed [vajra];
thus the Mātṛkā-vajra shall be adorned with all the letters.
Having worshipped it according to the rule and according to one's capacity with divine meat, liquor, and so forth—
Then, with all heroic offerings, one should extract the Vidyā.
Having rendered the world, along with its equipment, free from defects, O Supreme Goddess, one should first extract that which resides at the tip of the eastern peak.
After that, from the Vajragranthi, one should extract the fourth [letter] preceded by the Ālayā;
then, having extracted it together with the Daksina (the letter *u*), it is adorned by that same [Daksina].
This second [mantra], which has the form of a city of the Sun (*varṇasūryapura*), is thus proclaimed.
O Goddess, one should extract [the letter] situated in the wind-corner from the end of the lower station;
that third leader of letters is joined with the one situated in the southwest.
This step is extremely fierce, causing the destruction of the three worlds.
Furthermore, the vajra-knot should be given; it possesses great power and is situated upon that [step].
It is joined with what is below it and adorned by the first musical instrument.
Adorned on the head with the letter *pha*, the seed-syllable is like ten thousand suns;
having extracted the first of the letter *a* and placed it upon the head of the first of the letter *sa*,
one should enclose this extremely formidable seed-syllable between two *sa*s.
Furthermore, O Bhairavī, make the first letter of the syllable *aṃ* reside within the *saṃ*. Marked at its head by the end of *na* and adorned with the end of *pha*,
this is declared to be the *piṇḍa*, which causes possession in an instant.
Furthermore, O Dear One, that which is situated in the wind [direction] should be extracted from the lower group of nine;
this syllable, not joined with the letter of Nairṛti, is difficult to attain.
Again, O God, one should likewise give the syllable beginning with *aṃ*.
One should not join it with the final letter, nor should one give the head again in sequence.
The first [syllable] should be given as the vowel *ā* alone to complete the mantra.
For this seven-syllable word is the second, which destroys all evil.
Furthermore, the wise should not give that which has been vomited out (the letter *va*) joined with the final one (*na*).
Then, the "diamond-middle" (*vajramadhyam*, the letter *ra*) should be given, situated above the final one (*na*).
It should be adorned by the letter ending in *sa* (*sa*) and marked by the first of the four [consonants] (*ka*).
Having made it stainless with the letter *pha*, one should place the *piṇḍa* at the end of *māyā*.
Having extracted the *vānta*, O Goddess of Gods, it is situated upon *sādya*.
Enclosing the *piṇḍa* with the letter *sa*, it becomes like the fire of time (*kālānala*).

One should again give the "Vajra-middle" (va), endowed with the sixth [vowel] from the beginning (u); joined with the letter ending in *pha* (ph), it ends with the seed-syllable of the fire of time (kṣa). Then, one should give the letter ending in *dha* (dh), and thereafter extract the letter ending in *ma* (m) together with its vowel.
The third [mantra], the five-syllabled word, is proclaimed to be formidable.
O Goddess of gods, having extracted the letter beginning with *ya*, it is the one situated at the end (*sa*) and possesses great power.
Taking the fourth letter together with the head [letter], it is purified by the letter ending in *pha*;
then, having again extracted the letter ending in *va*, one should extract it along with its initial vowel. This two-syllable word is indeed the fourth, which destroys the time of death.
Furthermore, one should take the syllable beginning with *aṃ* and adorn it with the letter ending in *n*.
Adorned at the head with the letter ending in *ph*, this seed-syllable has the brilliance of the fire of time (*kālāgni*).
Having extracted that which stands between *ṭa* and *ḍa*, one should arrange it as that which stands at the beginning of *tha*.
Having first visualized the syllable *Śānta* (Śa), then again visualize it as established in *Jhānta* (Jha).
Then, with *Phānta* (Pha), purify the eastern [syllable] which has a second head (*dvitīyaśiras*).
Next, with *Vānta* (Va) preceded by *Sā* (Sa), there arises the state that causes the falling of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍapātana*).

One should again join the great *vajrāṇḍa*, which consists of three syllables, is most formidable and excellent, and is intent on terrifying the gods; it is situated as the sixth of the preceding [syllables] and is adorned with the letter *pha*.
Having done so, one should subsequently extract that which is to be concealed (*chādya*).
One should join it with the *kānta* [consonant], and then extract the *vānta* [consonant] again.

Having formed an enclosure (*sampuṭa*) with the *śānta* [consonant], one should extract the vowel together with its initial [consonant]. The sixth word consists of three syllables; it is formidable and has the nature of the Daityas' knowledge.
One should take the letter *ka*, which is beautiful and well-proportioned, bringing about the destruction of all colors;
that very same [letter], established in tranquility, joined with the letter *ja* and preceded by the sixth vowel (*u*),
and having made it variegated with the letter *pha*, one forms the *piṇḍa* that devours the sun.

Having formed a packet (puṭa) with the "vomited" (vānta) and "pacified" (śānta) [syllables], that very same thing is immediately the three-syllabled word taught as sevenfold, which causes the falling of the sun's orb. Again, it goes to the eastern peak, and again, it goes to the western peak.
The second [syllable] from the beginning, conjoined with the letter *pha* and purified by the letter *ma*, is to be concealed alone once more.
O Dear One, the third mark, preceded by the letter *va* and followed by the letter *ya*, is to be placed above and below. Furthermore, the letter *ya* is to be given again.
O Bhairavī, make the syllable *sānta* (sa), with its head (*ma*) placed upon it and joined with *nānta* (na);
and at the end of *dhānta* (dha), place the first letter (*sa*) together with its vowel.
The eighth *pada* is declared to be the deluder of the entire universe;
it consists of eight syllables, O Goddess of the gods, and increases all prosperity.
One should give only that which ends with the letter *ma*, and one should extract only that which ends with the letter *la*.
Moving backward through the combined consonants, place the letter *kha* situated after *ḍa*.
Then extract the "Vajra-egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*) inlaid with the third letter of the first group;
place it where *śa* resides as before, purified by the letter *pha*.
At the end, the word *sādyasasvara* (the vowel 'a' with 'sa' at its beginning) should be extracted as a nine-syllabled phrase;

it is remembered as a six-syllabled mantra that is most formidable and the destroyer of saṃsāra. Having extracted the letter ending in *ya* (i.e., *ya*), which is the Lord of Letters (*varṇeśa*), its head is adorned by the letter ending in *pha* (i.e., *pha*).
One should extract the syllable beginning with *kha* (kha), which is further adorned by *śa* (śa) and established in *śa*.
One should make it marked by *pha* (pha); this is the seed-syllable that attracts the three worlds.
Having again extracted the first of this [syllable] (*kha*), one should join it with *ya* (ya) and *sa* (sa).
Having again extracted the *vajrāṇḍa* (the syllable *va*) together with its final letter (*a*), which was previously adorned by three [consonants],
one should give that same *vajrāṇḍa* again, not joined with its final letter.
Having given the *vānta* (the syllable *va*) enclosed within the *sānta* (the syllable *sa*), one should extract it together with its initial vowel.
The tenth word is declared to consist of nine syllables and to delude the universe.
Again, having extracted the Vajra-egg (the letter *va*), one places the fifth letter of the first group (*pa*) in the middle of the letter *ya*;
having adorned it with the letter *ka*, that cluster ends with the Lord of Principles (*tattveśvara*).
Furthermore, its first [syllable] should be given, resembling the Destroyer at the end of the eon.
The eleventh word is to be known as a formidable and supreme two-syllabled [mantra].
Having extracted the middle of *ṭa* and *ḍau*, it is adorned with the sixth [vowel] followed by *sa*.
One should make the *phānta* (the letter *pha*) variegated (*saṃcitrita*), while the *vānta* (the letter *va*) is to be at the beginning and without vowel (*asvara*).
The twelfth syllable is extremely fierce; it is a two-syllable *kīlana* of the Moon.
O Goddess of Gods, having extracted the *mānta* (the letter *ma*), it is situated as the fifth from the first.
Having adorned it with mercury, perform the procedure once again in that same manner. Furthermore,
such [mercury] should be given, provided it is free from blemishes.
The two letters *ṇa* and *ḍa*, joined together as a single unit (*piṇḍa*) and adorned above by the letter *na*,
followed by the first letter of that [unit] which is devoid of life (*vānta* = *va*), O Supreme Goddess—
this is declared to be the great thirteenth word consisting of five syllables.
Place *ṭa* and *ḍa* in the middle; place *tha*, the first of the sibilants (*sa*), and the one situated after the sibilants (*ha*).
Adorned with the second letter of the first group (*ca*) and purified by the end of the *pha*-group (*ma*), extract once more that which is the first of the first cluster (*ka*).
This fourteenth word consisting of two syllables has been indicated by me;
it is the great terrorizer of the mantras of gods, asuras, and humans.
Furthermore, it is situated within the vajra-egg and established in the fifth position of the preceding [syllable].
One should again extract the first syllable of this, adorned at its head with the *phaṭ* sound.
This two-syllabled word indeed shatters all the netherworlds;
it is declared to consist of fifteen [syllables] and is the opener of the six cakras.
Having again given *ga* in the middle, illuminated by *kānta*, one should extract its first letter once more; this is the second-syllable sixteenth word.
Having again given *va* in the middle, adorned by the end of *nā* and the end of *phā*.
One should extract the "Vajra-egg" (vajrāṇḍa) together with the final letter ending in *sa* (the letter *pha*) from the fourth [group] of the first [row];
then the letter ending in *sa* (the letter *va*) at the end of the [fifth group], formed as a single cluster (*piṇḍabhūta*), followed by the first vowel (*a*).
This should be known as the seventeen-syllable phrase that shatters illusion (*māyā-prapāṭana*).
O Goddess, one should extract the letter *ya* joined with the end of *va*;

then the middle of *cha* and *ṅa* should be given again; then the end of *ḍha* conjoined with the beginning of *la*; then the end of *sa* joined with the end of *ma*; and one should extract the middle of *gha* and *kha*.
Having extracted the eighteenth word— marked at the head with *na*, ending with *ra*, adorned with *la*,
preceded by *sa* and having the third letter as its mark, ending with *va*, marked with *sa*,
and beginning with *ma*— it is known as "lifeless."

One should first extract the nine-syllable mantra, which possesses a formidable form and is worshipped by the eternal Lord of Yoga; it begins with the letter *tha* and ends with the letter *sa*, adorned by the fourth vowel (*ī*).
One should again extract its first syllable, adorned on the head with *pha*.
This is the nineteenth letter, a word difficult to attain.
Having extracted the middle of *jha* and *ḍa*, it is adorned at the end by *sa* and the fourth vowel.
Having made it auspicious and adorned, give it back to him as before.
The twentieth word should be known as two syllables, most terrible and dreadful.
Having extracted that from the middle, make it marked with the *lā* as previously described.
The previous fall (pāta) should be given again, free from further marking.
This is declared to be the three-syllabled, formidable word known as the twenty-first.
It is the mass of the Vajra-egg, containing the semi-vowels, and adorned by the fourth vowel at its end.
Again, having extracted the vajra-egg (vajrāṇḍa) adorned above by the letter *na*, one should again place the letter *ga* in the middle;
then one should again place that which has *śa* in its middle.
Again, the mass of the vajra-egg is adorned above by the letter *na*.

The middle of *ṭha* (*ṭha*) alone becomes the middle of *ḍha* (*ḍha*), conjoined with *sa*. Having made the end of *va* (*va*) marked by the end of *sa* (*sa*), one should extract it together with the first vowel. This is indeed the twenty-second word, the Lord of the Rāva family.
The eight-syllable [mantra] is taught for the shattering of a hundred cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*).
Furthermore, the mass of the diamond-egg (*vajrāṇḍapiṇḍa*) is likewise twice [the same], ending with the letter *sa*.
The diamond-egg is conjoined with the letter *pha*, and the diamond-knot (*vajragranthi*) is with the sixth [vowel].
That which is joined with *pha* and *anta* (the letter *na*) should be made twofold and adorned with *chādyaka-anta* (the letter *ya*).
This [syllable] joined with *ma*, *dha*, *sa*, and *anta* (the letter *na*), one should extract as *nirjīva*.
Having divided it threefold, O Goddess, the twenty-third [letter] is thus proclaimed.
The terrible *daśārṇa*, which causes the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) to tremble, is proclaimed [as follows]:
the middle portion should be given again, not made impure by anything internal;
then that very same *varṇeśa* (Lord of Letters) is adorned with the letter *pha*.
The Vajra-egg, not joined with the letter *na*, is adorned at the beginning with *ya* and at the end with *pha*;
having divided it twofold, O Queen of the Gods, the third is adorned with *ā*.
Having extracted the middle of *va* (the letter *ma*) and joined it with the third of the first group (*ta*),
and having marked it with the letters ending in *dh* and *s* (namely *na* and *sa*), one should extract that which begins with *sa* and is devoid of life (*jīva*).
This twenty-fourth word is to be known as the brilliant golden [syllable].

Again, having extracted Vajrāṇḍa, adorned with the sixth [vowel] and the letter *pha*, one should extract the letter *va* marked by the letter *sa*, preceded by *sa* and devoid of life (*nirjīva*). Again, O Goddess, one should extract that; it is known as the twenty-fifth word.
The supreme three-syllable mantra is said to bestow sovereignty over the three worlds. Having extracted the first letter from the first [group], place it at the end of the letter *la*.
Join it with the third letter of the first [group], and again place the letter *la* at the end of the letter *na*.
One should extract the first [syllable] marked with *sānta* (the letter *m*), which is lifeless;
for that is the great four-syllabled [mantra] consisting of twenty-six [units].
It is the *vajrāṇḍa* ending in *sānta* (the letter *m*) marked with the fourth [vowel *ī*], purified by the end of *phānta* (the letter *h*).
The supreme twenty-seventh syllable is that which is vomited, fresh, and lifeless;
it is declared to be the two-syllabled one of great power, the *Sādātrailokyadāmara*.
Make the best of letters, situated between *ga* and *ka*, and located between *mā* and *sā*.
Having extracted the letter situated at the end of the fourth [vowel], vomited from the head, marked by the letter *sa* and the digit,
and then having extracted the lifeless one preceded by *sa*, O Goddess, one should thus give it in two ways.
And the *vajrāṇḍa* situated between *ya* and *bha* is adorned with the pair from the east.
The middle of the father (the letter *ya*) is the second syllable (*bha*), adorned with the third vowel ending in *sa* (*e*).
Having struck it with the letter ending in *va* (*kha*) and the letter ending in *sa* (*tha*), one should extract that which begins with *sa* and is devoid of life (*ja*).
This is to be known as the twenty-eighth word, the Vasu-syllable (*va*), which destroys the universe.
Having again extracted the first letter, joined with the letter *sa* and endowed with the letter *kha*;
having made it joined with the first [letter], marked by the third letter *sa* and the letter *la*;
and having extracted the middle letter *ḍha*, adorned by the first three [letters].
The letter preceded by *cha* (cha) joined with the beloved (*ka*) should be given; again, that marked with the letter *sa* (*sa*) and ending with *ta* (*ta*) should be given;
that preceded by *sa* (*sa*) which has fallen [into place] should be given. This six-syllabled leader of the *pada* is to be known as the twenty-ninth, the life-force of the *codanāstra*.
Having extracted the middle of *la* and the middle of *sāśa*,
and having extracted the middle of *ca* and *gha*, that which stands in *khādya* is thus proclaimed.
Then the *sānta* (the letter *sa*) should be emitted; again, the *vānta* (the letter *va*) together with its final (*ta*) should be joined.
The *vānta* (*va*) struck by the *sānta* (*sa*) should be given, and one should extract that which begins with *sa* and is devoid of life (*nirjīva*).
Thus, there shall be a word consisting of thirty syllables, which bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
One should again extract that which is designated as having seven syllables, ending with *va*.
Then there is that which ends with *ḍha*, beginning with *la*, and likewise beginning with *ṇa*, rendered pure by the letter *na* itself.
Again, that same [syllable] is devoid of its mark (*lāñchana*), and then it is marked with the letter *sa*.
Having extracted the first letter from *nirjīva* (the letter *na*) and the thirty-first letter from the four oceans (*caturarṇa*),
this word is declared to be the dryer of the seven oceans.
It consists solely of the letter *ga* in the middle, with a *sa* at the end and a *sa* situated within the *sa*.
One should then provide the first [syllable] marked with *pha* on its head;
likewise, the fifth [consonant] situated between *ḍa* and *va*, ending with *kha* and marked by two *mā*s;
the middle of *ya* and *bha* situated as the fifth, and the middle of *ga* marked by three.
First, however, only *ḍha* should be given, with *ta* in the middle and marked by three;

then *cha*, with *ṇa* in the middle and alone; then *bha*, with *ga* in the middle; then that which stands at the end, with *kha* as the fifth letter; and finally *ḍha*, with *ta* in the middle and marked by three.
Make the letter *sa* (sānta) joined with the fifth vowel (*u*), and place it upon another *sa* (sāntasthita).
The letter *sa* (sānta) should be marked with two dots (*dvayāṅkita*) and adorned by being covered with a *sa* (sāntena bhūṣita).
One should make the letter *ra* (rānta) situated upon the letter *la* (lāntasthita), and the letter *ca* (cānta) marked with the third vowel (*tṛtīyacihnita*).
One should place that fifth [consonant] as the first [syllable], joined with two semivowels.

Place the second syllable with *ḍha* in the middle and the end-vowel *va*, enclosed by the final *sa*. Here, the thirty-second syllable is indeed the supreme one, accompanied by the life-force (*anirjīva*).
The terrible Rudrāṇḍapātana consists of thirty-two syllables;
it contains the Vajragranthi with the sixth vowel and is purified by the letter ending in *pha*.
It is marked by the letter ending in *ṭha* and the letter ending in *sa*, preceded by *sa* and joined with the "living" (*jīva*)—that [mantra] becomes twofold.
This thirty-third word consists of three syllables and possesses great power.
One should give the letter *va* joined with the letter *na*, followed by the letter *kha* and the two cities (*pura*).
One should extract [the syllable] joined with the first two of the former [group], ending with *sa* and joined with three vowels;
then, having placed the second letter of the middle [group] in the center of *ya*, one should extract that which precedes it.
Then, having encased the letter ending in *va* and ending in *sa*, one should extract that which begins with *sa* and is devoid of life (*nirjīva*).

The thirty-fourth [syllable] to be given is the six-syllabled word that slays Māra. Form the syllable *vajrāṇḍa* (vajra-egg) with the nasal *n* at its end and the letter *va* situated at its conclusion. With the letter *pa*, likewise surmounted by the head-vowel *ī*, form again the syllable *va* accompanied by the letter *sa*.

One should again bestow that which is marked on the head with the letter *na*. One should then give the letter ending in *ra* and the letter ending in *va*. Again, one should give the letter ending in *kha*, adorned by two [dots].
One should further extract the letter ending in *ḍa*, then the letter ending in *kha*, and thereafter the letter ending in *sa*.
The syllable *ca* with *gha* in the middle, mounted upon *kh*; *bha* with *pa* in the middle and followed by *sa* and the fifth [vowel];
*gā* at the end joined with three [consonants], then again *gā* ending with *ka*;
*vā* at the end preceded by *sa* and devoid of life—the word consists of fifteen syllables.
The thirty-fifth is the terrible [syllable] that swallows the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
The sixth is the adamantine egg (vajrāṇḍa), joined with the letter *pha* and purified by the letter *ma*.
The thirty-sixth is the two-syllabled word, beginning with *va*, devoid of life, and ending with *ta*.
Having extracted the middle letter of *gaka* (ga), the middle letter of *ḍava* (ḍa) with the sixth vowel (ū),
adorned with the third letter after *dhānta* (na), the letter at the end of *vānta* (va), that which begins with *sa* (sa) without the life-force (jīvaka,
i.e., without the vowel *i*), the fourth letter (tha), and the thirty-seventh letter (kṣa)— this is the invincible [mantra] beginning with *sā*.
Having extracted the seventh from the first, one should extract the letter ending in *dh* (dh) and the one ending in *m* (m).
Then, one should extract three letters beginning with the first of the preceding word;
furthermore, one should extract the letter ending in *v* (v), the letter ending in *ḍ* (ḍ), and the fifth after the letter ending in *gh* (gh).
Make the first letter "tha" joined with two "śas" (visargas) and ending with a "ra.
One should mark it with a final "na" and adorn the final "kha" with two [visargas].
Again, one should extract the final "ḍa" and the final "sa" adorned with two [visargas].
(10b) Again,
one should place the first and the semivowels together, joined with the third;
one should divide this four-syllable supreme word into two parts.
One should again extract the letter *ga* ending in *ta*, and place the letter *la* ending in *dya* situated after the letter *gha*.
Having joined it with the letter *na* ending in *ta*, one should divide that supreme word into two parts.
O Goddess, one should extract the letter *kha* ending in *ta*, and again the letter *ḍa* ending in *ta*, O Beloved.
One should divide this fifth [syllable] into two parts;

then, the sole [syllable] ending in *jaṅ* becomes a single mass (*piṇḍa*). One should join the one situated at the end of *cala*, marked with the number two, placed between *ṭa* and *ḍau*, and thereafter cause the one ending in *gā* to be given.
O Supreme Goddess, one should again extract the letter at the end of *ḍa* (ḍha) situated in the sixth position;
then the letter at the end of *ḍha* (ṇa) with the head of the third [vowel *u*], and again the letter at the end of *ṭha* (ṇa) alone.
This is joined with the beginning of *sa* (*sa*) and the beginning of *ma* (*ma*), and it is rendered pure by the end of *sa* (*ṣa*).
One should make the letter *gha* adorned with three dots (*bindu*), and make the letter *ḍha* marked by the fourth vowel (*ū*).
O beautiful one, having extracted the letter *ra* from the middle, place it upon the letter *la*.
Make the letter *sa* adorned with three dots (*bindu*), and make the letter *va* marked by the letter *sa*.
Having extracted this great wave-syllable (maholvaṇa) today as lifeless (nirjīva),
it is remembered as having forty, thirty-nine, and thirty-eight letters. O Goddess, one should again extract that which is to be covered (chādya), adorned with the syllable *pha*.
The edible substance, remaining within, should be given, purified by the Beloved alone;
that which has been vomited forth should be given within a vessel containing the letter *sa*; one should extract that which is beginningless and devoid of life.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, the forty-first [letter] is remembered as being one less than forty.
This four-syllabled word bestows all accomplishments.
Having extracted the syllable *ya* from the middle and marked it with two vajras (*ṃ*),
one should again extract the final letter of the *ma*-group (*ba*) and purify it with the final letter of the *ṣa*-group (*ha*).
One should again take the letter *sa* (sānta) and *la* (lānta), marked with the third vowel (*u*) on its head;
then one should extract the letter *ya* preceding this syllable. Next, one should take *la* joined with *na*, and then *ra* situated upon *la*.
Having extracted the syllable ending in *sa* joined with the triad, adorned with the final *sa*, beginning with *sa*,
devoid of life-force (*nirjīva*), the syllable of Rudra is thus extracted as the word. (11a)

The fortieth [letter] is the formidable one, worshipped by Mahābhairava; it is the letter *da* (dānta), followed by the letter *sa* (sānta). Again, it is marked by the sign of the fourth [vowel] *ī* (turyāṅka) at its end.
That which ends with *sa* (sānta) should be made solitary again, and then place the letter *ḍha* (ḍhānta) situated after the letter *la* (lādya).
Furthermore, the letter preceded by *sa* (sa), adorned with three vowels, should be concealed;
likewise, the letter ending in *ḍa* (ḍa) enclosed within *sa* (sa), beginning with *sa* (sa), and the lifeless one (*nirjīva*)—this is the six-syllable mantra.
The word joined with the forty-first [letter] (kha) ends with the fifth liquor (ma).
The letter *va* joined with the final *na* (vna) should be concealed; one should extract it alone.
The letter *sa* joined with the final *na* (sna), which is to be concealed, should be marked with the final *ṣa* (ṣāṃ).
O Goddess, that which stands between *ya* and *bha* (ya-bha = ya) should be marked with the third vowel (*i*).
Make the letter *va* joined with the final *na*, followed by *ra*, *la*, and *sa*,
each joined with three vowels (*i*, *u*, *e*), and adorned with the beloved *ka*.
Having extracted the one situated in the middle of *ḍa*, extract the one beginning with *sa* that is devoid of life.
Having formed a closed fist with the hand extended, one should take that which is present and devoid of life.
The eleventh syllable is indicated; it is the forty-second word.
It is the Vajra-egg, possessing a fourth head, beginning with *y* and situated in the fifth.
Having marked the end of *dh* with the end of *s*, one should extract the lifeless [syllable] preceded by the beginning [of *s*].

This should be known as the forty-third word, a great power consisting of three syllables. The end of *kh* should be made to stand upon the end of *s*; that end of *s* should be adorned with the end of *ph*.

The "Vajra-egg" (vajrāṇḍa) is marked by the sixth letter ending in *pha* (*ṣa*) and the letter ending in *na* (*ña*), followed by the letter ending in *va* (*kha*) marked by the letter ending in *na* (*ma*). The "Vajra-egg" is also marked by the fifth letter ending in *pha* (*pa*) and the letter ending in *va* (*ba*), preceded by the letter beginning with *sa* (*śa*) and without the letter *ja* (*jha*). This is taught as the five-syllable phrase, which is the fortieth [verse] increased by four.
One should extract the Vajra-egg (vajrāṇḍa), marked by the fourth letter of the *pha*-group and purified by that same [letter] of the *pha*-group;
then, having emitted it, one should again extract it marked by the final letter of the *sa*-group, together with its initial vowel and its own inherent sound.
This forty-second word is said to consist of two syllables plus five.
Having extracted the syllable ending in *v* marked by *n*, then that same one marked by the four vowels,
and then the syllable ending in *kh* doubled with its head marked by the second vowel;
The letter *sa* (sāntam) adorned with three dots (*tribindukhacitam*), marked by that very same [letter] as *ḍha* (*ḍhāntam*);
then the middle of *ṭa* and *ḍha* (*ṭaḍhaumadhyam*) should again be given; likewise, *ca* and *kha* together (*cāntam khāntam tathaikataḥ*);
*sa* joined with three dots (*sāntam tribindusamyuktam*); and make *va* situated upon *ḍha* (*vāntam ḍhāntasthitam*).
Having marked it with three dots (bindus), O Dear One, the end should be given again;
that very same [syllable] is then inscribed with a *sa* at the end, and again with a *sa* at the end, followed by *majīvaka*.
This is declared to be the eleven-syllabled forty-sixth *pada*.
The syllable *va* is adorned with the final letter [ma], and *va* is embellished with the letter *sa*.
Having extracted the first vowel (*a*), along with the fortieth letter [na] and the seventh [ta],
this two-syllabled mantra becomes the bestower of the fulfillment of all desires.
The *vajrāṇḍa* (the letter *va*) joined with the end of *mā* (the letter *ma*), and the *yabha* (the letter *ya*) alone in the middle;
likewise, the *vajrāṇḍa* conjoined with two vowels, and the *yabha* in the middle exactly as before.
Then one should extract the letter ending in *s* (*sa*) adorned with three suns (*ra*), followed again by the initial vowel.
The letter *khānta* (kha) joined with the second [consonant] (*ca*), and the solitary *ḍava* (ḍa);
having extracted *ṭaḍoma* (ṭa) in the middle, place *ghānta* (gha) situated within *khānta* (kha).
Place *sānta* (sa), adorned with three suns (*ra*), and make *vānta* (va) situated within *ḍhānta* (ḍha).
The letter *va* joined with the third vowel from the first (*u*), marked by that same [vowel],
and again situated after the *sa* which is deprived of its previous mark;
then the second number in the middle of *ya*, ending in *ḍa* and marked by *na*.
The fourth [letter] ending in *sa*, likewise that ending in *ḍha*, that ending in *pa*, and that ending in *pha*—

one should place these as a single cluster (*piṇḍa*) according to the sequential application. Then, one should cause the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*), ending in *sa* and *ṭha*, to become lifeless (*nirjīva*).
The eighteenth syllable is indicated, and that is the fortieth and the eighth.
This word is exceedingly fierce, causing the destruction of the three worlds.
The letter ending in *pha* (ph), the fourth vowel (*ī*), together with the adamantine *a* (a), and the semivowel *ya*, joined as a single cluster—this is the mantra.
To this, one should again give that two-syllable word which was previously mentioned;
it is the fifty-first [letter] in isolation, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) that shatters obstacles.
Thus, the poison-word is repeated, but with the semi-vowel *s* (sa) as its final member, preceded by the Mother (*mātrā*).

(12a) This fifty-first word consists of two syllables and bestows all accomplishments: the fourth letter ending in *pha*, likewise the one ending in *sa*, that which begins with *cha*, that which begins with *ya*, and the one ending in *sa*.
This seed-syllable (*piṇḍa*) is most formidable, the ender of all the lords of reality (*sarvatattveśvara*).
It consists of the letter *pha* (the fourth), followed by *va*, then *ta*, and ending with *sa*; these combined together form the single seed-syllable.
Then, the letter *ṭha* falls upon the first *sa*; this three-syllabled word is thus proclaimed.
The fifty-first word to be known is that which ends with *tva* and *īśvara*.
The letter *kha* at the end, in the form of the vowel *ā*, and the letter *ca* at the end, likewise the letter *kha* at the end in a single unit;
the letter *ya* at the end established as the fifth, and the letter *ga* at the end marked by three vowels.
The first [syllable] should be given in its own form; the second is adorned with three vowels.
The final [syllable] is that which ends in *va*, followed by that which ends in *ya*, situated with the fifth [consonant], ending in *ga*, and ending in *kha*.
It is peaceful (*sāntima*), with *ca* and *gha* in the middle, mounted upon the end of *kha*, and its head is adorned with three dots (*bindu*).
The first syllable of *vānta* (va) is joined with the same [syllable] (*va*), then *thānta* (tha) joined with the three dots (*mādyam*, i.e., *m*).
The first syllable of *thā* (tha) is joined with the end of *nā* (na), then the first syllable of *lā* (la) marked by two vowels (*e*).
The "Vajra-egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*) is joined with the end of *sā* (sa), and then the "Vajra-egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*) alone again.
One should extract the letters in sequence: *sāntam* (sa), *śāntam* (śa), likewise *ghāntam* (gha), and *lāntam* (la).
Then one should extract the letter beginning with *tha* (*thādi*) adorned with three dots (*tribindukha*), followed by the letter ending with *ma* (*māntam*) alone.
O Supreme Goddess, one should place the letter beginning with *ta* (*tādi*) upon the letter beginning with *la* (*lādisthita*), and mark it with the fourth digit (*turyāṅka*).
One should first extract the letter ending in *sa* (śa) joined with the letter ending in *ma* (ma), which is conjoined with the three vowels;
then, subsequently, that which stands in the self (*ātman*) beginning with *sa* (sa).
Then, the letter ending in *ma* (ma), the letter ending in *sa* (śa) together with the sixth [vowel], and that beginning with *la* (la) marked by the three vowels.

One should again extract the letter *ṭha* ending in a nasal (*ṇ*), enclosed by *sa*, followed by *sa* and *da*. This twenty-four-syllable mantra, consisting of fifty-two words, is to be known as the supreme;
it is to be known as that which brings about the destruction of all [obstacles] and bestows the accomplishment of the Great Melāpa.
The syllable *va* at the end is joined with the final *na*, and the syllable *ga* at the end is joined with the final *sa* and the *ṭha*-ending *ya*.
This three-syllabled word is proclaimed as the fifty-third.
The "Vajra-Egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*) is established with the final *sa*, and the fourth is adorned with the final *pha*.
Ending with *ṭha*, situated between *sa* and *na*, further purified by *na* itself,
ending with *ga*, joined with *ka*— this three-syllable word is supreme.
The fifty-fourth [letter] should be known as bestowing abundant success;
likewise, the fifth [vowel] joined with the letter ending in *ḍ*, situated after the letter ending in *kh* and marked by the number two;
the letter ending in *y* conjoined with the fifth [vowel]; and the letter ending in *g* adorned with three vowels.

One should again extract that very same [syllable] situated in the middle of *ṭha*. With a pure head-syllable ending in *sa*, one should place it where *ḍa* and *kha* end. Then, marked with a head-syllable ending in *na*, one should give the syllable ending in *ga* three times.

The third [syllable] is overlaid with two vowels, the "vajra-egg" marked with three vowels; the end of the *ṭha*-group (*ṭha*) enclosed by the end of the *sa*-group (*sa*), again beginning with *sa*, and falling [into place] once more. This twelve-syllabled, formidable mantra is worshipped in the world of the Sun.
The fifty-fifth [syllable] should be known as the devourer of all splendor.
Form the Vajra-egg (vajrāṇḍa), which is established with the letter ḍa and enclosed by the letter sa.
It is inlaid with the letter pha at the end of the letter pa; within this mass, it is like the stainless darkness of the end of time.

The "Vajra-egg" (vajrāṇḍa) is to be covered, adorned with three dots, and situated upon the letter *la*. It is marked at the top by the letter *na* and the letter *ḍha* is marked by the letter *sa*. Having placed the letter *sa* at the beginning, one forms the supreme four-syllable word.
Indeed, this fifty-sixth [chapter] has been fully revealed by me to you.

The Vajra-egg (vajrāṇḍa), situated on the head, resides at the end of the letter *ḍa*, established at the end of the letter *sa*; it is crowned by the head of the letter *pha* at the end of the fourth [vowel], and joined with the two vowels at the end of the letter *sa*.
Having bestowed this two-syllabled word that has fallen today,
it should be known as the fifty-seventh, which sets all accomplishments in motion.
Vajrāṇḍa is established with a final *sa* and purified by a beautiful [vowel].
O Dear One, this two-syllable word, ending in *ṭha* and marked by *sa*, with *sa* falling again at the beginning, is the fifty-eighth. It ends in *sa*,
is joined with two vowels, and is situated on the western horn.

That which ends in *ṭ* is inlaid with *n*; that which ends in *r* is established with *l*. That which ends in *s* is inlaid with three dots (*bindu*); that which ends in *ḍ* is variegated with *s*. (13a)
The letter *sa* (sānta), adorned with three dots (*tribindukha*), followed by the letter *ṭha* (ṭhānta) preceded by *sa* (sādya) and without the vowel *ī* (ajīvaka)—
O Goddess, one should bestow this syllable of great power in four ways.
It should be known as a thirteen-syllable mantra, with the sixth syllable being considered deficient [by one].

[It is] of great power, the cause of the destruction of the worlds of the Nairṛtas and Indra. The letter at the end of *ṭha* joined with the letter at the end of *na*, adorned by the letter at the end of *pha*.
Taking the final letter of that [group], it is embellished by the letter at the end of *pha*.
The letter *ṭha* joined with the letter *sa*, followed by the letter *sa* again, and then the letter *da*—
this third-syllable sixth word is to be known as difficult to attain. The letter *va* joined with the letter *ra*, followed by the letter *sa*, and adorned with the fourth letter *pha*.
The middle of *ṭa* and *ḍa* should be alone; then [the letter] ending in *la* marked with *sa*;
then the first [letter] beginning with *tha* marked on its head by *sa*, which is situated in the self (*ātma-sthita*);
having made [the letter] ending in *ya* marked by *na*; and the one ending in *ṭha* preceded by *sa* is cast down (*nipātita*).

The sixty-first syllable shall be the six-syllabled word, the most excellent of all excellences. One should extract the letter at the end of *kha* (ṅ) established as the fifth, followed by the solitary letter at the end of *ḍa* (ṇ). Then the letter at the end of *ya* (m) joined with the letter at the end of *na* (ṅ), and the letter at the end of *la* (ṃ) preceded by the first of *tha* (t) and ending with *sa* (ḥ).
The "Vajra-egg" (vajrāṇḍa) is joined with the sixth [vowel], made pure by the end of *pha*;
the "Vajra-egg" is established with the final *sa*, adorned with the fourth and the end of *pha*.
The first of *ṭha* and the first of *sa* fallen [therein] is known as the sixty-second word.

One should extract the eight-syllabled Kuleśāna, the most excellent among the most excellent of the *kulas*. Then one should extract the letter ending in *kha* (*kha*), and again extract the letter ending in *kha* doubled.
Having then placed the letter ending in *sa* (*sa*) therein, one should join the letter ending in *sa* with two vowels.
Having covered [the first letter], do not mark it with the final nasal (anusvāra), but again place the letter ending in *ra* within the letter ending in *la*.
Adorn that which ends in *sa* with three dots (bindus) to form the "vajra-egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*) situated at the end of *sa*.
Marked at the head by the fourth letter ending in *pha*, extract the solitary *śānta*.
One should join together in one place that which ends in *vāṃ*, begins with *thā*, and likewise ends in *sāṃ*.
That which ends in *yāṃ* is distinguished by two vowels; that which begins with *thā* is marked by an *nāṃ* at its end.

One should extract the thirteen-syllable, radiant mantra consisting of sixty-three words: the "Vajra-egg" (vajrāṇḍa), which is formed with the letter *ḍa* followed by the nasal *ṃ*, adorned below with the letter *sa*; marked at the head with the fourth letter of the labials (*pha*) followed by the nasal *ṃ*; and ending with the letter *ṭha* preceded by *sa*.
The destroyer of all netherworlds and the shatterer of all mechanical devices:
take the letter *ka*, preceded by *ra* and joined with the second vowel;
let it be followed by the end of *va* and the end of *ra* alone, and place the end of *kha* situated before *tha*.
Marked with three vowels at the head,

ending in *dha*, and situated after *sa*— know this six-syllabled word, which ends in *na*, is adorned above by *pha* and *va*, and begins with *sa*, as the "lifeless" (*ajīvaka*) word, the sixty-fourth [syllable], which bestows great purpose.
The letter *pra* should be given again, with the first two letters from the preceding [syllable].

The final letter is not present, being marked by three dots (*bindu*). The letter *ga* at the end is marked by the letter *na*. The letter *ṭha* at the end, preceded by *sa*, is the fallen word that sets forth knowledge.
The sixty-fifth [mantra] is declared to consist of six syllables, granting all desires.
Vajrāṇḍa joined with the fifth [vowel], purified by the letter *pha*,
is followed once more by its predecessor, the supreme two-syllable word.
This is indeed the sixty-sixth [chapter], which tears asunder all knots; it is the Vajra-Egg, conjoined with the end of *sa* and the end of *pha*, the Fourth State (*turya*), variegated,
and the Vajra-Egg situated in the center of *ya-bha*, marked by the second vowel.
The middle of "Ya" (ya) marked with that [the letter "ma"] at the beginning and adorned with the end of "Na" (na);
the end of "Tha" (tha) preceded by "Sa" (sa) fallen [therein]; the seventh and eighth syllables;
this is declared as the "Māyāntaka" mantra, the subduer of all the three worlds.
The syllable *śānta* (śa), likewise *yānta* (ya), and the *vajrāṇḍa* (ha) marked by *phānta* (pha);
in the middle of *ṭa* and *ḍau* (ṭa and ḍha), the *vajrāṇḍa* (ha) joined with *kānta* (ka) and adorned with *nānta* (na).
The syllable ending in *ṭha* (ṭha) preceded by *sa* (sa) is known as the sixth and eighth word when fallen [into place].
The seven-syllable mantra, whose nature is awakening, is the Lord of the Haṃsa-cakra chariot.
It begins with *sarva*, has *ṭa* and *ḍau* in the middle, and is marked by the third vowel (*u*).
It ends with *da*, is adorned with the second vowel (*i*), and is embellished at the end with *sa*.
The middle of the father [Ya] with the final [Sa] and the enclosure [Ha], adorned with the fourth [Pha] and the end [Kṣa];
the final [Tha] with the initial [Sa] fallen [before it]: this is the sixty-ninth word. (14a)
The six-syllabled mantra, most formidable, known as Khaḍgarāvaṇa,
consists of the Vajra-egg (the letter *ha*) joined with the end of the peaceful (*sa*), adorned by the fourth letter after the end of *pha* (*ba*).
Having extracted the solitary letter at the end of *la* (*va*), it is followed by the fifth letter from the end of *ṭa* (*ṇa*).
The letter *da* (dānta), followed by the second [consonant] *kha* (dvitīya-kha), then *sa* (sānta), joined with the final [vowel] *a* (nānta);

again, give the first seed-syllable (*ādya-bīja*), and here make it twofold ending with *ya* (yānta). The last [syllable] joined with the sixth [vowel] (*ṣaṣṭha*), likewise *sa* at the beginning, and the first [syllable] joined with three [vowels].
The seventieth syllable is known as the one ending in *ṭha* with *sa* at its beginning, which has fallen [into place];
it should be understood as bestowing the state of a Dhānaśvara and as a seeker of treasures (*nidhikarṣaka*), consisting of ten vowels.
Having extracted that which stands between *ṭa* and *ḍau*, [one finds] that which ends in *sa* and is situated after *la*, having two *yu*s.
The letter *ra* ending, the letter *va* ending, the triple-inlaid (*trikhacita*) *vajrāṇḍa*, situated after the letter *ḍa*;
that which ends with the five *paṅka*s, the inlaid letter *ṭha*, and that which begins with *sa* and is cast down—
this is to be known as the seventy-first [syllable], which bestows the accomplishment of being an eater of all things.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, there is no goal that cannot be accomplished with this six-syllable mantra:
one should place the letter *ga* at the end, followed by the letter *sa*; the fourth syllable should be adorned with the letter *pha*;
likewise, the first syllable should be made [with the letter *ya*]; and then one should again provide the letters *ṭa*, *ḍau*, and *ma* in the middle.
The word ending in *ya* with *pa* as the fifth letter following it, then the one ending in *thā* situated after *sa*,
then the one ending in *la* joined with the one ending in *na*, and likewise one should fashion the one ending in *rā*;
the word ending in *ṭha* preceded by *sa* is declared to be the seventy-second foot.

The eight-syllable mantra should be known as the agitator that dries up the seven oceans. It consists of the letter at the end of *ṭha* (ṭha) joined with the letter at the end of *na* (na), and is purified by the letter at the end of *pha* (pha).
Having again extracted that same [mantra] but omitting the letter at the end of *na*, it is joined with the letter at the end of *sa* (sa).

Having extracted that alone, together with the initial *sā*, this three-syllabled word falls again; indeed, it belongs to the Goddess of Gods. It consists of seventy-three syllables, ending in *la* and joined with one ending in *na*, beginning with *tha*, and adorned with two vowels.
The word ending in *va* is conjoined with the three vowels; then that ending in *ṭa* is placed with one ending in *la*.
That ending in *sa* is adorned by one ending in *la*, and that ending in *ṭha* is struck down by the letter *sa*.
O Dear One, the sixty-fourth word is the formidable six-syllable mantra:
the Vajra-egg (VA), established with the final letter (HA); the fourth (RA) adorned with the final labial (PHA);
the final labial (LA) conjoined with two vowels (Ī and Ā); and the final guttural (GH) joined with the nasal (NA).
The syllable ending in *ra*, followed by one situated in *la*, then again one ending in *sa*, marked with three vowels; then one ending in *va*,

together with *sa* and *da*, and finally the fallen [syllable]— this supreme six-syllable phrase should be known as the auspicious seventy-fifth, which bestows the sovereignty of speech (*vāgīśvarī*).
Make the letter ending in *śa* (*śa*), likewise the one ending in *śa* (*śa*) situated after the first [consonant], and the one ending in *ṭha* (*ṭha*) situated after the seventh [consonant].
Make the one ending in *na* (*na*) marked by the one ending in *ta* (*ta*) alone.
One should make the one ending in *bha* (*bha*) situated after the one ending in *ta* (*ta*), adorned with the fourth [vowel] and the one ending in *pha* (*pha*).
The seventh syllable, ending in *ṭha* and preceded by *sa*, is fallen [upon the vowel], cutting through the noose of craving. This seven-syllabled great secret is the seventy-sixth, most excellent.
One should make that which ends in *la* and stands after *sa* marked with the second vowel.
Place the letter *da* joined with three vowels, and the letter *sa* joined with two vowels;
cover it with the letter *na*, and fashion the letter *ra* situated upon the letter *la*.
Place the letter *sa* adorned with three bindus, and let the "Vajra-Egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*) be established upon that *sa*.
One should extract the letter marked by the end of *tu* (the letter *r*) as the head, followed again by the letter marked by the end of *pha* (the letter *m*).
That same [letter] should be adorned with the end of *sa* (the letter *m*), and then one should extract the letter *sa* alone.

Make the letter at the end of *tha* (the letter *jha*) marked by the end of *pha* (the letter *m*) as the head, and place the letter at the end of *ṭha* (the letter *ṇa*) preceded by the letter *sa* (the letter *śa*).
Ending with the letter *sa*, not joined with the final letter [of the alphabet], ending with *ṭha* and preceded by *sa*,
this thirteen-syllable mantra is radiant and a devourer of all diseases.
Known as the seventy-seventh, this word bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
One should place the letter ending in *ṣ* (ṣa), ending in *s* (sa), and standing upon three vowels (ī).
Again, one should extract the letter ending in *l* (la), and then again extract the one ending in *ṭ* (ṭa).
Again, the letter ending in *y* (ya) standing on the sixth vowel (ū), and again the letter ending in *s* (sa) standing on the first letter after *th* (tha).
That which ends in *la* is inlaid with that which ends in *ra*; make that which ends in *ṭa* followed by that which stands in *sa*.
Conjoined with that, it is the Vajra-egg, differentiated by the second vowel.
The first syllable is *vānta* (va), the second is *nipatita* (pa), and the third is the foot worshipped by the Sun (*sūryaprapūjita*, ra).
This ten-syllabled mantra is most fierce and auspicious as the seventy-eighth [mantra].
The peaceful [syllable] is the third (*śa*), joined with the first of the third group (*tha*) and conjoined with the seventh (*sa*).
Having extracted the letter *sa* (sānta) alone, it is adorned with the letter *na* (nānta) following the letter *tha* (thānta);
then the letter *ṭa* (ṭānta) is placed after the letter *la* (lānta), followed by the letter *da* (dānta) adorned with two vowels;
then the letter *ra* (rānta) is placed after the letter *sa* (sānta), further embellished by the fourth letter *pha* (phānta).
The eighth syllable is that which ends in *dh*, begins with *s*, is fallen (*nipatita*), rescues its father (*pitruttāra*), and is the best of its kind (*padottama*).
Indeed, the eight-syllable mantra is reduced by one [to seven] as the eightieth [mantra]. Having extracted only that which ends in *ṭh* and begins with *t*, mark it with the fourth vowel (*ū*).
Again, [the syllable] ending in *ra* situated after that which ends in *la*, marked with three vowels;
[the syllable] ending in *ṭa* joined with the fifth [vowel], [the syllable] ending in *sa* joined with two vowels;
[the syllable] ending in *da* joined with that same [vowel], and [the syllable] ending in *sa* joined with [the letter] *ca*.
The letter *pha* (end of *pa*), the fourth (*ta*), likewise the letter *cha*, the end of *ṭa* (*ṇa*), and the end of *la* (*na*) together;
the end of *ṭha* (*ṇa*) followed by the beginning of *sa* (*ra*)—this ten-syllable phrase has fallen [into place] as the supreme mantra.
It is declared to be the eightieth, which devours all serpents.
Having extracted the middle of *ṭa* and *ḍa*, which is situated after *sa* and *la*;
then make that which is situated after *śa* and *jha* conjoined with the second vowel.
One should extract the letter *sa* alone, conjoined with the same two vowels.
The letter *da* joined with two vowels, ending with *sa* and adorned by *na*;
the *vajra-aṇḍa* (the letter *ha*) joined with the sixth vowel (*ū*), purified by the letter *pha*;
the letter *ṭha* preceded by *sa* and fallen [downwards]—this is the eight-syllable mantra, the eighty-first.
This is remembered as the "Nourisher" (Āpyāyanī) and also as the "Reviver of the Dead" (Mṛtasañjīvanī).
Furthermore, that which is preceded by all [the vowels] should be given, joined with the sixth [consonant] and ending with the letter *sa*.
Again, there is the letter ending in *ṭha*, joined with three [vowels] and ending with *sa*; and again, the letter ending in *ṭa* situated after the letter *la*.
Furthermore, this [mantra], with the semi-vowels (*antastha*) interspersed, variegated by the fourth vowel (*ū*) and the letter *pha*,
ending with *ṭha* and beginning with *sa*, consists of six syllables and bestows peace upon all.

This is indeed the eighty-second [chapter], which always brings about peace and nourishment. It begins with the letter *sa*, followed by the *vajra-aṇḍa* (the letter *va*), then the letter *ṭa*, and again the letter *ja*.
Then there is the letter *sa* distinguished by three vowels (*e*), followed by the letter *tha*, the letter *sa*, and finally that which is joined with the end of the letter *stha* (*ṣa*).
The eastern horn, by its own nature, is the letter *ṭha* with *sa* at the beginning, cast down;
it consists of eighty-three [syllables] and seven-worded phrases, granting the perfection of omniscience.
It is *śānta*, *sānta*, likewise *yānta*, and *dānta*, distinguished by two vowels.
The letter *sa* (sānta) adorned with three dots (*tribindukha*), marked by that very same [letter *ḍha*] (*ḍhānta*),
the "vajra-egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*) joined with the sixth vowel, purified by the letter *pha* (*phānta*),
and the letter *ṭha* (*ṭhānta*) preceded by *sa* (*sādya*)— when these fall together, they bestow the attainment of the yoga of the eight treasures (*vasvarṇṇa*).
The eighty-fourth [mantra] should be known as that which bestows all accomplishments within six months.
The letter ending in *va* (va), the one ending in *tha* (tha), and likewise the one ending in *ra* (ra) should be placed above the letter ending in *ja* (ja).
The letter ending in *va* (va) should be given situated upon the letter ending in *tha* (tha), along with the letter ending in *ṭa* (ṭa) joined with two vowels.
The letter ending in *sa* (sa), followed by the one situated after it (ha), then the one ending in *gha* (kha) joined with two vowels (*e*),
then the one ending in *jha* (ña) alone, again the first of the *tha*-group (tha) joined with the three dots (*m*),
the "Vajra-egg" (the letter *a*) joined with the sixth vowel (*u*), and the head of the one ending in *pha* (ba)— this is the one of great power.
One should extract it like a fresh lump fallen below what has been vomited.
This is declared to be the eleventh [letter], the eighty-fifth word.
Again, the first of all [letters] is that which ends in *ṭ* and is joined with three vowels.
Having seen the letter *da* (dāntam) with the headless letter *i* (disvara-mūrddhānam), joined with the peaceful letter *na* (sāntam nāntena saṃyutam);
then again, preceded by all [the previous letters] (sarvapūrvam punarbhūyaḥ), the letter *gha* (ghāntam) situated after the letter *dha* (dhāntasthitam);
then the letter *ra* (rāntam) conjoined with the third vowel (*tṛtīyasvarasambhinnam*) and marked by that very same [vowel].
The letter ending in *ga* (ga) is adorned with the letter ending in *la* (la); the letter ending in *la* (la) is enclosed by the three vowels (*ī*, *u*, *ṛ*).
Again, it is situated between letters ending in *ra* and *la*; furthermore, the letter ending in *sa* (sa) is situated in the sixth position.
The letter ending in *śa* (śa) is joined with the letter ending in *sa* (sa), and the letter ending in *ṭha* (ṭha) is again enclosed by the letter ending in *sa* (sa).
The end of the first word is again joined with the letter *phā*;
this fourteenth-syllable, radiant pada is the eighty-sixth.
Again, having extracted *khānta* (the letter *kha*), followed by *sānta* (*sa*) and *ḍhāntasthita* (*ḍha*);
joined with the second vowel (*i*), ending in *yānta* (*ya*), and adorned with *sānta* (*sa*).
Beginning with *sādya* (*sa*), pierced by the third vowel (*u*), beginning with *kādya* (*ka*), ending in *sānta* (*sa*), and accompanied by the final *sa*.

Marked at the head with the letter *pha* (the end of the fourth group) and the letter *la* (the last of the labials), joined with two vowels; marked with the letter *sa* (the end of the sibilants) and adorned by that same [letter]; the "Vajra-Egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*) marked with three vowels;
and the letter *ca* (the last of the palatals), which is the final of the first group of consonants—this is the supreme nine-syllable mantra.

The eighty-seventh [syllable] should be known as bestowing the accomplishment of happiness and good fortune. One should extract the *piṇḍa* (syllabic cluster) consisting of the fourth letter of the labial class (*pha*), followed by the letter *va*, the letter *ra*, and the letter *sa* with the nasal bindu (*m*). Having extracted the solitary letter *ḍa*, one should then take the letter *pa* and the letter *bha* joined with three bindus (*oṃ*).
The syllable *khā* is inlaid with *na*, and the former end is again joined with the end.
This is declared as the eighty-eighth, beginning with *śiva*, possessing great power.
It is the six-syllabled word, O Goddess, which brings about freedom from old age and death.
The syllable *va* joined with *tha*, the final of the variegated group beginning with *pha*, the semi-vowel *sa* joined with *ta*,
and the King of Clusters (*piṇḍarāja*) followed by its own initial—
this two-syllabled word is indeed auspicious, being exclusively new.
The syllable ending in *ṭ* with three vowels on its head, followed by *thaliṃ* established as a single cluster (*piṇḍa*),
then the syllable ending in *pūrva* with the fourth vowel at the end— this is the supreme three-syllabled word known as "Nava" (the Nine). It bestows the state of Lordship over the Siddhacakra.
The syllable beginning with *ja* and ending with *na*, variegated by the final letter of *pūrva*,
and the final letter of *pūrva* again at the end— this four-syllabled,
supreme word should be known as the ninety-first, which brings all happiness.
Furthermore, the Vajra-egg (vajrāṇḍa) should be thus: situated in the fifth [vowel], marked by the end of *pha*;
