again, devoid of its mark, it is the end of *ḍha*, situated above *la* and *ga*;
then the end of *ya*, established in the fifth [vowel]; and the end of *ga*, joined with three vowels.
The letter *ga* ending in *pha*, marked again by the end of the preceding [letter], and likewise at the end;
this is the word of seven syllables, and likewise the ninety-second.
The letter *sa* ending in *ṣa*, mounted upon it, and variegated with the fourth *pha*.
(16b) That which ends in *khā* is inlaid with *va*; that which ends in *yā* is joined with two vowels;
that which ends in *sā* is joined with three vowels; likewise, from the beginning to the end, it concludes with *anta*.

The ninety-third syllable, possessing five colors, is the most supreme of all. Having extracted the letter *pha* (end of *pa*), the fourth (*ta*), the *vajra-egg* (*ṇa*), the end of *ḍa* (*ṇa*), the end of *sa* (*ma*), and likewise the single [letter] after that (*ya*); having extracted the solitary end of *ṣa* (*kha*), the end of *va* (*tha*), and together with the final end of *sa* (*ha*).
One should extract the third vowel joined with the *piṇḍa* (the seed-syllable). Then the end of the first [syllable], again the end of the letter *ca*, and the fourth syllable as the supreme word.
O Dear One, this glorious word should be known to consist of nine syllables plus four.
One should extract the letter ending in *śa* (śa) joined with two vowels, followed by the letter ending in *la* (la) alone.
Then take the letter ending in *kha* (kha) joined with three vowels, and make it enclosed (*puṭita*) by the letter ending in *śa*.
That [syllable] is adorned with the fourth letter ending in *pha* (pha), and its first part is the letter ending in *ca* (ca). Finally, at the end of this, there is the letter ending in *ta* (ta).

Form the word consisting of five syllables, the ninety-fifth pada, which expresses the purifier (Agni). It ends with the letter *sa*, is joined with two vowels, and has the letter *pa* situated at the beginning.
Adorned at the top with the letter *na*, it is the "Vajra-Egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*) joined with the sixth vowel.
Furthermore, the great sin of the past should be known as the four-syllabled supreme word,
increased by six; this is always the ninety-first [syllable],
ending with *va*, adorned with *tha*, and situated in the seventh position, ending with *sa*.
One should again give the first [syllable] with three vowels on its head, preceded by *p*.
This should be known as the ninety-seventh [syllable], a four-syllabled word.
It is beautiful, situated at the beginning, and further purified by the letter *ph*.
O Dear One, at the end of the first [syllable] and again at the end, there are two syllables, eight more;
this should always be known as the ninety-ninth, which causes the mountain of the Kula to tremble.
It is the letter *la* joined with two vowels, and the letter *sa* situated in the fifth position.
The letter *ḍha* is adorned with three suns; the *vajrāṇḍa* is situated upon the letter *la*;
the letter *pha* is variegated with the fourth [state], extending to the great end of that which precedes it.
The ninety-ninth should be known as the supreme five-syllabled word.
It should be known as ending with *sa* and situated within *sa*; one should extract the syllable ending with *ma* alone.
That which begins with *ra* and is covered by *cha* is declared to be situated there; it ends with *dha* and is joined with three vowels.
Again, having extracted only the syllable ending in *m* which stands at the beginning of the *chādyastha*,
and having extracted only the syllable ending in *s* from the previous *pāta*,
form the eight-syllabled verse, which is the most excellent of the excellent.
That which arises from the western horn, variegated with the letters *pha* and ending in *na*,
having extracted only that which ends in *sa*, and again the western horn;
it is inlaid at its head with the letter *na*, and again ending in *ra* and situated upon *la*.

It should end with *sa* and be joined with three vowels; it should end with *ga* and be enclosed by *sa*. Marked at the head with the fourth letter ending in *pha*, it should fall first and then extend to the end. This seven-syllable mantra, numbering one hundred, always bestows supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
The middle of that [ṬA] is with the final [SA], variegated; the end of that [YA] is with the seat [Ā] at the end.
That which is to be covered is joined with the one ending in NA, and again situated upon the one ending in LA.
With the final [SA] adorned with three dots, it is the Vajra-egg situated upon the final [SA].
Mark the fourth [syllable] with the letter *pha* at its head; again, perform the previous placement.
This is declared to be the supreme eight-syllabled [mantra], numbering one hundred and two.
The *vajrāṇḍa* is joined with five [units] at the end of *pha*, never rendered impure.
One should extract the syllable ending in *ṣ* alone; then again, that which ends in *n* adorned with two vowels;
that which ends in *v* joined with three vowels; and the syllable ending in *g* alone.
The previously mentioned [syllables] should be given again, making sixteen syllables in total.
O Goddess of the gods, I shall explain the meaning of these words to you according to their true significance:
the letter *gha* joined with the letter *pa*, the letter *sa* joined with the three vowels (*ī*,
*u*, *m*), the letter *la* joined with that same [vowel], and one should extract the letter *ra* alone.
The *pādya* [syllable] ending in *sa*, followed by the one situated in *sthita*, and then the fourth [syllable] adorned with *pha*;
having again applied the previous sequence, there are one hundred and four.
The six-syllabled word should be known as auspicious and the performer of all rites:
it consists of the letter ending in *m* (ma) joined with two vowels, followed by the letter ending in *ṭ* (ṭa) situated after the letter ending in *kh* (kha),
then the letter ending in *s* (sa) combined with three vowels, and finally the letter ending in *m* (ma) joined with two vowels.

One should again place the middle of *ṭa-ḍau*; one should extract only the end of *jha*. One should extract the end of *kha* joined with two vowels as the head, and the end of *ḍa* alone. Then the end of *ya* joined with two vowels, and again the first of *tha* situated at the end of *ya*.
The syllable-group (piṇḍa) marked with *gha*, situated within *pa*, established within *sa*, joined with *pa*,
and characterized by *pha*, is the devourer that swallows the three worlds.
It is *va* enclosed by *sa*, and then *sa* preceded by *sa* is cast down again.
It is taught that there are twelve syllables and one hundred and five words.
Make the word ending in *ra* joined with the fifth [vowel], and place the word ending in *ṭha* within the word ending in *la*.
Having adorned it with the word ending in *na*, place the word ending in *ṭa* again within the word ending in *sa*.
Furthermore, the letter *la* alone; then *yāṃ* joined with two vowels;
then that same *kevalin* again joined with the seventh [vowel];
the first of the *tha*-group adorned with the final of the *pha*-group; and *vāṃ* embellished by the fifth [vowel].
Having joined the Vajra-egg (VA) with its end (A), it is established with its own end (SA).
Then, having separated the fourth letter from the end (PH), and again having separated the end of VA (Ū), one takes the final letter of SA (HA).
That supreme state is adorned by the letter KA placed in the fifth position.
This word is to be known as consisting of one hundred and six syllables;
it is declared to be the filler of the supreme nectar.
It is adorned with the letter *ṣa* at the end of *nā*, and the letter *va* at the end, joined with two vowels.

Extract only the letter ending in *sa* (śa), joined with the third vowel (*u*), and adorned by that same [vowel] with the letter ending in *kha* (*khū*). Make the letter ending in *ṭa* (*ṭa*) situated after the letter ending in *va* (*va*).
Conjoined with the second vowel (*i*), it is purified by the letter ending in *pha* (*phī*).
Make the syllable *thā* end with the *vajra* (the letter *m*), and likewise make the syllable *ghā* enclosed by the letter *s*.
Again, place the letter *s* in the sixth position, further adorned by the letters *pā* and *phā*.

The letter *ṭha* marked with *sa*, followed again by that same [letter] with *sa* beneath it, and then *sā*, forms the ten-syllable mantra. It is said to consist of one hundred and seven syllables in total;
it shatters the flood of all obstacles and destroys evil portents and misfortunes.
Again, the western [syllable] situated on the peak, accompanied by a semi-vowel (*sāntastha*) and marked by the fourth [vowel];
then the letter *la* joined with the beloved [vowel *e*], followed by *va* illuminated by *i*;
having extracted the solitary *va*, it is adorned at the beginning with *tha* and at the end with *na*.
Having extracted only the *sānta* (sa), it is to be covered and adorned with the *nānta* (na);
the *vajrāṇḍa* (the seed-syllable of the thunderbolt-egg) is joined with the sixth [vowel] and purified by the *phānta* (pha).
The *vajrāṇḍa* is again established upon the *lānta* (la) and inlaid with the *kānta* (ka).
The eight-syllable Mahāghora mantra consists of one hundred and eight words;
it causes the destruction of all nāgas and is the ender of poisons, spirits, and planetary influences.
It is established within the Vajra-egg (vajrāṇḍa), ending with the letter *sa* and adorned by the fourth [vowel] following *pha*.
O Dear One, having made the letter ending in *ṭha* (ṭha) together with the initial *sa* (sa) into a lifeless mass,
this two-syllabled word is known as the one hundred and ninth. One should extract the letter ending in *sa* (sa), conjoined with another *sa* (sa), beginning with *kha* (kha), and taken alone.
One should extract the letter ending in *dh* (da) with the vowel *i* on its head; the letter ending in *th* (tha); the letter ending in *s* (sa); and the one following *san* (the letter *na*).

Having extracted the third letter from the preceding group (the letter *ga*), it should be covered by the letter situated after *dh* (the letter *na*). One should likewise extract the letter ending in *ṭ* (ta), joined with the fifth vowel (*u*), and the solitary letter ending in *s* (sa).
One should extract the letter *ma* joined with the letter *sa*, and indeed the letter *cha* alone;
the letter *va* combined with three vowels, and the letter *ya* alone. The "Vajra-egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*) is the letter *ya* presided over by two vowels and adorned with the letter *pa*.

In this context, one should join together into a single cluster (piṇḍa) the following: the letter ending in *ṭ* alone; the letter ending in *ḍ* joined with three vowels; that beginning with *ph*; that beginning with *r*; the "vajra-egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*); the letter ending in *y*; the letter ending in *ḍ* together with the final *s*; and the letter *s* joined with the sixth vowel. One should combine these into one.
The letter *ṭha* at the end, enclosed by *sa*, further joined with *sādi* (the letter *sa*), and without *jīvaka* (the vowel *i*),
is declared to be an eighteen-syllable word consisting of one hundred and ten [units]. The letter *ṭha* at the end, conjoined with the letter *na*, and purified by the letter *pha*.
(18b) Having extracted only the letter *sa* and the first *kha*, together with the final *na*;
one should again extract the beloved *ka*, and once more the *sa* situated after the *ya*.
One should extract the letter *ya* ending in *paṃ*, the letter *ḍha* ending in *la*,
likewise [the letter *ya*] alone ending in *ta* with its head adorned by the letter *na*.
Then [one should take] the "Vajra-egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*) traversed by two vowels, ending in *sa* and variegated by the letter *sa*.
Having extracted the letter ending in *s* (sa) alone, followed by the letter ending in *t* (ta) marked with two vowels;
then the letter ending in *ṭ* (ṭa) adorned with three suns (*r*) and marked by that same [letter ending in *s*].
Then, having extracted the letter ending in *n* (na) alone, followed again by the letter ending in *th* (tha) situated after the letter ending in *s*.
The syllable *khānta* joined with two vowels, and *ḍānta* marked with three vowels;
the *vajrāṇḍa* established upon *sānta*, and *ḍānta* adorned by *sānta*;
*sānta* inlaid with three suns—these should all be given first once again.
Ending with *la*, beginning with *tha*, and ending with *sa*—these are the sole leaders of the letters.
Having established that which ends with *ṭa*, begins with *tha*, and ends with *sa*, adorned with two vowels and ending with *pha*;
and having established that which ends with *ṭha*, begins with *sa*, one performs the supreme "falling of the lifeless."

This formidable twenty-seven-syllable phrase, consisting of one hundred and eleven [repetitions], is proclaimed as that which draws forth a great flood of blood. One should extract it ending with the letter *ga*, interspersed with the letter *na*, and solely concluding with the letter *cha*.
The letter *sa* (śānta) joined with three vowels, marked by that same [vowel] as the letter *ra* (rānta);
the letter *la* (lānta) joined with two vowels; then the letter *ṭha* (ṭhānta) situated in the sixth position;
the first letter after *tha* (thādya) conjoined with the third vowel, and joined with the letter *ṇa* (nānta) following *ṭha*.
Having extracted only the syllable *chā*, and again the syllable *ṭhā* enclosed by *sā*;
then the syllable *sā* fell once more, and finally the ten-syllable word was extracted—
this is proclaimed as the complete one hundred and twelve words at the end of the section.
Extract the letter *kha* with two vowels combined, and extract the letter *ḍa* alone.
Make the letter *sa* with two vowels on its head, and place the first letter of *tha* (i.e., *tha*) following that *sa*.
Adorn that with three vowels on its head, and further embellish it with two vowels.
(19a) This word "vajrāṇḍa," traversed by the three vowels, split into two parts;
join "vajrāṇḍa" with the fifth [vowel] and purify it with the letter "phāṃ."
O Supreme Goddess, one should make that which ends in *ṭha* and begins with *sa* lifeless.
This ten-syllable word indeed devours ten million Yamas;
it should be known briefly as one hundred and thirteen.
Having extracted the letter *nā* (with the vowel *ā*), it is placed at the end of *vajrāṇḍa*, which is itself situated at the end [of the preceding sequence].
By means of the former [syllable], the *vajrāṇḍa* becomes pure and is marked with the three vowels (*trisvara*).
Again, the letter *śā* is placed at the end, and the letter *lā* is joined with the three vowels.
Furthermore, make this word ending in *ra* and ending in *ka* into two parts.
One should extract that which ends in *kha* joined with two vowels, and that which ends in *ṣa* alone.
[Then] that which ends in *tha* joined with the fifth [consonant], conjoined with that which begins with *sa* and ends in *na*.
One should place the letter *ra* at its end, adorned with the fourth [vowel] and the letter *pha*.
One should first construct that adamantine egg (*vajrāṇḍa*) grown from the letter *la*, adorned with that [same].
The letter *la* is inlaid with the letter *pa*; one should extract the letter *ṭha* alone.
Falling at the end, it fulfills all hopes;
it is declared to consist of seventeen syllables and one hundred and fourteen [verses].
Furthermore, the mass of the Vajra-egg has a semivowel at its end and is illuminated by the fourth [state].
Having placed the letter marked with *pha* at the head, adorned with the three vowels and ending in *cha*;
having made it end in *va* and stand upon *tha*, marked with the second vowel;
having extracted the solitary letter ending in *ya*; and [placed] the letter ending in *ṭa*, adorned with the three vowels.
Having joined it with the peaceful sixth [vowel], one should write the two syllables ending in *sa* separately;

having written the word twice, one should add the syllable ending in *ya* joined with the two vowels and the letter ending in *pha*. Then, one should give the first cluster ending in *sa*, illuminated by the letter ending in *pha*.

Having extracted only the syllable *ga*, and then the syllable *dha* enclosed by *sa*, with *sa* at the beginning and falling at the end— this sixteen-syllable mantra, which bestows the fruit of all desired objects, should be known as the granter of the results of whatever is contemplated.
(19b) O Maheśvarī, this hundred is said to be increased by fifteen.
Again, one should extract the letter ending in *kha* with two vowels, and likewise the letter ending in *ḍa*.
The first syllable of the word *vānta* (va), joined with the third vowel (i);
the letter at the end of *kha* (kha), established on the seventh vowel (u); again *vānta* (va) situated on the first syllable of *tha* (tha) [i.e., *thā*] (tha);
*vānta* (va) conjoined with the third vowel (i); and then give the first syllable of the word *pada*.
Extracting only the letter ending in *ḍa*, one should extract only the letter ending in *ṭa*. Then,
the letter ending in *ca* situated within the letter ending in *kha*, and again the letter ending in *sa* joined with three vowels—
make the letter ending in *dha* have its head marked by that very [vowel] and be situated within the letter ending in *ḍha*.
Having extracted only the *yānta* [ya], marked with two vowels, it becomes the *vajrāṇḍa*.
Again, that same [syllable] marked with two vowels and ending in *s*, adorned with three vowels, shall likewise become twofold; it does not extend to the end of *ṅa*, *ka*, *ṭa*, or *ḍa*.
One should extract the letter *ṭha*, which is mounted on *la* (i.e., *ṭha*), has a great color (*mahāvarṇṇa*), and is marked by *sa* (i.e., *ṣṭha*).
However, the word "lifeless" (*nirjīva*) is that which is mounted on *sa* at the beginning (i.e., *sṭha*); it brings about the destruction of all things.
This should be known as the one hundred and sixteenth [mantra], which bestows great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*).
O Goddess, this twenty-one-syllable mantra has been revealed to you.

Having again extracted the Vajra-egg (the letter *va*), adorned with the fourth vowel (*u*) and followed by a semivowel (*ya*), it is marked at the head by the letter ending in *pha* (*pha*). Then follows the letter ending in *ṭha* (*ṭha*), together with the letter ending in *na* (*na*) and the one following *sa* (*ha*).
Again, having concealed the beneficial letter *varṇa*, adorned with *kānta* and ending in *ḍa*,
situated at the beginning of *sa*, and rendered lifeless (*nirjīva*), it becomes the wonderful *pāva*.
This [mantra] is known as one hundred [syllables] joined with seventeen at the end of five.
O Goddess of the gods, I have again given you the first syllable of this very word.
Furthermore, at the end of the previous [word], the two-syllabled word has been extracted.
Thus, one hundred and eighteen [names] have been declared to you according to their true meaning.
The *pādya* (the foot) marked by *kānta* (the letter *ka*) should be made; at the end of all [this], one should give again.
The first number is one less than a hundred increased by twenty; this is the *pada*.
The fourth is the *vajrāṇḍa* (the adamantine egg), ending with a *stha*, purified by *kānta* itself.
Furthermore, at the end of this [mantra], one should again perform that *kayuṭa* with the prefix *pūrvānta*.
It is recorded as consisting of three syllables and being joined with twenty, totaling one hundred words.

The syllable *pha* with the nasal *m* (*phānta*), followed by *sa* with the nasal *m* (*sānta*), then the *vajrāṇḍa* (the letter *ha*), then *pa* with the nasal *m* (*pānta*), and finally *sa* with the sixth vowel (*sa-ṣaṣṭhaka*).
This is the *piṇḍa* mantra, most terrible; one should extract it ending with the letter *ya*.
The *vajrāṇḍa* is conjoined with two vowels and purified by the syllable *phānta*.

The syllable ending in *va* is adorned with three dots (*bindu*); likewise, that ending in *ra* is proclaimed to be so. That ending in *gha* is preceded by *va* and marked with the fourth vowel (*ū*). The syllable ending in *pha* is adorned on its crest. The syllable ending in *ga* is joined with that which ends in *pha*, and furthermore, the syllable ending in *ṭha* is situated after *sa*.
O Goddess of the gods, this supreme eight-syllable mantra is devoid of a living soul (nirjīva).
One hundred and twenty-one [recitations] have been correctly prescribed.
Vajrāṇḍa, increased by five million, is purified by the very essence of Phānta.
The end of the first [syllable] and again the end of the last—this word consists of two syllables.
It is described as having a number of one hundred and twenty-two.
The Vajra-egg is firmly established at the end, adorned with the fourth vowel and the final consonant.
Having placed *ṭāṃ* at the end, joined with two vowels; *lāṃ* at the end, differentiated by three vowels;
*thā* at the beginning, situated with *sāṃ*; marked with the previous insignia;
then *vāṃ*, the solitary one; and again *yāṃ*, beautiful and variegated.
The six-syllable mantra known as Vedapāda consists of one hundred and twenty-three syllables.
O Dear One, it stands with the letter *ṭa* at its end, the letter *sa* at its end, and the letter *la* at its end; furthermore, one should give the first syllable again.
Then there is the letter *śa* at its end, the letter *da* at its end, and once more the letter *va* at its end, adorned with three vowels.
The Vajra-egg (VA), together with the sixth [letter] (Ū) and purified by the end of PHA (PHA),
having placed the end of DHĀ (DH) preceded by SA (SA) and rendered lifeless (NIRJĪVA), O lady of excellent complexion,
the word consisting of seven syllables and one hundred twenty-four [units] is extracted.
Furthermore, situated within the center of the vajra-egg is the letter *pha*, adorned with the fifth vowel (*u*).
At the end of the first [syllable] it is doubled, and at the very end is the supreme three-syllabled word.
This has been proclaimed to you as numbering one hundred and twenty-five.
That which ends in *śa*, that which ends in *ra*, marked by two vowels; that which ends in *va*, adorned with three vowels;
that which ends in *sa* and is joined with the seed-syllable of Vajra; and again, that which is situated between *dha* and *sa*.

One should extract the syllable marked by the end of *na* (ṇa) at the head, ending with the fire of time (kṣa); then the end of *kha* (ha), joined with the fifth vowel (u), and the end of *va* (pha) alone. Again, the end of *ṭa* (ṇa) conjoined with the end of *pha* (ra), and then the previous pair once more.

Again, that very same [syllable] is at the end of the pair, marked by *na* at the end; likewise, *va* is joined with *sa*, purified by *na* alone. Again, *ra* is situated after *la*, and *sa* is marked by three vowels.

One should extract the syllable *va*, which has two vowels (*u*) above it and ends with *sa* (i.e., *vauḥ*), alone. Then, one should take the middle of *ṭa*, *ḍa*, and *ma* (i.e., *ḍa*), adorned with *śa* (i.e., *śḍa*), and purified by the end of *pha* (i.e., *pha*).
This is the "Vajra-Egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*), presided over by three vowels (*ū*), and followed by the first and last [syllables] of the preceding [group].
It shall consist of nineteen syllables and one hundred and twenty-six;
this is declared to be the "Destructive Machine of Terrible Power.
It should be formed with the letter ending in *s* (sa) situated in the *cha*-group (*chādyasthita*), and the letter beginning with *y* (*yādyastha*) situated in the *ṭha*-group (*ṭhāntasaṃsthita*).
Furthermore, the effect (kārya) is situated within the sibilants (sāntasthita), the fourth state (turya) being variegated by the labials (phānta).
This is the Greatly Terrible (Mahāghora) Piṇḍa, intent upon devouring the three worlds.
Again, [the sequence] is the labial (kānta), the dental (ṭhānta), the sibilant (sānta), and that which stands at the beginning (sādya), devoid of the individual soul (jīva).

The word consisting of two syllables is said to be one hundred and twenty-seven. Having extracted the two [groups] beginning with *ka* in two ways, there is the great radiance variegated by that which ends in *pha*. Again, having extracted that which begins with *kha*, it is solitary; then that which ends in *ṣa* is joined with two vowels.
The letter *sa* is peaceful; the two letters ending in *tha* are firmly established at the back of the neck.

That which is marked by the letter *na* should be performed; furthermore, that which ends in *ra* is situated upon the letter *la*. Make that which ends in *ka* have three vowels as its head, and place that which ends in *ga* upon the letter *sa*.

Again, having placed it at the end of the sibilants (sa), purified by the end of the labials (pha), and then again placed at the end of the cerebrals (ṭha) together with the first letter (sa), O Goddess, one should bestow that which is devoid of life. (21a)
This indeed consists of ten syllables: the hundredth, the twenty-first, and the eighteenth;
joined with the one ending in *va*, the one established in the end of *sa*, the one situated at the end of *sa*, and marked by the sign of the end of *pha*.
Marked by the fourth, this great aggregate (*mahāpiṇḍa*) should be extracted as the solitary letter at the end of *ya*.
The syllable *vajra* (va), overlaid with two vowels (*ai*) and adorned by the letter *ya*;
the letter *ma*, joined with the letter *na*; the letter *ṭha*, followed by the letter *sa*;
and finally marked by the fourth vowel (*au*) and the letter *sa*: having thus formed these six syllables, one obtains this six-syllabled mantra.
This is proclaimed as one hundred and twenty-nine.
Again, that which ends with *ṭha* and is marked by *na* is purified by *pha*.
Having placed that which begins with *ka* in the position of *ra*, it is struck on the head by *na*.
Extracting only the *śānta* (the letter *sa*), make it peaceful and established in peace.
Not ending with an end, joined with an end, the *vajrāṇḍa* (the letter *va*) conjoined with the sixth (*u*).
Made pure by the *phānta* (the letter *pha*) itself, one should give it again, situated on the eastern mountain (*ka*).
The letter ending in *kh* (kha) with two vowels above it, joined with the letter ending in *y* (ya) and three vowels;
again, the letter ending in *v* (va) marked by that [same vowel], and the letter ending in *ṭh* (ṭha) situated with its initial [vowel]—
O Goddess of the lords of gods, this fallen syllable of Rudra is extracted as a word.
One hundred and thirty more have been declared to you according to their true meaning.
Furthermore, one should extract the pure *chādya* (the syllable *cha*), which is not established internally, purified by the letter *ṣa*;
then the solitary *kevalin*, beginning with the letter *e* and ending with the letter *ra*.

Place *khānta* (the letter *ha*) and mount it upon *thādya* (the letter *tha*), and adorn it with the three vowels (*e*, *ai*, *au*). Again, at the end, place the excellent five-syllabled word at the end of *pūrva* (the letter *pa*).
In brief, this is said to consist of one hundred and thirty-one syllables.
The Vajra-egg (VA) is enclosed by the letter SA; it is adorned with the fourth vowel (Ī) and the final letter of PA (PHA).
It is covered by RA and mounted upon the letter DYA, its head marked by the letter NĀ.
Again, the solitary letter SA is joined with the final letter of RA (RA) and the three vowels.
The first letter is joined with the final one; then again, the last letter of the eastern [group] is joined with the final one.
This is declared to be the six-syllable word, the supreme hundred and thirty-two.
Vajrāṇḍa is conjoined with the sixth [vowel] and purified by the final letter of *pha*.
(21b) O Dear One, one should again give the Vajra-egg together with Kānta.
This is declared to be a two-syllable word, numbering one hundred and thirty-three.
Again, having extracted the *vajrāṇḍa* (the letter *ka*) together with its internal vowel (*u*), marked by the fourth [vowel] (*ū*), and marked at the head by the end of *pha* (*phū*),
make the end of *ṭa* (*ṭha*) situated with the beginning of *sa* (*sa*).
O Goddess of the God of Gods, this is the supreme two-syllabled word, devoid of life-force (*nirjīva*).
O Maheśvarī, one hundred and thirty-four [syllables] have been declared to you.
One should extract the letter marked by the fourth [vowel], which is again the final letter of the labial class (*lānta*) in its pure form.
After that, one should extract the pure letter ending in *ch* (*chānta*), and then the letter ending in *kh* (*khānta*) doubled.

Having thus properly joined it so that the *sa*-ending is internalized and the sign of the end is absent, one should form the *ra*-ending situated within the *ra*-ending; the *sa*-ending should be conjoined with three vowels,
while the *ṭa*-ending is merely simple, and from that one should again extract the simple *sa*-ending.
The first [syllable] is *da* (dānta), mounted on *la* (lānta), with *tha* at its beginning, adorned with three vowels (*trisvara*).
The second is *va* (vajra), mounted on *ṇa* (aṇḍa), ending in *sa* (sānta), and adorned by the fourth vowel and the final letter *pha*.
The third should be given as the solitary *ke* (kevala), and again the solitary *va* (vajra) and *ṇa* (aṇḍa).
To this [mantra], the letter ending in *kha* (kh), adorned with two vowels, should first be given again;
having extracted the letter ending in *ḍa* (ḍ) alone, one should take the letter ending in *ṭa* (ṭ) adorned with the letter ending in *pha* (ph);
and having extracted the letter ending in *kha* (kh) alone, one should take the letter ending in *sa* (s) marked by three vowels.
Having placed the letter *ṭha* (ṭhānta) followed by the letter *ḍha* (ḍhāntasthita), it is struck by a head of three dots (*tribinduśirasāhata*).
The letter *ya* (yānta) has three vowels (*trisvara*) above it and is purified by the letter *pha* (phāntena).
Again, the letter *śa* (śānta) is followed by the letter *sa* (sāntasthita), and the letter *na* (nānta) is joined with three vowels (*trisvarayojita*).
Having extracted only the letter ending in *ra*, one should extract only the letter ending in *ya*.
Then there is the "vajra-egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*) conjoined with two vowels, followed again by the letter ending in *ya* marked by that [same].
Then the letter ending in *sa* with three vowels on its head, and the letter ending in *ṭha* struck by the head of the letter ending in *na*.
Furthermore, at the end of this *pada*, the *pūrvapāta* is proclaimed;
thus, one hundred and thirty-five [syllables] have been declared by me to you.
This [mantra], numbered as having thirty syllables, bestows the fruit of all desires.
(22a) The letter *va*, joined with two vowels and ending in *sa*, adorned by that very same [letter];
having extracted the solitary *sa*, [one places] the letter *ḍha*, beautified by three vowels.
Having extracted only the *chādya* (the cover) together with the *vajrāṇḍa* (the thunderbolt-egg) joined with the sixth [vowel],
and having again placed the first *pāta* (fall) at the end of this *pada*,
it is proclaimed as a seven-syllabled [unit]; there are one hundred and thirty-six [of these].
The first [syllable] should be given again; the third should be extracted again. That which stands alone in the middle of the vajra should be marked with three vowels.
Having extracted the final [syllable] alone, the vajra-egg (vajrāṇḍa) is marked with two vowels.
One should extract the letter *śa*, twice repeated, followed by *kevala* and ending with the fourth vowel (*ī*),
which alone is to be raised up. [Then] the letter *la*, topped by the third vowel (*u*), the letter *ṭa*, the letter *ḍha* with the fifth vowel (*ū*) attached,
the letter *ya* joined with the second vowel (*u*), and the letter *ja* marked at the end by the letter *na*.
Furthermore, there is the letter *ya* followed by the solitary *va*, marked with two vowels;
then *la* joined with *ga*, and again *ṭha* situated after *ḍha*;
then *la* conjoined with three vowels, and *sa* adorned with another *sa*.
Place the letter *gha* marked with the fourth vowel (*au*), then again the letter *ra* situated upon the letter *la*.
Extract the letter *sa* with three vowels above it, followed by the solitary letter *yā*.
Then take the "Vajra-egg" (*vajrāṇḍa*)—the letter *cha*—overlaid with two vowels, ending with the letter *na* following the letter *ra*.
The word *sāntam* (ending in *sa*) marked by *na* at the end is this "Great Power" (*mahābala*) pada;
furthermore, *ṭhāntam* (ending in *ṭha*) marked by *na* at the end occurs twice, first and last. One hundred and twenty-seven padas have thus been proclaimed.
The terrible *ghoraḍāmara* is illuminated by twenty-eight syllables.
It is the adamantine egg (*vajrāṇḍa*), established with the vowels and consonants, adorned with the fourth [letter] and the end of the consonants.
One should again apply the previous sequence at its conclusion.
This thirty-eighth word consists of two syllables;
having extracted only the first syllable, one should join it with the letter *pha* and the number from the preceding [group].

This word consists of two syllables and is the fortieth [letter], O illustrious one; it is deficient by one and brings about the weight of yogic power. Furthermore, the mass of the Vajra-egg contains a semi-vowel and is marked by the fourth [state].

That which is joined with *kānta* is declared; again, that beginning with *ka* and ending with *na*, and that beginning with *ka* joined with its end—this three-syllabled word is extracted. Thus, one hundred and forty excellent words have been proclaimed.
Furthermore, there should be the "Vajra-Egg-Mass" (*vajrāṇḍapiṇḍa*), ending with the fourth vowel (*turyānta*) and followed by the letter *sa* (*sānta*).
One should form a two-syllable word marked with the first *pātā* (the letter *pa*).
This is declared to be one hundred and forty-one.

The Vajra-egg (vajrāṇḍa), conjoined with the sixth [vowel], marked by the end of *pha* (*phānta*), and joined with the first *pa*, is this two-syllable word. It is indeed the fortieth [letter] when combined. Having established the four types ending in *sa*, the first pair is accompanied by the five.

The second syllable is marked with the number two, followed by the letter *pha* and another number, adorned with its respective vowel; this four-syllabled [name] indeed totals one hundred and forty-three words,
O Goddess worshipped by heroes.
Having placed the first letter with the semi-vowels within it, and the beloved's mark as a single syllable,
the word is said to consist of one hundred and forty-four letters.
The Vajra-egg is established with the final letter and purified by the fourth letter ending in *pha*.
Again, at the end of the first syllable, place the two-syllable leader-word;
I have described to you one hundred and forty-five [syllables].
Make the "Vajra-Egg" (vajrāṇḍa), which ends with a sibilant and is firmly established, likewise conclude with a sibilant.
Having again marked it with the beloved (kānta) and joined it again with the first vowel, a two-syllable word is thus indicated; this constitutes one hundred and forty-six [syllables].
Furthermore, the vajrāṇḍa-piṇḍa is situated in the fifth position and is joined with the preceding.
This has been taught as the forty-seventh [chapter] consisting of two syllables;
it is taught to contain one hundred words that devours the three worlds.

The syllable *khānta* (kha), adorned with the vowel *sāntastha* (u) and the consonant *sāntāṅka* (sa), is purified by *phānta* (pha) itself. This two-syllabled word, having been extracted, should be placed again as it was before.
This is declared to be the fourteenth [letter] along with the eighth, making one hundred.
Furthermore, one should provide the syllable *va*, joined with *sa* and *ka*, and conjoined with *na*;
then one should again give the previously fallen syllable, for this is indeed a two-syllabled word.
This is declared to be the hundredth [syllable], situated at the forty-ninth position.
The Vajra-egg is inlaid with the letter *pha*; having covered the Vajra-egg, it remains established.
Again, having placed the letter *sa*, it is joined with the sixth [vowel] and the letter *pa* ending in *pha*.
To this cluster (*piṇḍa*), one must further give the previously fallen great power.
This three-syllable word is indeed declared to consist of one hundred and fifty [units].
Again, that which ends in *kha* joined with that which ends in *sa*, marked by the digit ending in *sa*, and adorned with that which ends in *pha*;
the previous placement should be given again, and the two-syllable word is extracted.
This is declared to be one hundred and fifty-one.
Again, the excellent single-syllable foot beginning with *pūrva-aśri-gaṃ* should be added;
thus, one hundred and fifty-two, ending with *punar-vānta*, should be extracted.
Having joined the *śānta* [letter] into a *saṃpuṭa*, together with its consort (*sakānta*) as a single syllable,
one should know that this is the fifty-third word, the "Great Powerful One" (*mahābala*). Then,
one should again provide the letter beginning with *aṃ*, which is once more enclosed by the *śānta*.
This state, established in its own seat and devoid of life, is proclaimed;
it is called the Trailokyadaṃmara, expressed by a single syllable.
It is the supreme collection of one hundred and fifty-four words.
O Goddess of the gods, this has been proclaimed to you both in brief and in detail:
the great Vidyā known as Navā, which consists of one thousand four hundred and forty-six syllables, is the one that severed the head of Brahmā.
Named Trailokyadaṃmarā, she is auspicious and the performer of all rites;
she is the bestower of everything, the crusher [of obstacles], and the cutter asunder of the flood of evil deeds.
The Goddess of gods, the *Trailokyadaṃarā* Vidyā, when remembered even once, bestows fearlessness upon gods, asuras, and humans, and removes their fear.
There is nothing she does not accomplish, and there is nothing she does not achieve.
There is nothing that she does not give; there is nothing that she does not illuminate.
There is nothing that she does not burn; there is nothing that she does not devour.
There is nothing that she does not shatter by the power of the Goddess of gods.
She who shatters all mantras with her fierce [power], the foremost leader of all mantras;
the terrible one who is the fire for all mantras, the Bhairavī who brings about the dissolution of all;
she who crushes all mudrās and weapons, and who shatters all maṇḍalas.
She is the destroyer of all nāgas, the cutter down of all asuras;
she is the slayer of the pride of all causes, the exterminator of all the wicked.
She is the formidable mistress of all wheels, the fierce shatterer of all magical diagrams.
Consisting entirely of mantras, radiant, adorned with all the syllables of vidyā,
the Goddess who bestows all sovereignty is accomplished through mere recitation.
She who dwells within the crooked [channel] of one would take away even the head of Brahmā.

Bhairava, together with the gods, is remembered as the direct bestower of liberation through his vision. O Goddess, he in whom [this knowledge] does not descend is proclaimed to be eternally liberated.
O Bhairavī, the word and its meaning abide in his mouth.
That lord of heroes is worthy of the world’s worship; by the mere sight of him, he removes all impurity.
Indeed, the Khecarīs, the goddesses of the gods, and the daughters of Bhairava praise him.
O Goddess, all his attendants and all the deities abide at his feet.
Those for whom this crooked one remains fixed upon the head certainly desire him as the sacred ford,
that great mantra, that god, that great sacrifice,
that eldest one, and that which is ever to be worshipped— for whomsoever this crooked one may abide.
That is knowledge, that is the highest austerity, that is yoga, and that is the supreme seat;
it is the goal and the blessed equanimity for whom this crooked course remains established.
Whoever should write down and preserve this Mistress of the Wheel of Mantras,
she shall always be worthy of worship by all the gods and the sky-farers (khecarīs). O Goddess, wherever she resides, that place becomes a supreme sanctuary.
In this very world, O Goddess of Gods, by the mere recitation [of this] every day,
the entire wheel of rays residing within one's own body becomes manifest;
and by the mere utterance of the words, O sinless one, the extraction of the *liṅga* and so forth occurs.
O Goddess, the Mistress of the Gods of gods, she destroys [all obstacles]; of this there is no doubt. By the mere utterance of her name, the three worlds tremble violently.
Therefore, she should be known as Trailokyadāmara, the sovereign of the circle of mantras.
O beloved, that man by whom [this] has come to the path of his hearing, by whom it has been written, by whom it has been seen,
or by whom it has been seen in a book, is equal to me;
he is initiated in all tantras and is most excellent.
O beloved goddess, whatever vitality known as mantra exists within all those tantras situated in the four seats—
those which are waveless and supreme, and those headed by Kulakaula—
in all those tantras [resides that power].

That which is known as Vidyā—or that which is known as Maṇḍala—and that which is Raudra and Svābhāvika, all of that is swallowed by her; therefore she is the most excellent of all. Now, what is the use of saying more? There is nothing more terrible than she.
It exists within the entire essence of mantra, having emerged from the Four Seats (Catuṣpīṭha).
Its power, heroism, pervasiveness, cognition, and valor;
its form, the abundance of its colors, and its sequence of movement and utterance—all these are present.
O Dear One, the entire tradition and so forth cannot be described even by tens of thousands of Sādākhya-s and tens of thousands of Cakras;
for merely by grasping its name, one becomes like a creeper overcome by the wind.
The entire universe trembles; who is capable of describing her?
By the mere rising of whose slight smile all the quarters of space blaze forth.
Clouds fall like trees; who is capable of describing her?
Who is capable of describing her, by whose slight investigation of individual forms the principal mountain ranges are reduced to ashes?
(24b) Who is able to describe her who burns [all things] to ash?
Who is capable of describing her, the sight of whose power at the end of each foot and at the pause destroys all suffering?
By means of yoga, even those as massive as Mount Meru are consumed by her.
Who is able to describe her, from whom heaps of burning coals fall,
and by whose mere flickering sparks as vast as the celestial Brahmāṇḍas emerge with the brilliance of great fires? Who is able to describe her?
Who is capable of describing her, by whose mere analysis of the division of words and utterances this entire world is cast down?
She who is remembered as the lineage of accomplishments (siddhi) through the union with the Lord and Virāma.
Who is capable of describing that terrible Goddess?
O Bhairavī, by the mere thought arising from the conjunction of her [mantric] syllables, the entire host of sky-farers would fall;
who is capable of describing her?
By whose mere contraction even the Fire of Time (Kālāgni) is reduced to ashes;
who possesses singular steadfastness through practice—who is capable of describing her?
It is she whose power, within the wheel of Kuṇḍalinī, effects the blossoming of the lotus.
The head of Brahmā fell; who is capable of describing her?
The cave of whose throbbing belly was the locus for the manifestation of his virility.
The discus of Viṣṇu fell; who is capable of describing her?
O Beloved, who is capable of describing her, by whose utterance through the friction of the restless and lecherous [deities] the fierce *kula* falls down?
By whose pressure at the crossroads, from devouring the light of the peacock-crest (*kalāpīḍa*), [the world is transformed]?
Who is capable of describing that wheel of diverse onomatopoeic sounds,
by whose multitudes of shrieks and great crashing impacts [the world is shaken]?
Who is capable of describing that [power] by which even Sadāśiva falls [prostrate],
and by whose great roar the entire host of Bhairavas is dissolved and brought under command? Who is capable of describing that?

And who is capable of describing her, by whose hair-tufts— whirling as they move in circles— the [enemies] stationed in the circle of spears fall down? By the application of whose creative power (kalana) there occurs the dissolution of the skeletal frame of the Kula?
Who is capable of describing Mahākālī, from whom,
at the end of the kalpa during the dissolution, the twelve suns and the three fires fall swiftly from their own positions? Who is capable of describing her?

O Goddess, today I have thoroughly awakened the poison and the fire by reciting this Great Vidyā, the sole devourer that swallows the world. By her grace, may there be well-being for this entire universe.
Having heard this today, O most auspicious one, you have now attained peace;
today you are born, O fair-hipped one; today you are satisfied, O Bhairavī;
today you are worthy, O blessed one; today there is the blossoming of your eyes.
O Goddess of the gods, by the grace of the Goddess of the gods, they strive; O lady of beautiful limbs, may you be exhilarated by the surging wine of knowledge that intoxicates the great heavens,
and may you become radiant with splendor through that vision.
Today you live, O fair-hipped one; today is a great festival for you.
O lady of beautiful limbs, fulfill this [task] with the essence of mantras that spread from the pure embers, O you who desire the welfare of Jayadratha.
Thus, in the presence of the two [deities], who were resplendent with a row of crest-jewels of gods and asuras,
the secret of the Goddess— the essence of all the Agamas— has been declared exactly as it is.
O Goddess of gods, having encountered him— who is a rain-cloud for the forest-fire of saṃsāra— for the benefit of the worlds, you shall never again grieve.
You are satisfied, you possess full splendor, and you are most formidable;
you are worthy on the field of heroes, O fair-browed one, and you are most venerable.
What else shall I say to you? Speak quickly!

Thus ends the second chapter on the Extraction of Mantras (*mantroddhāra*) within the Wheel of the Trailokyadaṃmara, in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra of the Vidyāpīṭha in the Bhairava Stream, consisting of twenty-four thousand verses.
Having heard this from the mouth of Hara, Gaṇāmbikā, who is venerated by the world, [spoke].
With her body bristling with horripilation, she spoke again to Śaṅkara.
The Goddess said:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O supreme leader of all mantras!"
O Lord of the gods, you who are the embodiment of the mantra of the Great Terrible Sovereign of All;
O Mahāsaṃhārabhairava, the destroyer of great illusion;
O you whose nature is the protection of the three worlds and the upliftment of the universe!

"I am fully satisfied, O Blessed One; I am at peace, as is fitting for my happiness, through your grace, O you of great splendor who destroyed the enemies of the gods. Now, O Lord of the Gods, I desire to hear [this] according to its proper arrangement."

O Maheśvara, I desire to hear from you, along with its secrets, how meditation is performed, how pervasion occurs, how the worship of the maṇḍala is conducted, as well as initiation, consecration, spiritual practice, the rules of conduct (samaya), and so forth.
"Furthermore, tell me in brief all this which is more secret than the secret, capable of uplifting the three worlds, for the benefit of living beings. Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain, as I have been requested by you,
the Brahmaśiras-nyāsa for one's wife, according to the proper sequence. One should perform this nyāsa in an auspicious and pleasant place.
Having thoroughly worshipped both the Lord in battle and the lineage of gurus,
the Mountain [Śiva] should thereafter purify his two hands with a circular movement.
First, one should bind that [mudrā] upon the two hands smeared with fragrance;
thereafter, O beautiful one, one should bind it for the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions as well.
Immediately after, having bound one's own body, one should form the most formidable mudrā.
O Supreme Goddess, one should purify the consciousness of aversion through yoga.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, having generated the enemy of the heroes (vīrāvariman) and then contracted it,
one should cause the entire manifest Kula to rejoice through the union of bliss by means of the six-syllabled mantra.
Having filled that [space] with nectar through the divisions of sequential and non-sequential order,
one should thereafter effect the union of the nature of consciousness within the encapsulation of *bindu* and the end of *nāda*.
When the mental functions have dissolved and everything has become completely full, it abides entirely in a state of exhaustion.
Having rested for a very long time within that which has the form of an unbroken circle, resembling a tranquil ocean, until the state of contraction occurs,
the practitioner of mantra should recite the vidyā arising from expansion and contraction.
Within that [reality], there is that which is filled with the essence of bliss;
therein Bhairavī has arisen, and that is proclaimed as the Krama. It is filled with the abundance of exultation and bliss, and it is said to have arisen from the state of perfect rest.

Therein, one should meditate upon Śivā at the end of the reverse order, following the forward sequence, radiant with dissolution and reabsorption, characterized by expansion, contraction, and withdrawal. Thus, through these expansions and contractions, Mahāmudrā is revealed.
O Goddess, by means of this [mantra], one should perform the placement (nyāsa) following Vidyā, Śakti, and Śiva.
Thus shall be the internal six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) placement;
those which are called omniscience and so forth are the six limbs within the body.
In that state, those [energies] whose nature consists of contraction and expansion attain manifestation;
though always unmanifest through their own power when dissolved in Śiva, they are manifest [when emerging].
Therefore, this indeed is the six-limbed [rite], for it is not merely a ritual placement (*nyāsa*) consisting of phonemes.
(26b) Having thus become the Lord of Color, possessing the most excellent color and form,
he who is within the colors and whose essence is color should then deposit the family of colors.

One should perform the placement of the feet upon the manifestations of the words within the words that constitute the state of the instruction on the non-words at the end of the words. Having thus performed this supreme placement, one should thereafter proceed according to the gross sequence.
Through the practice of Mahāmudrā, by means of the division of emanation and reabsorption,
one should place [the mantra] from the head down to the feet, or from the feet up to the head. O Goddess, one should extract the Vidyā or the word that arises therefrom.
Thus has the placement (nyāsa), both external and internal, been fully explained to you.
O fortunate one, all collections of vidyās that are devoid of this are proclaimed to be like lumps of clay; they are not considered to bestow the fruit of accomplishment.
O slender-waisted one, by merely performing this arrangement,
the practitioner becomes the very form of Vātubhairava, a knower of the supreme reality.
Just as Vidyeśvarī has been described, so too is Ghorā, the subduer of the three worlds.
She is the one who carries away the head of Brahmā; she is likewise [inaccessible]. Difficult to behold and unassailable from afar—what is the use of saying more?
O Goddess of gods, by the mere act of nyāsa, she bestows the previously mentioned series of qualities.
"It shall certainly come to pass; there is no doubt, for my word is infallible.

Thus, O Goddess, have I explained to you this *nyāsa*, imbued with secret mysteries. Now, O Gaurī, I shall describe the meditation (*dhyāna*), which is very difficult even for the lords of the gods to attain.

Thus ends the third chapter on the procedure for ritual placement (*nyāsa*) within the *Trailokyadāmara-cakra* of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, a great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the *Śiraścheda* division of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavasarasvatī*.
Bhairava said:
I shall now tell you that which was declared to someone through great effort:
having rested in one's own ocean of the family by means of the previously mentioned placement (*nyāsa*).
In that which is without intrinsic nature, formless, free from duality, and devoid of affliction—
from which the principles (*tattvas*) unfold as the lords of lords—
and into which they enter, O auspicious one, remaining established therein; 15.20–21ab.
These five again become [manifest] through the application of one's own conduct and practice.
Indeed, that entire family of the wheel-bases consists of the *bindu* and *nāda*,
joined with the senses and their objects, radiant with the enjoyment of the sense-objects.
O Goddess, because [the mind] repeatedly enters into that which is pure by its very nature,
and because, O Beloved, everything enters therein and from there it departs—
that is one's own nature, one's own form, filled with indivisible bliss.
Mounted there, the supreme adept, at the dawning of the light of his vigor,
should contemplate [the deities] in their gross form as radiant Mahābhairavas—
possessing many faces and eyes, and terrifying with many arms.
With many bellies, necks, shanks, and feet that were terrifying,
with flames leaping from their hair that set ablaze the lords of the directions,
and crowded with tongues of fire issuing from the multitude of their wandering mouths.
They have rent asunder the shell of worldly existence with the violent tossing of their knitted brows;
they are formidable with the expansion of their lightning-like wrathful frowns, intense with the creepers of their eyebrows,
and they set ablaze all the quarters of space with the flames vomiting from within their ears.
Her eyes were like deep, sunken wells resembling vast pits;
her formidable cavities were like hundreds of Rudra-eggs difficult to fill, resounding from within.
Her face was radiant with stars that resembled the fire at the end of an aeon.
Her many eyes were like a mass of flickering flames at the end of an eon;
her lofty, withered face, with its upturned cheeks, was most terrifying;
and she was difficult to approach due to her massive chest, which shone like hundreds of thousands of fragments of the cosmic egg.
With garments ablaze from the fire arising from the depths of the hollows of her throat,
she is terrible and inflated, having shattered the shell of Brahmā’s cosmic egg with her great winds.
Her row of teeth was like a hundred great mountain ranges;
with the fire of her fangs, she consumed the sons of those upon whom she bit in her fierce rage;
and within the gaps of her terrible tusks, all the most excellent of the gods were trapped.
She has earrings fashioned from the entire Bhairava and Īśāna;
her beautiful crest is adorned with the six causal great skulls;
and she is decorated by the orb of the sun within the mass of her loose hair at the edge of her forehead.
She whose tongue was terrible with hundreds of spikes,
who caused the dissolution of the cosmic egg through the friction of her crown against the fierce-rayed sun,
and whose body shone with a multitude of millions of formidable, staff-like arms.

The Lord of the Wheel bears a neck pregnant with the deep resonance of secret mantras and a terrible gurgling sound; it is the abode where hundreds of wheels are perfectly merged, and its cavernous mouth resounds with a great roar that causes the cosmic egg to tremble.
She has the terrifying faces of a lion, a boar, and a dog, with breasts hanging down;
she is capable of sustaining the splendor of a hundred thousand cosmic eggs as cremation grounds;
she is emaciated, her deep belly appearing radiant with its parched sinews and veins.

Her broad hips are adorned with a girdle of skeletons, the cause of all things, while her deep and terrifying secret parts are covered by the hide of the enemy of the gods and encircled by fierce, crooked,
six-tufted venomous serpents.
Her thighs are resplendent with the brilliance of ten million Mount Sumerus ablaze;
her shanks shine with the light of hundreds of pillars of wish-fulfilling trees;
and her excellent garments are rendered motionless by the power of meditation arising from the impact of her feet.
She wears anklets that oppress all the assembled gods, has a terrifying face,
and stands on one leg with a severed head of Mahākāla— his cheeks swollen— serving as her tooth.
Her second foot is placed upon the skeleton of Ghoraheruka.
The eight wrathful kings, the lords of the terrifying and formidable Tathāgatas,
crush that fearsome one with the blows of their terrible feet.
Her limbs are made radiant by the ornaments of the lords of the nāgas of noble lineage;
she is adorned with garlands and ornaments fashioned from the heads and trunks of elephants;
and she wears a necklace made of stalks as numerous as the suns at the end of an aeon.
Her body was smeared with the drops from the tethered deer of the Lord of Speech;
she delighted solely in playing the lute made from the skeleton of Brahmā;
and she was greedily intent upon consuming all the blood poured out from the fresh lotus-stalks.
She shone with the weight of millions of cosmic eggs upon her khaṭvāṅga;
with some hands she bore the severed heads of Bhairavas, and with others she supported Mahākāla and Śiva at her side;
with some she held aloft blazing masses of fire, and with others the lords of serpents.

With some of her hands she was violently crushing the entire host of Brahmās until they let out piteous cries; with others, she was tossing about within the hollows of her palms the fierce host of Mahāviṣṇus;
and with yet others, she was utterly annihilating the blazing and highly exalted host of Rudras and their attendants.
With some of her hands, she crushes the fierce discus of Īśvara like a ball of honey;
with other multitudes of hands, she instantly squeezes the blazing mass of Sadāśiva like a cluster of grapes.
With some hands, she who is terrible with fierce fangs and of a horrific appearance crushes the entire terrifying wheel of Bhairava as it cries out;
likewise, with others, she [crushes] the entire most formidable family of the Tathāgatas.
With her masses of hands resembling sharp swords,
she crushes the fierce wheel of the hundred-sun-like serpents;
with those excellent hands, she completely squeezes and grinds it all.
(28b) The terrible Kālarātri, with her gaping mouths, incessantly casts about in every direction her wheel of fierce weapons that quivers and flashes as it revolves through the families [of deities].
With some of her terrible hands she devours the entire multitude of clouds and serpents;
with others she casts hundreds of thousands of cosmic eggs into her mouth-cavity from which [the flames] flow incessantly;
and with yet others she emits a fire of fearsome form, like the crests of peacock feathers.
With some [roars] that terrified [beings]— resembling the fierce flashes of lightning from the rending of clouds by terrible, sharp fangs,
and as violent as the great and horrific *saṃvarta* winds at the time of universal destruction—
and with some sets of six mouths terrifying with the flames of a laughing fire arising from their dreadful *aṭṭahāsa* laughter; ||| 17 ||
Weeping while some laugh aloud with mocking words,
and while others sing with mouths that are like the sacrificial pits for praising the best of the gods— unfathomable [is she],
who for a moment produces great roars and for a moment seems to cry out from all her mouths.

At that moment, she was for an instant wrathful, with eyes like those of the night of universal destruction; for an instant, her senses were intoxicated and her mind distracted. For an instant she wept, for an instant she roared aloud, and for an instant she was intoxicated by the play of a great laugh.
For an instant she was intent on devouring the world, and for an instant she resembled a tumultuous uproar of terror.

In one moment she is beautiful, and in another she is deformed; in one moment her own radiance is infused with camphor, and in another she possesses the form of the thousand-eyed Indra. In one moment she is the essence, and in another she is the playful manifestation of the universe;
in one moment she is worshipped by the circle of lords of reality, and in another she is fierce and devoted to dwelling therein.
For a moment she fell, for a moment she rose up, and for a moment she took on the form of the entire ocean;
for a moment she was worthy of praise, for a moment she was running, and for a moment she was inconceivable, resembling a great mountain.
In one moment she was variegated with a thousand faces; in one moment she was endowed with a thousand arms.

In one moment her hands held all the terrible weapons; in one moment she was intent on striking. She was to be meditated upon as five-faced in an instant, and in another instant she was possessed of a hundred faces.
In one moment she had a thousand faces of cats; in another moment she was variegated with the faces of jackals.
In one moment she possessed a hundred thousand faces of lions; in another moment her limbs were marked by the faces of bears.
In one moment she had ten million faces of *hālāhala* poison; in another moment she manifested a multitude of ten thousand mouths like those of female jackals.
In one moment she is endowed with the face of a lordly elephant, and in another moment she is to be meditated upon as having the face of a great horse;
in a moment her limbs are variegated with the faces of tigers, and in a moment she possesses a hundred thousand faces of owls.
She has faces on all sides, eyes on all sides, feet on all sides, and hands on all sides.

She whose knees, thighs, and hips are all-pervading; she who is fierce with her all-encompassing face, belly, and nose; she who possesses all-pervading form and perfectly all-pervading splendor; she who has all-pervading light and perfectly all-pervading speech; she who has all-pervading ears and all-pervading tongues; she who is both all-pervasively terrible and all-pervasively gentle.
Thus, Bhairavī, who is exceedingly terrible and whose sole delight is destruction, should always be meditated upon;
or else, she who assumes various forms according to one's desire may be meditated upon at all times. Who is capable of meditating upon her, O Great Bhairava, who is even beyond the supreme deity?
O beloved, no one else here can withstand her, except for him [the practitioner].
Or else, O beautiful one, one should meditate upon her as blazing with eighteen arms, radiant with five faces, glowing and bearing great weapons.
Or, having visualized her in whatever form is desired as dwelling upon the heap of corpses at Cakranāḍi, she is the destroyer of all lords of reality. (29b)
O Goddess of the gods, listen now to this [teaching] regarding the meditation on the aggregate as well as its individual components:
she is the goddess of the gods, the womb of compassion (kṛpodarī), who pervades all states;
yet, like a wall, she remains distinct from them.
Manifested and endowed with capacity, she is of one and the same form everywhere.
O Bhairavī, no distinction is to be known here; this is the ultimate reality (paramārtha).
As the last is, so are all; as all are, so is the one.
One should contemplate all those goddesses as having a single form, though they are very difficult to sustain [in meditation].
They have one face and eight arms, possessing forms identical to the central Goddess.
They are firmly established upon the spokes of the wheel, holding skull-bowls and goads.
Raising in their hands a sword, a skull-topped staff, a heart-lotus, a severed head, and a trident,
with great hand-drums at the tips of their hands and eyes resembling the three sacrificial fires—
what more shall I describe? O gods, they are manifest in their true forms.
O Bhairavī, in the ultimate sense, there is no distraction from the mantra.
One should meditate according to one's inclination and worship according to one's inclination;
whether separately or collectively, or even with a single word, O Dear One.
As is the worship, so is the meditation; as is the meditation, so is the adoration.
Thus, while meditating upon her, O beloved, what need is there for much speaking? Listen to it in brief, O dear one, regarding that lord of practitioners, the king of heroes.
"The form of the Goddess herself would become manifest; what more than this could be said?
Thus, O you who possess the wheel of the earth that is unrestrained by various winds, this noble destruction has been described to you, or rather, as it was.
I have described to you the meditation upon her who is worshipped by all the gods;
O lady revered by the lords of heroes, what else shall I tell you now?

Thus ends the fourth chapter on Meditation in the *Taulokya-ḍāmara-cakra*, within the third hexad of the *Jayadratha-māhāla*— the *Mahātantra* concerning the Severing of the Head (*śira-ccheda*) in the *Siddhividyā-pīṭha* of the *Mahābhairava-srotas*.
Having heard this, the Goddess of gods was struck with wonder and overwhelmed by fear.
With great difficulty, Jayadratha regained even a modicum of consciousness.

Then the goddess consoled him, and the mighty Mahādeva, having pacified Jayadratha, spoke these terrible words to those outside: [Note: The provided text contains two double-danda (।।) marks, indicating the end of a section or verse.]
Bhairava said:
"Excellent, O Goddess, O highly fortunate one, you who are saluted by all the lords of heroes! That you have indeed resolved upon this terrible and fearsome meditation is truly noble."
Excellent, O Lord of Sindhu, excellent! You who are a portion of me (the Supreme Being), you have not met with destruction while describing the true nature of the Goddess;
for, through the penetration of her grace, you have correctly perceived the future purpose.
"You are not lost; you have awakened, my son, and have been held by me here.
That goddess was not invoked by me, nor did I ascend to her station.
Now both of you have awakened simultaneously—what could be greater than this?"
Formerly, O fortunate one, when she resorted to a slight movement of her face out of desire, the entire circle of the Brahmāṇḍa then blazed up most fiercely,
and the head of Brahmā was struck down.
Having praised her again, O Subhagā, I have related [this] to you only in part;
indeed, it was not told in its entirety out of fear, O Daughter of the Mountain.
Today, however, it is told to you exactly as it is from within the Tantra.
Indeed, with a form that is perfectly tranquil and not agitated, O slender-waisted lady,
you two highly fortunate ones have clearly and safely emerged from this most terrible and wondrous crisis for the world.
Their enemy is the most terrible Mahāghorā, the fearsome Kālarātrī;
she is the wandering ascetic, the deluder, the beloved, who resorts to loud laughter.
She is the illustrious Mistress of the Terrible Face, who dwells within the heart of Aghora;
she is unrestrained by the heart-mantra of that color, bowed down by hundreds of great Mothers,
resembling a black kālāli bird, and like the throat of Śiva.
With teeth as hard as the fangs of a lion, adorned with various small bells and anklets,
with wheels revolving like those of a lion-king, and possessing the beauty of pendulous breasts and genitals;
with the sun and moon as ear-ornaments, and wearing a garland of ten million skulls.
She holds a skull-bowl in her hand, possesses beautiful arms, and has a face blazing with fire.
She is the bearer of hundreds of various wonders and the manifestation of various marvels.
She is the mistress of desires and various intentions, and her body is composed of various mantras and weapons.
The thirty-two supreme heart-mantras are the support for ten million vidyās;
they are the mother of accomplishment for the female messengers (dūtīs) and the bestower of the foremost siddhis for the heroes (vīras).
Abounding in the wheels of Kula and Śaṅkula, they grant the siddhi of the heroic sky-farers (vīrakhecarīs).

She is indeed the most supreme among all beings, the family deity of the families; she is remembered as the Queen of the Kings of Wheels (*cakrarājñī*) among wheels, and the Mother (*mātṛkā*) among yantras; she is the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*) among the Bhairavas, and the Supreme among the Goddesses of Sacrifice (*yāgeśī*).

She is the great illusion of the Asuras, the violence of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas; she is the edge of the sword for heroes, and even among the gods, she is the shower of wealth. She is the personified form of rivers and the supreme thunderbolt of the clouds.
The great tide of the oceans, the loud roar of the *vetālas*,
the thirst that drives away the two-footed, and among all four-footed creatures,
[it is] the supreme anxiety of diseases; it is the fang of all fanged beings.
She is known as Svāhā among the millions of gods, and as Svadhā among the ancestors;
she is known as Sudhā among all the nāgas, and as Oṣadhī among seeds;
she is the secret of mantra-sciences, and among yogins she is known as Dhāraṇā.
The Gāyatrī is the supreme crest-jewel of all meters and of the sacrificial fires;
she is indeed the Viśvarūpā among the Rudras and the Karṇamoḍhā among the hosts of Maruts.
Vārāhī is remembered as belonging to the Pitṛs; Lambikā is known as belonging to the Sādhya-s; she who is called Siddhā belongs to all the Siddha-s; Jayā is remembered among the Dvipada-s;
Kuṇḍamukhī belongs to the Ucchuṣma-s; and Kaumārī belongs to the Bālamātṛ-s.
Indeed, the power of Indra is remembered as that of all weapons; the power of Agni is remembered as that of the Vasus.
The power of Yama is remembered as that of the Kinkaras, and the power of Nirṛti as that of all Rākṣasas. That of Varuṇa belongs to the oceans, and that of Vāyu even to the Dānavas.
For the Rakṣasas, she is declared to be Dhanadā; for the Rudras, she is remembered as Saumikā.
For the Guhyakas, she is Īśānī; Gaurī is [the goddess] among all the Gaṇas.
For the planets, she is declared to be Bhāskarī; Śuklā is [the goddess] of all the Soma-drinkers.
Vaināyakī is indeed the [goddess] of the Daityas; Bhujagāśanī is that of the female messengers (dūtīs); she who is called Nidrā is that of all serpents; Mausulā is remembered as that of the Nāgas;
Carmamuṇḍā is that of the Bhairavas; and Bhadrakālī is the mistress of the progenitors (prajeśvarā).
She is Śivādūtī to the messengers, Kālarātrī to those who move toward destruction;
she is indeed the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) of the seasons and the sovereign of the Cintāmaṇi jewel and the treasures;
she is Nārāyaṇī among the lords of the immortals and Vaiṣṇavī among the Ādityas.
She is the night of the celestial maidens, Sāvitrī of all ascetics,
the twilight of the seven sages, and the sovereign goddess of rivers and mountains.
She is known as Nārasiṃhī among the lords of lineages, and as the mace of the masters of the discus.
In the Kula, Mahāmāyā is the mistress of the Śākinīs and the sovereign of the powers of yoga;
she is the radiance of the mantra-vidyās and the supreme beloved of the Kāminīs.
She is the crest-power (śikhā-śakti) in the Brahma-dhruva, and Sarasvatī in the jīva-cakra.

She is the intellect of all beings— including gods, asuras, and humans— and when these [beings] are withdrawn, she is known as Mārī. Thus, she is the family deity of the sciences of mantra, the scriptures, and the weapons.
She exists as the pervader of all Mothers;
her pervasion within one's own body has been proclaimed, and it is now being proclaimed once more.
O Goddess of the Suras, pervaded by which one attains perfect accomplishment:
having meditated upon the support of the play (vilādhāra), one should hold the mouth of the sound;
having comfortably reached the excellent void, one should enter the pure digit of the channel.
The end of the resonance of the *kalā* is the upward-moving syllable within;
it is the support of the channel of phonemes, the enclosure of the syllables of the support.
It is the resonance of the half-lotus of the enclosure, the *Rāvaṇa* [sound] by means of the rays of the fourth state.
By means of the rays and the wind-channel, one reaches the mantra [located] in the lotus-garland.
The garland, having entered the wind-sustenance, becomes composed of fire.
Then, the blazing [mantra], consecrated by the eye and joined together, is beyond the intellect.

Having thoroughly ignited the supreme *mahādi*, she blazes as the Great Imperishable (*mahākṣara*). Above the imperishable is the Great Canal (*mahānālī*), and within that canal is the imperishable again. Furthermore, the one called *punarnākhyā* is the Great Plague (*mahāmārī*), who speaks of the splendor of the movement of the Plague (*mārīcāraśrī*).
"Joined with *juṣam*, it is to be applied in the wheel of pervasion (*vyāpticakra*) through the splendor of the syllables of Mārī.
Thus has the supreme sovereignty of the Goddess of Destruction and Pervasion been described.
Having heard this, the Queen of the Gods and King Jayadratha [listened].
Having prostrated themselves upon the earth again and again,
and having repeatedly gratified the God with various kinds of hymns, they spoke once more to the Lord of the gods, the Sovereign of all, the Supreme Lord.
The Goddess said:
"By your grace, O Goddess, I have been rescued through the vision of your meditation;
even King Jayadratha has become utterly bewildered."
"O Lord of the World, by your grace, I have regained my consciousness and am no longer lost.

Thus [ends the passage] in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra (*Mahātantra*), within the *Bhairavasrotas* stream, the *Vidyāpīṭha*, the section on the Severing of the Head (*Śiraccheda*), in the third hexad (*Tṛtīya-ṣaṭka*).
The fifth chapter on Pervasion.
Having heard about pervasion, the goddess, the sovereign of the gods, having regained her composure,
the fortunate one again asked this supreme secret.
(The Goddess said:
"O All-pervading Lord, by your grace I have heard the entire secret;
yet, O Lord of the God of Gods, I have not heard of the proof and the sign."
O Blessed One, at the time of the extraction [of the mantra], the names of the goddesses were not heard by me; indeed, they were not heard at all.
O Blessed One, whose ornaments are the best of serpents, please tell me this.
Bhairava said:
Listen, for I shall declare a most wonderful secret that has not been told to anyone; that I shall now tell to you.
O Goddess, at the time of extraction, one should observe these signs of anxiety:
earthquakes, the shifting of lumps of earth, horripilation,
the cries of birds such as *siddhas*, and the arrival of unexpected wealth.
Each one [of these] is very far from the attainment of merit at the time of animal sacrifice:

those with liquor or wine in their hands; likewise, those with the Vedas and scriptures [in their hands]; or women with children in their hands, or those with disheveled hair and well-adorned with flowers.
Having set out for the sake of the celestial maiden, she who was adorned went at the very front. A Vaiśya woman skilled in the art of weaving followed, as did one holding a banner and an umbrella.
Chariots, elephants, and horses were there; for her, life itself would become nectar.
Curd, honey, sesame seeds, parched grain, ghee, dūrvā grass, and cow dung;
or one who is beloved by her husband, with flowers in her hand or in full bloom;
or one whose desire is for another, who delights in passion, who ends in passion, and whose speech is of passion.
The fulfillment of one's intentions, the face of desire, the face of reality, and the face of success—
these signs indeed manifest for the practitioner as previously described.
Those who possess auspicious marks are praised as bestowers of fruits both in this world and the next;
they are like those who grasp the lightning-bolt of knowledge, who seize the moon and the sun,
and who shatter the dark cloud of ignorance while remaining free from the rain of evil.
Those with extra limbs, those with missing limbs, the blind, the lame, and those afflicted with leprosy;
those carrying smoke, fire, or staffs in their hands; those wearing black garments;
those who are hostile, wicked, or deaf; and those who are base or four-footed [animals].
Those with broken horns like bull-fighters, those whose joints are dislocated, those harboring enmity, those devoid of affection or respect, those of contrary conduct, and the foul-mouthed—
avoiding these as one would sacred fires, one should recite the Śiva-mantra during the rite of atonement.
One should extract [the mantras] from the excrement of a bull, a cow, a cat, a rat, a *viḍvaroha*, a donkey, and a camel; likewise, by means of the incense known as *prāyaścitta* and the mantras,
[one should extract those mantras] beginning with a single syllable, consisting of either one or an odd number of letters, each separately.
The final [section] is said to consist of a full hundred [verses], with thirteen additional syllables.
Just as their names are specifically and individually distinct,
so shall I proclaim in their entirety all the names of the Vidyās in their proper order.
Mahāmārī, Brahmamārī, and likewise Kālarātri;
the supreme Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī, the other, Kālamekhalā;
Bhañjanī, Mohanī, and the exceedingly powerful Bhagnasthā.
Yogeśvarī, Parā, and another who is called Kharheṣikā;
likewise Jharjharī, Ḍhāḍhā, and Rudrarāveśvarī;
furthermore Karaṅkamukhī, and [Haṭu]tpalūṣikā.
Bhairaveśvarī is another, and likewise Ḍhakkāriṇī is supreme;
Vidyarājīśvarī is yet another, as is Ha(ḍa)bherūḍikā.
Another is Rākṣaseśvarī, and likewise another is Sarvottamā;
Mahāmāyā is yet another, and Parāvāgīśvarī is remembered as another;
Viśvakarmā is another, and likewise Viśvarūpā is another.
Likewise, there is Kuṇḍamukhī; another is Romarājeśvarī;
another is declared to be named Cāmuṇḍā; and another is Cintāmaṇī. Kālāntakṛntanī is Kṛtyā, and Kularājeśvarī is the supreme one.
Another is Jīvacakreśvarī, renowned as Viśvalakṣmī;
she is sometimes called Viśvamūrti and sometimes designated as Prakṛti.
Thus, through these various names, Mahāmārī is possessed of great power.
O beloved, I have proclaimed to you this [tantra] named Saṃkarṣiṇī;
hereafter, O Goddess, I shall explain in due order and according to the truth the determination of the limbs, which bestows the fruit of great accomplishment.
Having worshipped the *mātrikās* as before, but excluding the *prastāra*,
one should extract the vowels from the human skin and the leather of the dog;
[then] the disciple and the teacher, being greatly delighted, [should perform] the limbs (*aṅgas*) of the Goddess of the God of Gods.
O Agni, Lord of all vidyās, I remember the Praṇava and the Natis;
I remember Śiva, who is restrained by the Supreme Śiva and who stands at the forefront of Umā.
Having taken [the teaching] from the Great Lord of Yoga, I remember it before Vīranātha.
One situated in the center of the wheel should extract the Mahābhairava [mantra] in reverse order.
Then, from the sequence of Kālamukha, which is stepped upon by Kālāgnisūdana,
