the word "Khāhi" is joined in two ways, and the wheel is rotated in two ways by means of the offering.

In the word *bhojye*, one should abandon the fever (*jvara*); then, the syllable *mahi* is joined twice. Furthermore, after that, the syllable *aggre* is joined twice, followed by *avarma*. One should apply *ūhāruddham*.
Then, having joined *tarjanam* twice, one should recollect *mahocchuṣmāgra*.
(33b) Before the Lord of the Kirāta kings, the Lord of Granthi, situated at the tip of the junction,
should again recite from the midst of the fire with a drop perfumed by the supreme *hā-ha*.
With sword in hand, having extracted the mortar and entered the pestle,
he [took] the essence of the *śala* tree and the sacrificial animal from the seed-vessel; having extracted the binding,
he [performed it] in two ways, and then again as one through the mind and the face.
Furthermore, [the fire] Aparāmitatejas is at the tip; it is Agni, threefold again.
Having joined the triad of Bindu and Śakti, cause it to move and vibrate in two ways.
The pair of Jalpa and Hara, situated in the midst of Parameśvara, are twofold.
In the northeast are Rahas, Cānila, and Śakti; then, further north, are Caṇḍa and Ākha.
Likewise, there is Garjana and the Vyūha formation, along with Gaṇṭhīśa and Dvividha, each accompanied by Indu.
The first and the last two are the foremost messengers, unbearable due to their weapons at the middle and the beginning.
Thus, this heart-mantra known as the most auspicious (*śivatama*), which grants all desires, consists of one hundred and fifty syllables; one should apply it to the vessel-possessor (*pātrāveśinī*).
One should meditate upon the syllable *Oṃ* joined with *namas*, followed by "to the Blessed One, the foremost" (*bhagavate 'gryagaṃ*).
One should join the word *sadāśivāya* with the full [syllable] *pūrṇam*, and apply the short vowel.
One should extract the triad *īhyehi* ending in a short vowel, as well as *bhagavan*. Then again, one should join the short vowel to *brahmaśiva* and likewise to the *vaṣaṭ* syllable.
The long [vowel] has the syllable *oṃ* as its mouth and is indeed the supreme space (*parama-vyoma*).
It has the short space (*hrasva-vyoma*) as its body, and likewise [it is] the pervasive space (*vyāpin*). Likewise, it is the form of space and short, and everything is likewise pervasive.
It is incomparable and changeless, and likewise has a short finale;
it is joined with a short finale, for it is indeed the very state of Nidhana.
It is stainless and without appearance, the abode of the supreme state, and that is the Imperishable.
By the short [syllable], he is non-different, vigor, and the unique form without interval;
by the short [syllable] is the presence of all, as well as the abode of all.
Śiva and Niśūdana, Śiva and Satya are the two fixed syllables.
(34a) Short, the secret and the most secret, and dwelling in the cave itself—
I meditate upon him who rests upon the couch of Śeṣa at the forefront of the mass of Brahman, the True Brahman.
The Viśvedevas are the time of sleep; Bhava is distinct from Ālaya.
Bhava is the maker of Nirbhava, possessing another tone, joined with Dharmarāja.
By means of the vowel, Yajñapuruṣa is again the giver of the six sacrifices.
Brahmā and Śānti are distinct, and likewise Viśveśvara is distinct.
Nārāyaṇa and Viśvamukha, as well as Śānti and Atiśānti, are each distinct.
Avikāra (the Unchanging) is indeed distinct, while Prakṛti (Nature) and Vikāra (Modification) are distinct.
The Supreme is indeed the Great Beyond; by nature it is distinct from the end.
It is individually immeasurable and truly individually unstable.
It is conceived as having individual powers and paths, and likewise as having individual faces of emptiness.
The harshness within the harsh is distinct; the life-force of the great elements is distinct;
the indestructible protection is distinct, as is the eternal arising;
and the state of the Great Lord, which is not surpassed by heaven, is distinct.
At the end of *dhvanideśika* is *jīvasākṣiham*; *bhūjā* is separate.
*Mahādeva* and *sahasrākṣī* are each separate, as are the two vowels (*svarau*) at the end. At the end of *mahāparameśvara*, *sarvavāsapada* is separate.
Furthermore, the fruit of the tree of Vāsudeva’s knowledge is to be known as it truly is:
it possesses all flavors, yet it is distinct; it is a state of pure witness, distinct [from the objects witnessed];
indeed, it is the very state that is without beginning, middle, or end, and which culminates in the ultimate syllable (Svar).
Thus, the state of the vowels indeed bestows the supreme liberation.

Then, before the word "Bhāskara," the words "Agniṣoma" are placed separately. [The mantra continues with] "Be gracious," followed by the Supreme Self, the Sun, the syllable Om, and the Sustainer of Life.
Thus, there are three hundred and six syllables;
the head of the Goddess, which is the support for eighty-one words, is indeed unsurpassed.
Known by the name Brahmaśiras, it resides within the three-fold interval pervaded by Brahman.
By its constant practice, one is indeed liberated after six months.
The syllable *oṃ*, the power of Bhava, and the word for Caṇḍa—each on a separate lunar day.
O Goddess, thereafter one should recite *kapāliniḥ pratigṛhṇa devī jahā bījam*.
Then, one should recite *jagat ca prajvala ca eva hanti chinti* with the words separated;
and joined together, one should recite *hanti bhinti* twice again.
At the beginning of the text: *gṛhṇa moḍau ca jaṃbhi oṣṭambhi oṃ namaḥ*.
Then: *mohi ovaṃdhi opyevaṃ jaṃbhayaivaṃ* again and again.
Afterwards: *paramacaṇḍeti śīghram ānaya vai punaḥ*.

Furthermore, having joined the *pratoda* with the *savyūha*, and likewise the *mahocchūṣma* with the power of *bhava* followed by the salutation (*namaskāra*), one should restrain [the breath]. This seventy-seven-syllable *śikhā* of the Goddess is of great power.

One should always employ divine women for the purpose of subjugation, as well as a Naga maiden. Following the opinion of Bhimapani, there is the syllable *Uṃ*, the power of existence (*bhavaśakti*), and thereafter: "O Goddess, come, come! O Great Plague (*Mahāmārī*)! and what follows.
At the tip of the weapon (*astra*) is the deity; these two are placed twice.
With the *visarga*, it is the Lord of Knots (*granthīśa*); with the two expanded *jahas*, it is *Pharīmaṃ meghamāla mahāmāye*. This is the sequence.
Having extracted *māyeśvari*, one should extract the word *vidyut*.

One should give the three [syllables] beginning with *kaṭākṣa* and extract the three [syllables] beginning with *kṣapaya*. Then, having placed the word *udari* (in the secret place), one should establish the form of light (*bhāsvarūpa*).
One should utter "rūpeśvaryai te sacchaktivirūpe" before her;
then, with the face blazing, one should extract "caṇḍeśvari" while positioned in front.
In the street of the Void (śūnyavīthi), there is Ghoranāśa, and in front of him is Vīranāyaka.

With weapons in hand, she stands before him, threatening with the words, "I shall seize the house!"

One should place the syllable *dhā* at the forefront of the "Vajra-body" (*vajraśarīra*), and likewise the other, the Sovereign of the Wheel-King (*cakrarājeśvarī*), as the bearer of the earth (*bhū-bhṛt*). Furthermore, at the tip of the *nisvana*, there is a sound like a dark cloud breaking apart; thereafter, [one should place] that in front.
Having made two pairs of fists, one should again extend the index finger at their tips;
then the goad and the threatening gesture at the tip of the Bhīmāstra;
then the word "mukhi" at its tip, and then the word "hraṇḍa" at its tip.
Thus, one should remember the hundred and forty-three syllables in the rite of invocation for Viśvaiśvaryānātravara:
Vaitārī, situated between the true Śakti and the Vajra, is encased within the Bhīmā weapon.
The Kirāta [should utter] a great sound, and the three Caṇḍālas together;
having raised them up as they descend in two ways, one should remember the face of the invocation.
Bhaṇḍīratha should extract the excellent mass of the Kṣalaja.

Thus, one should visualize the face of Vajrasāra as fourfold; one should extract the pure Śakti situated at the tip of the mouth of Sarvāvarta. It should be stated that the two words "kalikāla" are to be dropped.
Having extracted the syllables for Vidhvaṃsanakarī in their proper sequence, one should join them with the syllable for Tarjanī; these six indeed abide as a vajra.
Having joined the first and last [syllables] in order, enriched by the bindu and the ākarṣa, one should apply them.
Then one should remember the syllable *A* at the end of the anus, as the knot within the heart.
It is joined to the seat of the Vajra-wind and restrained by the terrible weapon (*bhīmāstra*).
Thus is this formidable armor, ignited by the syllables of the twilight.
One should apply [the sequence] for the destruction of enemies and for the attainment of the subterranean and celestial realms:
having given three [units], one should proceed in two ways; then, having given three, the earth [unit] should be placed three times at the front.
One should remember the syllable *cakrāṃ*, extracted from the Lord of Kings (*rājeśvara*), as the foremost of great sounds.
Having placed the sound *rita* in two parts, one should add the syllables *roma*, *hala*, and *akṣara*. From the fire of the most fierce and wrathful one, the word *jvalat* is doubled.
One should thus heat it with fire in two ways, for one must indeed burn the body.
Having extracted [the essence] from the terrible practice, one should employ it in the most formidable rite;
having extracted it from the submarine fire (vāḍavāgni), one should again make it tranquil in two ways.
Blaze! Having thus extracted [the seed-syllable], one should indeed cause it to blaze forth.
Standing between wind and fire, one should meditate upon it enclosed within the power of the bindu. First are emptiness, water, fire, and wind; thereafter is the substance.
Having extracted [the mantra] with the sixteenth [syllable], one should join it with the supreme final [syllable].
Another messenger, having delivered [it], should extract the Kālāstra. Thus, this excellent weapon of the Goddess consists of eighty-eight syllables.

One should remember the most terrible [mantra] known as Aiṣīka, which destroys all evil ones. O Goddess, this has been declared by Vidyeśvarī according to the proper sequence for the determination of the limbs, bestowing the fruit of all accomplishments.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Limbs," in the *Trailokyāḍāmara* section of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, a great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses belonging to the third hexad of the *Śiraccheda* within the *Vidyāpīṭha* of the *Bhairava-srotas*.
The Goddess said:

"Therefore, O Maheśvara, Lord of the Gods and Sovereign of the Suras, explain from this point forward the worship that grants all desires, as well as the means of accomplishment for the Goddess of the God of Gods. Bhairava said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme worship of the Goddess,
performed in a solitary, secluded, and formidable place, such as a terrifying cremation ground;
or in a divine garden, at a confluence of rivers, or in an excellent temple of the gods.
(36a) Either on a famous lordly mountain or on the shore of the ocean,
in a most terrible empty house or in a divine temple of the Mothers.

Or, as in the case of bathing [the deity] at a *liṅga* and so forth in the courtyard of the temple, one should worship the God of Gods and the Goddess at night while staying in one's own home before that [image]. One should stand to the east of the Goddess and face the direction of Varuṇa (the west), which is not pleasant.
One should cleanse the cavity of the ground by means of three silver stakes, or having properly cast the triple *puṣkara* into a vessel empowered by the *hāhū* mantra; then,
having covered it in that same manner, one should raise up the temple of Śakti.
One cubit, two cubits, or even four or eight;
sixteen or thirty-two cubits, according to one's desire or as one pleases—
firm, sixfold, divine, and produced from a divine grove.
Having prepared a very smooth, perfectly level, and glossy thread,
one should draw [the design] in front with divine, even, pure powders, white, yellow, and red.
It should be square, with four gates, and adorned with bells and chowries.
One should draw a supreme temple, complete with a mirror, a parasol, and so forth, along with a railing and filled with various abundant flowers;
in its center, one should depict the deity and the abode of the deity, exactly as they appear.
I shall describe it thus, by omitting Mount Meru:
[it should be] shaped like a broken egg, with a face of flames and beautiful speech.
One should draw a trident in the center of that, beginning with the seven sprouts of the deity.
One should draw a wheel above the trident, with thirty-two spokes in its expanse;
resembling a fire that has consumed all wealth, it possesses the prowess for the destruction of worldly existence.
In the center of that, one should draw a wheel whose form is like the full moon.
O embodiment of the Kula, the vajra is similar to a nine-petaled lotus;
it has eight facets and possesses the brilliance of a blazing fire.
In the center of the peak of Kulabhairava, adorned by the Goddess,
and enriched by those who guard the syllable *dhruva*,
one should draw the external wheel of the sky (*vyomacakra*) of the distinct letter *ja*.
One should draw the city named Bhāskara, which is like the sky, circular and divine,
possessing the radiance of the sun at the edge of the firmament; it is filled with great heroes and has the form of eleven Rudras, resembling refined gold.
Then, outside of that, one should draw the circular city of Vāyu.
Outside of that, however, one should draw the Śakti of the form of the sky, possessing two eyes, two arms, and two faces,
who causes the house of Vāyu to whirl, together with her attendants.
Outside of that, Māyā is sevenfold, having an even form in cow’s milk;
she was previously proclaimed through various mantras originating from the Bhūcarya family.
She is present at the gates, as well as in the corners and the intermediate directions.
Having placed the *lokeśvarīs*, one should place the female messengers (*dūtīs*) and handmaidens (*kiṅkaras*).
Having first performed the casting of the thread (*sūtrapāta*) as before by the true teacher,
the bodies of reality (*tattvadeha*), characterized by all [the principles], should be deposited.
Having taken a human peg or even a golden peg,
one should draw the forms of the principles (tattvas) with silver or with the peg itself,
according to the tradition and separately for each distinction of the principles.
Listen, O Vīmi, to the arrangement at the end of the Jñānapīṭha:
Bhaiṣiṇī at the end of the Praṇava, and Preṣaka at the tip of the Astra;
having joined them according to rule, one should place them in seven ways.
Nārāyaṇī is at the central crest, while Saiḍphisūkarī is on the two sides;
Māheśvarī is the fourth, the mighty Śūlabhedī.
These are the family deities (kuladevatā) in order upon the upper, lower, and middle parts of the trident.
One should assign Brāhmī, Āgneyī, Raudrī, and the one known as Acyuṣmā.
Then, above the trident, there is a wheel with thirty-two radiant spokes.

One who knows [the mantra] should install it as consisting of the deity, conjoined with the thirty-two [phonemes]. Having extracted [the seed-syllable] along with its power (śakti), one should likewise remember Ghorabhīma.
Then, the fever [syllable] joined to the half of the heart [syllable], followed by the bindu, which is like a vajra.
In its own nature, it is equal to the jar (kalaśa), possessing a most beautiful form with many tigers;
indeed, it is terrifying, having half-arms joined by vigor in sequence.
All [the syllables] from the first joined with the seventh are preceded by the bindu.
In the fire of Cāndra is Nārāyaṇī; likewise in Bhīma is Sainhī,
and also Raudrī, as well as Saurī, Brāhmī whose form is fire,
the seventh Kularājeśī, Śaśāṅkī, and Mahābalā.
Devoid of roots, footless, and of noble lineage, they are five in number, each long and distinct.
Residing amidst the terrible weapons of Time, they are remembered as the thirty-two families:
Aṭṭahāsā, Harā, Harā, Śṛṅkhalī, and Madakoṭarā.
Haranā, Ādamaṇi, Bhadrā, Drāgini, Pilipiñchikā, Māṃsādarī, Matravasanā, and the eighth and fourteenth [days],
as well as the full moon, the new moon, Bharūdrī, and Khaṇḍamastakā.
Śivarātrī, Bhadrarātrī, Kularātrī, Vibhīṣaṇā;
Ṣaṣṭhī, Amararātrī, Jñānarātrī, Khaśekharā;
Vaṅkāśīvadravaktrā, Kṛttikā, and Kṛkilāsinī.
Vidyunmālā, Vidyunmukhā, Mahācchuṣmā, and Mahodarī—
these are indeed the Kula queens in sequence at the edge of the temple of the wheel.
They are the support for the nature of reality (tattva), crowded with thirty-two [deities] through ritual placements (nyāsa).
Jīvehavabrahmahī, Kāla, Srotīṣaṇātmaka, Tarjanī, Khecara, Mātribhūtā, and Svasaṃjñitā; Nṛsiṃhī, Bhairavānanda, Siṃhabhīma, and Uṭṭahāsaka.
(37b) Then Mārttaṇḍa, Vārāha, Śrīghoṇā, and Duṣṭavarṣaka;
these [are located] in the corners starting from the southeast, in successive order.

One should install the eight Bhairavas according to the distinction of their essential forms (*tattvarūpa*) at the ends of the [syllables] *ka*, *la*, *ḍu*, *śa*, *aṅka*, and *rā*. Then, one should again place the *praṇava* (OM) once.
Subsequently, the vowels (*mātrikās*) together with the *bindu* are to be installed, excluding the vowels *i*, *e*, *o*, and *au*.
And at the edge of the sky is Dhruva, and likewise again the Praṇava.
There are the Ṛṣis, the Vīrarudras, and the Yoginīs of various natures.
Those who are peaceful are indeed within the midst of the splendor, along with the neuter vowels beginning with the fifth.

One should install [the syllables] "varjitātraṃ," the other vowels, "yognaya" with the bindu, as well as "śamaiścāva," "niketaśca," "haro rudra," "haro bhṛmi," "nivaṃkurokṣa," and "śabda" in the eight suns of the heroes.
One should accomplish the wrath [mantra] by employing the vowels beginning with *s* (śa), excluding the neuter ones (*ṣa* and *sa*).
Having joined them, one should apply them to the *bindu* sequentially according to their order:
Hara, Kṛttivāsas, Viśveśa, and he who is indeed Rukma.
Aja, Paśupati, Śastra, as well as Nīlalohita,
Viśvādaka, Hari-hara, and Bhūtavigraha—
these are the eleven Rudras who constitute the body of the hundred Rudras.
One should always worship [her] on the forehead, she who is the support for ten million Rudras. Terrible like fire, yet uniquely peaceful, her form is the *bindu*;
joined with the fourth vowel, one should extract [the syllables] individually.
Lampaṭā, Vimalā, Krūrā, Kallaṭā, and Virūpinī;
Mahodarā, Mahākāyā, Vāyasī, and Śivakokilā;
Hariṇī, Hāriṇī, Bhadrā, Ucchuṣmā, and Cuṇḍacuṇḍikā.
Haṃseśvarī, Meghanādā, Duṣṭārādhyā, Gaṇeśvarī,
Dhūmrā, Kāpālinī, Kaṅkaṭā, and Madotkaṭā. (38a)
Kolāhalī, Ratnanābhā, and another, Ketumekhalā—
these are proclaimed as the twenty-eight Khecarīs at the end of the [twenty-eight] crores,
divided into groups of seven each, in the Śasyarddha Ocean of Milk.
One should worship [the goddess] Khecarī, who resides in the power (*śakti*) upon the support of various jewels;
she is liberated from fear itself and is likewise born of emission (*visarga*).
One should extract the two pairs in due order according to the rule.
Ṛṣabhā, Vihagā, Kaṅka, Kaṅkolī, Kālaśarvarī;
Visphārī, Nauṣā, Niṣṭhā, Mekhalā, Musalāyudhā;
Ulūkhalī, Paṅktibhujā, Bindujā, Vitpavitrakā.
Hala, hālā, khuvadanā, vitrāsīvṛṣadaṃśikā, sarasā, kakubhā, kūrmā, dantā, śarmā, jijakā,
kalūṣī, kalikailā, kaṃdalā, and sāgniśekharā.
Bhiṇḍera, Vicitrākṣa, Prayapa, Sṛgbhuja, Visphoṭāṃśī, Gaṇḍabhuja, Lohaliṅgā, Narottama, Devara, Śāviṣṭacīra, the goddess Meghā, and likewise Praṇī.
Meghamālā, Dṛḍhanakhā, Bhūyiṣṭhā, Bhūcarī, Kṣamā, Prabhāvatī, Bhadravatī, Karoṭī, Vīraśekharā, Śyāmā, Hayā, Śikhā, Rohī, Kakāṃśā, and Kākamekhalā.

The six mothers, who are composed of Śiva and consist of the nature of the higher principles (*tattva*), should indeed be worshipped in manifold ways by the disciple through the impulse of the Guru; they grant the desired objects for those who move upon the earth.
One should place Jvarapāṇīśa in a single way within the midst of the fire.
One should join [these] with the twelve vowels individually, together with the Bindu:
Kardama, Nahuṣa, Aparāvaṇa, Kālaśekhara, Dhūrjaṭi,
Viśvamūrti, Kakurda, and likewise Śivā.
Suśivā, Śivādūtī, and likewise Kāladūtī;
there are exactly four door-keepers and exactly four servants.
Indeed, at the corners of the temple and at all the separate doors,
having properly arranged them with one intervening space, the messengers (dūtīs) are placed at the middle doors;
[the goddesses] Madhyamā and Karabhī are positioned with the Astra-mantra in between, amidst the flames.
One should remember eighteen kinds of weapons in the eight directions, as if they were placed within a vessel:
the trident, the spear, the sword, the skull-topped staff, the noose, the mace, the skull-bowl, the thunderbolt, the lotus, the plow, the axe, and the mirror.
The conch, the discus, the bow, the banner, and likewise the sword;
the Vajra, the Pāśupata weapon, and the Pināka bow of exceeding splendor—
these seed-syllables of the weapons are situated in the center, adorned with the Māyā-vowel (ī) and the Bindu.
The weapon-mudrā is joined with the Mātṛ-mantra according to its numerical count.
One should apply the eight seed-syllables of the [vowel] groups to the three deities.
Joined with the *kāla* (visarga) and the *bindu*, one should contemplate the eight guardians of the world (*lokapālāṣṭaka*).
The Mātṛkā consists of eight groups and is endowed with the sixteenth [vowel].
One should extract it in sequence according to tradition, both collectively and individually.
[One should likewise extract] the planets, the stars, as well as the days, fortnights, months, and years.
The seasons, the months, number, time, and night;
the perfected ones (siddhas) such as Unmattabhairava, the vows and the secondary vows;
the yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, obstacles, and the guhyaka-servants.
The serpents, mountains, islands, rivers, and likewise the oceans— all these,
as well as those not explicitly mentioned and known as "mixtures" (saṃkara), consist of the Mātṛkās. Indeed,
from the weapons (astra) up to the mixtures, they are situated outside this square.
At the edge of the ocean of beauty, one should worship her who grants all desires;
she is Kālāstra, Kālaśakti, the one called Padā, and Dāhikā.
Then there are Pratodā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Khecarī, Vīranāyakā, Hayagrīvā, Siddhā, Raktā, Śuṣkā, Karotpalā,
Kālarātrī, Mahāmāyā, Saṃkhā, Aṣṭau, and Sahānidrakā.
The power called *mātrikā* is known as the object of perception (*grāhya*); that called *prāṇa* is designated as *ghora*.
Up to the end of my own power, there is the one called *guhya*, as well as the *mudrā* of great strength, Vikaṭā, Pañcavaktrā, and she whose face is like a lotus.
The fifth is named Ūrdhvaliṅgā, the great power of Mudreśvarī.
She is the true Śakti whose essence is one-faced; among those who are three-faced, she is the one to be grasped.
From her upward-facing aspect, she is known as Atighorā, whose nature consists of the Mātrikās.
For Viśvarūpā indeed [is worshipped] thus with the seed-syllables of the faces in their proper order; one should worship the entire [deity] in succession according to the rule among the incarnations,
together with the secret mudrās and [the syllables of] the navel of the wheel.
The practitioner of the lunar [mandala] should place the six limbs in sequence, starting from the eastern direction, at the end of the outer eight-petaled lotus,
at the edge of the inner path of the octagon,
joined with two digits (kalās).

Having thus previously established the divine ocean of mantras in the temple of the deity, one should then duly install the root-deity in the center of the eight-cornered *aṭṭahāsa* pavilion, each in their respective place.
One should meditate upon that which is explained as the *saṃkarī*, illuminated by the Egg of Brahmā (*vidyābrahmāṇḍa*),
its essential nature determined according to the injunctions of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*).
Listen, O sirs, as I proclaim the arrangement of this mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*).
Having the form of a blazing river, with a radiance equal to ten million suns;
adorned with various wonders and ornaments, shining with hundreds of diverse gold pieces;
wearing garments of various gold, and surpassing hundreds of golden moons.
Holding a golden lotus and a pitcher in her hands, with golden anklets jingling,
her hair adorned with a fresh parting-line, and her locks dark and curly.
The goddess has a very long braid as her refuge, a hundred-fold radiant golden garland,
teeth like those of a young goat, and a smiling face upon the earth.
With eyes and arms like a pair of yokes, she stands with a beautiful pearl necklace at her slender waist.
Sumavā by name, the essence of all principles, possessing the digits of the lotus and immortal youth,
should worship the deity on her left for the attainment of divine desires and fruits.
Mounted upon a great serpent, she is renowned as Aṭṭahāsa.
The father of the world, Bhairava, should be meditated upon by the Goddess on her right side;
he has ten heads and a hundred arms, is radiant with a thousand hoods,
holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and has a lotus for his seat and a sword for his footstool.
Indeed, [the goddesses] hold a garland, a lute, a club, a clap of the hands,
a trident, a bull, a lotus, a fruit, a water-pot, a noose, a flame, a spear, and a bow;
they carry a vessel of solar nectar, and the remaining nine possess the splendor of young jasmine flowers.
Indeed, O Earth, Śaṅkara manifested that [form] with nine eyes, possessing his own natural form,
appearing as both lion and boar, black, and with horses above; thus he is known as Aṭṭahāsa, the imperishable one whose supreme form is the universe.
Seated upon his throne, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns,
Bhairava, the Lord of Bhairavas, meditated while seated in the midst of the sacrifice.
In the midst of the glory of his boisterous laughter, the Great Radiance was not confounded.
The Goddess, whose body is the cosmic egg, stands upon a tiger in the ocean of the eight letters beginning with *varṇa*;
she is always to be meditated upon at the time of initiation, situated between Śrī and Bhairava.
She is likewise to be meditated upon during worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and the practice of union (*melaka*).
One should meditate separately upon Saṃkarṣaṇa and Aṭṭahāsaśrī individually.
The first three, the last three, and the fifth, eighth, tenth, and seventh;
Yuga, Kāluṣya, Viśvātman, and the thirteenth, Viśvarūpa.
The sixth [day] has four, nine, one, and two pairs;
Viśvarūpā consists of eight [days] preceded by one, three, and sixteen [days]. (40a)
The twenty-sixth [syllable] lasts for seven nights, while the first three belong to the triad beginning with Trivaktra;
the sixteenth belongs to Caturmukha, Amarendra, Śeṣa, and Yugas.
Having understood the unsurpassed syllable of Vidyā through such a division, [one should practice].
The Supreme Being (Sontamaḥ) is the primordial nature (prakṛti), while the various distinctions are the transformations (vikāra) described as differences.
Then, having meditated in this manner upon the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and the food offering (naivedya) in their proper sequence,
one should diligently unite them with the preceding mantras in order.
One should perform the smearing, the intersection of the lines, the inspection,
as well as the mounting of the pedestal, with the Netra-mantra. Likewise, the seizing, the inspection, and the entrance of the disciple [should be performed].
Padmanātha must perform atonement for embodied beings;

therefore, the purificatory rite (*pavitra*), the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) should be properly performed in sequence with the Heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*). The food offering (*naivedya*) should be performed with the Root-vidyā (*mūlavidyā*).
The offering of enjoyments is performed by Śiva alone, accompanied by the proclamation of the name and lineage,
according to the sequence of the purification of the paths (adhva-śuddhi), using the heart, head, and weapon mantras in their proper order,
with vessels made of black glass that take on various forms and modifications.
One should offer the food offering (naivedya), along with garlands, ointments, and ornaments.
Indeed, using a conch or a mother-of-pearl shell as the arghya vessel, there should likewise be a separate drinking vessel.
From that vessel, one should place four lamps made of ghee and wicks in the eight directions.
One should offer various kinds of meat, diverse drinks of many sorts, and lotuses with their stalks— both individually and collectively—
in manifold ways.
Numerous foods to be licked and sucked, and various kinds of solid foods; cakes, large quantities of clarified butter, and flower ornaments.
One should present all these offerings mixed with wine, meat, and blood.
Having thus worshipped the Goddess extensively at the end of her excellent pedestal,
one should then perform a circumambulation and offer oneself as well.
Then, above that,
the disciple— overwhelmed by the state of devotion and having fasted well— should enter there, clothed in a dyed garment, accompanied by the Lord of Teachers.
The silent hero, intent on meditation, [should enter] the abode of the Vīrācārya.
The disciple should sprinkle it with the weapon-mantra, and likewise separately with the heart and head mantras;
he should adorn it with flowers mixed together and fumigate it with ghee.
Furthermore, for the fashioning of the eyes, one should do so through another opening using a white cloth, or again, a yellow or black one; likewise,
[one should adorn it] with various flowers, gems, and excellent ornaments.
The disciple, facing either east or north, should have him cast a flower.
Upon whichever [deity] the divine flowers are seen to fall, he should then mark him with that name ending in *Śakti* and perform the fire-oblation (*homayet*) for him.
One should worship the deity individually with the garment of Agni and with [one's own] eyes,
according to the ritual of *madhuparka* and so forth, as desired and to one's satisfaction.
Together with the disciple and the preceptor, one should perform a circumambulation of the Goddess.
Afterwards, he should cause the pledges (samaya) to be heard according to the sequence for one who has received [initiation].
Having again performed a circumambulation, he should offer the sacrificial victim (paśu) there.
Then, with the arghya and madhuparka offerings, the disciple should worship the Goddess once more.

If someone, impelled by that [teaching], should become a guest out of devotion, he too should be accepted right there along with his disciples; what is greater than that? One who has not been born into the lineage, who is not a devotee, and whose conduct is wicked—[he is not to be accepted].
He who forcibly beholds the sacrifice perishes at that very moment.
Therefore, one must then maintain secrecy regarding the deity within the applications of the Vidyā.

For one who constantly possesses the hidden reality, all accomplishments are within the palm of the hand. That person who practices the worship of the God for seven days finds that worldly accomplishment, which grants the fulfillment of desires, has come into his hands.
He who worships for one month becomes dearer than even his own guru;
then, the disciple becomes eternally possessed—of this there is no doubt.
The second [type] is the practitioner (sādhaka), who, having attained perfection, may wander the earth like a Siddha.
In the third [birth], he shall become a universal monarch (cakravartin), the lord of the lords of kings;
in the fourth, [he attains] the enjoyments of the asuras; in the fifth, those of the guhyakas;
in the sixth, the sovereignty over the hosts (gaṇas); and in the seventh, he shall become equal to the moon.

In the eighth [stage], he becomes equal to Brahmā, possessing terrible prowess; in the ninth, he is like Kadrū; and in the tenth, he possesses a universal form. When the eleventh sacrifice is performed, he indeed becomes a mantra-adept who acts as a creator.
In the twelfth [year], the practitioner goes to the auspicious abode of the Lord.
When the mantra-practitioner has attained dissolution into the Lord through the sacrifice of the Vidyā,
he is then liberated from all bonds and attains the unsurpassed state.
Thus, after this offering of flowers has been performed by the wise Lord of Teachers for the first time with the disciples, he should afterwards lead them to the fire-sanctuary,
located on the southern side of the sacrificial ground, or to the east, or to the northeast.

Then the teacher and the disciples should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) for all the deities. Having offered more than a hundred oblations for each mantra to those whose bodies consist of various principles (tattvas), they should subsequently purify the disciple by means of the *tripuṣkara* [mantra].
Having prepared the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and consecrated the fire (jātavedas),
the disciple, being disciplined, should thoroughly purify the path of the egg (aṇḍādhvan). Then,
from the well-distributed heart and the ends of the feet, he should separately [visualize] that which is characterized by the syllable OṂ.
Having performed the first hundred [oblations] with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*, one should offer [the oblation] to Brahmā-Śiva.
Then follows the purification of impurity, the burning of the bonds (*pāśa*), and the cleansing of the eight primary [principles].
The cutting of the topknot, the burning of the bonds, and likewise the proclamation of the Kula;
the application of the lineage name and especially the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi).
[These involve] the paths of Kalā, Māyā, and Niyati, as well as Prakṛti and the paths of Puruṣa.
Just as the path is joined with the gross and subtle paths by means of the worlds-path,
so too one should further join the city situated on the path of Īśvara.
Thus, through this intermediate yoga, one proceeds gradually from the lower to the highest.

When the pure mantras of the path of reality have been mastered through ritual practice, one should proceed to the imperishable syllable. Thus enjoined by the Guru, the disciple—whose girdle is the sacred sound—should not be given the consecration; rather, it must be bestowed on the eighteenth day.
Totaka resides within the fragments; Śakti has a body composed of fragments.
She may be made of seven grains or even of sandalwood.
All of them bear a single form within the splendor of the Aṭṭahāsa [temple].
The universal form [is worshipped] with the previously mentioned divine lotus, well-adorned with the elements and seed-syllables, according to the prescribed sequence of ritual movements;
it is filled with the divine waters of various sacred fords and exquisitely perfumed with diverse fragrances.
One should well-adorn the dwelling with one or many flowers,
fumigate it with many incenses, and likewise perfume it thoroughly with fragrances.
Having thus prepared the excellent jar, one should face the intermediate direction during the sacrifice.
One should consecrate the water-pot with various excellent, divine mantras.
Thus, having joined this water consisting of knowledge with the form of Śiva,
it should be poured eight times upon the heads of the divine [deities] as well as the disciple.
And the preceptor who has received initiation, like Utko Viśvamekhalā,

having then worshipped [the deity], the Guru who bestows the command (ājñā) shall grant permission once more. Having thus obtained permission, he should then perform the sacrifice according to the prescribed rite.
(42a) Having performed the sacrifice in the midst of the excellent waves of the ritual, one should then begin the recitation (*japya*).
This is the supreme vow known as "the Madman" (*unmatta*), which arises when one is overcome by passion.

Having performed the sacrifice for a full year, one should then arrange the ritual offering. Alternatively, [the altar] is rich in the form of the earth, subject to various transformations, supported from below by the earth and other elements, and adorned within with various flowers and cloths.
Her face was radiant with eyes like those of a cakravāka bird in flight;
she possessed two eyes on her even (pair of) breasts, while on her uneven (breasts) she had but one eye.
Just as all [beings] are supported by the Āsuri-cakra, so too were the Daityas and Dānavas supported by her.
Furthermore, having seen [the deity] with four faces, or six, eight, or ten faces—
whether with two faces from the front and back, or otherwise—
with all [these forms] joined together, he is terrifying with two eyes.
Thus is the vow named Udbhūtaka, which strides through the three worlds.
For the Unmattakas likewise possess various forms, fierce and excellent;
they are heroes bearing clubs and spears, and their hair is always loose and disheveled.
The reciter, Maunī (or Ḍhaṇṭa),
who is devoted to the form of the deity, should first place the deities at the edge of the cloth according to their respective forms;
then, together with the jar, he should previously recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times.
Having prepared the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and sesame seeds with Puṣkara and the other ingredients,
one should offer a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) from that vessel, accompanied by the two mantras beginning with "jñāne" and ending with "dvāntābhyām.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should perform the sacrifice again according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having offered eight thousand oblations of clarified butter, one should employ the three rites.
Having performed this, the practitioner of mantra should constantly recite [the mantra] while offering oblations according to his capacity at the three Puṣkaras;
by doing so, he shall always bring his own body under control.
On the surface of the cloth, the excellent mantra, devoted to the proper ritual practice,
shall accomplish all the siddhis for the practitioner who applies it according to the sequence.

Endowed with a hundred *kalās*, one should first recite [the mantra] one million times. Thus ends the seventh chapter, concerning the procedure for the sacrifice and other rites in the *Trailokyadāmara-cakra*, within the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the *Siraccheda* in the *Vidyāpīṭha* of the *Bhairava-srotas*.
Bhairava said:
Therefore listen well, O beloved one, to the siddhis honored by all the gods; I shall proclaim those that are most excellent, arranged in ascending order.
The three [mantras] beginning with Tripuṣkara, along with the previous vessel and the deceased,
instantly bring about peace that crushes all malevolent planets.
One should offer eight thousand oblations according to the method prescribed for the Puṣkara-ādhya.
Through the power of the great sacrificial fire-offering, the practitioner shall accomplish his desired goal.
And by means of the oil of the great *reṇḍa* plant from the Asura region, along with *abhireṇḍana*,
he shall bring to life the Daityas and thousands of Rākṣasīs.
The maiden from the eastern marsh is indeed the *mūlāvidyā* (root-ignorance) in its encapsulated form (*saṃpuṭā*).
She nourishes the father and son within seven days, O Lord, without hesitation.
And the encapsulation of the *vidyā* should be written with the aforementioned substances and with the sprouts of the *emā* plant.
Having intensely agitated the lords of the gods through a thousand oblations,
he remains absorbed in the initiation within the midst of the sacrifice, following the inner reality of knowledge;
situated within the row of skulls, he should draw [the mandala] with the color worthy of worship.
For by this constant protection, one is liberated from all mortality;
one attains victory in battle, having conquered even the gods and asuras.
These very [deities], situated within the vessel, perform the sacrifice and the subsequent libation.
Remaining there, or having entered [the body], the maiden speaks everything. Likewise, situated within the wheel, the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), the lamp of space, the stone, and the fire,
she herself speaks of the three worlds, abiding between the forehead and the thumb.
(43a) Thus, through the differentiation of karma, the characteristics of the entire collection of sūtras are well-expounded; listen as I proclaim them to you in that same manner.
O limb, when one has meditated upon the Lord of Universal Form, renowned as the Five-Faced One,
entirely within the garment according to the procedure taught in the sacred tradition,
one should perform the recitation (japa) before him; that is the most excellent of vows regarding reality.
The heroines proceed by means of the *vīrāsana* posture; they live according to celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Or else, through the commonality of power (*śakti*), they regard a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal.
Established in truth, in their proper place, and in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), they obtain the fruit at the time of eating.
Having understood that Akṣamālā is indeed the very form of Śakti, born from the sprout of power (śaktikandala),
one should always and constantly remember her as such.
Through meditations, with the rosary, in fire-offerings (homa), in recitation (japa), bathing, and libations (tarpaṇa).
One should indeed practice with certainty and resolve in this manner day and night. Through the vow and the Lord of Vows, the practitioner should conduct himself exactly as prescribed;
thus, by means of play, he attains everything that is desired.
One who has undertaken the Kūṣmāṇḍa vow shall obtain thousands of worldly accomplishments and hundreds of heroic powers within six months;
or, devoted to the Taptakṛcchra penance for six months, one may subsist on barley-gruel (yāvaka).
Or, conjoined with the waxing moon, the practitioner may attain the other world.

Having prepared one hundred palas of the fourfold caste [substances], consuming one hundred palas at a time, the mantra-practitioner subsists on heated cow’s urine and does not eat until the end of the mandala.
Likewise, by offering blue lotuses with the triad beginning with *Pūjyarāja*,
and having offered divine *kṣetrapāla* yantras in many ways,
as well as ten thousand blue lotuses with honey, he directly beholds the messenger (*dūtī*).
A woman who gazes thus is either a female friend, a maiden, or a beloved servant; or else she is half of that [in intensity], being a *piśācī*, a *yakṣiṇī*, or a *kinnarī*.
Or an *āsurī* woman, one lacking feet, or a daughter of a *gaṇa* may take [the offering].
Having offered eight thousand oblations at the end of the powerful, the hair, the field, and fire, one pacifies excessive rain; indeed, drought brings forth fruits.
By means of the *śma* mantra, one indeed [subdues] showers of stones, clouds, winds, and lightning;
by means of blood, showers of blood and mountain-lightning [are likewise subdued].
By the mere sight [of it], the masses of clouds [are destroyed]; by touch, the yakṣas and rākṣasas.

One who knows the mantras slays Daityas, Dānavas, and Pannagas with ease. Having offered oblations from cow-dung, *śiṃśapa* wood, and *nyagrodha* wood— avoiding the *vaḍa* tree— and having worshipped with the *tripuṣkara* formula, one shall obtain the daughter spoken of by Agni.

Dwelling on a mountain in a cremation ground, he performed his recitation for another year. In the eastern direction, at the site of Indra, he offered oblations with a thunderbolt; at Tripuṣkara, he remained disciplined under a *bibhītaka* tree, proclaiming the principles (*tattva*) through the splendors of Brahman.
Then, having recited [the mantra] eight hundred thousand times at night, the practitioner will constantly see a Brahmarākṣasa named Bhukkurupiṇḍākṣa.
Through the power of his prowess, the practitioner shall attain divinity.
Then, being thus naked, adorned with ashes, and possessing the *arjana* [flower],
one should recite the mantra ten million times while offering oblations at the three lotuses (*tripuṣkara*) with a hundred *pala* [of fuel] according to the previously mentioned supreme number.
Through the power of knowledge, valor, and daring, the practitioner of mantra attains the status of the Lord of Devas;
by means of heated cow’s urine,
the practitioner of mantra obtains abundant desires and agitates the three worlds, attaining his every wish in full measure.

The minister, wearing rudrākṣa beads and a deerskin, seated upon a seat of antelope hide, ate only what came at the proper time, engaged in great austerity with self-restraint. Terrifying all beings, he recited the mantra sixteen lakhs of times.
Having prepared a well-cooked offering of abundant sesame, lotus stalks, and half of a half-pala,
the best of mantras, joined with the splendor of the center, should worship the cloth with flowers.
Having thus manifested the goddesses of Fortune from the midst of the fire as witnesses, one becomes truly happy.
Enjoying the pleasures of the wealth being enjoyed, one may live as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure;
thereafter, one attains the form of the Lord, which is the refuge of the Great Māyā.
As before, for the sake of the couple, he should cause ten lakhs of modakas to be prepared in the proper sequence;
having offered oblations of sesame seeds measuring a jujube fruit (*badarīphala*) according to the five-limbed ritual, he should offer them.

In another great sacred field (*mahākṣetra*), the mantra-practitioner, having properly smeared Mount Utpala with *tripuṣkara*, should perform more than ten million recitations of the Vidyā at the Kṛttikā forest. With his face smeared [with ashes], he should worship Halabhūṣaṇa.
The proud one, whose support is Bhairava, should worship the supreme bearer of the razor’s edge with the flower of power (śaktipuṣpa) within the cloth of the fire of reality (tattvāgneya).
As before, he whose self is the bilva fruit should recite the mantra for the seat of Rāvaṇa.
But by its own nature, it is the self of its own nature, the self of its cultivation through non-duality with the Self.
It is the Lord of Serpents, the root of the two worlds, the root of the root, the beautiful casket;
it is the support for the receptacle of sexual union, yet it is also the very essence of sexual union itself.

With his mind withdrawn from all objects, with his consciousness fixed on the state of being, and as a self-awakened knower of himself, he is joined in yoga with his soul disciplined; honoring the truth, he should always recite the mantra.
Indeed, like rain at the end of time, he experiences the fruit impelled by Time.
Then the practitioner, taking alms-food, milk, ghee, water, or even other things day and night,
while his mind is focused on Aṭṭahāsaka,
the Lord of Heroes himself beholds him as he is being honored by both [deities] in the void.
By means of the measure of the corresponding lunar day, or through the power of yogic capacity,
the practitioner, together with the deity, shall go to the Lord at the end of time.
[This is] endowed with the five.
(44b) The recitation, the Cāndrāyaṇa fast, and the installation upon the cloth [should be performed] one hundred thousand times;
on the Tripuṣkara mountain and the Utpala mountain, it should be joined with the Parvati rite.
Having offered one hundred and fifty thousand oblations together, one becomes an enjoyer of the purpose of the ritual application.
Having fashioned a sword made of human iron from the materials of battle,
one should seize both the Pallava and Parvata mountains along with this entire world.
Having first prepared a sacrificial seat (viṣṭara) with those two [substances] along with sesame seeds,
and having offered one hundred thousand oblations according to the prescribed rule, one becomes a lord of the earth.
Having thus taken up a sword and offered oblations, he becomes the subduer of the roar of the battle-drum.
Having offered the oblation, one should utter the *uccāraṇa* of the *vibhītaka-gaṅkāta*. Then,
from the midst of the fire, the form of the Yakṣa emerges according to the wealth [of the practitioner],
appearing like a flower upon the head of the lord of adepts (*sādhakendra*).
Having thus cut the base and tip of the foot, as well as the other [parts] of the Nyagrodha and Śiṃśapā trees,
and having brought them under the control of the Brahmarākṣasa, one should likewise fashion the two earth-digging tools (bhūmīdīraka) from the heartwood of the Palāśa tree,
joined with Parvatila.
Having fashioned an upper cloth from a sword, one should perform half a hundred thousand oblations at night.
Then, the most terrible Kṛtyā, along with the wives of Siddhas,
Vidyādharas, Nāgas, Asuras, and forest-dwellers, shall come under the control of the practitioner.
Having gone to the abode of the Naga and taken sesame seeds and lotuses, one should combine mustard seeds with rock salt and [anoint] them with nectar. Then,
while observing the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, one should remain facing southward with eyes fixed in anger.
One of great renown should offer one hundred thousand oblations into the Kravyāda fire while reciting the mantra.
Then, he should meditate upon the blazing fire as being consecrated by the Śakti-rope,
which is accompanied by smoke and is known to be of the nature of the supreme self.
Standing in the center of the wheel consisting of the letter *M*, one should pierce the three channels with the trident.
Having the breath as its support, the wind enters the channel that carries the universe;
having filled it from the two wings of the channels, one reaches the ocean of existence.
Having seen the ocean of existence, they were swallowed by it; then, beholding the nectar-water of omniscience,
they opened their own eyes and abandoned that which is terrifying due to the sound of non-existence.
The hero should take the *ḍhaṇḍhara* (a type of vessel) while being served food by messengers amidst great sounds;
then, having taken the sword— the portion for the deity— and the crest of the cloth,
he should enter the waterless abode of the Nāgas very slowly.
Then, from her own home, the Naga maiden of the lord of the best of serpents brought forth for Giriśa mercury,
a sword of alchemy, sandals of great majesty,
a garland, a lute, a drum, seeds, and likewise a supreme jewel.
Or, having confiscated all his property, he should banish him from his own place.
The practitioner, joined by excellent maidens, should proceed with the piercing [of the channels].
He shall dwell eternally under the control of the abode of the Nāgas, as long as the sun, moon, and stars endure.
Having recited the mantra over a clod of earth either by name or without naming it, one should throw it into another womb.
In this way, the Nāgas accomplish their desired aims using conch shells and other objects;
they are joined with the infinite Vidyā, which completely restrains the openings of the internal channels.
The power of the intellect is the knower, and that is the power of consciousness;
one should recite the vidyā at midnight for more than a year as an intermediate practice.
Upon reaching the end of one's own inherent nature, one shines like the space of both.
Having seen it thus— resembling the rising sun, revolving like a water-wheel,

situated within the cave of the heart, and joined to the lotus of the spinal column (vahni-padma) with the brilliance of the submarine fire— one shall obtain the supernatural powers (guṇas) such as atomization (aṇimā).
The self emerges from the machine, possessing the brilliance of blazing fire;
he is the trident with its tip pointing upward, the excellent wheel terrifying with its hundreds of spokes,
emitting thousands of various flames, and having a splendor equal to a mountain of gold.
Capable of bearing a thousand thunderbolts and formidable with hundreds of garlands of lightning,
whether you charge against the enemy army or against the strength of a rival elephant,
you are like a great cloud belonging to the Lord of a Thousand Lightnings.
(45b) Or, having meditated upon [the deity] on the head of those with fangs, one becomes a bestower of peace. Furthermore, there are garlands, ointments, food, and facial collyrium.
He for whom there is cultivation [of the practice] after having given his very name—
whether it be recitation or the support of sexual union— is a practitioner of the lower support.
Having smelled the scent of blood, he destroys his beloved in an instant.
Having performed the sacrifice at night, those sovereigns of the wheel of the Saṃvarta [fire] meditate upon [the deity] dwelling within the cave of the heart; revolving like a water-wheel,
they possess the form of quivering flames of fire, radiant with the flashing weapons of knowledge.
For by the power of the universe, the Universal Self is ignited as the syllable *Vāṃ* within the central channel;
situated at the top of the channel of the trident, like a stinging insect at the tip of the neck,
it is thus employed externally to strike the Egg of Brahmā.
Having meditated upon the sky as before, one should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds mixed with lotuses in due order; then, having performed the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) in sequence,
when this has been done, there, in the midst of the forest, for the practitioner—
The circle of the Wheel of the Mistress of Yoga (Yogeśī) exists directly within the Goddess.
Having seen the wheel of the Mistress of Yoga, he who should worship it in due order—
with his mind fixed on that and his thoughts absorbed in that mantra— shall become the lord of the Khecarīs.
Having offered the previously mentioned substances into a bronze fire-pit before the image of the Victorious One (Ajinastha) during the eight months of the great fields,
one should observe a monthly fast, consuming eight morsels of food increased by one each month.
Having bowed, one should constantly mutter [the mantra] directed toward Jātavedas,
until the fire of the sky, rising above the resonance of the bell,
is joined with the pillar that is the foundation of the science of sound.
With his face turned downward, he steadied himself like a revolving jar or a wheel of a chariot;
then, by his own strength, he released the fire.
Causing the worlds and the nether regions to whirl with the three thousand-fold crackling flames,

he should sustain [the practice] and fill the void of his own sky with the resonance of the joined sounds. Then, one should again meditate upon that very form, with two arms and a face, [holding] two discs.
In this way, one should summon those with two legs and those with four legs—
women of the *raṇasiddhas*, *yakṣas*, *kanyās*, *nāgas*, and *vidyādharas*. Likewise, goddesses and celestial nymphs (*apsaras*) come to the practitioner of their own accord.
Thus, within the eight-fold enclosure of the fires, one should know the complete set of the eight Bhairavas. All around, there is a blazing mass of flames, with an external lotus-seat,
terrifying with various hollows of fire, weapons, and the Bhairavas of the peaks.
One should perceive the blazing circle of the moon, a consciousness that breathes forth with sound;
having drawn up the moon and sun from the splendor of the upward-pointing flame of the fire of the *arccis*,
one should bring them down by means of the power of the internal radiance of the trees.
Bring also Deveṃdradayitā, as well as the daughter of the King of Serpents;
bring Suradayitā, who possesses the great splendor of the primordial Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara),
and likewise Lakṣaṇā, Kalāsāra, Sakala, Āśrita, and Akṣara.
The mantra proceeds beyond death until the dissolution of all beings (ābhūtasaṃplava).
O Vrajaśiras, the twilight [mantra] likewise [proceeds] to the fire of the eight [directions] and the northern fire;
release it upward into the fire of the discus, and downward into the thunderbolt and the mortar.
The immensely powerful one stood at the beginning and end of the *dhamadham* sound, and in a state of agitation,
he whirled the mass of the world-creation like a ball on a stick.
Then, [the goddess] whose form was visible and invisible, possessing great wealth such as victory and the like, [appeared].

The treasures known as Nanda and Padma come to the practitioner’s house when one has fashioned a rosary from *śrīphala* fruits and placed it upon the seat of the Abode of Śrī. For one desiring enjoyment, the great *Mahāvidyā* of the *Śrīsampuṭa* [is attained] through the most excellent *śrīphala* fruits.
(46b) He performed six hundred thousand rites based on the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Having offered one lakh oblations at Sāgratripuṣkara, he was thereafter established in the sound of glory.
Then, from the midst of the fire, the Mistress of Vidya, the supreme refuge, together with Suśrī, appeared simultaneously;
the practitioners beheld her directly. From that time forth, he became the son of Śrī, a lord of various jewels and wealth.

The practitioner enjoys enjoyments until the dissolution of all offerings. (In front, indeed, with the Vadhanaṃsena mantra,) having applied the immobilization (*stambhana*) within the *vidyā* and the *brahmaśikhā*, [he places] the nectar of the fragments at the end of the palate.

The practitioner, having himself experienced it, should direct his own stream [of breath] through the left nostril, not upwards, as it enters the cave; he should listen with half an ear to that which is situated within the midst of the great laughter of Śrī,
between the two palates and the entire interior above.
Through the two channels, Iḍā and Suṣumnā, the girdle of sound rises upward;

and like the sound of the half-syllable *Sa*, one should exhale with the hundredfold radiance. Filling the abode of the elements, one should contemplate the imperishable syllable within the path of sound.
Having indeed reached the hair-pores through the immortality of both the seen and the unseen,
she becomes the supreme Sarasvatī as if through aesthetic unity;
as the Mistress of Knowledge within the essence of sound, she rises up entirely and transcendentally.
Having joined the *iḍā* and *suṣumnā* together with Aṭṭahāsa and Śrī, one should—
having placed the four *kalās* (along with the half-measure of *tāla*, which consists of the nature of the new moon)—
unify them and pierce through the Vidyā within the interior of the *visarga*.
With the *prāṇa* and *apāna* as the two gatekeepers and *samāna* as the minister of meditation,
one should pierce through with the *udāna* and remain equal [in mind] for a period of time, contemplating [the goal].
By means of this yoga of practice, having meditated for a year or more—
The practitioner who possesses the *piṇḍa* mantra floats as far as the state of Sadāśiva;
indeed, he attains that very state of Sadāśiva, which is of the nature of Śiva.
Having uttered *sat-śivā* and proceeded to the syllable *bhūta-śivā*,
one should thus meditate upon the *sahṛdaya* and practice the vow previously described.
Having abandoned the sacrifice at the hundred thousand *tripuṣkaras*, one should thereafter extract it.
Having performed the supreme divine sacrifice, one should first offer sweetmeats (*modaka*).

Having mentally resolved upon the previously mentioned numbers, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*), having reached the edge of the sacred field (*kṣetra*), should meditate with the prescribed lotuses, accompanied by the *savi- -bha* and *akṣata* offerings.
At the conclusion, before the eight musical instruments and the like, upon a sacrificial seat made of well-crafted wood,
in front of the clothed image as described, the couple— performing the sacrifice, radiant with splendor, and possessing abundant prosperity— worship the Lord of the World.
Having reached that state,

he partook of the nectar from the mouth of the Lord, which flowed like a downpour of rain from the elephant-faced god; it resounded through thousands of streams as it rose upward, forming an archway for the couple.
Likewise, seated upon a grass mat, possessing a radiance like the form of nectar,
one who subsists on water-alms, fruits, roots, or ghee should meditate for up to a full year upon [the deity] while consuming only grain-particles, water, grass, wind, and so forth.

Then, through the attainment of *saṃskāra*, the practitioner directly beholds Śiva himself as Tuṣṭi, possessing a body of loud laughter (*aṭṭahāsa*). Just as [the deity] exists within, so too is there the manifestation of the form externally.
One attains equality with its form, or else one abandons my own form.
Having thus performed the ritual application, one should perceive that which is called the Four-Faced [Wheel].
One should accomplish the Wheel of Pairs, known as the Three-Faced, precisely in due order.
Having correctly understood the specific characteristics through the particular oral tradition of the teacher,
Vīrendra, who had entered a void-well, attained happiness while practicing.
That wheel known as Ekavaktra is the destroyer of all worldly wheels.
Indeed, I shall proclaim the characteristics of all the lineages according to their general and specific features, as they truly are. (47b)

In the Great Kalpa, Mahāmāyā is indeed the characteristic that extends to the very end of all things. Having bathed well with both [types of] vows, the Lord of Heroes (Vīrendra), whose charioteer is Śakti, subsisting on alms,
should recite eight hundred thousand [times] before the Prākyaṭa [mantra].
Having performed one hundred thousand recitations on Mount Tripuṣkara according to the previously mentioned procedure,
the practitioner of mantras should offer a quarter of that number as oblations while consuming [the substance] as prescribed.
Divine dust, mixed with a pala of poison and black mustard seeds, [is used].
Having thoroughly mixed [the ingredients] with great ghee and the three oils derived from mustard seeds, one performs the rite of *udbhramaṇa* (causing flight) with a thousand [recitations],
while *bhojana* (feeding/enjoying) is performed with double that number.
Likewise, there are the rites of *staṃbhana* (paralysis), *mohana* (delusion), *kīlana* (pinning), and *bhedana* (splitting).
One should not contemplate killing as having three qualities, nor likewise attraction;
sealing is performed by means of a sixfold yoga, and sealing is likewise [performed].
Or else, the practitioner who has performed the sacrifice should perform the mental [sealing] with the heart-mantra.
From the tip of the staff of power (*śaktidaṇḍa*), the wheel should proceed to the family of the Yogīśvarīs.
Having offered the *argha* to one's own Śakti (filled with the form of the *argha* for the Śakti),
one enters the house of the Yoginīs— the end of the cloth, the form of Māri.
Then that Siddhayogeśī, having seen the preeminent practitioner,
should take his flowers with her own flowers and,
having extracted them, certainly unite them with the nectar from the joined vessel.
Therefore, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the Yoginī, acting as the agent of confusion,
utters the sounds *phaḍ*, *phe*, *phar*, and *ṛ* from the cavity of the sky.
The practitioner, joined with the Śakti, proceeds toward the group of those who are to be grasped.
In that divine, supreme world, having eaten nectar according to his desire by means of his own power, Śaktisārathi shall go to the supreme state of Śiva. (48a)
Or rather, one should grasp [the vessel] while supporting it with the power of Śiva;
indeed, while performing the worship of the *argha* offering for Śakti, one should place the seat of Śakti upon the peak of Śakti.
By means of the yoga of Śakti, one should join one's own seat through the yoga of Śakti.

One should mutter [the mantra] until death, the supreme time; then, by his will, one goes to Śiva. Seated to the left of the eight powers of Śiva, I, subject to the principles (tattva), categories (kalā), and powers (śakti), uttered the emission of the manifest (sakala-udgāra).
Having tied a lion’s tail,
hairy at the tip, around his neck, he should offer incense at the fire of Śiva at night with a lamp;
for the body [of the drum] should be made resonant by Śaṅkarī, and not merely sweet-sounding.
As he sings the Uttara [Sāman] while seated upon the upward-pointing crest of the cloth,
the practitioner forcibly beholds the divine, direct lineage of yogis.
He gains mastery over the formidable Brahma-protector of the Universal Lamb.
Having seen [the deity], one should mark [the disciple] with the *śakti*; for him, one should remove the flowers.

Having joined the *puṣpāñjali-yoga* at the head, one shall obtain the desired [result]. Having completed the excellent sacrifice within the temple of the interior of the primordial syllable (*ādyarṇa*), [one attains success].

Having written the name within a female skull (strīkapāla) using lotuses, one should then place [the syllables] in the fire, the sesame seeds, the sky, and the end of the mantra; thereafter, the protective spell (vidyā) becomes applied,
and one is liberated from all calamities.
One who goes playfully toward the city of the king of serpents shall reduce it to dust;
in the battle between the gods and the asuras, the Avadhūta shall obtain victory.
Likewise, at the end of the guardians of death, one should draw [the deity] with lightning and weapons.
When the moon and sun have risen, one should worship with all the persons [present].
One should worship with the flower of Śakti and incense it with the previously prepared incense.
One should recite the body-mantra of the Goddess in a loud, resonant, and melodious voice.
The deity, having indeed entered the body of Śakti very gradually,
lets out a lion’s roar and exhales forcefully from the crown of the head.
One should worship again with the limbs of Śakti, with various incenses and liquors,
with various hymns and shouts of victory, and with various auspicious flowers and fruits; one should worship with garlands while crushing [the obstacles], and indeed with the Piṇḍadhātrī.
When this has been performed, the Goddess, residing within the mass of power (*śaktipiṇḍa*),
speaks of the events of the three ages and reveals the circle of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍamaṇḍala*).
Like one situated in a dream, she speaks of that which is born from the multitude of all lineages (*sarvakula*).

The Lord of the Skull (Muṇḍeśa) speaks everything that has entered the heart when the sword is at the end of the thumb in the sky of the heart, and when the lamp and so forth have entered the vessel; likewise, he speaks when the mace has entered the eye,
or when [the gesture] has been extracted by the movement of the monkey.
Having fixed the speech within the *kīka* (the palate), one speaks everything residing in the heart;
that which is in the heart [is expressed] by the tip of the palate, reaching as far as the crest of the form of Time (*kālamūrti*).
Having beheld all that within the cave of the heart, the practitioner obtains his desired goal.
The Vidyā that penetrates the beginning and end of the heart resides in the heart as the Lord of the Heart.
United with the syllable *yuṃ*, having the appearance of the sun, and fixed within the form of *ma* for a limited duration,
one should recite it at night with self-restraint, [the tongue] reaching the palate like a water-pot.
Bound by the subtle power (*kalā*) at one's own palate, firm as a water-pot during the retention of breath (*kumbhaka*),
and having seen it wandering through time, one should purify its abode in the heart. When joined with that, one attains true being (*sadbhāva*) and, by will, ascends through the sky.
Thus, with the mind fixed on the palate, having perceived the interval between the Kalās at the end of the Earth-element,
one should bind there the entire syllable along with its Kalā.
They drink away various diseases in many ways [with the sounds] *hu* and *go*.
Because the intellect and mind are unshakeable, one does not fall under the power of death.
Thus, like the moon with its digits fixed upon the tip of a stake,
wherever it undergoes waning, there indeed is that waning perceived.
The Brahman is the destruction of the Brahman, yet he is the bearer of the burden within the heart;
like the root of water at its sweet summit, the thread of Brahman is the Virāj-tree.
Even while she is passing through the spring season, one should contemplate her as being like a chariot wheel.
Having seized him with anger at every point on the potter’s wheel by means of a thread from the region of the heart, she should breathe out until the very end of the heart.
Brahmāṇī, from the root of Brahman down to the soles of the feet and up to the crown of the head,
draws the entire collection of sense organs toward the possessor of attributes by means of the attribute itself.
Having seen his own self established by its own lamp, a mortal shall go beyond death.
Then, having thus made himself fully compliant, he dwells within the great city of Brahman;
emitting a powerful roar like that of the enemy-destroying arrow,
he— whose support is the nectar of the digits— resounds with the syllables of the heart within the heart.

Having applied [this] here, the master of mantras, the lord of knowledge, shall go beyond death. Having repeatedly drawn [the breath] according to each respective *tantra*, he reaches the end of that;
[he reaches] the limit of the principle of Brahman (*brahmatattva*), from the root to the tip, the Lord of the Parts (*avakaleśvara*).

One who is incomplete should be bound with a digit (kalā), and one who is half-equipped should be bound without [the full] equipment. Having released [the breath], one should withdraw everything—the semen, the physical body, and life itself.
And thus, having established the earthly mandala from the root of the elements, [one proceeds].
One who is overcome by anger and joy, or is arrogant,
[should see] a buffalo in a copper casket on the road at a washerman's yard;
a cheek [ornament] enclosed in a bronze casket, or a sword in a golden casket.
Thus, indeed, the Śaṅkvaṣṭaka was proclaimed of old by all the Āgamas;
it was given to me at the beginning by the Supreme Self, Śiva, who was pleased.
Through this very knowledge as it has been described, there is the application of the various ritual procedures.
Intoxicated by the sacrificial cake of a mortal, he rushes toward the state of Bhairava through his audacity;
[this occurs] in the joints of one who practices equanimity toward cold and heat.

Facing away from the other [directions], one should proceed with the water in the jar (*kumbhāmbu*), having established the directions through one's own utterance; being the self of the reality of *sattva* rooted in the heart, and skilled in the four paths,
one should worship that fourfold self within it.
Bound by the heart to the heart, and girt with the upward-tending *kalā*,
having brought down that *kalā* to its root, one should contemplate me— who pervade the four paths from root to root— as consisting of all *kalās*, well-observed through the limbs of *kalā*.
The whole has attained the parts, and the whole is of the nature of the parts;
then the one who knows the lute perceives the Self as having that very nature, its own inherent being.
The Swan, having traversed the lute... [enjoys it].
Having performed the movement and arrival of the wheel of one's own livelihood without deliberation,
having offered water for the feet and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite by means of the *śaṅku*,
[one offers] the sun of the empty destruction to the earth, the cow, and the bull...
Meditating upon that divine form of Mārivigraha situated upon the cloth-painting,
enriched by offerings, incense, and the *akṣagāma* [mantra], one should remain solitary during the night,
[worshipping] with *suṣanta*, *śakti*, and flowers— [the remainder of the verse is missing].
Then, even with great effort, one should not lead this lotus [of the disciple] away from the Lord of Yoga;
having praised him with the Heart-mantra (hṛdayāṅga), one should cause him to proceed along the path free from defects.
Then, within that vessel, [one should place] various... [items].
Beholding that terrible Puruṣa, who deludes both gods and asuras,

one should honor him with an offering of power (*śakty-argha*), having taken hold of the essence (*sattva*) with the mind. Then, having praised him with the *Hṛdaya* and other mantras, one should offer great incense.
Having worshipped [it], one with a spear in hand should cast it according to one's desire.
One should properly contemplate that auspicious [spear], which is remembered as the ripener of the essence of nectar,
until the end— [only] by means of that.
(50a) When the vessel made of spikes was pulled by a rope through its mouth,
Śakti, naked and seated upon three shaven heads, [acted].
One should appoint an attendant (*kiṅkara*) for the invocation;
having recited [the mantra] enriched by seven syllables, one who holds the command should issue the dispatch with two separate [mantras].
By means of the application of the ritual according to rule, there is the restraint of beings and gods.
Then, at that time— in that supreme [state]—
they enter into a single, undifferentiated absorption within that field; they do not possess wealth,
nor do they engage in any worldly transaction.
This very benefit was [bestowed] by him, who holds a *śakti* in his hand, for Śiva,
for the one whose womb is Śiva (*śivagarbha*), and for the Hero (*vīra*) from the most formidable [source].
And in this field (*kṣetra*), she is the deity of desire for the terrible *yoginīs*.
Having thus instructed [them]— [and they having] prepared the incense—
one should feed the Śakti in front [of oneself], while one calls oneself "Śiva.
Having eaten through the six lotuses in this manner, one is liberated again in the seventh.
The deities mentioned in the Kalpa [must] certainly go there in various ways;
likewise, having offered the *argha* and partaken of the *caru* in the prescribed order for those deities who have arrived, one should proceed with them by means of that [vessel].
Thus, she too goes toward the king of the eight stakes (as previously described).
Right here, this Bhairava-self, with his physical mass dissolved, shall become Śiva.
Having quickly demolished the eight stakes, he [should go] to the south of the wall of stakes.
Having attained the fourfold state, which is turned away from all lunar [defilements],
he dwells eternally in the cremation ground as the fire that consumes the oblation of the four paths.
With a trident and a skull-drum in his hands, he wanders through the city for the sake of alms.
Having quelled the tumult, the couple [the husband and wife] offered alms into the hollow of their joined bowls;
and Caṇḍikā, having uttered "May it be well!", said, "May the circle of the house be pleased."
Having spoken thus, one should dispatch [the mantra] there with the *bilva*, *ḍamaru*, and *susthana* [mudrās].
One should cause it to be dispatched loudly by the dispatchers, bearing the *ḍamaru* upon their heads.
"I am Bhairava, the King Śaṅku; Bhairavī is Śaṅkumālinī."
"I offer libations to the fire of the vital breath within the circle of the Yoginīs. While speaking thus, whatever one may give or eat there—
whether by means of a handful or according to the ritual rule— that should be considered as being offered together.
When this has been done, one should then see there the massed form of the *piṇḍa* within the space of the heart; having seen it, one should pierce the channels—
[piercing] the left, the right, the middle, and both the left and right sides.
King Kevalāntaśaṅku and his queen Padākhamucchvasa [possessed] a vessel of knowledge joined with the breath of joy;
the King of the World (Bhramarāja), having performed the ritual, [attained] the vessel of the mantra-mortar.

In the same way, King Kuśa brought Antī, who was wandering at will through Kālāṇḍaka and Vilambaka, together with her fire and her attendants; thus he made her his minister according to the prescribed rite,
she being endowed with consciousness.

Through valor, one should bring forth the wheel of yoginīs along with their attendants (kiṃkaras). Having offered them arghya according to desire and having recited the mantra ending with the crest-syllable (śikhottara),
he proceeds at will together with those four whose nature is Bhairava.
Bhairava is the one to be meditated upon by Bhairava; he is Bhairavī and his very self is Bhairava.
Having pierced through the terrifying Bhairava with the terrifying activity of Bhairavī, he stands as Bhairava amidst those terrified by fear, arising from the goad of Bhairava.
(51a) Being thoroughly mixed with the ghee of Bhairava, one thus becomes Bhairava;
having made the seat of the Sakala [deity] the essence of the four-part kalā.
Thus meditating upon Śiva above, one should pierce that enclosure.
Having entered into Śiva through Śiva-śakti, the Śakti [resides] within the essence of Śiva. Meditating inwardly upon the innermost [layer], one should behold the right and left [channels].
One should offer four oblations with the *suvi* mantra, ending with the *agnīṣoma* mantra.
Having offered with the central crest-mantra, one should extract the crest (*śikhā*) as the foremost of heroes.
With the extraction and the giving of oneself, one is "self-giving" (*svadānā*), and thus foremost among the foremost.
Having ascended beyond the fire, the crested one [the vital breath] takes the form of the tip of a lute;
behold the sun situated within the mass of the body, shattered by the three fires.
One should then direct the left and right [channels] through the bridge of the left.

Having caused successive absorption into the characteristics of the *kalala* and the *ekakāla*, one should direct the Lord of Life toward the sky-faced *sallakṣaṇa*. Having performed the internal ascent (*antaroha*), one should bind [the breath] with the thunderbolt-bond (*vajrabandha*).
At that very moment, the mortal attains the state of the immortal;
supported by the eight qualities, he lives the life of the Yoginī-kula. Enjoying the most excellent flavors at will, he proceeds to Śiva.
By means of the power of Śiva, one should oneself extract the abundant [essence] during the arising of the wheel of Vidyā.
The one who is deaf and mute to suffering should join [the self] to that which causes the cessation of Rāvaṇa;
[this occurs] incessantly through the sender, the sending, and the object sent by the true messenger.
The Yoginīs shall unite him with the sender, who is like a crest of fire.
Then, if she is one whose self is perfected through the simultaneous arising of Śiva and Śakti,
she should worship the Śakti within the wheel and proceed toward the face of the Hero.
Having given that incomparable stone to him, the practitioner should again make a request from the heart: "By means of his instruction, may the mantra-master attain the state of Bhairava.
(51b) By means of his instruction, the mantra-master shall attain the state of Bhairava.
Having uttered the syllable *hruṃ* over the lotus in the field [of the heart], one should summon the great-sounding [deity] into the fire that consumes raw flesh.
Then, for those who follow the mantra (*vidyā*), having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) once,
the mantra is enclosed within the heart-mantra in the radiant eight-spoked wheel.
