To Nābhi and Dhyāya belongs the Mistress of Knowledge (Vidyeśī), radiant with a multitude of vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
Between the two goddesses [is] the blazing [deity], resplendent with companions and servants.
One should worship that which resides within the earthly [element], revolving like a water-wheel (*kumbhacakra*).

Again, one should meditate upon the excellent city as if it were the revolving wheel of a wandering chariot. All the deities and the various guardians of the field (*kṣetrapāla*) arrive in manifold ways; having granted their desires according to the prescribed rite, they depart.
In that same way, one should meditate upon the Lord of the Assembly (Sambhramendra) as being like one's own self;
having joined him with the two Vidyeshvaris, one should worship the deity there in the Tantra,
along with the Kula deities and the Kula Bhairavas.

Having worshipped Saṃkariṣṇī, who dwells within the Dhruva-star and the path of the Sun, they subsequently rained down nectar from the center of the sound of the bell and lotus. [The practitioner] should request this supreme vow through external yoga... [of her].
Then, having conquered those two along with them, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) shall go to Śiva as Time (kāla).
Or, having performed the sacrifice in this manner above the opening of the cavity, he should contemplate it;
having burnt away the cavity, he should go for refuge.
Having offered twenty-five thousand oblations of guggulu resin mixed with mustard seeds and half-puṣkara flowers into the fire that crackles, hisses, and emits smoke,
[one enters] the interior of the chasm, which is heated by the fear of that fire.
Having entreated Vīranātha for his favor, the Daitya maidens go to the beautiful and enchanting surface of the earth; indeed,
the lord of practitioners, having taken up that knowledge which is fierce with the power of its splendor.
Having offered him a seat made of various wonderful jewels,
they indeed cause the consoler to drink a beverage equal to nectar.
Having experienced a bliss ten times greater than that of heaven, the practitioner,
mounted upon hundreds of various heroes, proceeds at will to Śiva.
Having joined [the disciple] with the channel of the *saṅkariṣṇī* in due order, he [proceeds].
Performing no ritual action whatsoever, one should become like Time itself;
having made [the victim] go head over heels, with his head severed by enemies from above and below,
one should join him [to the mantra] and recite the Vidyā after having prepared the complete seat.
Having uttered this incomparable sound, as long as it proceeds further and further until a mass of sparks (*khapiṇḍaka*) arises between the two, like fire and wind,
that which has arisen is the Self known as *bindu*; one should worship the internal earthen [element].
If one’s own self should also cause even that [state] to revolve toward Śiva—
the perfect one who is the source of all forms for the sake of the incomplete, who is free from duality, and who is the refuge of the full— then,
having drunk the nectar from the skull-cup, one shall proceed at will like Śiva himself.

The knowledge [of the mantra] consists of nine syllables beginning with *na* and ending with *ga*. One should remember it as being progressively higher than the nine gates. One should contemplate the upper wheel, consecrated by the mantra, resembling a full moon and blazing with light;
within the interior of that luminous space, one should contemplate the supreme space.
At that very moment, one floats in yoga; through that, one goes to the perfected state (*siddha*).
In the second [moment], the ninefold [group] likewise, together with the noble one, causes the wheel to expand.
Thus, for oneself and for another, at every door, he is the king of wheels.
Blazing with the fire of the two lineages and radiant with the splendor of the *kula*,
one should bring it to complete saturation by means of the mass of the *saṃkarī* [mudrā].
It possesses a belly like a hundred moons and is intense with hundreds upon hundreds of streams.
As he drinks the foremost of the lives of those to be accomplished, there is the destruction of his own self by himself;
for as many times as there are oblations, [the process occurs] from the lotus of the throat into the self within the self.
Having spent that many thousands of years, one shall go to the mouth of Śiva.
In this very manner, having restrained the self within the self by means of the third [vow],
one should meditate on the inner life-force within the wheel, supported by the full moon.
Ascending separately and individually toward the upper [edge], and further up to a hundred faces;
fallen upon the eight goads, intense with hundreds of falling streams,
one should collect it together like a chick with the sovereign discus, full of vigor.
One who is appointed should join the time [of practice] with the heart, feet, and arms raised;
indeed, with the two weapons, one should hold the trident in the middle of the burning [region], and the trident held all around.
Having bathed [the deity], one should draw it forth with morsels of food, and perform the drawing in various separate ways.
And in sequence, marrow, fat, hair, bone, sinew,

blood, skin, and flesh— these eightfold natural constituents are modifications of the senses; likewise, the state of being a bull is considered to have the form of a chariot or a jar through its various limbs.
She should bathe him, lead him away, and instruct him in all the secret sources [of the practice].
When this has been done, then within six months,
his memory will be gone, his mind sealed, and he will become submissive, like a horse.
Every six months they drink the supreme nectar.
Eating well according to their desire, they do not enter the state of Supreme Śiva;
rather, from the body of the king, they cross over to the excellent abode of Supreme Śiva.
In the fourth section, one should meditate on the divine heart-wheel as supreme,
throbbing with fire, liberating and bestowing grace upon the forms of those to be accomplished;
one should remember it as piercing [the heart] with the two previously mentioned wheels, like a wielder of weapons.
From those two, one should grasp the essence obtained by Śaṅkuśakti;
the tip of the power of the chariot-wheel and the horse should be grasped, and the bliss of power should resound.
Having worshipped with supreme bliss, one should exhale again with a gift.
Having joined the individual soul with power within, the practitioner of mantra becomes a traveler on his own path.
The five persons beginning with Forgiveness (Kṣamā) are the Vidyās; the ninth is the fifth [of the group].
The city of Prabhākṣmā and others exist separately,
having been joined with the splendor of the King of Kings from of old;
just as there is a distinction above the sky-canvas due to the differentiation of various forms.
Likewise,

as if for the sake of that purification, having lifted up the mass from the root of the well by means of the rope of power, which revolves in the form of a wheel and a pitcher, they drink the excellent extracted essence according to their desire, as if drinking from their own vessel.
One should remember [the deity] ending with the *sthala-bindu*, who has crossed over by means of the boat of peaceful knowledge (*śāntavidyā*).
Worshipping at the root of the tongue, which is surrounded by the threads of the bound soul (*paśu*),
one should again cause [the disciple] to grasp that which is joined together, according to the direction of one's own [spiritual] power.
Having become one who intoxicates with the honey of passion within the three worlds,
one should indeed contemplate the root of the goad.
Having sprinkled the very root of the self, it becomes the power that sustains the life of the object to be accomplished.
One who meditates for years, having thoroughly drunk [the essence], attains Śiva.

[He meditates on] the six flavors in the six channels, possessing the digits of twelve kalās. Having meditated on the six syllables at the tip of the nostrils, he touches the kuśa grass with his hand.
Having turned back at the portion of Caṇḍordhva, Śāntā, Vidyā, Ātman, and Māyā [are established];
Pratiṣṭhā indeed extends up to the end of Sūryā, comprising the configuration of twelve kalās.
Constantly situated between Rauva and Ūrddhva is the unbroken form of the Sadhya.
Having reached the lowest of the low path, one should [visualize] Soddhasa and Surodhaka;
indeed, one should kiss Atsalamukha in Revatī and Ucucuṃbaka in Dhūmaka.
Having agitated the secret dead [semen], one should contemplate it as having arrived through *pūraka* (inhalation).
One should remember that [the sign] with a stone-like face at its full extent as having its root and base like a thunderbolt;
or at the proper time, one should remember the tip of the hook and the single corner of the mind.
Thus, in the case of the Moon and Jupiter, [one should contemplate] the wheel that sustains life and the life-sustaining vitality.
The practitioner attains the power of moving through the sky; having overcome Time, he goes to Śiva.
In this very way, by means of the radiant wheel of power, which is imperishable and unshakeable.
The chariot-pole, struck by the wheel— [being] struck, it was pulled and dragged with force by the elephant,
which was trumpeting loudly like a jar of the lineage,
its breath hissing as it shook.
One should whirl [the vessel] with the *rathāṅga* [mudrā]—[according to the mantra]—and [perform] the collection.
Having grasped the *piṇḍa* and sprinkled it, one should contemplate Brahmā in the tip of the *iḍā*.
[One should contemplate him] in the throat, the heart, the navel, and the pair of *yoni*s.
Quickly joined with the seven oceans, one should grasp the wooden vessel (or the leaf-cup for a moment),
the soul that sustains life and approaches all the senses.
Having directed it, one should draw up the mass [of vital energy] rising from the tip of the *brahmanāḍī*.
On the seventh day of the new moon,
having brought a ball of meat for the sacrificial animal— knowing the ritual procedure for the pegs and lotuses— one should satisfy the three worlds, radiant with Vīrabhairava.

The minister [should proceed] further; he should move through the sky for half a *vicāra*. Having uttered the eight and nine [syllables] joined with the *saṃkara*, and having consecrated them together as a single mantra consisting of word and essence, he should contemplate the Śakti situated within the wheel (*cakra*).
She, blazing with the rising of the scriptures, [is] there the descent of Bhairava.
One should firmly hold the support, which has the base of the trident as its fixed foundation.
For she, the bestower of boons, consists of various jewels and is the sprinkling of nectar from the hollow of the throat.
With the brilliance of a blazing sky, that Suṣumnā entered the body;
bearing hundreds of rays of wind, it attained the momentum of a torrential stream,
resonant with upward surges and possessing a form like hundreds of meteors.
One should cause the destroyer of beings, who possesses all the senses, to waver with the terrible weapon;
then one should take up the half-black weapon from that [place] and the support.
Having abandoned the state of being a support for what is grasped, and having removed the inherent nature that dwells upon existence,
one should withdraw all the channels through inhalation and contemplate the Self. One should lead the essence of the tongue from its root-base into the interior of the whole.

Having brought that state of peace into the heart, one should meditate upon it with the nature of wisdom (*vidyā*). When liberation from cessation is attained, one should abandon the arising of whatever arises.
Having thus made this state of equal flavor within oneself, the sense-faculties indeed become inexhaustible.
When one who possesses the nature of mantra is engaged in practice, whether gathering [the materials] or performing a grand collection,
the practitioner may go to supreme death or, by his own will, proceed to the Lord. This is the ninth [chapter], concerning the ninefold knowledge of the words, according to the excellent vow.
Having joined [the breath] separately at each door, one should rotate the nine doors. Contemplating the mantra within the heart-lotus— the enclosure of the essence—
one should rotate all the doors while meditating upon the end of the dissolution.
And one should worship Jaḍa, and all [the others], with the last one named Mahāmārī;
likewise, the yogin [should worship] Saṃśmaśru, Maukṣiṇī, Kāla, and Caṇḍacaṇḍā within the mouth. Thus, by means of the differentiation of faces, [these are used] in all rites for the yogin.
Meditating upon her who mingles [all things], one may effortlessly obtain what is desired.
Thus, by meditating on her who mingles within the expanse of the heart, along with the cosmic egg and its girdle,
one shall indeed shatter all the doors.
Having stationed herself at each door, she indeed dwelt below;
having appointed the fire-mouthed [deities] and gazing upon the circle of the sky,
the four-faced Goddess again began to consume the sense-faculties.
By three [fires] and two [factors], it quickly digests at the end that which is consumed—
the fat, marrow, semen, and life-force— along with the excellent essence of the Brahmin's body.
Vāṅgirā resides within the stalk of the *śakti* at the gateway of the *suṣumṇā* in every way;
Jayantī is the sender, and she has entered the circle of the excellent door, the foremost among those to be sent,
having reached the lotus-calyx which transcends the nature of existence.
Having thus appointed [the mantra], one should again employ it with forms that are very gross and terrifying—
fearful, most dreadful, and contemplating its own essential nature. Whether possessing many faces or a single face, one should shake it like the gaping mouth of night.
Again and again, one should brandish the sacrificial animal's lump of flesh, repeatedly tossing it up.
Having bound the animal to a wooden post according to the previous method of binding the victim,
one, seated on one's own seat and having performed the ritual heating, should then recollect the Supreme with one-pointed mind.

Having joined the excellent deer, which is like the form of a cow, to the upper part of the self of the Lord, one should lead it according to the nature of existence; having placed the best of animals within the belly of knowledge, one should establish the foremost of the eldest in the north.
Having brought the Lord of the Piṇḍas from the divine world by means of his own support,
and having united with her whose mind is established in the *saṃkarīṣṇī* [state] and who has withdrawn her physical form,
one should indeed drink the nectar arisen from the serpent-lineage at the three junctions of the day together with the Śakti.
Having bound the sacrificial animal within the *jyeṣṭha* [channel] with the enclosure of the terrible weapon-mantra,

having restrained its movement with the triple noose and enveloped it with the attire of Kulabhairava, one should unite it within the realm of Rudra, which is encircled by the supreme source of the Kula.
Having deluded [the opponent] through intimidation, one should indeed conceal [them] with the *māyā-astra*.
Having concealed [them] according to one's will, one should then contemplate them by means of the power of existence (*bhava-śakti*).
Having sealed [them] with the *cakra-mudrā*, one should open the surface of the earth.
Having produced a transformation of form, joined with the ungraspable through the power of reality,
and having gathered the threefold nature of desire, one should proceed toward the essence and the non-path.
Having correctly perceived the sacrificial animal according to its characteristics as appropriate, the beast [becomes] a beast.
(55a) Even so, one should either deposit it as a whole or extract it;
for this is known as the extraction of the *piṇḍa* when performed in its entirety.
O sir, listen as I describe the manner in which that protection was stolen by you:
through the mouth, eyes, ears, nose, breath, wind, and semen;
and from the fat, marrow, vital seed, life-force, flesh, body hair, and blood.
The ligaments are the primary constituents, while the modifications are the lords;
thus, twenty-three [categories] are to be grasped by those who subsist on ether and life-force.
Their characteristics, however, consist in their sustenance according to the distinctions of the locations of the senses.
O, I shall declare in its entirety, according to the divisions and subdivisions of the principles (tattva),
[the piercing] with the Kālāstra weapon, with the eyes ignited by the Bhīma-śaṅku,
with the two Bhoja [weapons], the nose and ears, and with the true power (sacchakti) the region of the navel.
One should draw up the *apāna* wind by means of the *tarjanī* (index finger) and the *liṅga*, and through *rūhā* one should bring it forth.
By means of *tvayā* it is to be grasped, and this state of possession (*āveśya*) occurs through the power of *bhava*.
One should lead the marrow (*majjā*) by means of *vratodena*, and through *siddhi* one should collect the semen (*śukra*).
One should extract the marrow with *mātrī*, the flesh with *teṇa*, and the life-force (*jīva*) with *hayā*.
One should take the *rāsnā* with *aghoṣma* (or *bhīṣma*), the blood with *sarvaśakti*,
the collection of bones with *dohaka*, and the sinews with *mātriśakti*.
From the *āsuri* [plant], the *prakṛti* should be taken; from the *khecarī*, the sense organs (*indriyas*);
and all the limbs from the *brahmahā*. The marrow is brought forth by the power of intoxication from the *dhātara*, the *vrata*, the *udena*, the *majjā*, the *pītalā*, and likewise the *haritā*.
One should indeed apply the manifestation of the objects of the senses as very black;
one should apply the internal [manifestation] resembling the primary wind (*mukhyānila*) as entirely yellow.
The modifications (*vikāra*) are to be grasped as green, but for me, the supreme ones are indeed very black.
Indeed, with a wrathful appearance like the color of fire, he may likewise, according to his will,
bring about at his pleasure the augmentation of the sacrificial animal.
Just as one would prepare a vessel full of milk on the night of the full moon,
so too should one prepare the supreme great sacrificial animal dwelling in the world;
having consecrated it, one should forcibly summon the Vetāla into the house of the Vetāla.
Or, one should join the end with the seed-syllable of Vāmā; having worshipped the Lord of Paśus during the entry of the Kṛtyā, one obtains the fruit of the Kṛtyā.
Having offered lotus-balls (*puṣkara-modaka*) into the mouth of this very true Paśu...
Then, having drawn out the tongue with ten thousand [strokes], one should cut it.
Having quickly grasped that very [tongue], the practitioner who has performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and is devoted to the Vīra-vidyā shall become free from old age and death in this world.
That very [mantra], well-enclosed by the Vidyā of Śira-nātha,
one should join as desired with the Utpala and the Satya-puṣkara mantras. Having joined it with the Trimātṛkā and the five limbs, one should then apply the Kadumbhrama.
Having combined the creepers with guggulu and dates, one should cook them in this manner.
Thus, this excellent *pañcāmṛta* modaka, consisting of twenty-five ingredients, is the best for the consumption of the noble devotees at the conclusion of the sacrifice.

Then, having thus fed those two excellent Bhojakas, the great beast instantly regained its own herd, which resembled a massive mountain. Thus, he now sprinkles [the world] with wine and the water of Śiva.
Incensing the courtyard with incense, the animal indeed goes out in two ways;
having made a mass of flesh for the animal,
the Brahmarākṣasa named Ketupādapa emerges with a most terrifying roar.

By means of the *ketupāda* mantra, clarified butter, and the power of the *vidyā*, the practitioner, having enjoyed the three worlds for a very long time and having performed his duties, shall go to Śiva at the time of death.
Now, in this manner, there are the five [mantras] consisting of five limbs each: Khaḍga, Daṃṣṭrin, Naṭī, and Ṭiṭṭibha.
Then a black dog or a cat shall deprive him of his five limbs.
He is born as a cowherd dog, and there are four further [rebirths] among the lowest of outcasts.
One should collect an even number of seeds together with a corpse;
having joined them with the blood of the seed-sower, one should place them within the hollow of a woman’s skull,
bind them securely inside that vessel, and fumigate them with incense.

Having thus performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) for twenty-one days, or even for fifty days, in an empty house, a deserted well, or a place filled with austerity, while contemplating [the deity] (*skandavakā*), one should remain amidst the waters.
One should bind him with the body that is to be mixed, together with his own body.
At the three junctions of the day, one should recite the king of incantations one hundred and eight times.
One should worship the excellent vessel and cause it to increase through meditation alone.
Standing upon the fifth head, he whirled the entire interior of the universe with the four kings of the Śakti-cakra-śūla, arranged one above and below the other;
[he whirled it] with the vessel-shaped weapons of the gavākṛti type, which were sharp-edged like the tips of flames.
Filling the excellent well as he submerged the vessel in its center—
thus, by means of the ritual prescribed by rule over twelve months,
that Brahmarākṣasa, who was like a blazing fire at his birth, indeed fell.
Known as Niraṃdhaka, naked, and resplendent with fifty arms,
he is one hundred yojanas wide, one yojana long, and high;
possessing a thousand illusions, of a fierce nature, his weapons are rocks and trees.
He had four feet, a hundred mouths, deformed eyes, and a donkey’s bray;
he resembled a smoky fire, with smoke puffing from his mouth;
he was adorned with thousands of plow-shares and blazed with hundreds of lightning bolts.
With a face made terrible by fangs, filled with hundreds of various clouds,
enriched with thousands of various illusions, and armed with hundreds of various lightnings—
thus did that lord of the Brahma-rākṣasas appear before the mantra-practitioner who had performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Having formed this resolve, the foremost of practitioners should go to the abode of the celestial beings. Then, that bull among adepts, protected by the Brahma-rākṣasa, [proceeds].
Having conquered the three worlds by force, he exercises lordship over the gods;
having enjoyed the divine state of the triple heaven and having subdued the *brahmarākṣasa*,
the mantra-practitioner proceeds with ease to the supreme Sadāśiva.

Having worshipped Mahāmārī from the beginning of the crest-mantra (śikhā) to the end, she is indeed consumed for the sake of subjugation; O Śacī, she is brought under control in an instant. For clothing, collyrium, food and drink, fruits, roots, and ointments [are likewise employed].
By taking [the mantra] and applying it after reciting it correctly, one becomes submissive;

having caused the goer and the act of going to enter into union, one brings the universe under control. In the excellent seed-mantra of a thousand cows, there is liberation comparable to a supreme boon.

Having caused [the substance] to flow, one should bring about possession through the fruit of milk. The four [methods] known as *tarodhi*, *ardhasanna*, and so forth, are for the purpose of killing the enemy.
First, one should bind a seat made of a hundred *badhva* plants upon the chest.
When there is no non-contemplation and no error, that wandering of the mind does not go far.
By the upward stroke of the divine breath, one should expel it from the heart;
having gathered the vital breaths within oneself, one should contemplate the state of non-existence.
Meditating on the eight syllables above, one should offer three kinds of sacrificial animals.
Thus, having offered a hundred animals along with the crest-lock (*śikhā*),
the practitioner of mantras attains liberation after enjoying whatever pleasures he desires.
In this very way, the fruit of the ritual action as taught in the tradition is attained through the sequence alone;
indeed, it is perfected by uniting with the goddess Śikhā and by the power of Saṃkarī.
Just as one might strike with blue [pigment], one should cause [the opponent] to tremble with yellow.
One should attract with red [light], but cause hatred with yellow. One should kill with that which has the form of collyrium, and paralyze with smoke-colored [light].
The arrival of wealth occurs with gold-like [light], and nourishment with the luster of snow.
As previously described, that golden-hued [light] rises higher and higher like a golden mountain;
it has the form of a red lotus at one's own heart and is intense with hundreds of falling streams.
One should meditate on the goddess of golden luster as the limit of one's own intrinsic nature.
Thus, through the practice of six months, the practitioner of mantras becomes a manifest lord of the forest.
In this way, one's self becomes like a red lotus, possessing the brilliance of freshly ripened barley.
By means of the designation "Sāṃkariṣya," the form with its characteristic marks was revealed:
the golden-rayed [deity] with true delusion, possessing dots and hollows;
and the arrival of the floating [form] everywhere within one's own body in the shape of the deity.
One should contemplate [the deity] resembling the sky, intense with hundreds upon hundreds of streams [of nectar].

Having filled [the disciple], one whose self is the mantra of the target (sādhya) should always perform recitation while meditating. Performing in this manner according to the rule for the duration of a year, [one attains success].
Then the wise one attains [success] and becomes like Ośanas in person.
Furthermore, by the oblation of *śaryā*, he likewise becomes a master of collyrium (*añjana*).
Constantly reciting at night while meditating on the characteristic of the *mṛla* [mantra], he achieves this.
Having fasted according to the prescribed rule for a year during the waxing moon,
the knower of mantras shines upon this earth like the Lord of Speech himself;
he is like a water-pot on a tripod, with his own seat placed above and below in a joined enclosure.
Having heated milk until it resembles the moonlight and is like a collection of tears,
one should practice the Vidyā within a space of eight *aṅkuśas* inside the house, its form fully armored.
Having joined [the mantra], one should constantly recite it and offer oblations of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and sesame seeds.
Devoted to the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, or subsisting on fruits and roots,
the practitioner of mantra should now perform the recitation (*japa*) four times fifty thousand times.
He shall become a master of speech among all the gods in this world, appearing like Vācaspati himself.
And thus, through constant practice, one is liberated from all calamities;
all diseases perish, and one is not overcome by old age.
The Yoginīs, having attained the *melaka*, proceed to Śiva through their own purity.
O Lord, the mighty Saṃkariṣṇī, joined with the supreme eye,
formerly sat at the edge of the field of alms, devoted to her vow.
He should wander for alms, moving about while proclaiming his voice,
eating whatever is obtained without ever being satiated. He should use only three bowls, eat from a single bowl, and wear a garland made of bowls.

Having offered into the fire of the hundred flesh-eaters (śatakravyādāgni) oblations consisting of honey-mixture (madhuparka), the lotus of the king, and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta)— oblations placed in a vessel and joined with a vessel, deposited in a worthy recipient (satpātra) or a small vessel (pātrikā) at night— the vessel remains full.
Chanting the *sahavidyā* loudly and making a resonant sound,
one should instantly summon Aghora, the Lord of the Field (*kṣetrapāla*), who is seated upon a corpse.
Together with him, one should perform the sacrifice known as *śakti*.
There, one should sprinkle the sacrificial animal with the radiant *kulārāja* [mantra].
By that means, the application of the ritual procedure is performed correctly, beginning with the *argha* and ending with the flowers.
Having thus joined [the elements], one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the *mṛta* [mantra] itself.
Then, whatever activity of the family deity (kuladevatā) becomes directly manifest,
one should duly offer them the *arghya* and *pādya* according to the previous ritual arrangement.
Having joined the sacrificial victim (*paśu*) with the remainder, one should traverse the sky together with those [deities].
Having experienced the arrow of another age, one attains Śiva by will. Likewise,
[one attains him] beneath a *vibhītaka*, a *nyagrodha*, a milky tree,
a *bhīma* tree, beneath a *kiṃśuka*, or beneath a *vacana* or a *phalguna*.

Likewise, for one who performs this rite while standing on a mountain peak according to the procedure declared in the sacred tradition, offering an excellent animal for each [deity] until the conclusion of the application of his own power, he beholds the eight Bhairavas.
Endowed with yoga, one should wander together with them, and finally enter Śiva.
Thus, at the foot of a reed or *arjuna* tree, or at a crossroads in the lineage of the [spiritual] directions.
In the conflict between Tālārjuna and Aśmaka, or at Śūnyaliṅga,
the Śāktas, acting as directors of animal sacrifice, performed the rite of inciting enmity;
they beheld the heroic spirits within the splendor of those equal to the auspicious ones.
Thus enjoined by this specific ritual procedure, O noble-souled courtesan, recite [this mantra] to the Leader of Dharma; you shall attain all desires.
With clarified butter and milk, [offer oblations] into the fires at the steps of Bhīṣma and other [sacred sites].

Having offered a thousand oblations for half a month, one attains a lifespan of a kalpa here through the power of this [rite]. Likewise, by offering three hundred oblations each at the three junctions of the day and night for a month, O King, [the deity] is indeed summoned.
A Yakṣa, Piśāca, Gandharva, Nāga, Vidyādhara, or Apsaras—
drawn forth by the opening of the yoga-yoga— is brought within a month; indeed,
by means of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and guggulu, day and night, according to the prescribed number.
By means of those two, he brings forth a maiden; through them, he enjoys the worlds.
Observing vows, eloquent in yoga, and following the conduct of Bhīṣma, he indeed beholds the eleven Rudras at the end of the year, at the end of the month, and at the end of the day.

Thus, by means of the earth-walker (*bhūcarī*), one sees [the signs] in one month; by the sky-walker (*khecarī*), in six months. By the *saṃkulā* and from one's own family (*svakula*), one sees them when the year is complete.
Or else, after eight years, whether fallen or not fallen.
The *sāla* trees, possessing buds and subject to transformation, were touched by the stalks of the *sendriya* plants;
they were neither adorned nor anointed, and while the earth was not covered by men, it appeared as if it were.
In that great field (*mahākṣetra*), the king stood with his sword, facing eight times eight [enemies].
In the midst of that, one should extract the Śākta limb known as Viśvarūpa;
or else, one should worship Bhāskarākṣa during the Mahāyāmala sacrifice. Upon it, one should place fragrant flowers prepared in a great vessel.
One should offer flesh arising from the four wombs according to one's own number;
indeed, having sounded the conch with power, one should loudly utter the *vigraha* mantra.
One should perform the oblation while burning great incense, as previously prepared;
with the guardians of the directions, one should offer eight full oblations of great clarified butter.
Then, with the *tripuṣkara* mantra itself, one should offer all kinds of meat and the best of fruits.
One should offer ten thousand oblations (*homa*) for each of the world-protectors (*dikpāla*) in front;
and one hundred and more oblations behind for Vāruṇī.
Having joined Bhairava with Bhairavī and having assumed the form of Bhairava, [one should perform the rite].
One should whirl the Varṇabhairava mudrā along with Bhairava;
for while whirling it, one whirled the Bhairava of the Bhairava of the Year.
Having meditated thus upon the Bhairava who is to be known, Bhairavī surely beholds him.
Having thus seen [it] within, she suddenly let out a most terrifying roar as she crushed the supreme mountain Meru from the outside;
threatening the Supreme Lord, she blazed with hundreds of rising meteors.
Agitating the intellect of living beings and illuminating the vault of the sky,
Mahāmārī, Mahākālī, who causes great agitation and wears a girdle of serpents,
approaches the presence of the practitioner, accompanied by her female and male attendants.
Having seen her— who appeared like a multitude of monks, whose roar was like that of churning ocean-milk,
who blazed like hundreds of lightnings from the fire of the great kalpa,
and who stood upon half a seat— uttering a loud cry of "Vigraha," he prostrated himself.
Having generated one's own left limb, one should fill it with the two-fold tranquility arising therefrom,

together with lotuses and flowers gathered for the *argha* offering. In this manner, one should likewise perform the *argha*, the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) for Kālasaṃkariṣṇī.
Having engaged [the attendants] at length according to his desire and according to his capacity,
and having properly performed the offering together with the eight great sacrificial animals,
Mahāmārī— whose body is the cosmic egg and who causes all things to arise— became pleased.
Having grasped it, the practitioner [drinks] his own nectar-like [essence], which is like ambrosia;
or, by his own will, having attained the state of the Lord of the West, he may live for as long as he desires.
Whether by his own will or through the Great Plague (Mahāmārī), he attains supreme Śiva or Halāyudha. Having employed the weapon-mantra and recited it in his own home,
the practitioner, having enjoyed his desired object, attains Śiva even by his mere wish.
On a fierce day of the planet Mars, while wandering toward the south, west, or northwest,
one should take the seeds and the front cloth into the house;
then, having reached it, one should meditate according to the methods of the mantra, the gaṇas, and the āgamas.
Having joined and restrained [the breath], one should cause it to resound according to the previous method.
Having entered the interior cavity and reached the mouth of one's own banner (*svaketu*),
once entered, one brings that [object] under control at that very moment, as if in play.
Appointed by means of the *śaṅku-yoga*, he forcibly brings forth semen. Without grasping it, [he consumes] the entire circle of the phallus along with the impurity (*asurva*) and its residue;
having emerged from that cremation ground, he is liberated together with the crushing of that [residue].
Having drawn it forth and crossed over, he forcibly burns the excellent city of Sūryāgra,
which has been left behind, while the ocean is agitated; then, having brought it down with its face turned toward the earth,
he burns the form of Rudra through meditation and sports as he pleases.
In front of the soil from a field productive of that [desired object], from an anthill, or from a divine fruit,
one should have the head rubbed by those with deformed nails and hair.
One may worship the house at will and fumigate it with its excrement.
One should offer five hundred thousand oblations at night into the Kravyāda fire; indeed,
by performing this at the three junctions of the day for five days,
one brings even Devendra, together with his wife, under control through the power of the name, provided he has not yet reached five hundred years of age.
Having thus performed the rite of bathing— contemplated as arising from the three, two, and nine [syllables],
with the head [of the vessel] newly fashioned and devoid of the designation "eye"—
I am smeared by that act of bathing, seized by the wind and fire of the noble lady.
(59b) Having mastered the mantra Pilivāgaitha, one burns and torments an enemy in an instant by means of recitation at night; indeed,
the enemy becomes a great weapon [against oneself].
One should place pure molten tin (trapu) up to the edge of a leafless vessel.
Likewise, when [the mantra] is placed upon an *aśvattha*, *bilva*, *kiṃśuka*,
or *śalmali* leaf, it can paralyze, immobilize, delude, and cause one to wander.
Thus, surrounded by the Bhīṣma-tree with milk in his mouth,
he causes the mountain-like wife to tremble and whirl about.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should offer *kadru*, sour gruel, a king, a limb, sesame, and black [sesame].
One should propitiate the lords of treasures (*nidhipāla*) and the guardians of the fields (*kṣetrapāla*).
From the beginning— [starting from] Mount Vindhya— with mustard seeds together with sesame seeds,
one should propitiate the divine cavern (*vivara*), which yields tenfold qualities.
Then, having thus offered oblations three times with guggulu resin along with clarified butter,
a person should extract the power of the world of the nāgas together with a well-satisfied araṇi wood.
In the same manner, a person should likewise offer oblations with śapharī fish together with guggulu.
The minister, the manifest Lord of Speech himself, took pleasure in the *saṃnāyya* oblation from his own breast;
having joined it with the middle *saṃnājya* stream within the form of the Self-cow,
he directed it toward the three *puṣkaras*, meditating upon them as being like the Lord.
In the middle [of the practice], one should visualize the form of the deity as moving like a cow;
for a month, one should offer the first oblation to the gods on a mountain peak,
or else in the heart, or in a sword, or in a vessel containing water and a goad.
The Goddess Vidyeśī, who dwells in dreams, likewise proclaims the three worlds.

At night, in the temple of the Void as described by Haṭha, one should recite [the mantra] while assuming the lion-gesture (siṃhamudrā) at the mouth. O Guhyamātṛs, this is for the purpose of bringing [the deity] during the night.
With the milky sap of the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *vaśyā*, *nyagrodha*, and *kiṃśuka* trees,
one may summon yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and asuras for both husband and wife. (60a)

Thus, having offered the lords of the Vidyādharas and the Nāgas according to the prescribed ritual, she indeed brings them under her power by force at the end of the night. Bhairava, skilled in weapons and mantras, is devoted to the worship of Bhairavī.
Having performed the sacrifice, one should offer blood while fasting for a year;
standing at the forefront of the vow, one should remember the alms and proclaim it with a loud voice.
Having proclaimed it seven times, ending with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), the *vigrahālikā* [is completed].
Yoked and facing forward in the field, one should move like a well-sounding wind.
Having entered the sacrifice and the breaking of the fast, which are the essence of the form of the Lord,
one should worship the Triple Puṣkara, whether it be divided or even when not present.

He beholds all ten Rudras together with their families; indeed, half of that [merit] is obtained according to his desire through the refuge in the Name. By his will, having enjoyed pleasures in the world of Śiva, he shall go to Śiva.
When the *abhividyā* of one's own family deity is properly applied,
it attains all desired objects when employed with single-minded concentration according to one's wish.
Having first joined this one *vidyeśī* of the family, [one achieves the goal].

One should meditate on the wind element, having drawn it into one's own armpit, as it supports that enemy— who is equal to the daughter of the King of Mountains (Pārvatī), who bears the foremost weight upon the tip of his spear, and who is encircled by the wheel— at every point.
Having placed it at the front of the eldest of the ancestors, within the interior of one's own wheel,
one who has attained perfection through yoga may wear it for six months along with the *sapiṇḍa*; or,
like a performer in a crowded assembly, the officiating priest may wear even a single one according to his desire.
Established in the wheel of yoga, one should recite [the mantra] while facing upward toward the wheel of the stars;
there, at the tip of the path of the lion, one certainly attains true bliss through the six [senses].
Having yoked the self, which is to be accomplished through the path of the senses (*govīthi*), to the foremost path of yoga;
having joined the self as if it were the self itself, like a driver who draws [the chariot] toward the auspicious arising of fragrance at the top of the new vessel.
In this very way, having reached the portion of the night with the foremost of the elders facing forward,
one should indeed worship the vessel of men by means of the king of yogas.
Now, the mortal body itself is the chain known as Kṛttikā.
Placing the practitioner upon his shoulder, he carries him wherever he desires in an instant.

By means of the *kṛtyā* spell, the knower of mantras attains mastery over humans, *kiṃnaras*, serpents, *siddhas*, *gandharvas*, and *dānavas*. Through the *adhīṣeṇa* [spells], he attains the state of a sovereign.
Then Bhairava, the lord of the Kula, having joined the Bhairavī-possessed one with the wheels,
let the Vāyubhairavas attend;
[he who is] the entire ancient face, the sky-face, the face facing toward the face.
Seated upon the primary female organ, she is both the manifest and the unmanifest, the syllable and the non-syllable.
With ten thousand streams and without breath, she is the totality whose form is composed of space.
Together with the visualization of her forms, she is perceived within the hollows of the cow-shaped [cavity] by means of the vowels.
Just as one who is afflicted by weapons [is healed], Bhairava bestows knowledge through the recitation of this mantra separately.
"Drink the nectar constantly; like a true animal (satpaśu) before, [drink] with force! Satisfy [the deities] known as the 'doers' (sakariṣṇu); O King, [thus you shall attain] true Śiva."

The wise go to Śiva even at an untimely hour by their own will. By reciting [this] with a circle of sages, one certainly destroys pestilence and other misfortunes. Having become thus, one obtains the state of Maheśvara.
He who practices the heroic conduct of a great hero, possessing true knowledge;
who is the common support, established in the three elements, and attended by those free from fear;
who causes that which is full of delusion to revolve with a thousand blazing rays.
And during the recitation, one should draw up the semen through this path of the channels;
one should bring it to the primary mouth by means of the visualization of the "goer" (*gantṛ-bhāvanā*).
Drinking thus the excellent essence, the practitioner becomes a sky-walker.

Restraining the breath within the cavity of the eyes, he should recite the Vidyā one hundred and eight times, starting from the end of the eyebrows up to the limit of the inner space, and exhaling again.
Meditating upon the half-moon digit (*kalā*) of the *kalaśa* from the north,

and being established in the state of non-meditation through meditation, one beholds the entire Rudra-maṇḍala as it truly exists; having seen it thus, one forcibly consumes the head of Time (*kālaśiras*).
Supported by the power of the eight qualities, he proceeds at will toward Śiva.
With the *argha* and *madhuparka* offerings of Śakti, he should drink the nectar of Śakti and Śiva,
both externally and internally, sustained by the application of the yoga of Śakti.
Holding the edge of the sword of power, he is indeed the practitioner of the vow of true power;
he is the possessor of power, whose self is the seed of power, who delights in the crest of the power of the crest,
and who, with his lineages, is the sixteen-syllabled one of the Goddess whose body is crowded with lineages.
Having thoroughly restrained the upper and lower [breaths], one should cause the wheel of the heart of the person to be acted upon to flow upward;
having thus worshipped it in the heart, the wheel of the head and eyes should be made to exhale.
In this way, indeed, the sequence ending with wind is sown within the two eyes of the universe of the person to be acted upon.
The wheel, shaped like a road-pot, should be rotated with the seven-syllable mantra.
Having sealed it as before with the mudrā, one should lead it into the house according to the ritual procedure.
Then, having thus performed this unsurpassed sacrifice with the *paśupiṇḍa*, [one attains success].

"Having drawn forth the wheel of the sky-farers (khecarīcakra), worship it according to the separate rite. From those two, another wheel—the wheel of the sky (khacakra)—is the wheel of the breath (ucchvasa). It is perfectly even and devoid of form; it is the excellent single state of both."
Having become a sky-farer together with her own [consort] according to the prescribed rite,
she proceeds through the sky, moving freely through the auspicious firmament.
In this very way, the Earth-dwellers (bhūcarīs) move about with a single wheel;
moving while remaining hidden, they traverse the auspicious path. Having joined themselves within the innermost core, they possess their own gatekeeper-forms.
Having made the foremost cloth [the object of worship] through the recitation of mantras as the Mistress of Mantra and Knowledge,
one should offer the *argha* for Śiva with one's own power according to the ritual of *argha*. Having joined those two with the water of Śiva as desired, one performs the *tripuṣkara* rite.
Having offered one hundred thousand oblations into the fire according to the procedure for the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*),
one should then offer the cloth-tree (*paṭavṛkṣa*) and again take recourse in the excellent *puṭa* vessel.
Having once more joined the auspicious corpse with the flower within that [vessel], it shall ascend into the sky.
When one thousand full oblations have been completed,
the immensely powerful Yakṣa king, Vaṭa, having struck down the image of that [deity],
will bring the flower under the control of the lord of practitioners.
Thus, one should perform the rite for a child under a *nyagrodha* tree using *vibhītaka*,

*harītaka*, *dhava*, *kārjuna*, *śoka*, *jīra*, *bilva*, and *śrīdruma* trees; and thereafter, one should carefully collect the three types of mustard seeds and the three pungent spices (*trikaṭuka*).

One should offer oblations with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), the *śivapuṣpa*, nectar, and the three purifiers (*tripuṣkara*), even when life is being gathered from the limbs, separately indeed with the fruits of prosperity. Together with Bhāyanī, one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) with the clarified butter of the venerable Brahmā.
One should perform the oblation for one hundred thousand units at each tree, in front of the cloth [banner],
from the door-keeper up to the end of the world, employing a single fire as desired.
Then, one who knows the nature of that scripture and the Self beholds him who is the very embodiment of reality.
By the power of destiny, at the conclusion of his vow, he beheld Yoga before him; as well as the Gaṇas, Guhyakas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rakṣasas,
and Dānavas, the Kṣetrapālas, the great Bhūtas, and the beloved wives of the gods, along with Śrī.
Just as that which was desired has been declared, so too, having attained it, the practitioner of great power shall restrain [all] by means of such valor with the *adhanāpuṣpa* flower. (62a)
Enjoying at will even those very objects of enjoyment desired by the mind,
the practitioner attains residence in the same world as Śiva (sālokya), according to his wish, in the form of Śiva himself.
Then, in this very manner, the weapons, radiant with the forms of deities, [are likewise attained].

Having meditated and observed the injunctions of the scriptures, he who is designated as the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) may, according to his will, accomplish his purpose as he desires in the eastern or upper [direction]. Having enjoyed the divine cavity of the cosmic egg, he shall proceed to the state of Sadāśiva.
In the Pitṛ, Sāvitrī, Jyeṣṭhā, Īṭkā, Yāmya, and Arka [nakṣatras], during the period of retention (*dhāraṇa*),
and in the dark fortnight excluding the day of Jupiter,
having performed the sacrifice with a *śaṅku* according to one's ability, and having worshipped [the deity] before the two vessels joined together;
Free from the memory of wandering, obstructing the impurities of the past,
he should, according to what is obtained, meditate upon the well-collected sacrificial offering;
without agitation, through the application of the prescribed method, he should quickly [realize] his own nature continuously.
Having stationed him with an interval and likewise having raised him up, the wielder of illusions,
having incited Dhāyodhaman, joined him with another; then,
having reached the opening in his own niche and entered the inner chamber, he [acted].
Having entered [the vessel], one should meditate with the mudrā that obstructs the rays of light through knowledge.
One should remember the two vessels above and below, adorned by the space of Śakti.
Holding them as desired, one should effortlessly lead [the offering] to one's own abode.
At the forefront of the sacrifice of one's own *śaṅku* and *śakti*, [the deities] consist of the goddesses of the directions beginning with Vidyā.
At night, by means of the three *puṣkaras*, one should place the Lord of the Directions face upwards.
By means of the three *puṣkaras*—[consisting of] the lines, the two nights, and the pungent substances—the *puṣkaras* [are established].
Having joined the previously mentioned sesame seeds in due order within the fire-house on the earth,
one should heat them together with half a *lakṣa* [of recitations] arising from the interior of the rays and flames,
having joined them externally in one place while restraining the vital breath (*asu*).
Even by raining down a shower of sound, one should cause [the offerings] to be sacrificed to the lords of the directions and sub-directions;
(62b) one attains sovereignty over all and, at the end of time, shall go to Śiva.
Having joined each secret mudrā with its respective vidyā as before,
one should consecrate the auspicious kumbha one by one with each [mudrā].
One should employ the rotation [of the wheel] like the water from the heart-lotus through the power of the wheel.
Above the *dhamadhamā*, within it is the wheel of knowledge (*jñānacakra*).
At its apex reside the prāṇa and apāna; there stands Mandarīśa, the mortar.
By means of the blowing of the breath, he causes this abode of Brahmā to revolve.
Having again swallowed the entire circle of the universe along with the upward breath,
he brings forth the physical body as before through the gathering of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Likewise, he [brings forth] the life-force (*jīva*), the nectar (*amṛta*), and the semen (*śukra*), according to the nature of his own internal cavity (*sampuṭa*).
Having thus eaten from the *kālaśiras* vessel, if he wishes to go to Śira,
he should offer the *saṃkaras* separately according to his means,
joined with three *puṣkaras*, along with sesame, *kravyāda*, and *yāvaka*.
Desiring [the result], one should offer oblations at night according to one's desire;
the terms *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *phaṭ*, *svāhā*, and *svadhā* are joined [to the mantra].
There is the movement of those with agitated faces, and the piercing by terrifying *reṇḍas*.
Likewise, having performed the fire-oblation (homa), one becomes a subduer (vaśya) when using *śiṃśapa* wood;
paralyzing (*stambhana*) occurs with conch powder, and causing distraction (*jambhana*) occurs with bones.
Causing delusion (*mohana*) is achieved with black sesame seeds, while worship is performed with *śastra*, *reṇu*, and *eraṇḍa*.
One should perform the ritual of pinning with *vadara* and *eraṇḍa* seeds, while the disintegration of the mantra is achieved with their husks.
One should employ great oblations mixed with clarified butter for rites of pacification and nourishment.
Binding with a thread made from the skin of a civet cat (*viḍgaga*), a musk deer (*gaṃdha*), a cat (*baṃdhin*), or a leopard (*dvīpin*) [is prescribed].
Binding the eyes [of an enemy] is achieved with the flesh of a crow; deluding them with the flesh of a vulture;
killing through the oblation of *kāṣṭhy-aṣṭha*; and [killing] with poison and *rājikā* [black mustard].

The vision of spirits is attained through a great sacrifice of clarified butter; the vision of what is desired through white mustard seeds; the acquisition of Yakṣas through a mountain goat; Piśācas through a Śaphantī;
a Kṣatriya ruler through an offering of bones; and a Brahmarākṣasa through donkeys.
In this way, by following the previous sequence and by means of a single [method], one should accomplish the rites for kings, yakṣas, piśācas, kṣetrapālas, and kinnaras;
for siddhas, gandharvas, and nāgas; and for brahmarākṣasas and kṣapācaras.
One should bring a maiden from the houses of the Daityas or the gods;

then, according to one's desire, [one gains] Apsarases with rice and flowers, wealth and prosperity with lotuses, and the goddesses Śrī and Sarasvatī with blue lotuses and beautiful red lotuses respectively.
Then, having thus obtained the knowledge of the field-offerings from a friend,
she displays millions of perfected signs and enjoys all the worlds.
With sacrificial fuel-sticks from milk-trees, she becomes Prasena in ten ways, as follows.
Behold the universe as it is perceived in a dream;
the practitioner of mantra effortlessly brings about various swift movements and attracts manifold riches, acting according to his own will like a leader of men.
Likewise, dried [into] ten parts or five as enjoined by the ritual rule,
they drive it away with the "fist-gaze"; thus they drink the water once,
cultivating their meditations in due order after having brought it forth.
Having combined three *puṣkala* measures with sesame seeds, one should offer them into the *kravyāda* fire within a cremation ground.
By means of fifty thousand [recitations], the practitioner shall obtain the aforementioned attainment of Pātāla.
Through the second [mantra], one attains the status of a lord of men; through the third, the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*).

On the fourth day of the vow, one obtains the status of a lord of Yakṣas; on the fifth, that of a Khañja; on the sixth, one attains the state of a Bhūcara or a Kinnara. On the seventh day, one gains the lordship of the Guṇas, and on the eighth, the rank of a Vīranāyaka.
In this very way, having fashioned the root of the axe in the shape of a tube with a jointed opening,
one should make its tip like fresh grain and hollow it out so as to contain the *śakti*.
Having thus placed the flame at the front, one should kindle the fire evenly.
Standing in the midst of the circle of the furnace, performing thousands of meditations and sports as desired with the cauldron and mortars, one should enter [the state] according to one's wish.
Roaring, he forcibly makes the river bend its course;
agitating it with the flapping of his wings, he might even consume the ocean by force.
He belches forth his mother, blazing like a meteor and a thunderbolt.
In this very same way, [the light] issues forth in a thousand ways from both nostrils.
Moving with the leftward-turning [breath], it arises through the awakening of prior wisdom;
likewise, the radiance shines like the light of Indra, that which is to be released and that which is beyond release.
Just as a silkworm encases its own body with its own saliva,
so does the Self, having divided itself, bring the world under its own control;
likewise, gradually bringing about destruction from that ancient city.

One does not fall under the power of death; having been led away, one shall go to the auspicious state. One should kindle the fire within the cavity of the navel by means of the fifty seed-syllables of the channels (*nāḍī*), minus one, together with the seven families.
One should meditate on the seven families as having emerged from the openings within the seventh power, amidst the enemy armies of the previous primordial wisdoms;
just as they went, so they have arrived— one should join them within the *saṃpuṭa*.
One should summon the life-force (*jīva*) into the lotus-cavity of the outermost exterior;
by means of those two, one should indeed employ the self, accomplishing its similarity to the [supreme] Self.
Fire is at the end of *barhiḥ*; *nārhitaḥ* is the seventh, and intellect (*buddhi*) is with eight.
The vehicle of the ray-sound is free from conceptual construction, beyond the path of the intoxicated,
and possesses four parts; it is established as radiant as a city.
Having correctly applied [the mantra] with "sudāda" (giver of good) at the beginning, one should apply it sequentially for anger and joy.
By thus drinking the nectar of mortals, one becomes immortal, freed from death. Having applied the Vidyā at the beginning and the end within the mouth, according to the previously stated number.
Having performed the recitation (*japa*) at the mountain of the Buddha, which is fourfold and square,
the householder, having worshipped his own [deity] in his own home,
[should do so] with pungent substances in the excellent eye, for indeed [this is done] by the name of the wheel of syllables.

Indeed, having written [the mantra] in the color of *śimī* with poison produced from the foot [of the deity], using ashes from a gambling ground and a cremation fire, and having placed it thus along with milk and the rising [planets],
one should smear it with that mud and pierce the field with the limbs [of the deity].
Then, indeed, having thus caused [the deity] to descend, one who has reached the infinite face of the time of knowledge,
having offered incense before the image with perfumes and the like,
and having addressed Agni in the four directions, should worship him with blue lotuses.

One should recite loudly the three syllables *viṣṭa-kadra-pyaṅga-miśre-yāṃ* with a beautiful tone, together with the syllables of the ritual application (*viniyoga*) directed toward the body of Māri. Having performed the recitation a thousand times before the fire at night, one should face the southeast.
At midnight, the best of arrows should effortlessly strike with its rays.
Or else, indeed, the entire [mantra] is spoken by the mouth of the mantra;
it is to be placed within the two *preṣaka*s, and is to be performed fourfold in the upper part.
The Bhairava [mantra] should be grasped by the Bhairavī; it has eight limbs and its body is the eight Bhairavas.
One who is detached should cause it to be grasped through power; filling [the vessel], one should dispel worldly existence (bhava).
Having thus bathed, others indeed [should grasp] the form as previously seen.
One should meditate upon the syllable *Vā* (*Rllaṃ*) at the mouth; one should always remember the *vidyā* to be grasped.
Having obtained it from the mouth of Uṣṭraśaṅku, one should continue until the true essence is attained.
Having experienced that supreme nectar which is like the essence of wine, one becomes immortal.
Thus, in the western face, the excellent speaker, employing the method of the Vidyā,
should meditate upon the four-faced one and recite [the mantra] for six nights while offering oblations of rice and *tripuṣkara*.

Standing high upon the lotus of the triple vessel, assuming forms at will according to her desire, she extends as far as the interval of the six corners; she is indeed the root, the nourisher of Śarva, and the six-faced one.
Furthermore, she is the traveler upon the four paths, possessing a form that transcends the fourth state.
Having worshipped with a mind as it truly is, one should exhale both [breaths] accordingly.
Likewise, having meditated upon the various elements and roots of the body, such as the mass of pure semen and so forth,
one who is established in self attains the end of his own three-fold state and perceives it effortlessly.
Having thus joined the seven syllables of the aforementioned color and meditated upon them in their proper sequence,
one should reach the interior of the *śaṅku* (the central point) and assume whatever form one desires.
Then, closing the eyes, one should look at the other with the gaze of desire.
Likewise, having bound forms of various kinds— numbering beyond count—
to stakes like sacrificial animals, and having sprinkled them day by day with food and drink, death shall not come under one's power.
Having always obtained the supreme nectar of the field as it truly is,
the practitioner of mantra attains lordship after seeing and heating the true path. The divine [power] that moves upward through the upper-facing [channel] proceeds according to one's desire.
One should recite with logic according to the ritual procedure, by means of the arrangement of the other faces;
likewise in the cities of Fire, Sun, and Moon, according to the arising of sound and non-sound.
Having joined [the breath] at the eight gross arisings, one attains the arising of both auspicious and inauspicious faces.
Above that, O Śūladṛṣṭi, is the great whirling Sahasrāra,
which possesses the terrible radiance of ten thousand fires and is unbearable due to various flames.

One should perform one hundred recitations with *pūraka* (inhalation), twice that with *kuṃbhaka* (retention), and three times that with *recaka* (exhalation). Thus, the *haṃsa* [mantra] is recited a thousand times.
By means of half of this effort, one should meditate upon the lotus of the heart situated between the vowels and consonants.
As if the netherworld were a whirlpool, and as if the three Puṣkaras were on fire,
with the root and stalk unsevered, and with the resonance of the *ucchvasa* and *saṃghoṣa* sounds,
one should meditate upon the entire universe as equal, brought under control by the auspicious play [of the breath].
Then, as if drawing it up to the tip of the nipple through the application of former yoga,
he brings forth for the perfected ones (siddhas) a form consisting of the seed of Śukra and other [substances]. Drinking at will that perfected, supreme nectar of the perfected ones, he enjoys it.
A mortal attains immortality and, by his own will, the supreme state.
O Goddess, resembling cow’s milk, you are the embodiment of the form of the universe;
having overcome the fear of Time, you travel the path of the digits at the end of all things.

One should offer oblations of sesame seeds scented with three *puṣkara* fruits and *matsyalikā*, and recite mantras while visualizing the goddess standing before one, possessing four horses, a chariot, and a banner;
she who is the support of the digits in the form of a stream, and who is intense with hundreds upon hundreds of streams.
One should contemplate her raining down above King Śaṅku as the bestower of desired objects.
For the sake of intelligence, she resembles a flock of birds; for increasing nourishment, she is a flood of blood;
for attracting wealth, she is like gold; and for the performance of power (*śakti*), she is a torrent of water.
Or else, within the inner wheel known as *saṃskāra*, which is manifold,
one should meditate upon the four paths (*caturadhvan*) in the sacrifice and recite the mantra a thousand times.
Having indeed bound the *ūrdhvajihvikī* [mudrā] with the syllables *urvī*, *du*, *prā*, *hareṃdre*, and *indrī*.
Chanting in the middle of the night, he beholds the Kaulika family.
Through that, by means of the previous yoga, there arises the union of another yoga;
the practitioner of mantra transcends death and becomes the sovereign of his own will.
(65b) Having bound Kālī on the path of the ocean of honey, in a place devoid of hermitages,
she [is] the goad that brings about the upward movement of the *liṅga* by means of the machine of the *śaṃkṛṣṭi*.

At the forefront of one’s own sacrifice, being free from dependence, one who partakes of the non-terrible within the terrible— by means of the hook, the support of nectar emerges, and one becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*).
The yogi should recite "Śara Vyoma" until the arising of the hook of hooks.
Having proceeded with the goad of the visible oṣṭha-śaṅku, one becomes a cakravartin.
Thus, according to the divisions of the stages of life (āśrama), this knowledge belongs to householders;
likewise, after receiving the command of the guru, there is the consecration (abhiṣeka).
For the various transformations have diverse substrata and undergo changes of manifold forms.
[He is] smeared with red, white, and ashes; his eyes are unconquered and he has a hundred eyes.
He possesses the five mudrās, the seven clans, the Kaula mudrā, and bears the eighteen [attributes].

Moving by power, moving through power, the power of space, and the movement of power in the sky; bearing the form and the skull-topped staff, observing silence, possessing the fivefold [senses] like an elephant, and maintaining the state of wandering;
he is a celibate student due to the simultaneous arising of various words and states.
Just as it is for those who have reached the final goal and for wandering mendicants bearing their emblems,
so shall I describe in brief the vowlessness (avrata) of all others;
first, according to the previously stated rule, [one should perform] the binding of the body with the vows.
Barefoot and with hair disheveled, wearing red and black garments,
adorned with a trident, a lotus stalk, and garlands, yet lacking limbs and a beard— such was the naked mendicant (dikpaṭa) whom I encountered.
Having been abandoned by him through his grace and favor, I indeed subsisted on alms.
One who bathes with water and ashes, bathing three times a day while remaining between the [outer and inner] limits,
should recite the Vidyā day and night, remaining steadfast for the sake of alms.
With the palate, the tips of the teeth, and the tongue well-positioned, one should remain firm.
When she rests upon the tips of the teeth and tongue,
Mahākālī, who is like a great skeleton and possesses great power, is liberated. (66a)
One should indeed mutter [the mantra] as Saṃkariṣṇī; Kālī is the supreme chariot of Time (Kālaratha).
For one day one should wander through the villages, for five or seven days at the city gate;
for a month and a half-month on the triple-pathway (tripatha), and for six months in the confluence of rivers.
The year is indeed a single tree at the crossroads;
one should maintain the fourfold Kṣatriya power throughout all times in its four divisions. On that cloth, the form of the Goddess should be depicted according to her description and as desired.
First, as previously described, she is in the manner of the Khecarī [mudrā].
Adorned with a bell and a skull-bowl, she stands upon a half-khaṭvāṅga, a mountain peak, or a banner;
seated upon a severed head, she gazes toward the northern direction.
To his right, one should have the god drawn in his true form, like a bull standing between two mountains,
with a body possessing the majesty of a loud laugh,
adorned with bells and chowries, and decorated with a canopy and mirrors.

One should install the deities who consume various kinds of meat, whose seats are supported by Bhairava, who are firm, who are joined above with the *sarvagā* [deity] by means of the syllables *ḍha* and *ḍha*, and who are endowed with various garlands and ornaments. These [deities], along with their respective faults (*saddoṣā*), should be consecrated.
One should worship Bhairava, who possesses a form such as that [described], who is of noble lineage, and who wields a weapon named after the *satyasava*, the *oṣṭaka*, and the *aṣṭhānta*.
One should honor him with these [offerings] when one has abandoned the commands of the king, which are like those of a beast.
One should worship Aṭṭahāsa-Mahākālī together with offerings of raw flesh and blood.
Whether seeking enjoyment or liberation, or even when something has been requested somewhere, one should offer it thus.
O Tongue, may there be such perfect rest; O you who are well-rested from fatigue, may there be the repose of exhaustion.
Likewise, one should extract the common *prāṇa* from the northern [channel]; thus the eight *kravyāda*s are proclaimed. One should offer a hundred oblations into the *rathantara*.
One should offer unbroken *mahājya* with that ladle into the sacrificial vessel (*pātrajīvaka*),
day and night, mixed with cow-dung and *sapharī*.
In this very same manner, one should burn incense mixed with mountain-borne *utpala*.
Chanting the mantra according to the method of whispering (*upāṃśu*), while pronouncing the *vigraha* [mantra] aloud; having bathed at the close of day as prescribed by his vow,
he should daily worship the digestive fire within the stomach by means of the rite of the vital-fire (*prāṇāgni*).

Having extinguished [the fire] with the remainder, one should offer the *caru* obtained through begging, dedicating it to the two deities; indeed, one should offer it in two portions. Or, having taken up a portion from the vessel of food, one should sprinkle it with *akṣata*.
Having offered oblations into that very fire, one should offer them again into the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*).
One should sprinkle the ground with *kula* [liquids], and the seat is the *Kuladevatā*.
Having touched the vessel with the *saṃkula* [mantras], one should utter the recitation of Bhairava.

One should cause the Great Heroes (Mahāvīras), who possess bodies that traverse both earth and sky and are worthy of supreme purification, to be grasped by their retinue; one should protect with the Rudras and sprinkle [with water].
One should [protect] the guardians of the directions with the mudrās and weapons, and the remainder with the forms of the Mātṛkās.
And having mentally offered this [oblation] with all the companions through the doors,
by means of the five faces beginning with Dhruva, and having first brought forth that which is known as the Heart (hṛt) according to the previous nomenclature,
one should indeed offer the group of eight in this manner until the end, and then consume it as prescribed.
Having eaten until the fire of the stomach has subsided and its heat has calmed,
one should meditate upon one's own deity as it was when first generated and then dissolve it.
Then, having performed the external offering (*arpaṇa*), one should properly perform [the purification] with water.
Having performed the *agnihotra* sacrifice again, one should recite [the mantra] for the remainder of the night.
The external [elements] are the Sun, Moon, and City; the excellent chariots are those of the previous state.
Like the flow of wealth, they are divided into eight parts within the direction of the hundred moons.

She is the foundation and abode of the cosmic egg, the universal bell of great sound; she is the source of the gods, the mother of all beings, and filled with the [twenty-four] principles and so forth.
The surface of the earth, divided by the distinction between the grasped and the grasper, was like the reflection on a mirror; thus, by that [reflection] which was possessed of fourfold delusion,
there arose a loud laugh within it, and those who possess the full digits [of wisdom] rejoiced therein.
The Supreme is the nature of supreme knowledge, the soul of the universe, the auspicious dissolution.
It is the womb of the fourfold *kala*s—*saka*, *cona*, *upama*, and *ādhāra*—and the arising of the rising with its parts; it is indeed the King, the source of the arising of peace.
Having gathered together, as if from a single essence of thread, those two powers that are difficult to withstand,
and having restrained them one after another within the tree of the body,
one’s own innate wisdom— arising from the self— blazes forth by means of the internal humming sound of the breath.

Furthermore, having applied oneself to cessation (*nirodha*), one should sleep within the interval of one's own *vidyā*. Having transcended the states beginning with that of the king (*nṛpa*), there is the subsequent concentration on the fourth state (*turya-dhāraṇa*). Having seen that intermediate state, which is the source of the arising of the locus of sound, [one attains it].
In that external Lord, the universe is the supreme nest of Brahman;
it is proclaimed by the knower of mantras himself as being pervaded by the path of Saṃkarṣiṇī.
Blazing with splendor, she is manifested with a loud, boisterous laugh.
She is of terrible form, exceedingly fierce, yet gentle with a smiling countenance.
Furthermore, having performed the sacrifice properly and in great detail according to the ritual,
one should offer the *arghya* to the deity and worship the *piṇḍa* with the *piṇḍa* itself.
Reciting this, the practitioner indeed offers the *māri-piṇḍa* to the exceedingly powerful Mahākālī;
having offered one such oblation, he should consecrate his desired goal.
Once consecrated according to the rule, he shall come to know the divine power of asceticism (*tapas*).
He attains the lordship of the gods Rudra and Bhairava,
or else he enjoys manifold pleasures in the world of Vāmāri.

Having enjoyed the state of the interval of time, one united with the Goddess shall go to Śiva. Thus the Goddess Ghorā, the *Ḍāmarā* of the three worlds, is the bestower of accomplishment through the yoga of following the sequence of the words and by the piercing of every vajra.
When she is properly differentiated, she is then the sovereign of a thousand colors.
When she is worshipped as divided sixfold according to the divisions of the wheels (cakras),
then the goddesses at the end of the words have been briefly described as before.
I have [offered] one hundred and fifty-four of these to you;
among them, O Goddess of gods, you reside within the enclosure of heat. First is the six-spoked wheel, and beyond that is the twelve-spoked wheel.
Outside of that, there should be a sixteen-spoked [wheel], then a twenty-four-spoked one;
from that, a thirty-two-spoked one, and then one twice that number is prescribed.
Thus stands the arrangement of the six wheels, situated according to the division of the words.
And here, the *ānulomyagatā* [mantra] is applied according to the division of the *pada*s.
One should worship *Trailokyadāmara* by distinguishing each goddess individually;
likewise, by distinguishing the lords and through the differentiation of their movement between locations.
And through the application of the successive coverings (*āvaraṇa*), one should attain the reality (*tattva*) of the divisions.
Here, there are six divisions for the first [covering] due to its connection with the subsequent coverings;
twelve for the second; and those same [twelve] constitute the third.
In this [system], twenty-four [petals] are proclaimed for the twenty-four-spoked [wheel];
here, sixty-four are cited for the thirty-two-spoked [wheel].
O lady of beautiful hips, it is likewise through the fivefold division and the piercing of the heart.
In the sixty-four-spoked wheel, that many divisions are proclaimed. Having thus understood these divisions, one should subsequently [arrange] the wheels according to the sequence of their retention;
by virtue of the primary importance of each, and through the distinction of the remaining syllables.
The goddess Kṛṣodarī, O god of gods, attains infinity;
she is endowed with eight excellent thousand-spoked wheels.
It should be known by the Guru at all times in this Viśvadaṃmara [Tantra]:
"The one and only Paramākālī has spread out into infinite divisions;
however many varieties of forms there are, O slender-waisted Goddess of gods."
That alone is declared to be the single *tāva*; it is differentiated according to the distinctions of ritual action (*kriyā*).
In reality, O beloved, there is no difference here, for it possesses the nature of the solitary hero (*ekavīra*).
O beautiful one, it may be combined, separated, or even a single word.
O King of Eyes, that which is on the chariot should be known here as entirely equal;
whether it be without limbs or with limbs, one should diligently worship it under this name,
as well as Sarasvatī, Brahmā, and Nara and Nārāyaṇa.

O fair-hipped one, O beloved, this *Trailokyadaṃarā*, which is endowed with power and accompanied by its secret doctrines, was not previously declared to Vasiṣṭha in its true essence; today it has been proclaimed. This [tantra] is the slayer of the head of Brahmā.
The attainment of all higher consciousnesses arises for the souls of practitioners from the recitation of this [mantra], O Goddess of the Gods; within six months, there is no doubt of this.
It is perfected as the bestower of great enjoyments and the giver of hundreds of great wonders.
She is the constant bestower of wealth and grain, the giver of manifold prosperity;
she is renowned as the granter of various supernatural powers (siddhis) and the provider of all success.
She is the Terrible One, the Excellent Heroine, the Fierce and Wrathful, who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
She is the pervasive one, the nourisher, the fierce one who brings about the destruction of violent evil;
she is the destroyer of faults regarding the great commitments, the slayer of wickedness and poverty,
the shatterer of the great illusion, the performer of all rites, and the auspicious Śivā.
Thus has been explained this formidable wheel, the essence that bestows all accomplishments;
it is secret, the ultimate mystery, and grants liberation to men through its recitation.
What more shall I speak now? O Gaurī, O fortunate one, mistress of the practitioners, I have declared the *Cetasiḍdhi* along with its secret, together with the *Nīlikhā-tantra*.
Thus [ends] the third hexad in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraścheda* section of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavasrotas*.
The eighth chapter, the procedure for the sādhana of the Trailokyadaṃarācakra,
[is concluded]. Having heard this, the Goddess, whose prowess is the fierce Vidyā,
being entreated by the King of the Sindhus, spoke again to the Lord of Gods.
The Goddess said:
I have heard this most excellent essence, the supreme and most wonderful secret;
by remembering which, I rejoice again and yet again.
Now I wish to hear about that other [form] known as Pratyaṅgirā,
who destroys the faults of all impurities, who brings down all good fortune,
who is indeed the Great Plague (Mahāmārī) through her recitation, and who bestows great peace.
She is indeed truly named "The Destroyer of All Fierce Machines.
Bhairava said:
(Listen), O lady of beautiful hips, I shall declare the secret that destroys sin.

O Goddess of the Suras, this is the terrible rite of Pratyaṅgirā, which crushes all calamities. Of this Kālī, there are seventy-seven crores of yantras born from her body; therefore, she consists solely of mantra.
Having gone to the garden of the best of mountains accompanied by his preceptor and disciples,
his body smeared with abundant sandalwood paste and delighted by wine,
he there worshipped the stone image according to his means.
Then one should extract the Vidyā, which is like twelve thousand suns.
One should first extract the Praṇava, then the Haṃsa joined with Agni (Ra),
