conjoined with the Bindu and the Ākāśa (Ha), forming the Piṇḍa, ending with Sarva and Antaka.
Having extracted the *bindu* and the three syllables, then the double-tongued *bhairava*,
[one sees] the *piṇḍa* mounted upon Citrabhānu, resembling ten thousand suns.
The *haṃsa* (ha) is established upon the lunar day (*tithi*, i.e., *u*), adorned with the *bindu*.
The *kuṇḍala* (ka) is established upon fire (*vahnī*, i.e., *ra*), marked by the head of the destruction of fire (*kṣaya*, i.e., *ṣa*).
Having joined these with the *bindu*, one forms the fifth supreme syllable.
Having extracted the *paśu* alone, then the *haṃsa* joined with two vowels;
then the *paśu* again, as it was, surmounting the *vāyu* adorned by that very same [vowel];
then again the *kāla* alone, and the *vāyu* marked by the destruction of fire (*agni*).
The letter ending with *va* (va), accompanied by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and marked with three vowels (*ā*, *ī*, *ū*),
followed by the letter ending with *śva* (śva) mounted upon a goad (*kuśa*), then the letter beginning with *ca* (ca) enclosed within fire (*ra*),
then the letter beginning with the sixth vowel (*ū*) marked by three vowels (*ā*, *ī*, *ū*), and finally ending with the letter *va* (*va*) marked by that same [sixth vowel].
The fifth [letter] and the first [letter], marked by two vowels, ending with Varuṇa (va) and alone;
O Mistress of the God of Gods, [this is] the prohibition, adorned above by three suns (three *ra*s).
Having extracted the animal (*pa*) alone, adorned with two vowels, [and] the *haṃsa* [syllable].
One should extract the first [syllable] of the sixth [group], adorned by the seventh [vowel] joined with fire (ra);
then the one called Aṅkuśa, which is the first of the fifth [group]; and then Soma alone.
Then Puruṣa, traversed by two vowels, and again Vahni joined with the sixth [vowel].
One should again give the compassionate Lord (the letter *gha*), marked with the abode of fire (*ra*) and the letter *kha*;
then the absolute nectar (*amṛta*, *ha*) mounted upon Varuṇa (*va*), adorned with the great goad (*mahāṅkuśa*, *ū*).
Then one should give the first letter (*ca*) mounted upon the end of *kha* (*ha*), preceded by the womb (*yonipūrva*, *e*).
The first [syllable] of the sixth [group], conjoined with two vowels, is Maheṃdra; then again, that same one alone.
Before this, one should again place Varuṇa at the end, alone.
Puruṣa should be situated in the thirteenth [position]; Gaṇeśa is marked by the letter *ra*.
The fire-goose (*vahnihaṃsa*) alone, joined with the moon and the goad (*aṅkuśa*), is the moon-studded *śirātrikāṇa*;
then again, the solitary moon.
One should extract the fire merged with Varuṇa and the pure Vāyu.
One should extract the prohibition, the goad, the fire, the wood, and the massed [elements], as well as the horse,
the variegated triple-sun, and that which ends at the tip of the earring.
Make this phrase ending in *bhairava* and containing the word *dvijihva* (two-tongued) twofold.
Then [place] the *puruṣa* alone, followed again by the bow with its arrow;
then one should make that phrase repeated twice, beginning with *padmāsana*.
One should again place that [syllable] joined with the sixth [vowel] situated in the middle of the fire (the letter *ra*).

The letter *ya* alone should be given; fashion this word in two ways. Then the "womb" (*yoni*, the letter *ha*) should be given first, and again at the end of the sun (*sūrya*, the letter *ra*), like a *piṇḍa*.
This word, repeated twice, shatters all yantras. It consists of Vāyu joined with the Praṇava, Soma conjoined with Kāla,
followed by Mukhadāraṇa, Niṣedha, and Dantavāhana.
Then, that [syllable] situated in Varuṇa (va) should be joined with the fire-syllable (ra) and the letter for destruction (kṣa).
Next, one should place the first [syllable] of Amṛta (a), together with the third (i), situated in Candra (sa).
Then, the fifth [syllable] alone should be given, ending in Bhairava (ha) and joined with Caṇḍa (cha).
One should give Varuṇa alone, and Pavana adorned with the Bindu.
[The letter] Daṃtura is mounted on Varuṇa and beautified by the third vowel (I).
That which is called Amṛta is situated upon Paśu, and the first of the fifth [group] is alone.
One should extract the nectar (amṛta) conjoined with Vāyu, and then Varuṇa alone;
likewise, one should extract Vāyu alone conjoined with the bow and the goad.
Having extracted the Bhairava weapon three times, it should be provided with the consort of Fire (Vahni-bhāryā).
This most formidable and auspicious Vidyā is known by the name Pratyaṅgirā;
she should be understood as the bestower of all prosperity, the crusher of all mantras,
the destroyer of all malevolent sorcery, and the annihilator of all evil deeds.
(70a) No knowledge equal to this has been proclaimed within the wheel of mantras.
When a mountain-dweller recollects a most terrible mantra while devoid of worship, [it becomes effective].
Then those mantras curse him; therefore, one should always remember her as Pratyaṅgirā, who neutralizes sorrows, yantras, and malevolent incantations.
Then she should be known as Pratyaṅgirā, the auspicious Mahāyogeśvarī.
O Gaurī, she who is difficult to attain in the three worlds has been revealed in this tantra;
she is proclaimed to consist of ninety syllables and is the destroyer of all sins.
Abiding in the midst of the expansion of one’s own consciousness, Kālī brings about the end of Time itself.

One should meditate upon her who is manifest, beyond the ignorant and the indifferent, who is the source of wonder and terror for the three worlds; who is as formidable as the fire at the end of an eon, observing a vow of a hundred thousand-fold intensity; who possesses a splendor like the hue of the *kālikā* and *kokila* birds, and is most terrifying.
Four-armed and solitary heroine, radiant with three eyes,
mounted upon a great corpse, bearing a begging bowl and a khaṭvāṅga staff;
holding a noose and a mace in her hands, she is greedy for fat and blood.
Extremely lofty and most terrifying, with a sound like the wind at the time of universal destruction—
such is the Kṛtyā for the destruction of machines and the crushing of Khārkhoda;
one should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess for the suppression of malevolent magic.
In rites for pacification (*śāntika*), she has the luster of a pure necklace, the moon, or snow;
in rites for enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), she has the white and red radiance of another supreme [form], who is withered and has a withered face;
and in rites for attraction (*vaśya*), she has the luster of a pomegranate flower and resembles water mixed with saffron.
One should always visualize [the goddess] as resembling vermilion during the rite of attraction (karṣaṇa);
during the rite of immobilization (stambhana), she resembles Indra’s weapon; during the rite of paralyzing (stobha), she is like an emerald;
during the rite of crushing (jambhana), she is like gold; and for the rite of burning (dahana), she is like a mass of flames.
For the rite of eradication, one should visualize her as resembling smoke; for killing, as blackish-brown;
for causing flight, as covered in dust; and for bewildering, as like a dry feather.
One should contemplate the union of the colors of the crow and the cuckoo for the sake of the goal;
during the agitation of the cavity, she resembles a fierce fire and a cavern.
When situated in the sky, she has the appearance of her former form, and in pure liberation, she has the form of the pure moon.
One should meditate upon the auspicious Goddess, who assumes forms at will like a wish-fulfilling gem.
In a well-concealed place or in the teacher’s house, one should worship the goddess Kṛṣodarī;
there, the most excellent of teachers, having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus—
One should worship the Goddess there (in the center), abiding in the previously described meditation, within a square, bright, four-gated [mandala] adorned with the power of one's will,
offering various garlands and various special kinds of liquor.
Having worshipped according to one's means with various fragrant scents, hundreds of various flowers,
diverse excellent incenses, and likewise the sounds of various musical instruments,
one should thereafter perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as desired, using firewood of the "hero" (vīra) variety in a secluded place,
one should offer oblations into the "heroic fire" (vīrānala) according to the requirements of the ritual.
Just as the preliminary consecrations and other rites were prescribed for the first six [chapters], so too should they be performed here.
Having prepared it, one should offer the great flesh— or whatever else— with a concentrated mind.
Having thus performed the oblation, the wise teacher should then admit the disciple,
who is pure, dexterous, disciplined, and who delights in the conduct of the heroes.
One should cast the flowers used for sprinkling while holding them with joined palms and looking at the lotus of the heart.
In the Mahāyāga of Ekavīra, which is devoid of mudrās, limbs, and the like,
one should subsequently initiate [the disciple] near the fire as previously described.
Having thus initiated him, one should subsequently consecrate him.
For once he has been consecrated and has gained knowledge, he should thereafter begin the practice of accomplishment.
Having gone to a garden on a preeminent mountain, free from all dualities,
subsisting on alms and liberated from attachment, he should accomplish what is desired by his mind.
The practitioner of mantra should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times and perform oblations with a tenth part of that amount.

From the midst of the fire at the conclusion of the oblation, Mahālakṣmī arises together with the finest clarified butter for the sake of the preeminent practitioner of firm vows. Accompanied by her, he indeed goes to where the goddess Karaṅkiṇī resides.
O fortunate one, through one hundred thousand recitations, the *pātāla* [subterranean realm] of that [deity] is accomplished.
Then, desiring the great assembly (*mahāmelāpa*), one should perform this rite:
having gone to a terrifying cemetery, one should seize an excellent corpse.
Then, with a serene mind, one should have that well-adorned vessel placed upon the altar;
having mounted its back, one should recite the vidyā without fear.
O virtuous lady, after a hundred recitations, the gods and goddesses arrive.
One should offer them the respectful oblation (argha), having pierced one’s own left side.
Then all those [goddesses] shall grant success to the great-souled practitioner.
By this very procedure, one should always accomplish the Vetāla.
One whose limbs are smeared with fish oil should touch the corpse placed upon the altar;
then, a Vetāla of terrible appearance quickly rises up. Having let out a thunderous, vajra-like loud laugh, he speaks:
"Tell me, what oblation shall I offer? What may I do for you?
Shall it be the elixir of taste, the sword, the pill, or the cloth;
or perhaps the netherworld, the immortal hero, or the ritual procedure that fulfills all desires?"
Take many wish-fulfilling jewels (cintāmaṇi) that you desire in your mind.
Remaining silent and composed, one should not desire anything at all.
O heroes, having slain him, one should devour him with a mind free from conceptual construction.
By consuming this flesh, the practitioner becomes as long-lived as Brahmā;
endowed with qualities such as [freedom from] wind and other ailments, he possesses great strength and prowess.

And one who proceeds without having digested [the practice] shall attain nirvāṇa in the end. O Goddess of the gods, the Unborn One always performs all common means of accomplishment— the rites beginning with pacification and ending with killing, as previously described.
Or rather, that which subdues even the minds of the gods by its power—
this ritual of the Goddess, as it was correctly spoken by the Lord of the Gods, is the essence of all the Āgamas.
Now hear another most secret procedure, the *Pratyaṅgirā*, which bestows accomplishment and is delightful with infinite virtues.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, the ritual of Pratyaṅgirā, in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraccheda* of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavasrotas*.
Bhairava said:
Now I shall proclaim another supreme procedure.
The essence that bestows all accomplishments, known by the name *Trailokyasādhana*, which devours supreme mantras, shatters the obstacles of *kṛtyā* and *khārkhoda*,
is the Great Kālī Pratyaṅgirā, the bestower of all prosperity.
The supreme sovereign of all mantras, named Maṃtraḍāmarikā,
went to the terrifying cremation ground at night and extracted the Vidyā. Always honoring Mātrikā with heroic offerings, he remained firm in his vows.
One should extract the incomparable mantra that consumes all supreme mantras.
One should extract the *tāraka* (the syllable Om), followed by a pair of *haṃsas* (the syllables Ha and Sa).
Then, the final [syllable] accompanied by emission (*sṛṣṭi*), and again the pair joined with the long [vowel].
Furthermore, one should extract the pair alone in four ways:
the beloved joined with two vowels, and the *haṃsa* joined with three vowels. This word should be made twofold; one should extract the *soma* alone.
(72a) Again, [one should visualize] Fire grown out of Varuṇa, then the solitary Puruṣa;
then the Niṣedha situated at the beginning of the fifth [vowel], adorned with Fire and the Bindu.
One should extract Gaṇeśvara situated in fire (Ra), which is conjoined with the tearing of the mouth (the letter A).
Having extracted Soma (Sa) alone, one should divide this syllable into two. Again, from among the six, one should extract the first (the letter Ka) alone, and then extract Fire (Ra) alone.
The seventh [letter] preceded by *yoni* (the letter *i*), the first of the fifth [group] (*pa*) which is always fierce,
situated in the wind (*ya*)— O Goddess of the Gods, it is beautiful and always formidable.
That very same [syllable], ignited by fire (*ra*) and adorned with the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*).
One should again extract the *cāpādya* (the bow-born), then the solitary *varuṇa* (water),
then the roaring one mounted on the wind (*vāyu*), joined with the cause of the mouth;
preceded by the womb (*yonipūrva*) in its own form, one should extract the fire situated in the jar (*kumbha*).
Having extracted only the *astra* (the letter *pha*), one should place *varuṇa* (the letter *va*) accompanied by three vowels (*ai*).
[Then] *daṃtura* (the letter *ra*) mounted upon *varuṇa* (the letter *va*) and joined with the abode of fire (*agni*, the letter *ra*).
Having extracted only *kaṃbha* (the letter *ba*), it is marked with two vowels (*au*).
One should again place Vahni and Kevalin, then Aśva together with Praṇava,
and then Caṇḍa situated within one's own self, joined with Mukhadāraṇa. Candra should be alone, and Niṣedha struck by Aṅkuśa.
The "protruding" [letter] (da), pervaded by the three vowels (ai), preceded by the womb (i) and the bindu;
the Lord of Knots (tha) joined with the "tearer" (ṛ); and Varuṇa (va) alone at the end.
Having extracted Vāyu (ya) alone, make this word twofold.
The *haṃsa* (ha), the fire (*ra*), the *ḍambara* (*ḍa*), the *piṇḍa* (*ba*), adorned with the *bindu*;
the *kuṇḍala* (*la*) encased in fire (*ra*) and joined with *kālarudra* (*ma*) and the *bindu*.
Again, the god *kuṇḍala* (*la*) situated in fire (*ra*) and marked by that [same] instant (*kṣa*).
Having marked it with a bindu, one should again extract the kuṇḍala;
it is conjoined with fire and kālāgni, and adorned with the most excellent bindu.
Furthermore, O Goddess, one should extract the deity Kuṇḍala situated in the auspicious lunar day;
one should extract that great seed-syllable with the *visarga* in two ways:
the sound joined with fire and endowed with the *visarga*.
Then, at the end, append "bhīmaśaṅkuṃ" and this word twice.

This mantra, which concludes with a salutation (*namaskāra*), is known as the "Mantra-Purifier" (*mantraprakālana*). It is proclaimed as the supreme among all mantras, named *Pratyaṅgirā*, the bestower of all prosperity.
Ekavīrā, the pacifier of great sins, spoke previously: "O Great Goddess,
even if one were to kill the entire universe, including all moving and non-moving beings, and even if it were filled with Brahmins,
one is not tainted by sin, even if done out of desire."

O Goddess, Mistress of the Lords of Knowledge, by remembering you three times, even one who has committed the sin of uprooting a *liṅga* or the like, or who has killed his guru, father, or mother, is purified. You are the shatterer of supreme mantras and the devourer of hostile yantras.
It pacifies malevolent magic, destroys the evil deeds of others, and is the sixty-four-syllable Vidyā that removes the sins even of mantras.
What more shall I say? Listen, O you who are worshipped on the lotus seat!
O Supreme Goddess, there exists no knowledge equal to this for destroying great sins; what else shall I tell you? One should worship her on a mountain peak or in a well-concealed, excellent house.
O lady of excellent vows, within the six-cornered world that is smeared with fragrance,
one should install in its center the goddess Bhīmā, who devours mantras;
she resembles ten thousand fires of cosmic destruction and is intent upon shattering the shell of the universe.
It was fashioned with wings from the sky-dwellers, had great serpents for its girdle,
and was difficult to approach, emitting a terrible roar like the crashing of clouds.
One should always meditate upon Gṛddhadhvajā, who stands before one, adorned with ornaments of snakes,
whose mouth is filled with human heads, who possesses the splendor of ten million times ten thousand flashes of lightning,
and who has the faces of a lion and a boar between her two breasts.
She was utterly withered, with eyes like hollows, terrifying even to fear itself;
her throat resembled the dark hue of a crow, a cuckoo, or a black bee;
she had long hair, long fangs, and long entrails hanging down.

One should contemplate her as having eighteen arms, five faces, and a great roar; she holds all weapons, is radiant, and possesses a universal form. She carries a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and is adorned with human skulls.
Having meditated upon the fierce goddess holding a lotus in her heart, brandishing a sword and a dagger,
intent on playing the *tuṃbu* drum and the lute, with an elephant hide raised in her hand,
and bearing a trident and a *ṭaṅka*— one shall destroy all hardships.
Having meditated thus, one should place the slender-waisted Goddess, the God of gods, in the center; thereafter,
one should worship her with all the offerings for heroes,
including divine mahāmāṃsa, fermented liquors, and [meat] derived from goats, fish, and so forth.
One should worship with many roasted and fried items, both cooked and raw,
as well as with *surā*, *madya*, *āranāla*, *śīdhu*, *raktāsava*, and so forth.
Having gratified the Goddess of the gods with various garlands, perfumes, and incenses, [one should proceed].

One should worship the Mistress of the Śūras with various kinds of foods, such as *lopikā*, conch-shaped wafers (*śaṅkhavartī*), and so forth, while remaining free from stinginess regarding wealth. Thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the meat of wild animals.
Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, O Goddess, one should then cause the disciple to enter—
well-disciplined, with eyes bound, and always following the conduct of a hero (*vīrācāra*).
Having made him cast flowers [to determine his destiny], O Mistress of Gods, one should lead him from there to the site of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Therein, the Guru should initiate that disciple by means of the previously mentioned yoga.
Then, as before, he should consecrate him with all the royal services.
Having received permission, the excellent practitioner should thereafter begin the practice (*sādhana*).
The procedure for establishing a residence on a mountain peak or a riverbank follows this sequence:
having sat there, he should consume roots and subsist upon the nectar that has arisen.
One should meditate upon [the goddess] Cakrabhedakī, who resembles a coral staff;
situated in the center of that [lotus], one should recite the mantra while remaining thus established within one's own self.
O highly fortunate lady, one should offer three hundred thousand human lungs as an oblation.

Then, from the center of the fire, the goddess Bhayānakā emerges as the Great Goddess with her tenth part; he should proceed together with her. There, that worshiper shall always become a lord among practitioners (*sādhaka*).
Then, having gone to the mountain ridge where the famous cave is located, the practitioner,
having fasted on the great night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
should kindle a fire-pit and perform oblations there.
When one offers guggulu mixed with clarified butter up to eight thousand times,
then the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, quickly trembles;
and from there, lovely, charming women with beautiful smiles emerge.
All of them assumed various forms, adorned with every kind of ornament;
they always possessed the gait of elephants in rut and were sixteen years of age.
They had broad hips and ample breasts, which were full and elevated.
O Beloved, trembling with prostration before the feet of the practitioner, they, being terrified, address that practitioner who is worshipped by the gods:
"Come, come, O Lord of Heroes! To Pātāla, the ocean of enjoyments!"
We shall enjoy ourselves here together until the dissolution of the earth,
drinking excellent wine with its accompanying snacks— a place ten times more beautiful than heaven.
"Drink there, O Lord of Heroes, or bestow it upon others, O All-pervading One.
Having heard this from them, a man should then enter there together with them;
endowed with great majesty, he shall abide in golden celestial chariots.
Having worshipped there the great lord Hāṭakeśvara, the king of gods,
and having drunk the sāttvika beverage, one shall dwell until the moon and stars [end]. O fortunate one, at the conclusion of the kalpa, one shall enter that body of the Lord.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the *melāpa*, one should apply [the ritual] as before.
One attains success as previously described; no specific distinction is prescribed.
O Goddess worshipped by the lords of heroes, now hear about the production of the *kṛtyā* at the beginning.
Having gone to the terrifying cremation ground, equipped with a formidable collection of materials,
one should take eight great tridents and fashion them into banners; one should then suspend animal carcasses, lumps of food, and lotuses from those very [banners].
Having placed eight *rudrākṣa* beads upon the head and a sacred thread with great mantras,
one who stands upon the back of the corpse should kindle the funeral pyre in the center with its own wood on a ground smeared with great blood and adorned with the funeral garlands of the deceased.
There, the practitioner should offer oblations of human flesh mixed with *karpūra*.
As long as he offers them up to one hundred times, the entire earth trembles;
in the second [round], there is a conflagration in the cardinal and intermediate directions and a great clamor.
In the third [stage], there arises the sound of lightning and thunder;
then, from the midst of fire, a great *kṛtyā* of terrible form and fearsome appearance suddenly emerges,
having opened her most horrific mouth.
When the practitioner speaks thus, O Lord, what task shall I perform?
Shall I pulverize the four mountains, dry up the great oceans,
split open the netherworld (pātāla), or crush the earth into dust?
(74b) Out of anger, I shall crush either the Giver of Wealth, or Yama, or Time itself;
or the Lord of the Nairṛtas, or Indra, or Vāyu, or even Agni.
"Tell me, what shall I destroy for you who have come from another world? Shall I bring Brahmā here? Tell me, what may I do for you?
For what purpose have I been summoned? O Lord of Heroes, tell me your command."
Then one should speak to her exactly as it has been conceived in the mind;
she then bestows all that upon the practitioner without obstacle.
Thus have the great siddhas and their rites been correctly revealed.
The Āsādhinī Mahāvidyā is remembered as the bestower of all good fortune;
it swiftly cuts through the bonds of supreme mantras and provides protection against others.
O beautiful one, by remembering her even once, she destroys the effects of malevolent sorcery.
The goddess consisting of red nectar is remembered as the bestower of happiness, prosperity, and fortune.
Through the practice of Vasudhārā at the *dvādaśānta*,
she should be known as the one who grants wealth and grain to the great-souled practitioner.
Emerging from the *kaṇḍa-cakra*, endowed with twelve rays,
this most terrible *kalā* (the wielder of arts), through its connection with the stroke of lightning,
O Goddess, brings down the hosts of *siddhas*; of this there is no doubt.
On such a Monday, conjoined with the sixteenth lunar digit (kalā),
she who is intent on reviving the dead instructs the wise man;
indeed, through the expansion of the wheel of desire and by means of that agitation, [she brings about the goal].

One brings this entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, under one's control. Having entered into the interior of the wheel of wind, by means of the yoga of the wandering bee, one can cause even mountains to tremble from their places; how much more so the army of an enemy?
Fierce and resembling Vajrapāṇi, she is the supreme goddess proclaimed by Kālacakra;
together with a sharp sword, she shall slay the entire host of enemies.

Having meditated upon the Goddess of gods, Kṛṣodarī, who performs all actions, who has arisen from the world through her own nature as peace, nourishment, subjugation, and attraction, and who has arisen filling the world with the manifestations of the splendor of her own nature— [The practitioner] should contemplate her.
These two are equal to the Goddess of the lords of gods, auspicious Siddhipratyaṅgirā;
for they accomplish whatever tasks are held in the mind here,
just as the thousand-syllabled Goddess took away the head of Brahmā.
Just as she is the Mistress of the Wheel of Thought, so too is the supreme Mistress of Laṅkā.
These [mantras] are proclaimed to consist of one thousand syllables;
this pair of *Pratyaṅgirās* bestows all accomplishments and is auspicious.
Or rather, since the reality has been explained according to its true nature, what more do you wish to ask?

Thus ends the tenth chapter, the ritual of Pratyaṅgirā, in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraccheda* section of the Vidyāpīṭha in the Bhairava-stream.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O mighty-armed one, saluted as the cause of all; wielder of the trident (marked with the crescent moon), intent upon your devotees;
the Goddess Matacakreśvarī, who wears a garland of a thousand syllables.
Likewise, O Lord, the Mistress of Laṅkā is adorned with a thousand syllables;
O Supreme Lord, please graciously explain her to me,
how she is joined with the secret yoga and endowed with the means of accomplishment.

O Lord of the gods of gods, O Destroyer of Tripura, speak to me out of your grace! O Lord of gods, having manifested the essence of virility and having ignited the lineage of Jvālinī, [offer] the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the sacrificial oblation (caru) to the east.
Mounted upon the lineage of Mahākālī, he spoke with a loud roar.
Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Mistress of Bhairava, to that which I have been urged by you."
The great secret, incomparable, which causes the dissolution of the universe,
which brings about immersion in an instant, and which dissolves the causal elements.
This ritual procedure is exceedingly fierce, a devourer of *bhūta* and *apasmāra* spirits;
it is the crusher of the evil dreams of the Kali age and the dispeller of calamities. It bestows all auspicious fortune, is the essence [of all rites], and is the consumer of the power of Mahāmāyā.
Now hear in brief the incomparable method for the divine [realization] of that which is complete,
peaceful, eternal, and characterized by imperishability;
which is eternally satisfied (or ever-content), pure, and beyond the reach of the means of valid cognition.

Of the all-pervading Lord Bhairava, whose nature is consciousness and supreme bliss, she is the totality (sakalā), rich in the expansion and unfolding of the supreme, consisting of creative potency (vīrya),
inlaid with a thousand rays, and garlanded by a thousand lords.
She is the sovereign of the wheel of a thousand powers, beautiful with a thousand gardens;
she churns a thousand *piṇḍas*, resplendent with a hundred thousand forms.
She is the great sinner who drinks the five [poisons], terrifying with a thousand falls.
Abounding in the blossoming of the five jewels, she is the sovereign of the lords of the five jewels;
she is the formidable one who seizes the five planets, the tearer asunder of the five knots,
the giver of the five, the remover of the five, and she whose garland is the lineage of leaders.
She is perfectly immersed in the Vedas, radiant with a thousand syllables;
she is Maheśvarī, established in the state of the intellect, Caṇḍī, Kāpālī, and Kālikā.
She is manifested through the fourfold division of speech by means of the sequential yoga.
Arising from the first conception of the Supreme, she is filled with the bliss of her own radiance;
devoid of all phenomenal expansion, she is waveless and beyond lineage (*niṣkulā*).
Then, adorned by the three powers, they behold her in her true form.
Therein, the triad consisting of will, knowledge, and action becomes contracted;
because it abides in a state of non-differentiation, I am indeed nothing other than pure consciousness.
Then that Goddess Gītā, the Mistress of the Kula, beholds forms;
for she is the pure Madhyamā, intensified by both Will and Knowledge.
O Goddess, from her, through the differentiation of manifestation, speech arises.
When that very same [power] is intensified by will, knowledge, and action, it is the supreme power (parā-kalā).
Even when it is in the state of articulated speech (vaikharī), because it bestows the fruit [of liberation], it is indeed called the "explosive" (sphoṭa) and is Vaikharī.
And when it is joined with the four [powers] within the interval of the preceding vitality (vīrya)—[the powers of] will, knowledge, action, and bliss—then...
In the wheel of light and bliss, variegated by the sun and moon, there is the sun;
its sun is there, and therein the moon; and that of the moon is there. These three are within the triad, and that shines eternally.
There, indeed, is the sky within the sky; when that sky has expanded,
and when [the body] vibrates there, both therein and not therein, then the wheel (cakra),
possessing the splendor of the seat known as mantra, unfolds.
It possesses a thousand syllables and a thousand eyes;
it is garlanded with a thousand suns, enriched by a multitude of a thousand rays, and resplendent with a thousand moons.
It bears individually the splendors of a thousand fires of the end of time.
The fivefold— that which has flowed forth and fallen into the five locations,
ascended into the cavern of the five objects, the Lord of the lords of the five jewels—
that mantra is incomparable and formidable, the devourer joined with the Sun.

I shall explain its extraction; listen, O Bhairavabhāminī! Having gone to a terrifying cremation ground, or else to a temple of the Mothers, or to the house of the Guru, O Īśānī, accompanied by a messenger and with a serene mind—
Having adorned her well and anointed her with sandalwood and agallochum, one should cause the two— the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*— who are surrounded by a garland of flowers, to tremble.
Having caused the *golaka* to flee from there and having rubbed the body of that *kuṇḍa*, [one should proceed].
Thereupon,
O slender-waisted one, having grasped that great substance with her mouth, she placed it in his mouth,
and then, having done so, she placed it back in her own mouth.
One should examine a vessel mixed with great *āluya* (lotus root);
with that, one should prepare the *argha* vessel which bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.
Then, one should worship the Great Goddess Mātrikā, the Mother of Mantras.
Having become one whose body is that of an Avadhūta and remaining in the state beyond conventional conduct,
the practitioner of mantra should spread out the Mātṛkā preceded by the eight groups [of consonants].
Having worshipped it with perfumes, incense, and so forth, as well as various garlands and offerings.
Then one should extract the supreme Vidyā, the Mistress of the Wheel of Thought (Matacakreśvarī).
Having first extracted the Savior (Tāraka), then Mahānārāyaṇī;
having extracted Puruṣa and Haṃsa, joined with Mukhadāraṇā.
The first [syllable] of the third [group], by its own nature, is without a vowel (asva) and is situated at the root;
it is Vāyu joined with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and marked with Gaṇeśa (the letter *ga*).
Then there is the one ending in Varuṇa (*va*) mounted upon that, and Fire (*ra*) marked with the three vowels (*i*, *u*, *m*).
This indeed consists of ten syllables and bestows the fruit of all desires.
It has a twice-born [letter] as its excellent form, Śakra [the letter *sa*] marked by three vowels,
the first of the fifth [class of consonants] in its own form, and the Person (*puruṣa*) situated in the auspicious lunar day.
The word *Gaṇeśān*, enriched with three dots (*bindus*), is the supreme five-syllabled [mantra];
this is proclaimed as the second. Now hear the third:
[the syllable] *Dviji* (or *Dvijihva*) mounted upon *Varuṇa* (Va), with its head (*m*) pressed down by the goad (*a*).
The syllable *Śakra* (Śa) joined with *Aṅkuśa* (U), followed by *Jihvīla* (Ra) marked with the three vowels (*Ā*,
*I*, *U*), then *Haṃsa* (Sa) conjoined with *Varuṇa* (Va), marked at the head with *Praṇava* (Oṃ).
Then the letter following *Cāpa* (Dha) alone, and *Vahni* (Ra) adorned with the three vowels (*Ā*, *I*, *U*).
The six-syllable word is taught as the characteristic of the entire collection;
having extracted the end of that which begins with *ṭha*, it is endowed with great delusion (*mahāmoha*).
The fourth word consists of two syllables and is endowed with *paśu* and *makṣaya*.
Having placed the solitary *puruṣa*, it is joined with *haṃsa* and *dāraṇa*.
The first part of this word begins with *ā*, while the second is devoid of its ornament.
One should give the first word beginning with *kāla*, overcome by delusion (*mohana*),

and the fifth word consisting of seven syllables, which is pure and begins with *soma*, combined with three vowels; having extracted the pure *indra*, [one places] *puruṣa* whose vehicle is a crane (*vaka*).
One should offer the bow joined with the *praṇava*, or the bow alone.
The face of the deity consists of the four-syllabled word marked by three vowels.
Again, having extracted Varuṇa, which possesses three vowels, it is of great power.

The seventh word consists of four syllables: it ends with *varuṇa* (the letter *va*), is preceded by *panadruḍha*, is accompanied by *mukhadāraṇa*, stands upon the fifth vowel (*ī*) of the prohibitive class (*niṣedha*), is preceded by *yonipūrva* (the letter *ya*), and is joined with three dots (*tribindu*). This indeed is the seventh word, measuring four syllables.
One should extract Śakra alone, preceded by the *yoni* (the letter *ai*) and the two vowels (*i* and *u*).
Gaṇeśa is situated in fire (*ra*), with its head mounted by the two vowels (*i* and *u*).
One should give Amṛta alone, accompanied by the three vowels (*a*, *i*, and *u*), as the prohibition.
The eighth syllable should be known as the fifth; this is the word that bestows great benefit.
One should again extract two syllables prior to this word:
the negation (na) surmounted by three vowels, and the nectar (amṛta) situated in the sixth position.
The *cāpādya* (bow-initial) alone should be given; the prohibition is marked by three vowels.
The ninth [mantra] shall consist of six syllables, and this fifth [mantra] is of great power.
Having extracted the *haṃsa* fourfold, it is joined with the "mouth-tearing" (*mukhadāraṇa*).
Amṛta and Niṣedha are variegated by the three Suns;
the tenth syllable is to be known as the foremost letter, the most excellent of the excellent.

One should extract the *puruṣa* (the letter *na*) alone; the *haṃsa* (the letter *sa*) adorned with two vowels (*ai*); the *vahnī* (the letter *ra*) preceded by *kāla* (the letter *ka*), conjoined with the *aiśvara* (the letter *i*), and then the *kevala* (the letter *ha*) alone. Then the *varuṇa* (the letter *va*) endowed with three vowels (*au*), which is the supreme five-syllabled word.
The eleventh has been declared to you, O slender-waisted one:
the *puruṣa* alone is to be given, joined with two vowels;
likewise, the *haṃsa* ending in *varuṇa* mounted upon *kāla*, also ending in two vowels.
One should give only the *niṣedha* (prohibition) joined with the five dots (*pañcabindu*) and the beginning of time (*kālādya*).
Again, there should be the mark of time (*kālāṅka*), which is the letter of Varuṇa marked by two vowels.
Both the nectar (*amṛta*) and the prohibition (*niṣedha*) are marked by three vowels.
This twelve-syllable word consists of two letters and is a great seat (pada).
Therefore, four *kalās* should be given; then one should give again the first [syllable] of the third [line].
This is the horse mounted upon the vital points (*marmas*), the Time conjoined with the venerable lunar day (*tithi*).
The beloved [mantra] consists of three vowels, the head [letter], and five syllables;
this thirteenth perfected [mantra] is the attractor of the three worlds.
Having again extracted the *puruṣa* [syllable] and the *prāṇa* [syllable] adorned with two vowels...
Furthermore, the first [syllable] from the third [group] should be given, along with the downward-pointing trident (śūla) and the Samardaka.
One should take Vāyu joined with the Praṇava, Gaṇeśa joined with Vahniveśa, and Varuṇa ending with [the syllable] Varuṇa; thus one should extract them as a single aggregate (piṇḍībhūta).
One should extract the fire-syllable (*vahni*) with three vowels on top and the short *ḍa* vowel;
then the fire-syllable, the infinite (*ananta*), and the fire-syllable again, struck by the head of *ḍa* and marked with the *bindu*.
Having done so, one should place the bow and then enclose it within two fire-syllables.
Together with the previously mentioned *prameya*, the *bhīmaśaṅku* is fivefold.
This sixteen-syllable *pada* is indeed the most excellent of all;
it is declared to be the fourteenth, which destroys the terrors of the three worlds.
One should extract those two [syllables] from the beginning of the word;
one should give the *haṃsa* alone, and place that which resides in its own self within the lunar [syllable].
O Dear One, one should give the first syllable as *kāla* (ka), followed by the solitary *vahni* (ra) joined with the auspicious lunar day (*tithi*, i.e., the number 15).
Then one should give the *candra* (ca) situated in the *piṇḍa* (the vowel *u*), topped by the three vowels (*e*).
This seven-syllabled word, O Beloved, is the fifteenth *pada*.
Furthermore, one should cause this pair of full vowels to be placed here again:
the fire-vowel (Ra) conjoined with the resonance (Nāda), and the water-vowel (Va) which is the prohibitor (Niṣedhaka).
Adorned with the three vowels, those two constitute the five-syllabled word that has been extracted.
This sixteenth word is the resonance of the wheel of the Rāviṇī;
it consists of *prāṇa* joined with the *bindu*, which is the nectar and the negator.
Adorned with the three vowels, these two constitute the supreme three-syllabled word.
O God and Goddess, the seventeenth [letter] is the illuminator of the central breath (*madhyaprāṇa*).
O God, Gajendra is situated in the mouth (*vaktra*), requested for the purpose of splitting the face.
Make the *haṃsa* itself the prohibition (*niṣedha*), adorned with the three vowels.
This is proclaimed as the eighteenth word, beginning with the letter *pū*.
One should extract the letter *pa* joined with *dāraṇā*, followed by the letter *va* alone.
Then comes the letter *a* joined with three vowels; this is the nineteenth, most excellent word.
O Supreme Goddess, one should extract the three-syllabled mantra which is filled with the destruction of the entire universe;
then, one should extract the *paśu* together with the *praṇava*, followed by the *haṃsa* alone;
then the twenty-first letter preceded by the vowel of the third musical note (*ṛ*), which is the syllable of prohibition (*ni*).
Having extracted the four-syllable [seed-mantra] adorned with the long double-tongued [visarga],

and again joined with the visarga, there is this supreme three-syllabled word. It begins with Gaṇeśa, is conjoined with the long vowels, and consists of the Haṃsa-mantra adorned with the three vowels.
This word should be given in two parts: the twenty-first [consonant] with four vowels,
the Vāruṇa [letter] (va) conjoined with three vowels, preceded by the Bow (cāpa) [letter] (jha) joined with Fire (ra),
and then the Vāruṇa [letter] alone, joined with the "mouth-torn" [syllable] (pha).
The horse-headed one with three suns for a crest, possessing four oceans and the supreme foot;
known as the twenty-two-fold [mantra], it brings an end to all that is evil.
O Sulocanā, the "double-tongued" (ja) and the "with-visarga" (haḥ) should be given twice;
then, joined with a long vowel, the "swan" (ha), radiant with three vowels,
should be made twice— these two excellent syllables constitute this six-syllabled word.
The twenty-third [syllable] should be known as that which cuts through the lineage of enemies.
It is the syllable Ananta (Ha), encased by fire (Ra) and adorned with the circle of the Bindu (M).
One should give the solitary Puruṣa (Sa), and the Haṃsa (Ha) embellished by two vowels (Ā and Ī).
One should extract the letter *va* (fire), which is preceded by *ka* (time) and conjoined with the eighth vowel (*ū*).
Then one should take the letter *va* (Varuṇa), conjoined with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), followed by the five vowels (*a-e-i-o-u*) and the crescent moon (*bindu*).
This is followed by the end of the trident (*kṣa*), and then the letter *va* (Varuṇa) mounted upon the elephant (*la*) and struck by the goad (*ha*).

The twenty-fourth word consists of the two syllables *amṛtam* and *niṣedham*, adorned with three vowels and joined with the eleventh letter [the nasal ṅa]. One should then extract the word *puruṣam*, followed by *haṃsam*, adorned with two vowels.
One should extract the letter *puruṣa* (pa) joined with *bindu* (m).
Then there is *amṛta* (sa) overcome by *dāraṇā* (r), followed by the solitary final letter of *varuṇa* (va).
Then *niṣedha* (kṣa) overcome by the three vowels (*ai*). This is the six-syllabled [mantra], the twenty-fifth.
This step is extremely fierce and grants the accomplishment of the *melāpa* immediately.
Having established the prohibition mounted upon the fifth, it is again to be taken as solitary.
This step should be made twofold, adorned with four syllables.
This twenty-sixth [syllable] indeed bestows the fruit of all desires.
Then, take the first of the fifth [group], mounted on fire (the letter *ra*), and place it upon the venerable lunar day (the letter *ti*).
Having extracted the solitary moon (*ca*), make its own nature twofold in syllables.
The number of syllables is twenty-seven in my verse, as before.
One should extract the *haṃsa* twice, then the seventh figure, the *puruṣa*,
and then the solitary *haṃsa* joined with the "mouth-opening" (*mukhadāraṇa*).
In the same way, having extracted that [syllable] from the womb and so forth, adorned with three vowels and belonging to Śakra,
it should be known as the incomparable six-syllabled twenty-eighth word.
Having drawn out the bow along with the arrow, one should again raise up that heroic power.
Extremely terrifying, reaching to the throat, adorned by three udumbara fruits,
and joined with the fire-bindu, these *piṇḍas* are like ten thousand suns.
The sixth [letter] and those beginning with the first [of their respective groups], ending with Varuṇa (va), should be given alone as they are pervaded by two vowels.
Then the letter beginning with the bow (ca) should be given alone; furthermore, one should extract the horse (ha) situated at the vital point (marmasthita).
Then one should take the bow conjoined with the goad (aṅkuśa), and subsequently extract the fire (ra) and the horse (ha).
Adorned with three vowels, those two constitute the supreme ten-syllable mantra.
It should be known as the twenty-ninth [mantra], which brings an abundance of enjoyments.
It begins with Gaṇeśa, includes the *praṇava* (oṃ), consists of two arms, and is established in Varuṇa.
Adorned with two vowels on its head and decorated with the three-syllabled fire (*vahni*),
this three-syllabled word is proclaimed as the thirtieth.
Time (*kāla*) should be given according to its own form, adorned with two vowels, [and] the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Adorned by that very [letter], beautified by the three vowels of fire (Ra),
it should be known as the thirty-first, the supreme four-syllabled word. Again, [the syllable] ending with the earring (Ku), joined with fire (Ra), is the vital breath (Ha) situated within time (Ka).
Having made the horse (the letter *ha*) adorned with two vowels and the [letter] *ya* embellished with three vowels,
this thirty-two-syllable word consists of three parts and is the most excellent of the excellent.
It is joined with *mukhadāraṇa* and the seventh [vowel] along with *kālahaṃsa*.
One should extract that supreme thirty-third syllable, ending with Varuṇa (Va), mounted upon that [same vowel], adorned with the three vowels of Fire (Ra),
and preceded by the Yoni (E), which is pervaded by three feet consisting of four syllables.
O Maheśvarī, the thirty-fourth supreme syllable is joined with *mukhadāraṇā* (mouth-tearing), followed by *kāla*, the *kṛṣāṇḍa* (the seed-syllable *ha*) presided over by the three vowels (*ai*).
This three-syllabled mantra, O Parameśvarī, bestows peace upon all children.
The eighth [letter] of the *vāruṇa* [group], preceded by the *ūṣman* [letters], is mounted upon a horse;
its face is adorned with three suns— this is the thirty-fifth syllable.
Adorned with three colors, it is the supreme destroyer of all misfortune.
Varuṇa and Vahni are joined with the terrible-faced one;
the swan is inlaid with three suns—the three-syllabled, supreme state.
The thirty-sixth syllable is proclaimed as your supreme perfection (*siddhi*).
The wind-syllable (*vāyavya*) is conjoined with two vowels, and its time is established once again.
One should then give the first of the third [group], its head conjoined with the seventh.
The horse-mantra, situated in the vital points, further refined and established for the propitiation of guests,
beautiful, adorned with three suns, consisting of six syllables, and supreme—
this thirty-seventh [mantra] should be known as that which causes the destruction of all enemies.
Again, having extracted the end of this [syllable], one should take Gaṇeśa (Ga), the Obstructor (Ni),
with its head conjoined by the seventh vowel (Ū), marked by the three vowels of the northwest (Vāyu),
known as the thirty-eighth syllable; this is the supreme three-syllabled word.
The syllable *āṃ* [is] water (*āp*) conjoined with two vowels; *vāhna* [is] fire (*vahni*) adorned by the auspicious lunar day (*tithi*);
[and] *hayatrisvara* [is] conjoined with three vowels. This supreme three-syllabled word, numbering thirty-nine, has been correctly revealed to you.
The Vāruṇa [letter] (va) is presided over by two vowels; the Vāyavya (ya) is alone.
Then the Vāruṇa (va) is mounted by Vāyu (ya), with its head (m) presided over by the seventh vowel.
This great three-syllabled pada should be known as the fortieth.
One should extract the syllable *Śakra* (Ś) alone, marked with the two vowels preceding the *Yoni* (Ī);
then the syllable *Kāla* (Ka), established upon the venerable lunar day (the letter *I*), beautiful and adorned with three vowels;
and finally the excellent four-syllabled word consisting of forty-one [units].
Furthermore, one should place the first [syllable] of the third [quarter], situated in the *padyamarman*, O Supreme Goddess. Having been pervaded by the *praṇava*,
one should again extract Gaṇendra, whose head is pervaded by the seventh [vowel].
That arm, ending with Varuṇa and situated there, is adorned with three vowels;
this six-syllable word is remembered as the forty-second.
Furthermore, Yama alone, adorned with two vowels,
preceded by the Yoni and joined with the sixth [letter] as the first, is likewise marked by that very [vowel].
Then Śakra and Niṣedha have their crests (mūli) occupied by three vowels.
The forty-third is to be known as the supreme six-syllable word.
One should extract the three: the Vāyavya, the Kālapuruṣa, and the Trident;
then the Medhya, which is established in nectar, followed solely by the Yoni.
The arm, with the two vowels raised, is indeed Śakra, the restrainer;
those two are adorned with three vowels, the supreme syllable of the god.
This forty-fourth [chapter] has been declared to you according to its true meaning.
One should extract only the arm [letter] occupied by the eighth [vowel] Kāla;
the Vāruṇa [letter] occupied by the seventh [vowel], its end, and that [group] combined together.
[Then] the arm [occupied by] three Sūryas [vowels], and the head [occupied by] the forty-fifth [consonant] with the five [vowels].
This five-syllabled word indeed bestows the siddhi of Mahābhairava.
O Supreme Goddess, the first of the third [group] and the second of the two [groups] are situated at the vital point (marmastha).
Again, that same pair, but with the seventh [vowel] added to the latter.
The sixty-fourth word known by me is "varuṇasthaṃ nadādyaṃ kṛṣāṇḍaṃ tṛsvarāṅkitam" (varuṇasthaṃ nadādyaṃ kṛṣāṇḍaṃ tṛsvarāṅkitam).
Again, [the next] is "kālaṃ tathā haṃsaṃ mukhadāraṇayānvitam" (kālaṃ tathā haṃsaṃ mukhadāraṇayānvitam).
The first syllable is *kāla*, followed by *kevala*, then again *vāha* situated upon *kālānala*;
then *caṃdra*, *trisūrya-mūrddhāna*, and finally the forty-seventh [syllable].
This great five-syllabled *pada* indeed bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).
Having extracted only the syllable *kāla* (ka), joined with the two vowels [e and i] to form *ke*,
and having again applied this same term (*ke*), one places it in the seventh position preceded by the *yoni* (the letter *m*).
Then, one places the fifth letter (*pa*) at the beginning, marked by the two vowels [e and i], and finally applies the *niṣedha* (the letter *ha*) situated therein.
One should extract the syllable beginning with *kāla* (ka), which is the Lord of the World (*bhuvaneśa*), joined with *medya* (ma) and adorned with three vowels;
this is the tenth syllable, the forty-first supreme word, exceeding the eight (*vasu*).
Thereafter, one should extract the nectar (*amṛta*) situated in Varuṇa (va), combined with the egg-born (*kṛṣāṇḍaja*, ka).
The wind [letter Ya], conjoined with the Praṇava; Gaṇeśa struck by the three vowels;
the nectar [letter Va] together with the five dots; and the Haṃsa situated in the seven vowels.
Then, the Cāpādi (the letter *ca*) alone, followed again by the Vāyavya (the letter *ya*) joined with two vowels (*ī*),
and the Niṣedha (the letter *ṣa*) alone should be given; then again that which resides in the Pādya (the letter *pa*),
and then the Yonipūrva (the letter *ya*) followed by the Vahni (the letter *ra*) adorned with three vowels (*ū*).
Indeed, this twelve-syllable mantra bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.
O Maheśvarī, this fifty-first word is declared to be the solitary one, wherein the double-tongued [S] is pressed by the goad [H] and rests upon Varuṇa [V].
Śakra joined with Aṅkuśa, then again the first one without Aṅkuśa;
Śakra with three suns on its head, and the fifth one alone;
Varuṇa traversed by the three vowels, and Gaṇendra situated in Vahni.
The *haṃsa* is the seventh head; the eight-syllable word is supreme.
The fiftieth [syllable] should always be known as that which brings about the gateway to all prosperity.
It should be applied four times and in three ways, with *kṣaya* and likewise enclosed by fire (*vahni*).
The fierce goad (*aṅkuśa*) is joined with the *bindu* and the *ḍambara*, being fivefold. It is the radiant eleven-syllable mantra, the fifty-first word.
Furthermore, it is Time (*kāla*) alone, which is the *raṃ*, the demoniacal [seed] possessing two vowels.
One should give the negation (ṃ) alone, followed by the fire-syllable (ra) topped with two vowels (e);
then the negation situated at the beginning of the fifth [group] (ma), mounted on fire (ra), possessing great power;
then the third at the beginning (ga) alone, the fire-syllable (ra), time (ka), and the goad (ṅa).
Furthermore, there is *varuṇa* alone, and again *niṣedha* alone;
then *cāpādya*, and likewise the five *piṇḍas* marked by the seventh.
That ten-syllable *pada* is indeed situated as the fifty-second.

Again, there is *kāla* (k), *kevala* (e), *vaṃśa* (ṣ), that which has two vowels as its crest (*dvisvaramaulinam*), *kuṇḍala* (m), the seventh mark (*saptamāṅka*) which is preceded by *yoni* (bh) and joined with itself (*svapiṇḍita*),
struck on the head by *aṅkuśa* (h), and again *kevala* (e) born from fire (r).
The syllable *ta* joined with the goad (*aṅkuśa*) and *va*, with *ru* as a restrainer;
the two [syllables] whose heads are stepped upon by the three vowels form the eight-syllabled auspicious *pada*.
This indeed consists of fifteen syllables and is the sovereign of all melāpakas.
O Maheśvarī, one should divide the syllable *haṃsa*—which has the color of prohibition—into two parts.
This four-syllabled word, O beloved, is the fifty-fourth.

The fifty-fifth [syllable] should be known as the Great Wrathful One (*mahākrodha*), likewise slow (*manda*), conjoined with the auspicious lunar day of Kālaśrī; it is beloved, has three suns upon its head, consists of four vowels, and is the supreme word that grants the accomplishment of all unions.
One should utter the double-tongued [seed-syllable] and the goad, joined together as a single mass.
Likewise, one should utter Indra joined with the goad, and the prohibition alone;
then the prohibition with the three suns upon its head, which is the supreme word consisting of four syllables.
This is indeed the fifty-sixth [chapter], characterized by the collection of all [mantras].
Again, preceded by the *yoni* [syllable], one should give the *Kālavaktra* with the fifth [vowel];
the Lord of Gaṇas (*Gaṇendra*), mounted upon fire, struck on the head by the *ḍambare* [syllable].
The fifty-seventh word is Vāruṇa, occupied by the seventh [vowel],
consisting of four syllables, greatly radiant, and bestowing sovereignty over the three worlds.
Vāruṇa is mounted upon Vāyu and its head is pierced by an *aṅkuśa*.
Having extracted Śakra alone, preceded by Yoni and accompanied by the seventh; the solitary Kevalin, preceded by Yoni and accompanied by the fifth;
Megha situated at the vital point (marmasthita), and again Śakra adorned with the seventh.
The fifty-eighth should be known as the supreme seven-syllable *pada*.
Again, having extracted *kāla*, one should take *haṃsa* adorned with two vowels;
then *kāla* at the beginning, followed by the fourth [vowel] as the head, and *kāla* beautified by the seventh [vowel].
The four-syllabled mantra is proclaimed, with the sixth syllable designated as "exclusive" (ekānta).
Furthermore, regarding this very king of mantras, one should extract the first three phonemes;
then, having extracted "Kāla" together with the goad (sāṅkuśa), it is established with the qualities ending in the trident (śūlānta).
The seventh [syllable] is to be joined; the sixth syllable is the sixtieth word.
Again, the first three [syllables], then Kāla alone, preceded by Yoni and joined with Vahni, and struck at the head by Praṇava.
Having extracted only the *dvīpa*, likewise the *śrītithistha* and the *antaka*,
the lovely seventh head, and the eight-syllabled supreme word—
this sixty-first [chapter], O Goddess, has been correctly revealed in nine ways.
The double-tongued one mounted upon Varuṇa, Śakra adorned with three vowels;
the first of the five, the solitary one ending in Varuṇa, joined with three suns. (81b)
One should place the arm together with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and joined with the venerable lunar day (*tithi*).
Then, having again established the *vāruṇa* [syllable] alone, preceded by the *yoni* and joined with the seventh,
one should place the first of the fifth [group] and subsequently cause it to reside within the fire.
O Goddess, the sixty-second word consists of eight syllables and bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).
Again, having extracted *kāla* (k), [place] *prāṇa* (ha) adorned with two vowels (*ai*).
Make the first of the third [group], the solitary one (*kevalin*), [the letter] *megha* (gha), situated at the vital point (*marman*).
One should again give the first letter of the third [vowel] with its head stepped upon by the goad (aṅkuśa).
Then, the horse (ha), which has grown from the venerable lunar day (ti) and is situated at a vital point (marman);
then the seventh vowel (u) with its head stepped upon by the seventh [vowel] (u)—this is the supreme word consisting of seven syllables.
The sixty-third [chapter] is the Great Fierce One, which bestows many wonders and accomplishments.
O Goddess, having extracted from this very [mantra] the first four syllables,
one should then append the fourth [syllable] joined with "Mukhadāraṇā."
Śakra, with three suns upon its head, is the supreme five-syllabled word.
It should be known as the sixty-fourth [mantra], which brings peace to all beings.
Preceded by the Yoni, marked with three suns, it is joined with the goad (aṅkuśa).
The fifth [letter] with the first [vowel], accompanied by the *praṇava*; the third [letter] with the first [vowel], well-combined;

then the two [letters] situated in the "glorious lunar day" (*śrītithi*); thereafter, that which is situated in "time" (*kāla*) preceded by "immortality" (*amṛta*); then the "womb" (*yoni*) preceded by the "two-vowel mark," followed by "fire" (*vahni*) and "cloud" (*megha*). One should extract it thus.
These two, adorned with three suns, constitute the sixty-fifth word.
It consists of eight syllables, is greatly radiant, and bestows the accomplishment of happiness and good fortune.
One should extract *haṃsa*, *soma*, again *haṃsa*, and again *soma*.
The sixty-sixth syllable is the supreme pada;
it is the negation (niṣedha) ascended to the seventh [note], beginning with the fifth, and condensed within itself.
This pada should be made twofold, each consisting of four syllables as before.
O Goddess, this sixty-seventh [chapter] has indeed been revealed to you;
furthermore, [it concerns] Time, the Kevalin, the Vital Breath adorned with the Goad.
The fifth [consonant] with the first [vowel], mounted on fire (R) and adorned above by the Praṇava (Oṃ);
Indra (L) together with the Praṇava, followed by the Yoni (Ā) and Vāyu (I);
the fifth [consonant] with the first [vowel] and fire (R), joined with the "mouth-torn" (E).
One should extract the nectar (Amṛta) by means of negation (Niṣedha), preceded by the womb (Yoni);
then [extract] Vahni with three vowels as its head. This ten-syllable word, O highly fortunate one, is the sixty-eighth; it is thus described as the granter of all desires.
O Goddess, one should again extract its first pair of syllables.
[Then] the Fire-syllable established in the Abode of Śrī, the Bow joined with three vowels,
and then the Fire and Varuṇa, O Goddess, each separately and individually.
Again, one should give the nectar (*amṛta*) with the goad (*sāṅkuśa*), followed by the moon (*soma*) situated in the seventh position;
then Gaṇeśāna stationed at the beginning of *kāla*, with its head surmounted by the *praṇava* (oṃ);
the double-tongued (*dvijihva*) alone should be given, and the prohibition (*niṣedha*) struck by the three vowels.
The eleventh syllable is a non-word (apada), and the sixty-ninth syllable is a word.
Again, the sixth syllable and so forth, ending with the three vowels, is the syllable *v* alone;
this word is to be performed in two ways, as the auspicious seventieth of the fourth [section].
Again, O Beloved, having extracted Varuṇa and Kāla once more,
having extracted these two in this manner, [one obtains] the seventy-first vowel, which is the fourth letter,
conjoined with the trident and the goad, and is simply the first of the fifth [group].
Having extracted only the *vāyu* [the letter *ya*], divide this word into two parts.
This supreme word of four syllables consists of seventy-two [units] and is established in the abode of Śrī; by that very [word], the hair on the head is overcome.
Make this third word, "kevalin," into two parts;
this four-syllable word is the seventy-second word [of the sequence].
The syllable *va* alone should be given, and *indra* should be placed after *gaṇapati*.
This seventy-fifth word is to be made twofold;
it shall consist of four syllables and is the destroyer of the ends of the three worlds.
One should extract the nectar situated in the *kuṇḍala*, pervaded by the *praṇava*.
Simply extract the moon and divide this word into two;
for this word of four syllables consists of seventy-six [units].
Having given the Lord of the Gaṇas (Ga) alone, followed by the one situated on the double-tongued serpent (Sa), and the son of Kṛśānu (Ra);
this [sequence] should be made twofold.
Then the forty-fourth [letter], the trident (Śa) endowed with the sixth vowel (Ū), and the cloud (Va) marked by the head of fire (Ra).
This word is to be divided into two parts: the fourth vowel (Ū) and the seventy-eighth [consonant] (KṢA).
Having extracted the *kāla* (the letter M) alone, together with the *haṃsa* (H), one should then take the solitary *kāla* (M) again, marked by the *praṇava* (OṂ).
The negation (niṣedha) established by time, accompanied by a long head (m),
and again this initial *ca* (cāpādi) should be given as a negation struck by three vowels (*trisvarāhata*).
This should be known as the eighty-first [syllable], the supreme seven-syllabled word.
[The letter] ending with Varuṇa (va), mounted upon Kāla (r), joined with that very same [letter] as a goad (a);
then again, the Lord of Knots (gha) alone, followed by the Vāruṇa [letter] (va) struck by a goad (a);
then Amṛta (sa) and Niṣedha (kṣa), with their crowns overcome by the three vowels (i, u, ṛ).
The eightieth word should be known as having six syllables and bestowing all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).
Again, having extracted *kāla* (the letter *ka*), it is adorned with *prāṇa-aṅkuśa* (the letter *ha*).
The first of the sixth [group] is mounted upon fire (*ra*) and marked by the head of the abode of fire (*ma*).

The first of the fifth [group] is with the goad (sāṅkuśa) and is situated in the nectar-wind (amṛtavāyu). The one beginning with the "crow's voice" (kākavācādi) is fire (vahni), ending with the trident (śūla), and is situated in *ka*.
Its head is traversed by the three vowels and adorned by that very same [cloud].
The beautiful nine-syllable mantra is reckoned to consist of eighty-one [units].
One should extract *haṃsa*, then *candra*, again *haṃsa*, and again *candra*. This becomes the eighty-fourth word, which effects spiritual absorption (*āveśa*).
Place the fifth letter ending with *varuṇa* (ṇa) in the jar (*kuṃbha*), situated in the first syllable (*kha*).
It is joined with *kāla* (ka), *śrī* (śrī), and the lunar day (*tithi*), and is beautiful, residing in the seventh position.
This word, consisting of eighty-three and four letters, bestows great purpose.
Having again extracted Amṛta (Sa) and Vahni (Ra) together with Aṅkuśa (U),
one should extract Mahāvāyu (Ya) situated in the Śrī-tithi (the ninth vowel, Ū), followed by Cāpa (Pha) alone.
That same [Pha] joined with Aṅkuśa (Ū) and adorned with the three vowels (Ā, I, U) is Vahni (Ra).
(83a) O Goddess, this supreme seven-syllable mantra, which brings about all prosperity, is the eighty-fourth [chapter], which is not to be recited together with the *asvata*.
Having extracted only the letter *kā* adorned with the goad (*aṅkuśa*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one should extract only the letter *la*,
together with that [goad], as the vital point (*marman*). Then,
there is the fifty-eighth word, the fire (*vāhna*), adorned with three vowels.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, this five-syllabled mantra bestows the siddhis of the Mahāḍāmara.
It should be given as the venerable *tithi-kevala*; one should extract the syllable of Indra (Śakra) situated in the sixth position.
One should take the *yonipūrva* (the letter preceding the *yoni*) which is the solitary (*kevalin*), followed by the third [vowel] and the second [consonant].
Then, one should extract the syllable beginning with the fifth [consonant], established in the [fifth] vowel, marked by the seventh [vowel].
The sixty-eighth word is to be known as consisting of the letters of Kāma’s arrows, ending in a *kuṇḍala* (an anusvāra), situated in the seventh [position]; this is the *prāṇakevala*.
Place the letter *ca* (the bow) at the beginning of *mṛtyu* (the death syllable), and then place the letter *śrī* (the auspicious one) according to the lunar day (*tithi*).
The "double-tongued" (*dvijihva*) shall be the seventh mark; the fourth letter is the supreme word (*padottama*).
This is to be known as the seventy-eighth [syllable], illuminating all directions and the sky.
Again, [one should place] Kāla, whose head is struck by the goad (Aṅkuśa),

together with Varuṇa accompanied by Vāyu, topped with the second vowel (Ā). By that same [method], one should likewise place Śakra (Indra) and Samīraṇa (Vāyu) situated on the auspicious lunar day (the letter Ṅa).
Having raised only the bow, one should raise only Kāla;
having placed Megha at the vital point, one should strike the head with Trisūrya.
One should take the first of the five as Kevalin, and [the letter] ending with Varuṇa as Kevala.
Having extracted the fire-mantra (VAH) in two parts, the first is illuminated by the fourth [letter] (Ū), and the second is conjoined with the seventh [letter] (SA).
This supreme mantra of eighty-eight syllables consists of twelve letters;
it is most fierce, the devourer of the great serpent-king of the Kula.
Having extracted Nārāyaṇa, one should place the seventh [vowel] Niṣedha;
then again, preceded by Yoni, Varuṇa alone should be given.
Again, preceded by Yoni, Puṇyavṛddhi mounted upon Vahni, together with the seventh [vowel], should be placed.
The ninety-ninth [mantra] consists of five syllables; it is the most excellent among the best of foot-verses.
It contains Varuṇa situated in the wheel of Vāyu, with its head struck by the Praṇava.

One should extract the syllable *puruṣa* as it is traversed by two vowels, and the syllable *soma* alone. Then one should extract *granthīśa* as it is traversed by three vowels, which is the fourth letter, the supreme state.
This is the ninety-first [syllable], unknowable, which causes the expansion of the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoman*).
One should extract the very first syllable of this word;
having extracted only "Kāla" (Ka) and only that which ends with "Varuṇa" (Va),
one should again extract only the fourth letter marked by fire (Ra) from the head.
The first [syllable] of the third [group], accompanied by the goad (saṃ), radiant with the fire-seed (ra) and the three vowels (i, u, ṃ);
then the cloud (va) marked by that [same triad]—this is the supreme eight-syllabled mantra.
O Vīreśī, this alone has been correctly proclaimed as the crest-jewel (avataṃsa).
One should again extract the syllable *kāla* (ka), adorned with the goad of breath (*prāṇa-aṅkuśa*).
It is joined with the nectar (*amṛta*) and the bindu, and embellished with the third vowel (*i*).
Before this, one should further place the pure essence of nectar (*sudhāsāra*) alone.
The Lord of the Knots, presided over by the three vowels, is the supreme six-syllable word.
This is the ninety-second [mantra], situated in the center of the womb of the union.
Furthermore, the first two syllables of this very king of words—
Having formed the bow (ca) together with the bindu (m), one should extract the other [syllables] as follows:
the letter preceded by Soma (s), marked by the goad (a), situated upon the moon (u), and established in the wind (ya);
then the Yogī (o), the Kevalin (au), and Fire (ra), radiant with three vowels.
The seventh head of Śakra, with seven syllables, is the extracted *pada*;
O Goddess, it consists of ninety-three [syllables] and bestows the attainment of lordship over the *cakras*.
It has two tongues, is mounted upon Varuṇa, and its head is adorned with a goad.
Indra together with that same [letter], then Soma situated in Vāyu; then Varuṇa alone, followed by Yoni, and then Aṅkuśa mounted on Fire;
this is the seventy-fourth word.
O fortunate one, the five-syllable mantra is renowned as the bestower of the siddhis of Śiva.
Again, the first [syllable] beginning with the womb (yoni) should be given, then the fire (vahni) alone;
again, O Goddess, one should give the final trident (śūla) preceded by the womb (yoni).
Again, the fifth [letter] is *kāla* (the letter *ka*), beautiful and radiant with three vowels;
this five-syllabled word, numbering ninety-five, has been thus proclaimed. (84a)
O Goddess, one should again fashion the fifth Gaṇendra situated there;
having placed him at the end of the bow (the letter *ca*), place him again within the fire (*ra*).
Having added the fire (*ra*) together with the Praṇava (*oṃ*), [place] the nectar (*a*) and so forth alone.
The syllable *megha* (me), with three vowels as its head, becomes the six-syllabled *pada*;
it is five-syllabled, possessing a terrible form, and capable of destroying the three worlds.
Then, the *haṃsa* (haṃ) mounted upon the seventh [vowel], followed again by the bow (*dha*) alone.

O Goddess of the Gods, having combined the letter of Vāyu (ya) as it is pressed by the goad (a), the face of Mahākāla (ma), and the letter Caṇḍa (ca) into one, one should extract the Leader of the Letters (the syllable *yamcam*).
Then, [one should take] the double-tongued (pha) alone, and again the first of the third [vowel-series] (u) together with the goad (a).

O Goddess, the ninety-seventh [mantra] consists of fire (ra), a cloud (va) marked with three vowels, and the supreme eight-syllabled lotus; it causes the heart-lotus to blossom. Again, having extracted nectar (sa), one places fire (ra) established in Varuṇa (va).
The first [syllable] is *kāla* (k) together with the sixth (*au*), and the first of the fifth group (*pa*) alone;
likewise, the first of the ninth (*ta*) and *kāla* (k), marked with three vowels, followed by the Lord of Knots (*granthīśa*:
*ma*). This seven-syllabled word, ending in *aṣṭa* (a) and *nava* (na), is thus proclaimed.
Again, take *prāṇa* and *granthīśa*; make this pair of words twofold.
This four-syllabled, formidable word is the ninety-ninth word.
O Goddess, one should extract *mahākuṇḍalakuṇḍeśa* three times.
Enveloped by the great fire, adorned with the circle of the bindu, it consists of four kalās; thereafter, the formidable Śaṅku is fivefold.
This nine-syllable pada is proclaimed as the hundredth.
This is the supreme essence of all mantras, which effects instantaneous possession.
Having again extracted the *paśu* [the seed-syllable], conjoined with the *prāṇa-aṅkuśa* (the goad of the vital breath),
it should be given preceded by the *yoni* (the letter *m*) and struck by the *aṅkuśa* (the letter *j*), being the first of the sixth [vowel].
This [syllable] is marked by that [bindu], and again it is the immortal, the absolute.
(84b) One should give the absolute Niṣadha, accompanied by Soma and the bindu.
That [mantra] has its arrows grown together within, its hair-tufts traversed by the three vowels,
the seventh syllable being the increase of merit (*puṇyavṛddhi*), followed by the four *kalās* of the deity,
obstructed by the *bhīma-śaṅku*, and it is that supreme *pada* consisting of twelve syllables.
These one hundred and one words of yours have been proclaimed.
One should extract those two which precede this very king of words;
one should extract the *praṇava*, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and the *piṇḍī-bhūtas*.
The letter Ka joined with the goad (Ra), Kāla (Ma) together with its friend (Sa) and the fifth vowel (Ū);
the double-tongued (Pha) overcome by the goad (Ra), followed by nectar alone (A).
Again, negation alone (Ha), then nectar again with the bindu (M).
The nectar (amṛta) marked with three vowels, and the bow standing with an arrow;
then the fifth [vowel] at the beginning, marked with seven, and again four morae (kalās) should be given;
joined with Bhīma and Śaṅku, there are ten and three syllables.
And one hundred and two words have been proclaimed for you, O fair-faced one. Again, the pair of syllables preceded by *yonis* (the letter *i*) and accompanied by the goad (*sāṅkuśa*),
having extracted *śakra* (the letter *e*) alone, one should extract the horse (*vāhana*, the letter *u*) along with the goad.
Then one should extract the syllable *taraṃḍi*, which is pervaded by the three vowels and situated in fire (*ra*).
At the end of the word, one should extract the four-syllabled *bhīmaśaṅku*.
This is declared to be the excellent hundred words consisting of one hundred and three syllables.
One should extract Varuṇa ending with the letter *m* (va), marked with three vowels (*ī*), and then Varuṇa alone;

then one should extract Prāṇa alone, preceded by the Bow (*cāpa*) and conjoined with the seventh vowel (*ū*). Furthermore, one should extract Vāhana situated on the Bow and joined with the goad (*aṅkuśa*).
The bow, the three vowels, the head, fire, and the clouds—these two [groups] placed upon the three suns;
O Goddess, one should join them together once at the end of the first and last [syllables].
This ten-syllable foot consists of one hundred and four [units].
Having extracted the fifth vowel, marked with the seventh [consonant],
preceded by the bow [the letter *j*], and surmounted by three vowels, one should give the Lord of Knots (*granthīśa*) alone.
The Yoni (L), preceded by Vahni (R), and Haṃsa (S) standing separately; then Amṛta (S) mounted on Vahni (R), followed again by Varuṇa (V) alone;
then the first of the sixth group (Ś) situated in the Śrī-tithi (the ninth letter, Ū), and finally Amṛta (S) as the seventh.
One should again arrange the two final syllables at the beginning of this word;
this word, consisting of seventeen syllables, is renowned as bestowing great benefit.
In brief, it is said to contain one hundred and five syllables.
O Goddess, the Mistress of the Gods, one should cause the third [syllable] to be placed here once again.
Then, perform the prohibition situated in the bow (ca) and so forth, and again mount it upon fire (ra).
Then, preceded by the womb (ya), with the praṇava (oṃ), and the lunar (sa), place it again in the wind (ya).
One should place the letter *Śrī* (Ś), the letter situated on the lunar day (*Ti*, *i*), the great wind (*Vā*, *va*), and the fifth from the beginning (*Pa*, *pa*) together with the goad (*Ku*, *u*).
Adorned with the bindu, one should then take the letter ending in Varuṇa (*Va*, *a*) along with the fifth (*Pa*, *pa*).
Then, the Lord of the Knots (*Granthīśa*, *Tha*) conjoined with the three vowels (*Ī*, *Ū*, *Ū*), and again fire (*Ra*) situated in time (*Ka*, *a*).
Śakra is the seventh, undivided; indeed, the two preceding [syllables] are likewise. This twelve-syllable word consists of one hundred and twenty-six [syllables].
O Goddess of the Gods, this has been declared to you as auspicious and bestowing nourishment upon all.
One should extract the seed-syllable of Time (*kālabīja*), the solitary one, the sound (*nāda*) accompanied by sound;
then the first of the sixth [vowel] established in Fire, and Śakra alone.
One should extract Vāyu joined with the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and Gaṇendra situated in the knot.
Having placed the head of the third vowel, one should extract Varuṇa;
the first of the sixth [group] situated on the ninth auspicious lunar day (Śrītithi), together with the first of the nectar (Amṛta) and the seventh.
One should again extract the two ends of the beginning at the end of this word.
The eleventh syllable is indicated as the seventh pada.
One should extract the "arm" situated in the fifth [pada], beginning with the fifth;
having divided that into two syllables, one should again make the first and the last [syllables] joined.
At the end of each foot, O Maheśānī, is the supreme six-syllable word.
This [mantra] of one hundred and eight syllables has been declared to you according to its true meaning.
The first [syllable] from the sixth [group], joined with fire (ra), is the nectar situated on the circle of the head (muṇḍala).
Having then placed the venerable lunar day (ti) therein, one should extract the fire (ra) alone.
This word should be made twofold, and then the resonance (nāda) should be made threefold.

O Goddess, one should extract the syllable Kuṇḍala, which is encased by Fire (Ra), mounted on the sixth vowel (Ū), and endowed with the Bindu (Ṃ). Then one should extract Bhīmaśaṅku, encased by Fire (Ra) and accompanied by the Visarga (Ḥ); this word is said to be threefold and exceedingly terrible.
It is remembered as consisting of one hundred and nine syllables, radiant with thirteen vowels.
Having extracted the pure *kāla* together with the *nāda*,
[one places] the *amṛta* situated at the beginning of the fifth [vowel], resting upon the fire and the sign of the zodiac (*rāśi*).
One should extract the Fire (Ra) with two vowels on its head (Ī), marked by the seventh of the double-tongued ones (Sa);
then Varuṇa (Va) and the end of Varuṇa (U)—these two joined together.
Then the Fire (Ra) with three vowels on its head (Ū), and the Bhīma-pile (Śa) twice again.
This nine-syllable mantra is indeed remembered as having one hundred and ten [syllables].
Again, one should extract only the syllable *kāla* (the letter *k*) with the seventh vowel (*ū*) as its head.
[One should also extract] the syllable *śra* marked by the seventh vowel (*ū*).

Again, there is the time consisting solely of *nāda*, not joined with *āda* and *anāda*. Again, there is the time distinct from *nāda*, joined with the seventh [vowel], which is four measures (*catuṣkala*). Then, one should extract Bhīmaśaṅku once more.
O fair-browed one, I have explained to you this ten-syllable *pada*, which consists of one hundred and eleven [units] and which brings about a body like a cloud. Furthermore,
[the syllable] *kā* is distinguished by the sound (*nāda*) and divided by the seventh [element], wind (*vāyu*).
Then, form Varuṇa and that which ends with him (the letter *ra*) into a single mass.
Again, [place] Vahni and Varuṇa, adorned with three vowels;
likewise, [place] that which begins with the bow (the letter *ja*), joined with Vāta, and situated in the ninth lunar day (the letter *na*).
The fifth [letter] and the first [letter], preceded by the womb (the vowel *u*), are declared to be joined together.
[This forms] Amṛta (the letter *ma*) accompanied by the long [vowel], which is Ananta (the letter *na*) struck by the seventh [vowel, *e*].
