Furthermore, perform the same at the end of this word as was done for the two preceding letters.

(86a) O fair-limbed one, this station of yours, which is proclaimed as having eleven syllables and being incomparable— exceeding [that] by twelve— is a hundred and twenty-two syllables; it possesses great power.
Again, having extracted Ananta (Ha), then the sixth [vowel] alone (Ū);
again Vāyu (Ya) alone; then Cāpa (Dha) situated on the sacred lunar day (Ti, E);
Fire (Ra) adorned with three vowels (Ā, Ī, Ū); and the fifth [consonant] (Pa) preceded by the goad (A).
Then, having separated it with a *bindu*, one should extract the first and last parts again.
Thus, the word consisting of eight syllables, numbering one hundred and thirteen, is extracted.
O Goddess, one should likewise place the fourth digit after the letter *kā* (the first of the word).

Again, one should extract the seventh vowel, the *paśu*, the *nāda*, the wind (*vāyu*) with the seventh vowel, and the *nāda* joined with three vowels; from this, one should take the first syllable. Again, the *nāda* marked by three vowels, and again the *deva* consisting of four parts.
Place the *yoni* first, then mount it upon fire; again, place it in the sixth position.

This great seed-syllable (*mahābīja*), pierced by the *bindu*, is the formidable *śaṅku*. Furthermore, this eleven-syllabled mantra, when joined with the thirteenth [vowel], becomes one hundred and thirteen syllables.
Now these words salute you, the Lord of the gods of gods:
the primordial food, mounted upon fire, marked by the swelling of the Bindu;
having extracted Time alone, together with the Nāda, endowed with Nāda.
O Goddess of the gods, having first given the third [syllable], one should extract the cloud (the letter *ga*).
O Goddess of the gods, [one should take] the wind (*ya*) mounted upon the vital point (*ma*), adorned with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*).
Then, joined with that, [one takes] Gaṇeśa (*ga*), marked by the abode of fire (*ra*), and preceded by Varuṇa (*va*).
The deity Vahni, conjoined with Tripura, is again four-syllabled;
Bhīmaśaṅku is fivefold, and the deity is again four-syllabled.
This sixteen-syllable word is indeed the most supreme among the supreme.
One hundred and fourteen [verses] have been declared to you according to their true meaning.
Again, having extracted *kāla* together with *haṃsa* and *nāda*;
then again, *kāla* alone at the beginning, and once more situated as *soma-kāla*.
Its head is pervaded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ), its beginning is the letter *ka*, and it is situated upon a bow.
It is the well-established Kālāgnirudra, joined with the two vowels [i and u], making the syllable *śukra*.
The first of the fifth [group] (*pa*) is used alone, and the one ending in Varuṇa (*va*) is also used alone.
The fire [letter] (ra) is conjoined with the fourth vowel (ī), and again joined with the goad (aṅkuśa, i);
it is placed at the end of the trident (the letter sa) and mounted upon the Gaṇa (the letter la), conjoined with the seventh [vowel] (u).
It is declared to consist of eleven syllables and one hundred and fifteen [repetitions].
This *pada* is proclaimed as the illuminator of all prosperity.
The first consists of five [syllables], joined with fire (the letter *ra*) and topped by the letter *e*.
One should extract Indra (I), enriched with the Praṇava (Oṃ), preceded by Yoni (M), and joined with Savāyu (V);
then Ma, Ma, joined with the goad (A), followed by Kāla alone (U).
Then Vahni (R) joined with the seventh (Ū), situated in Varuṇa (VA), and that which is at the beginning (A).
O one worshipped by the best of gods, one should perform the rite adorned with the three vowels and the fire;
the eight-syllabled word is radiant, numbering exactly one hundred and sixteen.
Again, [one should recite] Kāla, Kevalin, Nāda, and that which is endowed with Nāda.
One should extract the Lord of the Knot (the letter *ga*), as well as Fire (*ra*) alone preceded by the Yoni (*i*).
Likewise, one should extract Indra (*la*), which is the first of the sixth [group] and is conjoined with the Goad (*u*).
One should extract the Prohibition (*kṣa*), which resides at the beginning of the fifth [group] and is situated above the Wheel of Fire (*ra*).
The sixth [letter] with the first, accompanied by the sixth and adorned with three vowels;
the fifth alone as the beginning, which is Ananta, and that likewise [as] the end.
The double-tongued [letter] (Ṣa) pressed by the goad (U), and Soma (Sa) and Varuṇa (Va) separately.
Again, one should extract this very first [syllable] from the sixth and that which has ascended to the seventh.
The seventh mark is the Great Wind (mahāvāta), the most supreme state.
This peerless mantra consists of eighteen syllables and comprises one hundred and seven units.
Therefore, one should extract the second from that word, and then again three from the first; O Goddess of the God of Gods, one should extract these from this auspicious and excellent word.
O Goddess, one should extract Gaṇendra seated upon fire and holding a goad.

Furthermore, one should repeatedly extract the nectar alone, and then the trident. The nectar is established in time; it is fire, radiant with three vowels. This consists of eighteen syllables and eight words, totaling one hundred and eighteen.
Again, there is Kāla, Kevalin, Nāda, resplendent with the three tones;
Amṛtādya, Sāṅkuśa, Amṛta, and Niṣedhaka. Preceded by Yoni, situated in the Śrītithi, Kāla is situated in that which precedes it.
One should extract the great seed-syllable marked by the fourth [vowel], accompanied by the goad and fire;
it ends with the trident, is pervaded by the *praṇava*, and is situated above Gaṇeśa.
The first [syllable] from the sixth [group], alone; then Varuṇa again, marked with three vowels.
Then Amṛta at the beginning, mounted on the Moon (Candra), ending with Varuṇa and alone.
Then Vahni, conjoined with the fourth vowel, and that joined with the seventh.

This king of words, possessing great strength and prowess, has been declared to consist of one hundred and nineteen syllables, ten and fifteen each. Again, having extracted the syllable *kāla* (time), it is endowed with the sound *nāda*.
Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa should be given, followed by the trident (śūla) conjoined with the Praṇava;
then the seventh [letter], the great fire (mahāvahni), and Varuṇa adorned at the end.
Again, the third letter of fire—this is the seven-syllabled word.
This one hundred and twenty [letters] has been declared to you according to their true meaning.
One should extract the first of the five, mounted upon Varuṇa, with its head struck by Bindu;
specifically, one should extract Śakra alone from the top of the fourth.
One should extract the syllable *va* alone, followed by *ru*, *na*, *ma*, and *ṅkuśabhedita*.
Then one should extract the syllable *haṃsa* joined with the seventh [vowel, *ū*], forming a word of six syllables.
Thus, one hundred and twenty-one words have been proclaimed for you.
One should further extract the *paśu* (the letter *va*), which is pierced by the *nāda* (the letter *ra*) with the *nāda*;
the *śūla* (the letter *ha*) conjoined with the *praṇava* (the letter *o*), and the *vahni* (the letter *ra*) alone.
Then one should take the first of the bow (the letter *ca*) together with the *bindu*, and the first of the nectar (the letter *a*) together with the goad (the letter *i*).
One should form the Candra (moon) and Agni (fire) [seeds] mounted [upon each other], followed by the Yoni alone.
Having extracted the Śaṅku (thunderbolt), Vahni (fire), and Śakra (Indra) alone,
one should then extract Varuṇa along with the bow, and thereafter [the seed] alone.
This twelve-syllable word, preceded by the seventh [vowel] and followed by the negation,
consists of one hundred and twenty-two syllables, O you who are worshipped by the best of gods.
Again, one should extract the sound (nāda), the solitary one (kevalin), the wind (vāyu) conjoined with the syllable Om (praṇava),
the solitary lord of the hosts (gaṇarāja), and likewise the solitary double-tongued one (dvijihva).
Having extracted the fire (vahni) together with the goad (sāṅkuśa), one should then extract the solitary moon (soma).
One should extract the prohibition [of the syllable *na*] as being struck by the goad (*aṅkuśa*) of *kāla* (*ma*) and so forth in two ways.
The final [syllable *ya*] is struck by the three vowels; thus the nine-syllabled *pada* is extracted.
This is declared to consist of one hundred and twenty-three [syllables].

Again, having extracted the letter *kā* (the second), joined with *nāda*, [and] the first of the sixth [vowel] (*ū*) traversed by the three *svara*s (*ai*), [one obtains] *kū*. With that, [one forms] the final letter of Varuṇa (*va*) together with the goad (*ā*), which becomes *vā*.
Then, the first of the fifth [vowel] (*u*) with the goad (*ā*) is *ū*; then again, the nectar (*am*) alone.
Again, having extracted *va* and *ru*, and then *kāla* and *kevalin*,
[one obtains] the first syllable of the fifth [group], which is the essence (*piṇḍa*), crowned by the seventh vowel.
This nine-syllabled mantra constitutes one hundred and twenty-four [units].
Having extracted the *haṃsa* and the negation (*niṣedha*), divide that again into two.
This four-syllabled [mantra] indeed consists of one hundred and twenty-five [units].
Having extracted the *haṃsa* and the negation, divide that again into two.

O Goddess of the gods, these four syllables indeed constitute one hundred and twenty-five words; this has been declared to you according to their true meaning. Furthermore, four *kalās* should be assigned, beginning with the third, and likewise again.
One should place the syllable *megha* (ma) in the vital spot (*marmasthita*), followed by the syllable *tyāga* (ta) adorned with the fifth vowel (u).
Then comes the first letter of the third [vowel] (i), and the lord of the skull-bowl (kha); this five-syllabled phrase is the supreme one.
This indeed is declared to consist of one hundred and twenty-six syllables.
Furthermore, O God and Goddess, one should place the Moon, Fire situated within Varuṇa, and Vāyu together with the Praṇava; [then] Gaṇendra, Agni, and Kṣapānta;
ending with Varuṇa, that [mantra] should be established, with Fire radiant with the three vowels.
This six-syllabled mantra is to be known as the twenty-seventh, consisting of one hundred and twenty-seven syllables;
it is the state that bestows the fruits of great accomplishment, enjoyment, and liberation.
Furthermore, O Goddess of gods, one should extract Kāla together with Nāda,
and the Wind joined with that very [Kāla].
One should then extract the Trident joined with the Praṇava, and the Fire alone.
Furthermore, that [mantra] consisting of sixty syllables, beginning with the sixth [vowel] and endowed with three vowels,
together with *megha*— this supreme nine-syllable *pada*, O Goddess,
has been revealed to you as the one hundred and twenty-eighth.
Having again raised up the *ḍambara*, one should extract only the *kāla*.
One should then again extract the *nāda* together with the *nāda*, preceded by the syllable *tri*.
The *megha* situated at the vital point (*marman*) should be placed, adorned with the *praṇava* and the *vāyu*.
Having placed Gaṇeśa (marked by the sign of fire), Varuṇa situated within one’s own heart,
and Agni adorned with three dots, one should then extract Nara. Furthermore,
one should again place the triad consisting of Sūrya, Cāpa, and that very [Nara] along with Śara.
O beloved, O most worshipful one, adorn that with the bindu, the circle (ḍambara), and fire (vahnī);
the formidable *kuṃ* should be given five times.
Thus, one hundred and thirty-one words have been extracted.
One should extract the supreme, primary, and most excellent seventeen-syllable mantra.

One should extract the vital core alone, beginning with *Soma* and surmounted by the *Praṇava*. Having extracted that which ends with *Varuṇa*, one should likewise extract that which begins with the *Yoni*.

The syllable *niṣedha* joined with *indra* (the letter *i*) and conjoined with the fifth vowel (*u*), *varuṇa* accompanied by *nāda* (the letter *m*), and *soma* radiant with three vowels (*ī*, *u*, *m*). The syllable *niṣedha* presided over by the three vowels (*ī*, *u*, *m*): this is the supreme nine-syllable mantra.
O Goddess, these one hundred and thirty [mantras] have been revealed to you.
Having extracted the *haṃsa* alone, preceded by the *yoni* and accompanied by the *aṅkuśa*,
one should extract the fire (*vahni*) together with that very same [syllable], and then the fire situated within the water.
One should again extract the solitary [letter] pierced by the goad from the head;
the first letter of the third [vowel-group], together with the goad, shall be fire, radiant with three vowels.
The horse (a) joined with that very [letter] (u) is the eighth syllable, the supreme pada.
One hundred and thirty-one padas have thus been proclaimed for you.
One should extract Varuṇa (va), which is pervaded by three vowels (ū), situated therein at its end.
One should extract the syllable Niṣedha, which is pervaded by three vowels, followed by Śakra alone.
Then the seventh mark, Mahāvāyu, adorned with five letters;
this is declared to be the one hundred and thirty-second supreme word.
Again, having extracted Varuṇa, with his crown traversed by three vowels,
one should extract the letter at the end of that [mantra] which stands upon Varuṇa.
Then one should take Gaṇendra, joined with Fire (Ra) and struck on the head by an Aṅkuśa (U).
One should extract the *amṛta* (the letter *sa*) as it is preceded by the eighth vowel (*u*), followed by the *yoni* (the letter *e*).
Then one should give the *triśūla* (the letter *ha*) alone, and again the *soma* (the letter *sa*) situated in *kāla* (the letter *ra*).
This eight-syllabled word is marked with the three vowels and is the great fire (*mahāvahni*).
This [mantra] consisting of one hundred and thirty-three words has been extracted by drawing out the fourfold vital points (marmans), as well as the syllables *kāla* and *vāhna* alone;
thereafter, one should extract *varuṇa* joined with *mukhadāraṇa*.
The letter following *cāpa* (the letter *cha*) is mounted upon *vāyu* (the letter *ya*); the sixth [letter] followed by the first [letter] (*ṣa-ā*) is situated after the seventh (*sa*).
The seventh mark is the great wind (*mahāvāta*, the letter *ha*), and the ten-syllabled word is the supreme.
This auspicious [mantra], numbering one hundred and thirty-four, is the end of all.
Having raised up the letter *ka* alone, adorned with two vowels (*i*),
one should extract the letter *śa* preceded by the *yoni* (the letter *ī*) and marked by that same [vowel].
Then, the letter *ma* alone, adorned with a bindu (*m̐*), preceded by the *yoni* (*ī*).
The fire situated at the beginning of Amṛtā, the cloud, and the demon of the three vowels—
this indeed consists of eight syllables per word and comprises one hundred and thirty-five words;
it has been declared to you as bestowing the fruit of all prosperity.
Again, having extracted the Moon, which is the subtle seed-syllable situated in Varuṇa;
and having taken Varuṇa, which is presided over by the three vowels and is situated in Vāyu, [one should place it] upon the bow.
With the goad (Aṃ), the head (I) placed upon it, followed by the prohibition (Niṣedha, M), marked with the three vowels (Ā, I, U);
having extracted Indra (La) alone, adorned with the seventh vowel (Ū).
This seven-syllable word consists of one hundred and thirty-six [units].
This step, which is said to be the foremost of all vidyās, possesses great power.
Having again extracted the first of all [syllables], one should extract the three-syllabled step consisting of *kāla* joined with the *praṇava*,
and the trident joined with the seventh [vowel].
This has been explained to you according to its true meaning as consisting of thirty-seven [syllables].
Furthermore, the first of all should be given, and then again only the sixth and so forth.
O Goddess, one should extract the fire (ra) with its head pressed down by the goad (a).

O Goddess of the Suras, this five-syllabled mantra— consisting of the "double-tongued" (dvijihva), the one "overcome by three vowels" (trisvarākrānta), the first of the fifth [vowels], and the seventh— is the name of You; it yields the fruit of all desires and comprises one hundred and thirty-eight syllables.
Furthermore, [one should place] the nectar alone, then fire situated in Varuṇa;
Kāla joined with Aṅkuśa, the fifth [vowel] situated in the seventh [consonant].
Kāla established upon the auspicious lunar day (tithi), the beloved adorned by the seventh.
This six-syllabled word consists of one hundred and thirty-nine [units];
it is declared to be worshipped by all the Mātṛs and Īśvarīs.
Having extracted the syllable *kāla* alone and joined it with *haṃsa* and the *aṅkuśa*.
The negation (niṣedha) alone should be given, and that should be placed in the bow (cāpa). The double-tongued one (dvijihva) alone should be given, and again the negation alone.
That [negation] is conjoined with the third vowel; this is the seven-syllable word.
The one hundred and fortieth [verse] is the source of the arising of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).
Furthermore, the first of all [the preceding] should be given; it is situated in the seventh time-period.
The first of the fifth [group] would be "with the goad" (*sāṅkuśa*), while "prohibition" (*niṣedha*) is simply alone again.
And having placed that [letter] which is to be attained, [one places] Soma again situated in Fire;
then Varuṇa, occupied by the seventh— this is the auspicious seven-syllable mantra.
This is declared to be one hundred and forty-one.
The first [syllable] is the fifth, accompanied by the wind (vāyu) and overlaid by three vowels (*trisvara*), serving as a prohibition.
The second word consists of two syllables, the seventh being overlaid by the head (*śiras*).
This word, consisting of forty-two syllables, has been extracted.
It contains a negation marked by three vowels, beginning with the fifth [consonant] and accompanied by Vāyu (the letter *ya*).
It begins with *kalā* (the letter *u*), bears the mark of the *praṇava* (the letter *o*), and then Gaṇeśa (*ga*) alone once more.
The fifth letter at the beginning, the seventh letter situated [therein], and the seventh letter as its ornament— this six-syllabled word, joined with the forty-third [consonant],
is declared to be one hundred [syllables] in total, bestowing the fruit of all desires.
Having again extracted the *ḍaṃbara*, one should then extract *Kāmeśa*.
[This is] the "double-tongued" (*dvijihva*) mounted upon *Bhairava* and encapsulated by *Tejas*;
joined with the *bindu* and the *ḍaṃbara*, this *piṇḍa* is like ten thousand suns.
The letter *Ananta* (Ha) enclosed by fire (Ra), situated within *Kālāgni* (Sa) and accompanied by the *bindu*;
then *Kālāgni* (Sa) enclosed by fire (Ra), situated at the waist of *Ajīvaka* (Va).
Again, O Goddess, one should bestow that *Bhīmaśaṅku* (Jha) in four ways.

One should extract this syllable: *Amṛta* (A) mounted upon *Varuṇa* (U), its head pressed down by the *Aṅkuśa* (M), and the *Nāda* (H) conjoined with *Nāda* (H). O Goddess of the Lords of Gods, this eleven-syllabled word bestows great purpose.
O fair-complexioned one, this hundred and forty-four words has been proclaimed as the essence that bestows all accomplishments and grants the siddhi of the Great Assembly (mahāmelāpa), O Maheśvarī.
O lady of excellent complexion, this is declared to be the knowledge of these words;
it is considered to consist of one hundred and forty-five [syllables].
O Goddess of the lords of gods, at the beginning of the Vidyā, one should place a word for the purpose of illumination.
Salutation to Rudra, together with the Praṇava at its beginning, the one of great power.
Thus has this Vidyā of a thousand syllables been fully described.
O Sovereign of the Best of Gods, it is equal, neither more nor less than its progenitor.
This supreme Vidyā is proclaimed as Cakreśvarī;
she pacifies all sins and destroys all evil deeds.
She who pacifies all calamities, she who cuts asunder the flood of misfortunes;
the sovereign of all lords of mantras, worshipped by the entire host of Mothers;
the mistress of the circle of all Bhairavas, the queen of all the hosts of Rudras.
She who pacifies all evils, who crushes spirits and vetālas;
the sovereign of the assembly circle of all, the bestower of all prosperity;
the destroyer of the flood of all obstacles, and the devourer of all nāgas.
She who destroys the pride of all aggregates, she who causes all cakras to blossom;
she who dwells within the openings of all channels, she who causes the heart-lotus to expand;
she who is bowed to by all vetālas, she who is praised by all yoginīs.
Even after destroying the entire universe filled with Brahmins,
he is not tainted by sin if this [mantra] resides in his heart.
Even one who has killed his guru, his mother, an embryo, or his father [is purified].

By reciting this knowledge (*vidyā*) of terrible power even once, one is purified; indeed, by mere remembrance, it destroys the sins such as the uprooting of the *liṅga*. By reciting it once, O Mistress of the Gods, one becomes completely cleansed of all sins.
One who is uninitiated becomes initiated; one without the pledges (*asamayin*) becomes possessed of the pledges (*samayin*) by entering [this].
One who is unconsecrated becomes consecrated in the midst of all mandalas.
O Goddess, such a person becomes a sovereign among practitioners (*sādhakendra*), having fulfilled all vows.
There is nothing that cannot be accomplished through the grace of the Mistress of Knowledge (Vidyā).

She is known as the Fortune of Mantra (Mantra-lakṣmī), and she is likewise designated as the Fortune of Knowledge (Vidyā-lakṣmī); she should be understood as the Fortune of the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa-lakṣmī), and is similarly remembered as the Fortune of Mudrā (Mudrā-lakṣmī).
Maṇḍalākhyā, likewise Lakṣmī, and Bhairavalakṣmikā;
Siddhalakṣmī, Devalakṣmī, and Lakṣmī Vidyādharīśvarī.
The splendor of the great lord of the asuras, as well as the splendor of Rāvaṇa, is proclaimed as Matal-lakṣmī;
therein Lakṣmī is celebrated.
Atimārga-mahālakṣmī is celebrated as Kulalakṣmī.
Kauleśvarī, Kaulalakṣmī, Nityālakṣmī, Jayapradā,
and Viśvalakṣmī— these are proclaimed as the Vidyās of terrible prowess.
She is Ekavīrā when devoid of limbs, and she is Mahātantra when divested of parts.
"O Goddess of gods, I am not able to describe the multitude of her qualities even in hundreds of years called Sādākhyā, nor with tens of thousands of mouths.
Thus was the all-pervading Vidyā, perfected, described in a thousand syllables.
"Tell me quickly: why does she delight [in this], being devoid of the ancillary vows (*aṅgavrata*)?

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Extraction of Mantras," within the ritual procedure for the Mistress of the Wheel of Doctrines (*matacakreśvarī*) in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, a great tantra concerning the Severing of the Head (*śiraccheda*), belonging to the Vidyāpīṭha in the Bhairava-stream, consisting of twenty-four thousand verses.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Heroes, I have achieved my purpose by hearing this knowledge that is so difficult to attain.
Now, O Lord of the Gods, I wish to hear about its meditation."
Or rather, O Bhairava, tell me what her retinue is,
so that I may become free from doubt regarding the Goddess of the gods, O Hara;
and how she becomes manifest through meditation by the best of practitioners.
"O Leader of the Gods, tell me, what does she do when she has become manifest?
O you who are worshipped by all the Asuras and Suras, [tell me] all this.
Bhairava said:
Having attained a place free from dualities, with a mind firmly concentrated,
seated in a comfortable posture, and gladdened by the joy of wine.
Accompanied by a female messenger, with a serene mind and adorned with all ornaments,
well-perfumed and having consumed excellent betel, he is ever devoted to the conduct of heroes.
[He partakes of] the juice arising from the bliss of the household, as do the Kuṇḍas, Golakas, and Pramathas.
O slender-waisted one, having indeed joined that with the five jewels,
the Hero— possessing great enjoyments and embodying both power and the possessor of power—
should awaken her who resides within the center of the heart-lotus and whose nature is supreme.
Then one should meditate upon the Goddess in her manifest form, the sole devourer who swallows the universe—
shining with the hue of a crow or a cuckoo, resembling the throat of Śrīkaṇṭha,
mounted upon a crocodile and a buffalo, and adorned with eighteen arms.
She has five faces and distorted eyes, adorned with serpents and a cow-nose.
One face, O large-eyed one, is dark, terrible, and formidable;
the right [faces] are horse-faced, upward-facing, and elephant-faced.
One should always contemplate her who is known as Rāsabhā on the left and Kroṣṭravaktrā in the west, roaring with the sound of terrible thunderclouds,
filling all the quarters of space by the tossing upward of her hair.
With all her weapons held ready in her hands, she is radiant with a terrifying appearance;
she bears a sword, a shield, a skull-topped staff, a trident, and a battle-axe,
and is intent upon ringing her fierce bell while holding a noose, a goad, and a skull-cup.
She whose sole diversion is the playing of the great lute with its head-like lotus,
who is difficult to behold due to her fierce *tāṇḍava* dance while intoxicated by the wine of passion for the world,
and who has fashioned a crest-ornament from the heads of the lords of all the worlds.
She was radiant with a garland extending from the head of Tatveśvara down to his hands and feet;
she was terrifying, wearing a skull-ornament fashioned from Kāraṇeśvara;
and her ornaments consisted of masses of putrid corpses impaled upon the uneven points of a fishhook.
It terrified the entire shell of existence with its terrible and great roar,
and it was more intense than hundreds of masses of blazing fires at the end of an aeon.
She whose sole diversion is the play-ball of Brahmā’s lotus-stalk,
who has made the world-elephants her playground with the deep-sounding *dhanaṭāṅkāra* of her laughter,
and who is eager to consume the spreading poison from the hoods of the lord of serpents, Śeṣa.
Her waist was adorned with the excellent hide of a world-elephant;
she held a great, terrifying owl as a parasol; she was formidable and protruding-toothed;
and she was surrounded by hundreds of clapping hands from throngs of bhūtas and vetālas.
She is resplendent with eyes like a shimmering, terrible sword and adorned with earrings; her body is matted with the fierce flames of the fire at the end of the eon;
she is solely intent on devouring the great flesh of gods and demons.
She has great earrings hanging down to her ears from Saṅkarṣaṇa, the Great Lion;
her body is radiant with a multitude of severed heads as brilliant as the sun at the time of dissolution;
she possesses a lion’s face, a cow’s nose, and a true human face, and her formidable breasts hang down low.
One should then meditate upon her whose mouth is filled with human entrails, adorned with thunderbolts and lightning, and possessing the form of white pearl necklaces, the moon, and bright clouds;
seated upon a white lotus throne, resplendent with white garlands and wreaths.
She possesses a universal form and large eyes, adorned with every ornament;
she is mounted upon a great corpse, embellished with many arms,
possessing many faces and eyes, and radiant with many feet.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess, who is saluted by the multitudes of many gods and Siddhas, who is garlanded by heroes, and who possesses whatever form is desired;
such is she, the auspicious one who bestows peace as well as nourishment.

One should visualize [the goddess] as resembling vermilion, drawing [the target] under her control; for killing, O Maheśānī, one should always visualize her as black as a man’s hair and like a terrible mist, with the color of smoke, for the purpose of eradication.
For the purpose of paralyzing, she has the luster of molten gold; for stunning, she is reddish-black;
for deluding, she has the hue of a parrot's wing; and for causing enmity, she resembles a blue jay.
In the rite of disappearance, one should meditate upon Śivā as possessing her former form, the performer of all actions; thus has the meditation on Ekavīrā been fully described for the ritual.
Having meditated upon her, living beings in this world do not grieve intensely.
Now, O auspicious lady, hear at once about these goddesses who possess that same form:
just as the mass of rays of the sun shines as an undivided whole,
even so is the host of deities established here as an inseparable unity.
Rudrāṇī, as well as Caṇḍā, and another named Jvalitānanā;
another named Jvālājihvodarā, and another proclaimed as Bhīmā;
another known by the name Mahābhīṣaṇā, and likewise Lambodarī.
Viśvāntakī, and another named Kālagrāsaratā; another named Kālasūdanī, and another Hāhāhāsinī;
Mahābhairavā by name, and another who dwells in the cremation ground.
Likewise, there is Candramukhī, and another, Caṇḍayogeśvarī;
Phaṭkāriṇī, Mahāghorā, and likewise Phaṭṭabharūṭikā;
she named Mahārāvinī, and Haṃsinī as yet another.
Grāhiṇī, Māraṇī, and another, Mohanī;
likewise another, Khādikā, and another, Vidrāvaṇī;
and another is called Jīhikā, who dwells in the lap of Bhairava.
Another is Mahāmāṃsāśinī, and another is Tudanī;
likewise another is Truṭanī, and another is Mahākālī.
Another is remembered as Pāśadaṇḍadharī, and another is Khorvārī.
Mahāmārī, as well as others— Brahmāṇī, Maheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Yamadaṇḍinī,
Āgneyī, Vāruṇī, Vāyavyā, and Kālacakrikā.
Likewise, there is Yogeśvarī, and another supreme one, Mahākāpālinī; Yamaghaṇṭā, Bhairaveśī, Caṇḍeśī, and Bharūṭikā.
Another is Kṛtāntabhakṣaṇī, and another is Hṛdayānandinī;
another is Jvālājvalitadehā, and another is remembered as Huṃkārī;
another is Narāṃtravalitā, and likewise Phetkārarāviṇī.
Hanani, Kuṇḍavaktrā, and likewise Jvālānala; another is Kaṃbugrīvā, adorned with serpent-earrings;
another is Mahābhīmā, and another is Mahābhīmāṅgadā.
Bhīmā, another Krodhamukhā, and Śirojvalitacandrikā; Cāmuṇḍā, Caṇḍālī, and Kirītācchuṣmakāriṇī;
Hasanī, Bhṛtanī, and another, the supreme Trailokyatrāsanī.
Rudhirā, Asṛkvasābhojinī, Pāvanī, Vamanī,
Ghātanī, Khecarī, Vallanī, Sphāṭanī,
Garjanī, Ghūrṇanī, and another, Madonmādanikā.
Another dwells in the cremation ground, and another delights in the earth;
one has a beautiful smile and a thin face, and likewise all bear weapons.
Another holds a great ḍamaru drum, while another wears an owl-skin garment.
The one with broad arms, the great serpent, the one intent on many desires;
the one seated in space, the one whose body is space, the supreme one with the face of a great lion;
the one with great fangs, and the one with a skull-face amidst flames.
Another is Gṛddharoṣaṇikā, who dwells within the lotus of the heart;
another is Sarvabhūtadamā, likewise Hanahaṃkāriṇī;
another is seated upon a skull-throne, and [another] is seated upon the lotus of the great void.
Likewise, there is another, Kālarātrī, who bears half of Śiva’s body;
and another with a thousand forms, possessing the radiance of ten million times ten thousand moons.
Another has the form of the fire of love (*praṇayāgnivapuḥ*), while another is likewise incomparable;
then there is the supreme Mistress of the Kings of Weapons (*astrarājeśvarī*), who is radiant and most terrible.
There is also Meghamālā, Mahāmāyā, and likewise Vidyut yakṣikā.
Another is Duritakṣaparī, and likewise Bhīmakaraṅkiṇī;
Cātreśīlasmagātrā, and likewise Trailokyaḍāmarā;
another is Raktāsavapriyā, and [she who is] Trailokyagrāsaghasmarā.
Another supreme Mahāghoreśvarī is seated upon a buffalo throne;
likewise there is Nīlavarāhā, another with a terrifying countenance,
as well as Hayānanā, Gajāsyā, and another with six faces.
Kroṣṭacakrā is most terrible, the consumer of flesh, and the master of all mantras;
Huhuvaktrā is the power of yoga-illusion, possessing a most fearsome form.
Another is Caṇḍayogeśvarī, who reaches the end of the sixteen digits (kalās).
Another is Hakārārddhacarī, and another is the abode of the universe; likewise,
she who delights solely in devouring the universe, she who sounds the hand-drum (ḍamaru),
the terrible one who drags away Time, and the supreme one who is the source of all vidyās.
Amoghā is known as Aparā, and likewise there is another called Aparājitā;
another is Sarvamātrīmukhā, and the supreme one is Mahānandakarī.
Another is Sudhānandasravā, and the other is Nityānityoditā.
These goddesses are fully described; they all bestow the accomplishment of all aims.
All of them perform every rite and are established according to the movement of the wheel.
They have four arms and one face, and are endowed with severed heads and lotuses in their hands.
Carrying alms-bowls and staffs, they are formidable, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction;
all of them are devoted to the form of goddesses, yet all are greedy for flesh.
Just as one is, so are all; and just as all are, so is each one.
Indeed, all things are always distinct by their own nature and yet non-distinct [in essence].
Thus has this meditation been proclaimed by the Great Goddess, the Queen of Gods;
it brings benefit to practitioners for the sake of attaining their desired goals.
It bestows all accomplishments, it is the essence, it destroys all sins;
it pacifies all epilepsy and destroys calamities and afflictions.
"O Goddess of gods, worshipped by the immortals, tell me through the path of speech: what shall I say? [It is] that which accomplishes the three worlds and adorns the trembling earth.
Thus [ends the section] in the *Bhairava-srotas*, within the *Vidyāpīṭha* of the *Śiraccheda*, in the *Jayadrathayāmala Mahātantra*, in the twenty-four thousand [verse version], in the third Ṣaṭka.
The twelfth chapter, the narrative account of Matacakreśvarī.
The Goddess said:
"Now I wish to hear about the one of great power who draws [all things] toward her."
O Lord of Gods, O Great Īśvara, tell me that which is the supreme [teaching]: the *nyāsa*, the *avādīkṣā*, the *abhiṣeka*, and the *sādhana*. Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall now explain that which you have just asked:
having gone to a beautiful and excellent mountain, or to a cremation ground that bestows perfect siddhi,
or to the lovely shore of the ocean, or even to the house of the Guru.
Or else, O Īśānī, he may stay in the house of his mother, or wherever the Guru pleases.
Devoted to the conduct of a hero (*vīrācāra*), surrounded by female messengers (*dūtīs*), cherished and satisfied, fortunate, and anointed with sandalwood and agallochum; |||
Having thoroughly perfumed himself, having taken betel nut, and having consumed the auspicious five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
he should always construct a single maṇḍala for the rite of the heroes—
one that is symmetrical, bright, with four gates, and adorned with the mudrās and wheels.
The wheel is made of royal stone, with a red rim and great radiance;
it is endowed with thirty-two spokes, beautiful with a lotus-center,
possessed of sixteen petals, and covered with red powder.
Having thus decorated it, O fortunate one, adorned with arches and mirrors,
embellished with various kinds of upper coverings and banners,
he, being composed in mind, should hang a bell here at every quarter of the directions.
O highly fortunate lady, in these directions, place water-pots filled with unguents,
containing gold and flowers, and wrapped with silk garlands and cloth bands.

In the southeast (āgneyā), one should fashion a fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) endowed with all the auspicious characteristics; it should be circular with three tiers (trimekhala), and the sacrificial hearth (yoni) should be like the leaf of an aśvattha tree. One should always make the joints even and smooth.
Having thus accomplished [the preliminary rites], one situated there should begin here with the ritual depositions (*nyāsa*) and so forth;
by means of the King of Mantras at the end, one should cause the five purifications to be performed:
the purification of the place, the purification of the materials, and likewise the others.
The wise practitioner should perform the purification of the mantra and the purification of the ground. By merely binding the directions and smearing the site, one will attain success.
Materials become pure through sprinkling; this is the half-measure of yoga that has been prescribed.
Listen to the incomparable purity of the self within the characteristic of the *pada*:
having expelled from the body the impure wind that is bound by fetters,
and having abandoned it again into the ether at the end of the twelve, one then [proceeds].
One should contemplate a white lotus, consisting of Śiva, with a hundred petals, its pericarp fashioned from the moon, dripping abundant nectar;
[the nectar] returning from that place by the sequence of digits (kalās) to the heart-lotus.
There, one should contemplate oneself as residing within the heart, having the nature of consciousness (cit),
complete with all parts and limbs, manifest, and possessing a pure body;
endowed with the path of divine senses and enveloped by divine, excellent organs.

Having first contemplated [the mantra], the Mistress of the Gods should then perform the placement (nyāsa) in forward order (anuloma) starting from the first word; then, having performed it again in reverse order (viloma), she should subsequently place that entire [mantra].
Thereafter, with undistracted mind, she should contemplate her own body as having the form of the Goddess.
This is declared to be the impurity of the self, which lasts for twelve years for all ascetics.
Hereafter, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, listen to the purification of the mantra:
having abandoned the immeasurable male state as well as supreme inactivity.
O Goddess, by means of the expansion and blossoming of that [light],
those who have taken refuge in the undifferentiated state attain manifestation through the fortune of its unfolding;
at that time, O Goddess, one should remember the mantra— this is the supreme purification of the mantra.
(94b) And I shall declare another [method]; listen, O Pārvatī, according to the truth:
from the location of the *kanda* and *kuṇḍalinī*, by way of the lineage of the Guru’s mouth.
Having arisen, the knower of mantras, free from exertion, should take refuge in the fire;
the practitioner of mantras should then contemplate the mantra through the consciousness of supreme bliss.
O Bhairavī, at that time, there is the purification of the wheel of mantras through that recitation.
Furthermore, hear from me the purification according to the distinction between the higher and the lower. The light that unfolds as a triad within the hollow of the heart-lotus—
by striking the two [breaths] below, the exceedingly powerful fire brings about life and purification.
Through devotion, he attains oneness with those known as Nara, Śakti, and Śiva. Abiding within that wheel of their vibration, one should remember the most wonderful mantra.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, this is that supreme and yet non-supreme purification of the mantra.
Furthermore, O Maheśvarī, I shall again explain the purification of the mantra:
when the sun has risen on its day, one should recollect the mantra through the yoga of unifying it with that consciousness, extending as far as the station at the end of the twelve fingers.
By this Lord Khecarīvaktra, [the state of] Bhavana has been attained for a long time.
Listen once more to another [teaching], the purification of mantra which bestows the great goal:
O fortunate one, having come from that place as far as Ākarakuṇḍalī.
O fortunate one, by the rising of the moon, one becomes the leader of the netherworld (Pātāla).
This purification of mantra has been revealed through the sequence of the yoga of emanation (sṛṣṭi-yoga).
Furthermore, I shall tell you again the purification of mantra according to another division.
One should meditate upon that mantra, which is luminous and situated within the abode of the two eyebrows as the *bindu* between the moon and the sun—
the leader of the five causes, whose entire body consists of the series of digits (*kalā*)—
by means of the differentiation of the mind.
When employed here, this mantra shall bestow all accomplishments. O worshiper of the best of gods, this is declared to be the purification pertaining to the mantra.
It must be kept most secret, O auspicious lady, and should not be given to just anyone.
(95a) One attains the intermediate stage of giving known as "with-gift" for eight years.
Beyond this, O Pārvatī, hear now about the purification of the ground.

With the very last syllable, one should burn [the world] along with the series of spokes of the wheel as far as the fire of time (kālāgni) by means of the needle; then, one should nourish it again with masses of the essence of nectar,
indeed in the form of the interior void.

One should contemplate the power called the support (ādhāra-śakti) and the great lotus arising from it; upon that, one should likewise place oneself. O beloved daughter of the mountain, this is the purification of the locus (sthāna-śuddhi). Thus, O daughter of the mountain, the five purifications have been fully explained.
Having done this, O Goddess, one should then begin the sacrifice within the heart-lotus.
Therein are the bulb, the stalk, the excellent lake, and the boat;
furthermore, the lotus extending to the edge of the mandala, as well as the crocodile and the buffalo.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) up to the final form, O beloved, the Goddess likewise [should be established] again; one should worship her, who has arrived through the previously mentioned method, as the witness of all. Whatever object exists in this world, O Goddess worshipped by the gods—
O highly fortunate one, with each [of those] one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the pit of the navel with seeds born of the *jama* plant.
Having done this, O Goddess, one should then worship within the mandala.

One should place the Goddess in the center, purified by the limit of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). One should contemplate her in the form of a star, [emerging] from the vessel of curd through a stream of rays,
by means of the flow of three or four divisions, through union with the enclosure of honey.
One should establish [the deities] up to the limit according to the division of the non-differentiation of yoga.
One should worship the Lord of the Field (kṣetreśa), the Lord of the Gaṇas (gaṇanātha), the Rakṣas, and the Vāyu-gaṇas.
And one should worship the Mothers of the Directions stationed at the jar, O Supreme Goddess.
One should worship Gaṅgā and Kālindī at the two locations of the gates;
one should also worship the Goddess who has entered into the aforementioned meditation, as well as the other goddesses.
The Great Goddess Ekavīrā is always like the goddess Tārā;
one should then gratify the Goddess with liquor, meat, fermented spirits, and the like,
as well as with various offerings of food, cakes, and auspicious incense.
With sesame cakes and conch-shaped wicks,
with various and wonderful sweetmeats made of grapes and sugar-candy,
with other foods prepared from mung beans and black gram, as well as milk-rice (pāyasa), [he offered].

One should satisfy Śivā, the goddess of the gods who wears tinkling bracelets, by offering beef, human flesh, and likewise the flesh of elephants, horses, and camels, as well as various other kinds of meat from aquatic and terrestrial creatures— all of which have been steamed or fried.

O Maheśānī, for the propitiation of the Goddess of Devas, one should offer wine, *surā*, as well as *śīndhu*, *āraṇāla*, and *umbu*; the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), even though lacking actual nectar, and various other drinks.
Having thus gratified the devotees with the aforementioned offerings for Maheśvarī,
he should then cause the disciple— the hero, the hero of firm vows—
to enter, his eyes bound, his hands joined in *añjali*, and his body sprinkled and anointed.
Then, O Goddess, having been struck and purified by the one with the spear in hand,
he should cause the hero— the hero of firm vows,
whose eyes are bound, who has joined palms, whose body is sprinkled, and whose form is light— to enter.
Then, O Goddess, having struck and purified [the disciple] with the hand holding the spear,
one should cause him to enter and cast a full handful of flowers.
Then, one should open his eyes and show him the maṇḍala.
Then, O Goddess of Gods, one should go near the fire-pit (*vahnikuṇḍa*).
There, in the southern quarter, one should place the cooked sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Then, O Goddess of Gods, [one should proceed] around the perimeter of the pit with a step.
One should indeed perform the ritual preparations just as in the case of the first hexad.
O highly fortunate one, in that very same manner, one should purify the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
Likewise, one should purify the fire and likewise initiate the disciple in the middle [tanu] initiation.
The path of mantras, the path of words, that which is called the path of principles, the one named the path of worlds,
the path of kalās, and the one called the path of phonemes— [these are] the six paths according to their respective divisions.
By whichever path one wishes to consecrate the three disciples,
having established that [path] situated there, one should meditate upon the five [deities] within it;
one should perform the five rites, beginning with emanation, in each respective place.

O Maheśvarī, just as the first group of six was previously described, so should one perform everything; no further elaboration is recounted here. The Guru should, with his whole being, unite the disciple with the abode of Śakti.
Because he desires liberation, one should then initiate him into that very reality.
Indeed, having consecrated him once with a variegated jar that has been properly consecrated,
O Goddess, one should then impart the mantra to him.

O Goddess, one should grant her permission for the practice of mantra-sādhana. Having thus obtained it in this final birth, the best of men should afterwards please his guru by whatever means he may be pleased.
O highly fortunate one, that which is to be given should be bestowed by the wise one without hesitation.
Then, with permission, O Heroine, one should begin the mantra practice.
All this most wonderful secret has been explained to you.
Therefore, the practice of mantra-sādhana is now desired as it has reached its proper occasion.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, on initiation and consecration, within the ritual of Matacakreśvarī, in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the *Śiraccheda* in the *Vidyāpīṭha* of the *Bhairava-srotas*.

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the practice of the Goddess here, which is devoid of arduous means and has not been declared to anyone else. Having gone to a mountain region or a cremation ground, one of firm vows—
There, the lord of practitioners, upholding the hero’s vow and possessing a serene mind,
intent solely upon the potency of the mantra, should recite it according to the previously described rule. (96b)
Then, O Goddess, one should offer ten thousand oblations of a thousand divine couples;
or else, O Beloved, [offer] human flesh, or the resin produced from *jyotis*,
or pills of *guggulu*— these, O Goddess, are the best oblations when offered with the three [substances].
Thus, at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, the goddess Karaṅkiṇī herself arises from the midst of the fire to bestow boons upon the practitioner;
she grants him whatever boon he desires, of this there is no doubt.
She bestows either the state of a wheel-turner (cakreśvara) or even union with the Self;
of this there is no doubt, and she grants it to him in every way while he is still embodied.
From five thousand recitations, the goddess Kṛṣodarī [bestows these].
By means of an oblation of sesame seeds and guggulu resin, one will master the netherworld (pātāla).
In whatever place, on whatever mountain, one subsequently recollects the vidyā,
there that netherworld shall become the supreme [abode] for the practitioner.

Terrified by fear and overwhelmed with passion for the maiden, they all come into the lineage of the practitioner, possessing immeasurable splendor. O Goddess, he is their lord, like the moon among the stars.
My word is indeed true; there is no doubt about it.
There, the lord of practitioners shall live for a great kalpa, without a doubt.
Now, as for that which is taught as the practice for one who is devoid of [other] means of accomplishment:

Having obtained permission on the festival of the Lamp, one should recite the vidyā for a hundred [times] before the face of Śrīmukhā, O highly fortunate lady, remaining unwearied. Thereafter, one may enter one's own home there, free from fear of fire.
The accomplishment is as before; no specific distinction is elaborated here.
Having brought an unblemished corpse and having adorned it with all ornaments, one should place it upon the left side of the altar and seize its hand.
O Goddess of the gods, the high-minded one should rotate the right [hand] with the right;
then he should cause the Goddess, garlanded with a thousand syllables, to revolve.
O Goddess of gods, after three revolutions, that corpse will rise up hidden;
then, with five revolutions and a laugh like a thunderbolt,
it will undoubtedly arise and dance in the grove of men.
Vīravara himself took his hand upon his shoulder;
the two of them, delighted by the wine, danced together with one another.
He took a hundred *palas* of its essence for the purpose of drinking.
Having drunk that, he would indeed be satisfied; then, sitting down, he would say:
"Aha! This is truly a play we have just performed here together.
O Vīranātha and the rest, tell me quickly: what else shall I do?"
"Take the elixir, the alchemical mercury, the metal, or the supreme treasure-trove; or take the great siddhi of the subterranean opening as you desire.
Having heard this, the Vidyā then remained silent and withdrew.
Then he says to him: "Come, mount upon my back.
O Great Being, I shall go wherever you desire, even to the hollow of the peak of Brahmā’s world; I stand here as your servant."

"The entire world abides in your contemplation; you are indeed forever free from decay and death. Unopposed by gods or *siddhas*, you alone are truly one who has attained mastery through knowledge (*vidyāsiddha*).
Having heard this, he immediately mounts his back.
One should consider all the worlds as being like Hari and Hara themselves—
possessing great strength, great energy, and enduring until the end of the great kalpa.
Or else, by the command of the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśī), one should begin the churning process in the ritual procedure.
Accompanied by thirty-two heroic and immensely powerful forest-dwellers,
he proceeded toward another formidable forest, which was infested with wicked fanged beasts.
For the purpose of a moat, the ground was made sixty-four cubits deep and square.
One should have a wall constructed there so that no one sees it.
Then, in the center of that place, [one should prepare] an altar with thirty-two excellent animals.
O Goddess of the gods, at the end of the eon, eight males were then born from the four castes, O Mistress of the gods, two by two.
There were eight species of horses, eight species of donkeys, and eight species of buffaloes.
Having performed this sacrifice to the Goddess of the Gods according to the method of forceful practice (*haṭhavidhi*),
one should cause her blood to be taken by striking with swords, spears, and other weapons.
Then, one should pour that milk into the great adamantine cauldron (*mahāvajrakaṭāha*).

Having prepared the great altar with all the jewels there— marrow, fat, grease, and flesh— and with the meat of animals, he should establish Mādhava upon it; [therein] the great trident, smeared with blood, is situated within the churning-vessel.
Having fashioned a human head-ornament (puṃśīrṣa) for the arm, adorned with garlands of mantras,
and having well-increased it with bracelets and other ornaments,
one should indeed worship the goddess of gods, the terrible one, while remaining established in the previously mentioned meditation.
Then, O Dear One, one should wrap that thread seven times with hair made into a cord and encircled by a ring. Then,
making eight roars and uttering the sounds of a donkey, one should [proceed].
O Goddess of the gods, one should take refuge on the right side with that which arises from a buffalo;
one should take refuge on the left with the cries of dogs, tortoises, and rats.
Then, one should churn with speed, like Manthānabhairava.
O Goddess of gods, the entire earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves, trembles three times,
beset by lightning and thunderbolts;
and thousands of meteors fall toward the ten directions.
A most terrible cry of "Hā! Hā! and a great crackling sound arise there suddenly from a thousand [directions], horrific and fearsome in form;
and all the quarters blaze, filled with the howling of jackals.
From that, the great poison Kālakūṭa suddenly arises—
terrible, resembling Bhairava himself, and causing the destruction of the three worlds. (98a)
One should strike him with the *vajra* while recollecting the terrible *vidyā*.
Then he indeed perishes; one should then begin the churning once more.
Thereupon the Lord Bhairava, the leader, emerges in person.
Then, O Goddess, she spoke thus to the high-souled practitioners:
"Accept your desired boons; you shall surely laugh at me, there is no doubt.
You are Brahmā, you are Viṣṇu... [and so forth].
—And I shall give this; receive it, O best of men!
Since you have performed a most terrible and formidable deed, well done, indeed well done, O best of men! Therefore, receive it!
Having heard this, the harsh-voiced peacocks, crying out with their keka calls,
showered down rains of flowers from on high and repeatedly raised shouts of "Victory!
All these spoke thus to the great-souled practitioner.
Having seen the Lord, one should worship Him who possesses the form of Mahābhairava.
O virtuous lady, if she [the goddess] grants even the slightest boon whatsoever,
then Bhairava, the Lord of Gods, himself vanishes from sight.
By means of the seventh enclosure, the goddess Kṛṣodarī herself arises from the midst of that [mandala], pure as a pearl necklace and the moon;
the goddess has thirty-two breasts and carries water-pots in her hands.
The thirty-two sovereign goddesses are completely filled with the great nectar (*mahāmṛta*).
Upon seeing that Goddess of the lords of gods, the wise man should immediately prostrate himself;
she then becomes like a mother to him, honoring him with her own left-hand nectar.
She bestows breast after breast upon each of the practitioners;
she gives them a flask held in her hand—of this there is no doubt.
Having drunk from the excellent breast of the Goddess, which is difficult for those of unrefined self to attain.
O Goddess, having taken up the vessel filled with supreme nectar,
practitioners free from all afflictions attain the state of being his sons. (98b)

As long as the Goddess Mahāraudrā exists, so indeed do all things endure. Just as there is the power of agency and the power of withdrawal belonging to the Goddess, so indeed it comes to pass for high-souled practitioners; of this there is no doubt.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva; Mahābhairava-deva and those others who are the lords of Bhairava—
by him [the practitioner], accompanied by his own circle of leaders among adepts, the state of being worshipful for them has been attained.
Or what else shall I declare? For there is nothing higher than this. O Goddess of the lords of gods, no such means has been proclaimed anywhere else.
Therefore, I shall declare that which brings success according to its performance.
Having gone to a terrifying cremation ground at night on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, O Bhairavī,
worshiped by the best of gods, kindle a fire there with the wood of funeral pyres and tridents. Then, at night, one should offer human flesh as an oblation.
Adopting a formidable mode of conduct, the preeminent practitioner of firm intellect—
whenever that lord of practitioners offers even ten oblations,
the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembles.
Then, from the midst of that unassailable fire, there arises with speed a most terrible and exceedingly dreadful *kṛtyā* with a wide-open mouth.
She says: "O lord of practitioners, what shall I do for you now?"
"I shall split open Pātāla; shall I grind Sumeru to powder?
Shall I drink up all the oceans, or destroy the abode of Yama? Or else, tell me, shall I destroy the entire realm of Indra?"
"Tell me, shall I destroy Nairṛta, Indra, Vahni, Varuṇa, or Vāyu? Or shall I destroy Kubera or Īśāna?
Or tell me, shall I utterly destroy Kūṣmāṇḍa or Kālāgni?"
"Shall I crush Brahmā or Viṣṇu, or even the entire cosmic egg?
Speak quickly, O Lord of Heroes, that which is most pleasing to your mind. (99a)
Having heard this, the practitioner should state whatever is desired in his mind. Established in the state of a servant, she fulfills all of that.
Now, if one desires to accomplish the supreme possession of a stationary object (sthāvareśa), [he should proceed as follows].
Then, having brought a maiden endowed with all auspicious marks and having seated her upon a well-concealed, excellent throne,
she was dressed in red and black garments and adorned with a red garland gracing her neck.

One should place her upon an auspicious seat, completely covered with flower garlands; then one should burn incense continuously and recite the vidyā. At that time, the maiden trembles, reels, and laughs again.
One should ring the bell there while those established in the great mantras remain present.
Then the goddess Kṛṣodarī, the deity of deities, swiftly enters [the vessel].
Having left the ground, she stands there, and the person bows down before her.
One should gratify the Supreme Goddess with various offerings of food.
Then she will tell the chief practitioner whatever is desired in his mind—the entirety of the three times: the past, the present, and the future.
This news from within the belly of the cosmic egg speaks to the practitioner;
thus, with a humble mind, he satisfies the Goddess with devotion. Having prostrated before her, he should bid farewell to that Goddess of gods, Kṛṣodarī.
Now, O lady of beautiful hips, I shall explain the auspicious *karmaprasenika* [rite].
For the sake of preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), one should recite the incomparable hundred-fold mantra (*śatavidyā*).
Afterwards, one should employ it in the rite known as *prasena*, which is most excellent.

O Goddess, one should cause the *prasenā* to descend into a water-lamp, or into a sword-moon, or within the solar orb, or into the eyes of a maiden, or into the thumb, or into a very pure mirror, or into a great vessel.
O Dear One, [one may perform] the *āvatya*-piling with ashes here, or else without ashes.
Having swept [the site] with that and having addressed the Goddess of the gods, Kṛṣodarī, [one proceeds].
One should worship and perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the Goddess who bestows the great goal, and then recite her mantra.
Then, O Beloved, she will reveal there the past, the future, and the present, O fortunate one; behold this without doubt, O maiden!
When the preeminent practitioner, having performed ten thousand recitations, beholds this,
then this preliminary rite has been explained to you according to its true meaning.
Now, this procedure for the narration of dreams is being stated.
Having smeared a beautiful area of ground the size of a cow's hide with *alika* paste,
O Goddess of the lords of gods, and having performed the ritual preparation with mantras,
one should worship the Goddess of the gods situated within a water-pot at the head of the site.
Having worshipped the Goddess of the lords of gods with various kinds of offerings and many types of liquor, he respectfully made this request:
"O Goddess, how is the threefold time, which is of the nature of conceptualization, established?"
"How should I conduct myself? What accomplishment will be mine?
Which field should I resort to, and upon what companion should I rely? In how much time will my accomplishment be clear, and by doing what will it come to pass?"
For how many years shall I live? How much remains [of my life]?
O Great Goddess, who will live, or what kind of fear belongs to whom? O Goddess, what kind of gain, victory, or defeat is ordained for whom?
Tell me truly, O Bhairava, whether there will be abundance or famine, or what terrible disease shall afflict whom;
how many years shall the reign or the life of the two kings last;
and whatever else appears in my dream, speak of it according to reality.
Having spoken thus, he should recite the vidyā while sleeping in the presence of the God and Goddess.
Then, in his dream, he shall see whatever may be pleasing to him.
Alternatively, for the sake of subjugation, he should employ the incomparable [vidyā] according to the goddess.
(100a) Thus I shall explain it to you; listen, O Pārvatī, according to the truth.
Having diligently collected the dust from the feet of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), [one should proceed].

Having mixed [the mantra] with red *rocanā*, one should write the *vidyā* upon a highly auspicious birch-bark leaf, accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Having written it,
O fortunate one, one should worship it with all the services of red offerings.
Thereafter, the Great Goddess should cause the *prakṛti* to be fashioned from resinous incense (*madana*).
Having placed that [image] within her heart, one should fix the *cīrikā* (the written name) wrapped in red cloth.
Then, at the time of midnight, one should heat it in a fire of *khadira* wood.
O Goddess, one should recite the mantra while standing facing that direction.
In this way, within merely seven days, one will bring even Purandara himself, or Urvaśī, or Ahalyā, under one's control; of this there is no doubt.
Alternatively, by means of the yoga of meditation through the application of the noose and the goad,
one should join the mind to the mind with a meditation that is deep red.
Having withdrawn the pentad by means of the pentad itself through this practice, [one attains stability].
Having attained oneness with the two, one shall bring [the subject] under control within seven days.
Then, O Goddess, one should recite the Vidyā conjoined with the name of the person to be subdued;
then everyone, as far as the world of Brahmā, will be brought under control.
Now listen, O you who are honored by the lords of heroes, to another [rite], namely attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*).
According to this very procedure, one should then have an image made;
there, one should place a written note (*cīrikā*) inscribed with one's own blood.
O Dear One, one should heat that image born of passion in a fire of khadira wood until it completely melts;
then,
by the force of his arrows, he will come and fall before the practitioner.
O Goddess, it draws [the object] very swiftly from a distance of a hundred yojanas.
Such an excellent method of attraction is revealed in this tantra.
Now I shall explain, according to the truth, the art of enchantment (mohana) for those of middling capacity.
(100b) O beloved, having taken the blood from a parrot’s beak or from a pigeon,
one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) with it and fashion [an image].

O beautiful goddess, having performed the ritual with the Vidyā, one should cast beans mixed with thorns into the middle of a water-pot. For whomsoever this yantra is thus performed, he shall become as if dead.
Deluded, he does not recognize [the woman's] country, caste, family,
or conduct; then, having created a sense of awe in the subject, he should consecrate her seven times with mantras and proceed toward the blazing funeral pyre.

The student should cast that [substance] therein and subsequently proceed for one hundred steps. Having returned, O Goddess of Gods, the lord of practitioners, having empowered it once more with a hundred recitations, should cause her to grasp it without hesitation.
Whomever he strikes while enraged, he renders that person like a log, stupefied;
thus stupefied, that person then knows nothing at all.
O beloved, having thoroughly rubbed her [the woman] who is joined with the *tattvīvana* [mantra], [he achieves this].
Therefore, whichever charming woman the lord of practitioners applies a tilaka mixed with his own blood upon, she shall become his servant;
she will offer herself, her wealth, and even her thieves to the practitioner.
Then, having fashioned a terrible mace from the wood of a funeral pyre and having consecrated it with great skill while wrapping it in a cloth from a corpse,
the practitioner should indeed smear it with dust raised by women.

Having slain a goat before it, one should take its lukewarm blood and bathe [the image] with it again; then one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. From that time forward, she becomes perfected and shall delude the enemy army.

Grasping this terrible mace, the lord of men, standing upon the back of his elephant or chariot, should once call to mind the Goddess of the Gods. He shall then overcome the elephants and the [hostile] kings.
Even if he were alone, he could pulverize a terrible and utterly unsubdued army at the head of a host, equal even to that of Indra;
indeed, having extracted from its cave the very hero who had been struck down in battle, he would crush it.
With this, one should prepare a banner consecrated one hundred and eight times with mantras.
Upon seeing it, all the Śāntavas will flee in retreat;
utterly deluded, they will not even recognize their own selves.
Thus, having briefly described the destruction of armies,
O beautiful one, listen now to the method of immobilization (*stambhana*) according to its true nature.
Having written the name of the enemy on birch bark with yellow substances, [one should proceed].

Having performed the rite with the Vidyā, one should draw an impenetrable circle of Śakra; having thus drawn it, O fortunate one, that impenetrable enclosure for his activities will paralyze even the army of Śatakratu, intent on its march.
By such a procedure, O Goddess of Gods, one will paralyze the planets; or else, one may paralyze the fetus—of this there is no doubt.
Thus the paralysis [of the planets] has been fully explained; now hear, O beloved, the ritual for the planets (*grahakarma*).
Having consecrated a branch of the *śimī* tree or a creeper originating from a fragrant plant with mantras,
and being armored by the previously mentioned ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should gaze upon the person bitten by the planet,
[visualizing] the entire interior of the world-egg blazing with consciousness.
O Goddess, when the body to be treated is cool and the self is perceived as resembling [the deity],
that planet, terrified and oppressed by the mantra, approaches in the form of darkness;
trembling and agitated, it cries out and rolls its eyes violently.
Saying "I release [you]," he should indeed cast it away after having uttered a curse.
Now, for the purpose of destroying epilepsy, this ritual is being described;
listen to it, O fortunate lady, along with its secret, most wonderful [details].
(101b) From terrible sin comes this powerful thief;
therefore, first, for the destruction of that sin, there is the vision of the Goddess’s maṇḍala.

O Goddess of the lords of gods, that which must be performed for one bitten by a planet so that he may not remember it again is a four-legged vessel destroyed by the Vidyā. Or else, O slender-waisted one, one should destroy the body through the application of the Tantra.
O fortunate one, the high-minded man, having consecrated with the mantra the blood taken from a person struck by a weapon,
should apply the *tripuṇḍra* marks with it upon all the limbs of that person afflicted by epilepsy.

Then the king shall never again remember that [attack] which arose from the fourfold [causes]. Then, taking a corpse-ash (śāvaṅkara) mixed with *pura* and well-smelled, one should offer it as incense for one possessed by apasmāra.
Then, one who has been rendered unconscious by the smoke of four-legged [incense] should not remember that vessel.
Having taken the oil produced from the fat, marrow, and so forth of Kṛṣṇa’s dog,
one should then prepare the collyrium contained in a skull (kādyastha).
Having consecrated [the site], O highly fortunate one, when the arrival of thieves occurs,
he whose eyes are anointed with this [ointment] should again recite [the mantra] four thousand times.
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, there is a fourfold tube for the dog.
Having prepared it with seven types of seeds and tied it with a goat’s cord,
O Supreme Goddess, one should fumigate it with that incense;
then he shall never again even remember that vessel.
O fortunate one, having carefully extracted the noose from the one bound below,
and having worshipped the Goddess of the lords of gods, one should fasten it around the neck of the mantra.
By the power of this noose, epilepsy shall arise together and depart.
Then, O Daughter of the Mountain, listen as I describe the procedure he should follow if he transfers this [sin] onto some evildoer:
having caught a single live fish three times over, he should perform it.
(102a) O Supreme Goddess, having prepared a vessel with human flesh as the middle ingredient,
one should thoroughly mix it with that essence and form a ball of rice grains.

As soon as the thief has arrived, one should throw that ball into his mouth; then, having wiped it with his saliva, one should take it back again. O Goddess, to whomever it is given, he shall be provided with food by that very means.
O Goddess, he shall transfer that most terrible epilepsy [to another].
O beautiful one, this is known as the transference of epilepsy.
Now, therefore, I shall explain the wonderful protection of crops.
This [act] is extremely fierce, devoid of ritual conduct and proper behavior.
Having fashioned an iron trident with a sharp point and a most dreadful appearance,
one should fashion its middle shaft according to a measurement of twelve finger-breadths.
Then, by means of the laughter of the fingers, one should fashion two other [parts]:
the *catuṣkikā* should be two finger-breadths wide and variegated with lotus designs.
Thereafter, one should have a *dadr̥* made twenty-four finger-breadths long with a white tip.
Its width is half of that, and the length of the spokes is equal to that [width].
Having thus fashioned this most beautiful trident, O fortunate one,
it should be sprinkled with the five jewels and smeared with the menses of a woman.
Having performed this, one should worship therein the Goddess Kṛṣodarī, the deity of deities,
with extensive displays according to one's means, [visualizing her] garlanded with the thousand-syllable mantra,
mounted upon the peak of the spear of vital breath (prāṇa), and the Vidyā blazing intensely.
One should join the trident to the image and subsequently worship it;
then, having consecrated the trident with one hundred and eight [recitations],
the trident thus installed wards off clouds and thunderbolts.
Having emerged from the maṇḍala, O Goddess, she protects within the nature of the bee;
and with the mind, O Mistress of the Gods, one should recollect the army of the Vidyā. (102b)
O Goddess, one should perform the binding of the boundary (sīmābandha) as long as it is necessary for protection;
thereafter, one should cause the gross [form] to revolve, for it will provide complete protection.
Having beheld the terrible power of the trident, the lords of serpents, beginning with Ananta, [will offer their support].
Distressed by the bursting of the heart as they are whirled about by the central practitioner,
they flee in a faint, overwhelmed and agitated, with their own blood,
to whatever village, district, or city pleases him.
Whenever one recollects this very Vidyā conjoined with the *rañjikā*,
it will then draw away clouds or an unassailable thunderbolt;
or else, a branch from a *śimī* tree, having been consecrated with mantras, [shall perform the same].
Having performed this at the time of the arrival of the clouds,
the preeminent practitioner, having consecrated sand with this mantra once,
should, if enraged, scatter it into the sky; it will protect [the area] for a hundred yojanas.

One should destroy the masses of clouds that are difficult even for the gods to open. Then, having taken auspicious water, the practitioner, possessed by wrath, should consecrate it with mantras and cast it into the sky; thus he shall effect the destruction of the clouds.
When one has consecrated a black mustard seed and hurls it into the sky,
then that lordly practitioner, filled with wrath, destroys the masses of clouds by means of the application of the trident mudrā and the terrible *huṃkāra* mantra.

One should recollect the most fierce Vidyā while destroying the masses of clouds. Having consecrated with mantras a piece of wood, grass, a clod of earth, or a pebble, one should throw it into the midst of the clouds; then it will destroy them.
Having made a drum very firm and empowered it with mantras, one should strike it with force;
it will surely go to whomever it is directed, even if they are as firm as a mountain.
One should do this during the rainy season, as long as one is intent on protection.
(103a) To that extent the practitioner should properly protect it; there is no doubt in this matter.
O Goddess, in this way the supreme practitioner should protect the grain.
Now I shall proclaim the supreme method for subduing the *nāgas*.
Having first performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) by reciting [the mantra] eight thousand times,
one should take up a divine bamboo bow that has been properly consecrated with mantras.
Having gone twenty-one terrible *yojanas*, which were like the edge of a sword,
toward the front of the Nāga-pit, he, enraged with blood-red eyes,
should block the cardinal directions with stakes and mustard seeds.
Then, one should kindle a blazing fire there and offer oblations of black mustard seeds smeared with pungent oil;
indeed, he should offer twenty-one oblations as long as he performs the sacrifice.
At that moment, the lake, resembling the ocean, becomes agitated with waves;
then, rising suddenly and grasping his excellent bow,
he should discharge an arrow there after having intoxicated each [target] one by one.

Then that water is worshipped, for the serpent comes out of fear—terrified, with a trembling body, shivering and overwhelmed by dread. O blessed Ananta, you yourself are like this; how much more so the other lords of serpents?
They remain as your servants, together with their attendants, forces, and vehicles;
and the lords of the nāgas, overwhelmed by fear, undoubtedly bestow upon you elixirs, rejuvenators, swords, sandals, and earrings.
Or he may send it to wherever the lord of serpents, Doṣa, might prefer.
Thus has been told, O sinless one, the supreme Drāviḍa [mantra] of the Nāgas.
Now, O lady of beautiful hips, I shall speak of the great destroyer of poison.
The mantra-practitioner, having consecrated the water with mantras, should also strike the mirror;
other [water], consecrated for drinking, should be given when [the disciple] is thirsty.
Then he becomes free from poison, even if he has been bitten by the God of Death; or, O Goddess of the gods, he who has eaten poisoned food or who is about to die,
quickly becomes free from poison by drinking water consecrated with mantras.
Alternatively, O Goddess of the gods, having taken the poisons— Vatsanābha, Ātmaguptā, and others—
within the hollows of both hands and purified them by means of the previously mentioned nyāsa,
one should consecrate them with the measure (mātrā) of Hari, just as Garuḍa did for the poison.

Having taken the poison in his hand, though it was accompanied by nooses and goads, he gave it so that it would not cause affliction; nor did he kill it, for there was no loss [of power]. He whose nature is the essence of consciousness abides in the state of all-pervasiveness.
One who is apprehensive about his body, when administered [the medicine], transfers the poison [elsewhere].
In this world, there is no doubt that nothing can destroy it;
or else, by means of the yoga of digestion (*jārayoga*), one seizes the poison with the hand.
By means of the yoga of casting the net, empowered by the Queen of Vidyās,
one may then transfer the powder-poison to whomever one desires.
In this manner, O Goddess of Gods, one may play with serpents at will.
O beautiful lady, having joined the *vidyā* through the application of the noose (*pāśa*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*),
the wise one should then draw forth the serpent and dispatch it;
by means of the great coil-binding (*mahākuṇḍalabandha*), he may cause it to run or make it lie down at will.
O Goddess, whatever poison— whether of iron, a phallic emblem, or otherwise— is said to be virulent,
the lord of practitioners shall destroy it merely by sprinkling [the water].
He will utterly destroy even the poison known as "doubt" simply by remembering [this mantra].

O Goddess, I have now described to you the treatment for the five types of poison— namely, that which is stationary (*sthāvara*), mobile (*jaṅgama*), artificial (*kṛtrima*), metallic (*loha-ligaja*), and that known as *śaṅkā*. Now listen to the procedure for killing [the enemy] (*māraṇa*).
One should prepare the base for the effigy by mixing it with black gram and *aguru*,
stirring it with goat’s blood, and blending it with husks and charcoal.
Having drawn the figure of a corpse with bees resembling poison,
one should then encircle it with the Vidyā. Thereupon,
while performing great austerity, the steadfast one should draw [the syllables] there using soot from a crow.
On the day of the Raudra asterism, during the cruel period of the Krūra-vāraka, one should bathe that image again with hot water while reciting the *Priti-māyā* mantra in the heart. Then,
having gone to the cremation ground (*pitṛvana*), one should kindle the sacrificial fire there.
When it is blazing with fierce wood as fuel, one should heat her, whose face is turned toward the fire;

then, O Goddess, while she is thus heated, the man, filled with wrath, should place her back into the mouth of the fire. For as long as she remains in the fire, O Goddess, for that long the enemy is destroyed.

O Goddess, if the Grandfather of the world of Brahmā were to appear in person, then he would surely kill him; of this there is no doubt. This method of killing, which is free from the need for bringing [the victim] back to life, has been fully revealed.
I shall now describe the rite of inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*) by which it is performed against enemies.

O Goddess praised by heroes, having taken the feathers of two owls and the excrement of a crow, one should prepare an incense. Then, having fashioned a pair of images of the two persons to be targeted (*sādhya*), [one should proceed].
And those two buffaloes, fashioned from potent poison—
