having placed within their hearts two copper inscribed plates, O Goddess of the lords of gods— one should then fumigate them thoroughly with incense.
Having turned those two away, one should recite the vidyā while enraged;
they shall become mutually hostile in the presence of their enemies. There is nothing that is not commanded by you for them at all times.
Now listen to this supreme rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), which strikes terror even into Indra.
One should write it upon a circle of wind (*vāyumaṇḍala*) using blood derived from a crow,
or else, O Goddess, one should write it with poison mixed [with blood].
O Goddess of gods, that [mantra] written on birch bark and encircled by the Vidyā should be tied to a tree in a cremation ground, or to one presided over by the deity Wind, but not in a field.
The practitioner situated in the northwestern corner causes even mountains to be uprooted.
Now I shall explain another supreme method for agitating a city,
by the mere knowledge of which the adept attains a state of worshipfulness.
Having gone to a solitary, uninhabited place, the wise man, devoted to the conduct of a hero,
his consciousness intoxicated by wine, [meditates upon] Vidyākaṇḍodarādittā,
who adorns the entire world with throbbing lingas the color of vermilion.
Flooding either the region or the very air with streams of the essence of wine,
one should meditate on the Goddess for one month without constraint;
then all those people dwelling there will become agitated.
They come before the practitioner just as at the unsurpassed holy site;
they give themselves to the practitioner like givers of wealth,
and indeed, they bestow upon the practitioner the foremost circle of kingship.
For whatever jewel belongs to anyone, he bestows that very thing upon them.
This well-known "Agitation of the City" is called the means for attaining the treasure-store.
Having recited the mantra eight hundred times, one should thereafter commence the ritual action.
Having taken a white *rakṣoghna* (pesticide) plant that has been consecrated seven times,
when the time of evening has arrived, O slender-waisted one,
the practitioner of mantras should recite it over a leaf while looking at his outstretched hand.
Then, at the time of dawn, one should become unified with the world as a dense mass;
one should indicate that very state by means of signs such as the conch and the discus.
O Dear One, [one should offer] a wick arising from a garment of nectar, soaked in great oil.
Having placed [the mantra] at the tip of a sword and recited it, one should wander about free from fear.
Wherever the wick falls, there indeed is wealth in that form.
Alternatively, a small bowl (khorikā) should be prepared; the procedure for this is stated here.
Taking a small vessel made of iron and filled with ashes,
one should worship the Goddess therein according to one's means.
Then the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra twenty-seven times; then that pearl,
having been released there, quickly goes to the location of the great treasure,
its essence, and the elixir.
One should show the glorious face, the most excellent and supreme, to the practitioner.
Even by the most terrible *kṣetrapālas* or by extremely dreadful obstacles,
that Goddess cannot be obstructed by anyone here.
Having thus beheld that place, and having bound it through the application of the boundary-consecration (*sīmābandha*),
one should there recite the Vidyā of terrible prowess.
O Goddess, within three nights, one shall summon even a *nikara* who has gone to the world of the Nāgas.
When it rises up by itself upon the ground through the power of the God and Goddess,
the practitioner should employ it here as he desires.
O Goddess, this which subdues poverty has thus been revealed.
Now I shall fully explain how one may attain the status of the Lord of Śrī.
Having performed the sacrifice as previously described, one should place a silver water-pot there,
consecrate it a hundred times with mantras, and seat [the deity] upon an auspicious throne.
Then one should consecrate oneself with all the honors due to a king.
From that time forward, O Goddess, he becomes exactly like the Lord of Lakṣmī;
of this there is no doubt, for my word is unfailing.
This most auspicious descent of fortune has indeed been described to you;
by attaining this, men are liberated from all poverty and great fear—
of this there is no doubt— and they shall surely become blessed.
Now, the rite of transference (*saṃcārikakarma*) is briefly described for you:
having obtained a deceased object that is free from defects, one should [offer it] to the Supreme Goddess.

There, one should meditate upon the Goddess established in the previously described visualization. O Mistress of the Gods, one should install her in the Śrīgṛha with great offerings and with the abundant results of many fire-oblations.

Having established it before him, O Goddess of gods, listen to how the vessels are prepared according to the rule: having brought a vessel of liquor for Śauṇḍika, filled to the brim with the three faces of Viṣṇu,
one should install it before the Goddess.
Likewise, O Goddess, one should install a single *taṇḍola* vessel collected through the *vīrakrama* rite; furthermore, a vessel of ghee,
a vessel of buttermilk, and likewise a vessel of oil, O Goddess.
In the same manner, one should collect a large vessel of cooked meat;
likewise, O Daughter of the Mountain, having collected a vessel of sugarcane juice,
one should place them before the Goddess in such a way that no one sees them.
Thereafter, one should recite the mantra there, joining it with the most excellent *vara-rañjikā*:
"O Goddess, grant me all imperishable condiments,
so that I may remain constantly intent upon sacrifice before you."
In this manner, O slender-waisted one, one should perform the recitation for a period of one month;
from that time forward,
all kinds of condiments will present themselves before the practitioner in the presence of the Goddess, produced from six different regions.
The hero-sacrifice (vīrayāga) should always be performed; by that means, O Maheśvarī, it is eternal. This unsurpassed hero-sacrifice has been fully explained to you.
Now, if one desires inexhaustible wealth, then one should perform this rite.
Having gone to the abode of Hara on the appointed day at the time of the sacrifice,
he unweariedly brought that Rakshasa and the excellent youth;
having placed him in the center of the altar, he adorned him with all ornaments.
(106a) A man should mutter with his arms raised while it is firmly fixed upon his chest,
until that corpse, emitting a terrible sound, begins to tremble.
Then that greedy leader of Dviraṇyāpura spoke:
"I am he, the king of the Vetālas; why have I been summoned by you, O Lord?
Having heard this, the heroic lord remained unperturbed, O King.
"You are indeed inexhaustible; this collection of gold shall remain forever.
By the command now given to you by the Goddess of the Gods, O Vetāla, you shall thereafter become golden.
Having heard this, he then became golden.
One should always make expenditures here by cutting away one's own limbs;
for there is no doubt that these [limbs] will certainly grow back again for him.
O fortunate lady, with that wealth, one should satisfy the poor and the helpless.
O Goddess, one should constantly cause to be constructed ponds, wells, and tanks, as well as various temples and diverse sacrificial rites;
the wise man should likewise cause various means of spiritual practice to be performed.
No accumulation should be made here, for what has been done then perishes.
Thus has the inexhaustible accomplishment regarding wealth been described to you;
having attained which, a virtuous man indeed becomes like Vaiśravaṇa.

O Goddess of the lords of gods, by remembering [this mantra], one undoubtedly achieves victory in legal disputes, gambling, battle, and quarrels. Now, therefore, O Beloved, I shall fully explain the supreme rite for pacification (*śāntika*).
O slender-waisted one, listen to that by which peace may be attained for one who is about to die:
having brought a beautiful water-pot free from cracks and other defects,
and having filled it with milk, one should place therein the goddess Kṛṣodarī.

O highly fortunate one of slender waist, having worshipped [the goddess] who is endowed with the previous meditations and adorned with a necklace of large pearls, one should cause a water-pot consecrated twenty-seven times to be placed upon the head of whomever [is the recipient].
For whomever it may be, even for one on the verge of death, there shall always be peace.
I shall now duly explain to you the Yoṣṭika [rite] as it truly is.
Having prepared saffron mixed with *rocanā* and combined with the substance arising from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*,
one should write the name on birch bark (*bhūrja*) using the Vidyā ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
O Goddess, that name should be surrounded by the words of nourishment (*āpyāyana*).
Having placed [the substance] in a vessel of milk, one should satisfy it with the "milk-ray" (kṣīrakarā).
Thereby, O Goddess, there shall always be nourishment for the sādhaka;
he becomes pure, possessed of a nourished body, free from death, and without disease.
"Without doubt, this occurs immediately; such is the certainty of the scripture.
This is known as the Āpōyana [rite], and it was performed for King Jayadratha.
The goddesses who were previously extracted from the great wheel of Matēśvarī—"
O Goddess of gods, that treasury of rites which has been proclaimed for all the deities is common to them all, because they are all equal here.
Thus, indeed, through such distinctions, many varieties arise among the gods.
However many varieties of mantras have been described here at present,
just so many heart-born [mantras] are remembered for the God and Goddess;
for the ritual procedure for one is exactly the same as it is for all.

Each one should be known as a bestower of liberation, each one as a bestower of all perfections. The Goddess is declared to be one, according to the various divisions and sub-divisions of her stations.
Like the sun among water-jars, the Goddess of gods shines forth.
Thus, O Pārvatī, this entire beautiful secret has been narrated by me to you;
this supreme method of my teaching—
What more shall I delight you with now?

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Section on the Sadhana of Matacakreśvarī," in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra (*Mahātāntra*) concerning the Severing of the Head (*Śiraścheda*), within the Vidyāpīṭha of the Bhairava Stream.
(107a) The ritual procedure for Matacakreśvarī is completed.
Thus the Goddess heard from the mouth of Hara the entire essence of Kālī.
Furthermore, desiring to hear the secret, she spoke again to the Lord of Gods. The Goddess said:
"O God of gods, I have heard of the most wonderful jewel."
"I am fully satisfied, O Lord of Gods; I desire nothing else.
However, O God, there is a curiosity: how is it that she is Kuṇḍaleśvarī, who is to be contemplated within all cakras and who resides in the hollow of the kuṇḍalinī?"
She who is the Goddess, the Mother of the World, the Supreme Kālikā of the entire universe;
by the mere utterance of whose name the cage of bonds is shattered,
and of whom no other more terrible [power] exists within the belly of the world.
"O Lord of the Gods, tell me your name, O omnipresent one; by your grace, [may you] draw forth the life-force from the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile.
Having heard this, the Supreme Lord, the Indra of the gods, spoke.
[To] Umā, the mother of all beings, who is intent upon the protection of the three worlds.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O hero among heroes, to this wonderful ritual procedure.
It brings all prosperity, is most excellent, and bestows the perfection of all spiritual practices;
it destroys the fault of all intermixture and removes all sins, being auspicious.
Merely by uttering its name, the interior of the universe trembles.
By the mere utterance of which one obtains union with the Yoginīs—
that Śakti who shines as the Supreme, who abides in the division of the Supreme and the Non-Supreme,
who is the abode of knowledge and action, and who resides within the center of the wheels of Will and Consciousness.
Subtle, situated within the belly of the pulsating [nāḍī], and joined with the most subtle nectar;
known as Anaṅgadhenavī, she resides in the center of the heart-cakra.
Arisen from the bulb (kanda) as Kuṇḍalinī, she resembles a sleeping serpent.
Adorned with a multitude of arts, she is the devourer of all the kulas; rich in the splendor of the canopy of the world, she is the supreme refuge of all worlds.
She is unmanifest in the form of mantra as Kuladāmarabhairavī.
O Pārvatī, listen to her door from the perspective of ultimate reality (tattva).
Having gone to the abode of the Vīrendras, one should be anointed with sandalwood and agallochum.
With his consciousness intoxicated by wine and adorned with the five jewels, he—
worshipped by the lords of heroes— should spread out the *mātrikā* there, the mother of all speech, upon the ground smeared with heroic substances.
Having worshipped with various enjoyments, one should then extract the mantra:
the Great Void (mahāśūnya), its flow (tatpravāha), and the three powers (triśakti) fully adorned; then the Bindu, then the Moon, and again the Yoni as the eighth.
Then, O Maheśvarī, one should join it from the *viyoni* triangle;
O Bhadrā, the twenty-eighth [syllable] situated in the seventh from the *nāda*,
which is conjoined with the head of that *veśman* (the *dhāman*) and devoid of the prostration (*natipraṇava*).
O highly fortunate one, this *piṇḍa* is the supreme source of all mantras,
the lord of all mantras, the essence, and the illuminator of all mantras;
it brings about the presence of all [deities] and bestows the abundance of all supernatural powers (*siddhis*).
This is the essence that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, the unsurpassed *piṇḍa* of the Goddess.
O Goddess, when its recitation is performed correctly even once, the body, together with the vital breaths, trembles; of this there is no doubt.

Devoid of the heart, head, crest-lock, armor, eyes, and weapons; liberated from both meditation and the object of meditation; situated in the center of the inconceivable and the unshakeable consciousness;
vibrating within the supreme expanse; and the abode of all the digits of power (kalā).
Having awakened [the wisdom] from the hollow of the Ākāśacakra, which is beyond the outer ear-rings,
it arises from the mouth of the Guru like the revolution of a fish.
When six *mīna* [signs] are in the seventh *mīna*, through the *vidyuduccaṇḍa-yoga*,
one sees [the deity] blazing, with two rays as a beautiful crown,
and six *mīna*s at its base by means of the application of the whirlpool (*āvarta*).
When one should set the world ablaze by means of the application of the downward-flaming [mantra],
then one should utter the Great Piṇḍa from the Mīnāvarta.
At that time, there shall be a single staff, a single Liṅga, and a single Fish.
Then that Goddess of the gods enters the cage of the body;
the yogin, consisting of great bliss, then becomes the Śakti-piṇḍa.
Thus, she is remembered as Kuṇḍalacakreśī, Piṇḍeśī, and Kālikā.
One should form that *piṇḍa* into a small ball (*piṇḍaka*), placing it within the *kuṇḍa*;
having placed the *kuṇḍala* within the *kuṇḍa*, one should place the *piṇḍa* in the middle of it.
One should cast the *mīna* into the middle of that, and that [ball] should be situated within the whirlpool of the *mīna*.
The flame that has issued forth from that fish is the flame that enters the end of the earring (*kuṇḍala*).
The sphere (*golaka*) situated at its end is the recollection of the fourfold utterance (*caturuccāra*).
This is the auspicious knowledge of the *piṇḍa*, held as the doctrine of Kuṇḍaleśī.
Relying thus, O fortunate one, one shall attain supreme nirvāṇa;
he may cause the hosts of lions to fall and slay gods and dānavas.
The practitioner should forcibly perform the extraction of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).

The most excellent of practitioners, having bound the Anaṅgadhenavī mudrā, shall become capable of extracting the six flavors; of this there is no doubt. I shall now fully describe that mudrā by the name of Anaṅgadhenavī.
The practitioner, having assumed the bound lotus posture (*baddhapadmāsana*), with body, head, and neck held straight,
and with the area of the chest free from excessive tension, should encircle the hands in the *jāpa* gesture.
Having slightly opened the treasury of the thirty-two deities,
the practitioner [should bow] to that Supreme Bhairavī, the Mistress of the Supreme Deity, who resides within it;
he should bow to her with his own mantra, and to the other [deities] along with their retinue.
One should make the fish-catcher the foundational element,
held fast by means of the previously mentioned yoga of sacrifice. Let them enter into Śivabhairava,
who is protected by Śiva and filled with the supreme nectar within the vessel.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, this is that mudrā known as Anaṅgadhenavī. Indeed, she is the supreme among all mudrās, the supreme one who causes melting and agitation.
O Mistress of the gods, having bound this, one should extract the six flavors from the victim.
O Supreme Goddess, if one should bind this [mudrā] in the midst of a group of women,
then they all will melt away through the power of the Mistress of Mudrās (Mudreśvarī). Indeed, those thirty mudrās which were previously proclaimed by me—
Among them, this Mahāmudrā Khageśvarī is the foremost;
by her mere presence, the priceless Yogīśvarīs become agitated.
O you who are worshipped by the best of gods, having captured the bound soul (paśu) through the yoga of the net (jālayoga), [she brings about their agitation].

There, one should properly bind the flowing liquor of the six flavors. Having meditated upon the excellent fish within the place of the blazing mantra-araṇi wood, one should contemplate the Lord of the End (Anteśvara) here; by that, one should pierce the self.

In this way, after merely seven days, he forcibly seizes the sacrificial animal by means of the application of blazing flames; the animal is bound as if in a net. O fortunate one, he then crushes it underfoot with a great trap.
O Goddess of good vows, when one consumes [the substance] through the application of the stream by means of the left-hand practice,
using the exertions of the right-hand practice according to the distinction between the left and the right,
then, O Great Goddess, one should always take the fifth salt.
O fortunate one, by means of the great trident that pierces the adamantine knots,
he extracts the vital essence situated within the sevenfold sheaths.
Having gone there at the onset of night during the dark of the moon, O Maheśvarī, with consciousness blissful from wine and established in the abode of his former yoga,
he should stand in the center of the altar and bind the Mātreśvarī mudrā upon the shoulder of Hara.
Having bent the left knee halfway and extended the right one,
and having opened the apertures of the mouth while remaining in the previous mudrā,
one should then cross the hands and tear open the corners of the mouth.
One should slightly caress the tongue; the Mistress of the Triangle (Kuṭeśī) bestows bliss.
Then, fifty deities will indeed flow forth, as will all the goddesses—those presiding over various forms, the Mothers intent on weeping.
Out of joy, those consisting of great bliss arrive by the hundreds of thousands;
surrounding the heroic practitioner who stands there with immeasurable splendor,
they bestow the *caruka* upon that high-souled practitioner.
"By which [means] you shall become their lord, just as that Bhairaveśvara is;
so it shall be without doubt, for my word is unfailing.
Or else, O Goddess of the Gods, having formed the mudrā called Ghorarāvā,"
All the Mothers gather together; listen to that, my beloved.

Satiated by the *palāla* offering, his soul fulfilled, the lord of practitioners, with a serene mind, O Goddess of gods, shall go to the supreme cremation ground after taking recourse to the funeral pyre.
Having sat there, the Lord of Heroes, according to the sequence of the previous yoga,
should press down his right foot directly beneath his own anus;
having sat there, he should extend the part called *dhāma* while it is half-bent.
The body should be inclined to the right, with the right ear slightly tilted;
one should move it there a little and open the mouth with the left [hand]. The right [hand] should be placed in the cavity [of the mouth], and one should repeatedly stroke the tongue.
With his face turned upward, he should utter [the mantra] with the sound of a donkey’s bray;
and he should worship the goddess Kuṭeśvarī, the deity of deities, eight times with laughter.
Furthermore, O Daughter of the Mountain, one should perform the Ghorarāva [mudrā] in the center;
this is the mudrā known as Ghorarāva, which bestows the perfection of the melāpa.
As long as the practitioner performs it here up to seven recitations, [the result follows].
At that time, O Dear One, those Mothers, the Ḍāvis, and the Ḍāmarikas arrive,
raising a tumultuous clamor before the practitioner. Having saluted the lord of practitioners just as the goddess Karaṅkiṇī does, they stand there.
"O leader of practitioners, all of us say this:
wander with us wherever your mind finds pleasure!
Become our lord, for he is Bhairaveśvara."
Having heard this, O Goddess of the gods, he then gave them a cloud empowered by the mantra of Kūṭeśvarī from his own abode; for when that cloud is given,
he alone becomes their husband and their spiritual practitioner (sādhaka).
The Lord of the Wheel, possessed of great majesty and worshipped by all the lords of the gods,
the Hero, having assumed the mudrā of terrible sound and remaining in the family of Fishes upon the mountain peak, should perform this ritual procedure.
Having severed the great snare of delusion and having drunk the supreme wine from the mouth of the household,
O Goddess of the gods, one who has gone beyond suffering should perform the *duki* at night;
then the *yoginīs* will appear before the practitioner.

Having become their husband, he indeed rejoices like Bhairava. Then, seeing her deeply submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, the lover— who is intent on performing fierce deeds for her sake— [acts] with heroic and generous efforts.
Then one should perform for them the initiation that destroys the bonds—
known as the Nirvāṇikī— which is perfected and produces immediate conviction.
O beautiful one, having overturned the fish by striking it on its back,
she remains there within the womb, her body coiled in the shape of a ring;
she is five-faced, most terrible, a female serpent, and a devourer of snakes.
As long as a man summons that dream through the application of wrath,
so long does she appear in her awakening— terrible and agitated by the destruction of the universe.
Having torn open five mouths, the five lords draw [the victim] forth together.
And that serpent-like power (bhoginī), greedy for enjoyment, rises up in anger.
One who is established in the root of Śakti should direct her into another body;
therefore, she emerges again from the disciple’s body through the aperture (brahmarandhra).
O Goddess, as long as that heart has not reached the tip of the kuśa grass,
one should impel it together with the mind toward the dvādaśānta. Once it is joined there, until it reaches the station of the visarga, [one should maintain it].
O Goddess, as long as one maintains that unification while uttering "ciccida" (or "sva"), for that duration he is pierced and will experience a slight trembling;
accompanied by the bristling of his hair, he indeed shivers slightly.

Thereafter, there arises incomparable bliss caused by the manifestation of one's true nature; then, the state characterized by being the sole consciousness and the absence of agency is born. At that time, he indeed becomes liberated from saṃsāra—what wonder is there in this?
Thus has been fully described the initiation that is devoid of the sacrificial pit and the mandala;
it bestows all accomplishments as its essence and is difficult to obtain even among the gods.
One who is thus initiated indeed becomes Bhairava himself.
The hero who bestows curses and favors removes impurity by his mere sight.
Now, O Bhairavī, I shall describe another [practice] called Ghaṭṭana;
by practicing this, O Maheśvarī, the lord of practitioners becomes perfectly accomplished.
Having stepped upon the Bhairavī-mudrā, which is the vajra-cage of all the directions,
one should remain perfectly motionless, having compressed [the body] with the Saṃkocaka [mudrā].
Then one should cause it to tremble slightly, making the belly vibrate internally;
having performed that movement there, one should press it with skillful means. Then the bonds perish, and that which is Yama becomes manifest therein.
O fortunate one, by means of that manifest aggregate known as the three *piṇḍas*— namely Nara, Śakti, and Śiva— one becomes worthy of all accomplishments (*siddhis*).
At that time, one becomes the lord of all masters of mantras (*maṃtreśvara*) and a sovereign among practitioners (*sādhaka*).
This has been taught as the "striking" (*ghaṭṭana*) which reveals one's own true nature.
Now, O Supreme Goddess, I shall fully explain "suppression" (*nirodha*),
by which the suppression of the moon, the sun, and the mind may arise.
Abiding in the wheel of Kūṭeśvarī, endowed with all mental functions,
one should cause the moon and sun to be paralyzed through their union in the yoke.
Their sheaths are ever slightly opened, and they remain situated within the petals.
When one whose nature is the essence of consciousness, who is permeated by the true being of Śiva,
and who relies upon the seal of the "neither-exist-nor-non-exist" (amavya) through the abandonment of the obsession with grasping at what is unreal,
then cessation arises within the Supreme Self.
Henceforth I shall explain how the supreme realization arises within the Great-Souled practitioner regarding the Supreme Self.
Abiding in the wheel of Kūṭeśvarī, he should swallow the multitude of lunar digits.
Until that flood of rays is completely absorbed into the heart-wheel,
the Supreme Self shines forth through the yoga of contracting the body-mass (piṇḍa).
Within that essential nature, one's own self-awareness will attain realization of its own self.
This realization regarding the Supreme Self has been fully revealed by you,
through which the manifestation of the mudrās, mantras, and words arises as a vibrant awakening.
The throbbing Kaulika tradition has been proclaimed to you in brief.
Therefore, O Goddess, listen now as I shall describe the three voids (śūnyatraya).
O beautiful lady, Śiva is by his very nature unattached to phenomenal states.
It is never tasted by those [senses] preceded by great delusion;
therefore, it is called "void" (śūnya), for it is not like the extinction of a lamp.
When it is always completely full of its own essential nature.
Then, for the one of immeasurable splendor who has manifested the three powers within his own self, Śiva is said to be "void" (śūnya), yet the fetters are not [absent] as if he were dead;
for through the expansion, manifestation, and contraction of his potency, he remains within himself alone in the state of both dissolution and emergence.
When the immutable Lord Śiva assumes the form of the possessor of power (śaktimat),
then that which is devoid of both existence and non-existence should be known as "the Void" (śūnya).
Because his power has become fully established in its outward expansion, he is manifested by that very [power].
She is never stained by the states of the egg and the cosmic sphere;
therefore, because she is devoid of them, Śakti is considered empty of them.
O Goddess, the supreme consciousness is the Void; thus it is sung that consciousness is the Void.
O Goddess, when that incomparable power is of such a nature that it is empty of the qualities beginning with *prakṛti*, as well as the nine internal organs,
the objects of the senses, and the categories of the elements— [it remains] always pure like a sword-blade.
That great heroic form is neither stained nor diminished;
therefore, it is proclaimed as "Nara" (the Person) because it is empty of [intrinsic] attributes.
Thus, O Goddess, there is a triad of voids consisting of Nara, Śakti, and Śiva.
Listen, O beloved, to what is proclaimed in this supreme tantra regarding attainment here:

situated within the hollow of the heart-lotus is the stainless nature of consciousness; there, one drinks the multitude of lunar digits that exist externally through the activity of the mental fluctuations.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, O slender-waisted one, through this very practice of union and embrace,
there then occurs the manifestation of the void called "man" (narākhya).
Through meditative absorption into its true nature, the arising of all supernatural powers and qualities occurs for the preeminent practitioner within just one month; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, when one becomes the master of the wheel of channels through the union with the Sun, [the result follows].
O beautiful one, by abiding in the middle path and so forth, one attains rest;
then that void which bestows power becomes eternally manifest.
Established therein, the supreme leader of practitioners beholds the most excellent assembly of deities.
O Goddess, he beholds him assuming various forms without obstruction;
O Goddess, in the sequence of all mantras, his mastery arises.
Indeed, the practitioner performs piercing, causing to fall, and so forth, or even dissolves [into the deity].

Through the practice of the power of the mantra and the void, the practitioner of mantra performs, as if in play, the entry into another body and other such feats by means of the various types of living beings, including the dead; indeed,
he can produce thousands of forms from a single form in a mere instant.
O fortunate one, when the wheel of mantras, the wheel of vidyā along with its maṇḍala,
and the wheel of mudrās are firmly established within the wheel of power (śakticakra), O Goddess of gods,
everything becomes a servant to the great-souled practitioner.
Now, listen as I describe the nature of that which is proclaimed as the Void (śūnya) consisting of both aspects, known as Śiva— how it is in its auspicious essential form:
infinite, perfectly full, and radiant with the splendor of all-pervasiveness.
Devoid of beginning and end, free from the source and the effect; liberated from above, middle, and below, and devoid of action and qualities;
free from time and occasion, it transcends the dissolution of the moon and the sun.
Free from movement through directions or places, devoid of the quality of discursive thought,
beyond speech, the supreme abode even of all abodes, eternally divine,
the very nature of itself known as its own inherent being, the Supreme Consciousness, the Supreme Lord.
Free from all conceptual proliferation, beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition,
self-cognizable, self-luminous, awakening, and the unfailing nirvāṇa.
Through the very transmission from the mouth of the Guru, the state of being one-pointedly absorbed in its true nature arises;
there is no doubt that such a master of practitioners becomes perfectly accomplished.
Like Śiva himself, the master of practitioners is fully endowed with all supernatural powers (siddhis).
This consciousness of the triple emptiness has been proclaimed to you in brief.
Now, O beloved, I shall explain the supreme, waveless state,
by the mere realization of which one becomes endowed with all accomplishments.
Apart from this King of Tantras, this knowledge has not been investigated elsewhere;
it has come down through the lineage, established from mouth to mouth.
It is devoid of all ritual action and is like the ocean without waves.
O Supreme Goddess, this has not been told by me to anyone except you.
This fifth [chapter], known as the *Tristaraṅgāru-sāriṇī*,
is exceedingly subtle, the essence of the Guru, and a great source of joy for the intellect and heart.
It is the discernment between the perishable and the imperishable, the awakening to the continuity of the universe;
it is characterized by the absence of sovereignty, the great bliss, and the great dissolution;
it is that which has taken up karma, which brings an end to the existence of karma, and is the most excellent cause of karma.
That which is the stream of existence born of karma, yet possesses a supreme form, that eternal state— Om! That single-syllabled word, the awakener of all beings,
consisting of pure consciousness, non-dual, Śaṅkara, the irreproachable one.
Thus, I am that very one eternally; I am he, and I alone am this world through the nature of desire, fashioned by me alone. In every state, I alone abide within them, remaining unmanifested.
I conceive myself by means of myself, solely through the cause of my own autonomy.
And whatever wheel is fashioned by that conception— the entire universe of moving and non-moving things—
abides within all beings, yet transcends all beings and remains untainted.
(112b) That light-form which is the Self, I am that, the eternal seer of all; devoid of measure, yet called infinite measure, I abide within the absence of all measures.
The seer is beginningless, undecaying, devoid of qualities, and the fulfiller of all;
he is perfectly concentrated within the peaceful states that transcend the qualities of *sattva* and the rest. Like an ocean without waves, I am eternally possessed of a mind thus disciplined.
Even among beings who possess the wealth of the abode of consciousness, he is the investigator;
he by whom this realization has arisen—that "I am indeed that True Brahman"—is truly I.
Whatever exists while one is established in one's own samādhi is characterized by the qualities of the intellect and the other faculties.
I am the source and the Lord by whom they find dissolution;
likewise, I am the abode of the rays of light, peaceful, and resonant within the center of the heart.
Having realized the self that is devoid of the abode of Brahmā, one becomes pure in intellect—the sovereign of yogis.
The deluded soul, who is not detached from the objects of the senses and does not possess discernment,
and who is not disciplined toward *nirvāṇa*,
would then enter that beginningless bliss which is free from conceptual construction through that state.
By that [means] with which they yoke the eternal Brahman— the auspicious Lord who yokes the practitioner—
[he attains] the vehicle of intellect and mind along with its purpose within the sphere of the primordial power (ādi-śakti-maṇḍala).
Thus, by this path of Niṣvāta, one attains the state of Śiva.
When intellect (*buddhi*) has waned and the mind (*manas*) and ego (*ahaṃkāra*) have likewise perished,
one then enters the circle of Śiva by means of the supreme power (*paramā śakti*).
That consciousness which exists together with Śiva at the time of the dissolution of all beings— [that is the state attained].
In the sphere of the self-arisen power (*svayaṃbhū-śakti-maṇḍala*), that which is without deliberation and identical to the primordial awakening of the perfectly awakened one arises as vibration;
when it dissolves into the state of non-vibration, then one is Śiva, established in his own nature.
That which is unmanifold is indeed manifold; the awakened one is within the sphere of the intellect.
The nature of existence is beyond the senses, unconditioned, manifest, and devoid of becoming.
That state which belongs to that beginningless existence is not [attained] through becoming.
He should indeed meditate upon that Self as "I am that," the eternal seer of all.
When the Self of the unmanifest becomes manifest, [it is realized].
The absence of all entities for the sake of the Puruṣa is called Bhairava; by that Great Thread this world is woven.
It is the binder of all beings and the deluder of the moving and the unmoving.
Since the wheel (cakra) produced by this [power] consists of manifold states,
it manifests as waking, dreaming, and speaking when struck by the utterance of the Lord.
This Great Māyā, called Bhairava, is the knower of divisions through its fourfold division.
This subtle nature of the Puruṣa follows its qualities;
dwelling within all beings, it is perceived by one who has become [enlightened].
It is the protector of those whose minds are stilled and who are companions in the abode of Brahman.
Unperceived by those who have entered the world of darkness and fallen into delusion,
this most brilliantly radiant ray has emerged from the sequence of Brahman;
it is the supreme intellect of the yogin and the eye that is skillful regarding all objects.
For this [vision] is another, divine vision within the auspicious Vāmadeva;
it is subtle, supreme light, moving within the Supreme Lord.
Indeed, when one has abandoned all dharmas and has fully resorted to this [vision], [it is attained].
Then, liberated from the laws of space, effortless, desireless, and pure,
I truly become the power consisting of the Great Abode (mahāhara),
in which the succession of qualities such as sattva and the rest is dissolved.
There is nothing higher than my own state; that is the supreme state of Śiva.
In a single moment, he perceives the birth of all beings, their enjoyments, and their complete destruction—this is his everything; that is the supreme state of Śiva.
That digit which is conjoined with time is incomplete when devoid of time;
that digit reveals time, and that digit is indeed time itself.
It is she whose mouth swallows the digits of the moon, the sun, and the rest, as if they were morsels of food.
He by whom that *kalā* has been consumed is called "partless" (*niṣkala*).
For the Self consists of all beings; whose unity would not be lost?
The enjoyer, having become tranquil through the fourth state (*turyā*), is no longer deluded.
When the intellect (*buddhi*) does not perceive objects as its own purpose,
then, awakened by its own bliss, it attains the state of the Lord (*pati*).
In the web of conceptual constructions regarding bliss, and in the arising and perishing of merit and demerit,
there is the certainty that nothing exists which is not Śiva;
this is the contemplation that has arisen for those who are completely absorbed in pure consciousness.
This vibration which [occurs] from merits and demerits, but not at the time of the arising of the fruit—
though it exists within this body, it causes the dissolution and emergence of everything on all sides.
By means of this, I consider liberation to be as certain as if it were held in the palm of my hand.
Emerging from the left measure (mātrā), endowed with each respective abode (dhāman),
it perceives the self as the abode of consciousness and the qualities such as smell and so forth.
Therein, there is no suppression, no utterance, no deliberation, and no conceptualization.

The non-duality of time and destiny is a certainty within the waveless [ocean]; the universe, which has attained oneness within the one, is described by the intellect as it truly exists in its distinctness,
yet for that intellect there is no manifoldness.
In one who has abandoned dharma, who is detached, effortless, characterized by awakened intellect,
and absorbed in the state of non-duality— what longing can there be for pleasure or pain?
For that which is the observation of dharma belongs to the nature of the cessation of the qualities of the mind.
When the web of conceptual construction has been awakened and one is overflowing with the bliss of power, the yogin perceives that reality through the desire for the well-ascertained state.
I consider [the world] beginning with Śiva to be "I"; what longing can there be for merit and demerit?
Residing in the center of her circle of digits, blazing with light during the Vaivarta [kalpa],
she is the enchantress of all beings and the lawful consort of Śiva.
That consciousness which exists within all beings,
formless and subtle like the space within jars, is the witness of karma;
it is ungraspable by the bonds of action— what longing can there be for any worldly enjoyments?
Fully awakened by her own self-manifestation, she is the unfailing consort of Śiva;
by his mere will, he has made this entire universe consist of play.
He is non-dual with all beings, himself the Hero, himself the Lord.
Through the continuity of all phenomena, that state which was cultivated by me is my eternally existing nature, a non-conceptualization consisting solely of nirvāṇa;
when both truth and falsehood have subsided, peace has indeed arisen within.
Then, through peace, I am peaceful, abiding as the one who sports within embodied beings;
omniscient, all-pervading, and tranquil, I have no desire even for desires.
Always possessing all power and eternally satisfied, they know me as Nirvāṇa.
This universe is peaceful, variegated, of the nature of consciousness, and devoid of the mind.
By means of the intellect, the unborn perceives the unborn; such is the ultimate reality.
The perception of qualities such as sound and the rest occurs within the range of the power of manifestation.
That which has been concealed by the foot is Śiva in the ultimate sense;
it is the cessation of all sufferings, pervaded by power—of this there is no doubt. That which is satisfied with the bliss of the inexpressible is designated as Śiva.
The state of manifoldness has always arisen among beings as non-duality;
for all, peace exists in this non-duality according to the ultimate truth. Indeed, for one whose self is continuous, there is that which draws forth bliss.
That Dharma, being liberated from all bonds, is worthy of worship in its true essence;
in non-duality there is no bondage, and for one who is eternally satisfied, what desire can there be?
I alone am the supreme light, situated above all.
I am ungraspable, I am beyond intellect; I am unseen and unheard.
To behold the Self by means of the self, one must be free from the states of having become or being born.
I am the illusion (māyā) of all beings, the father and the grandfather;
I am the beloved, the destroyer of the universe, the unshakable and well-established one,
in whom this variegated universe has arisen and into whom it again sets.
O King, that which is the mere existence of the Self,
which remains by itself alone at the dissolution of all desires and is experienced with bliss—
that is the state completely cast off [of duality], known as Samādhi.

Free from qualities such as intellect and the rest, with the self grasped by the stainless [soul], having attained the state of pure consciousness— that samādhi characterized by sattva is indeed free from the body and mind, waveless and devoid of conceptual construction.

That primordial awakening is perfect enlightenment; it is the meditative absorption through which this entire universe is pervaded. It is that eternal state in which one remains awake. That bliss is unborn, subtle, and difficult for all to attain.

While awake, one should not dream of objects in the waking state, nor should one dream in a dream. Yogis remain asleep while awake, being liberated from both waking and dreaming. He who sleeps with the waking state does not indulge in sleep during a dream.
If one were to know that unborn [Self] which is sleepless and dreamless, then the existent is not seen in the waking state; it is seen through the dream of existence.
The Existent, the Self of all, perceives the longing for the dream of waking.
When the waking state has been dismantled— just as one awakens from a dream—
and through the discernment of phenomena that have become tranquil by means of inquiry,
then discernment is awakened in the waking state, free from the sleep of ignorance, even as one was previously in a dream.
The unborn one, not knowing the unborn and the unproduced, becomes deluded regarding the unborn.
That is proclaimed as the dream of one who is asleep, whereas that which occurs while awake is called the waking state.

The intellect that is devoted to Brahman and has attained its true aim experiences attachment toward various states of being while it is enveloped by waking and dreaming; however, the subtle intellect that perceives that [Reality] does not experience waking, nor dreaming, nor even deep sleep.
In that [Reality], neither waking nor dreaming occurs, nor is deep sleep possible.
For one who is detached from manifold existence, there is that which abides within, the auspicious and immutable.
When dreaming has reached the state of deep sleep, and for the waking one there is the changeless;
when deep sleep occurs within waking and dreaming, and waking occurs within waking at all times.

The universal commonality of all forms is consciousness in all these things. By myself, through my own self, I behold the Supreme Lord; seeing him, I perceive the one essential nature in all beings at all times.
Consciousness dissolves into consciousness as the supreme Self. One who desires desire may desire desire through desire;
indeed, that desire within desire is the eternal Brahman.
In one whose mind has attained the state of non-duality and is devoid of [the perception of] reality,
no bondage arises even in a slaughter consisting of the concealment of truth. That dissolution which occurs when the distinct collection of worms and insects is brought together is [true liberation].
Happy within, one who speaks of and listens to the supreme bliss is rare to find.
In the awakened one, the intellect dissolves; the mind remains in the mind. The vital breath dissolves into the abode; thus, all actions cease forever.
The single radiance consisting of the qualities of consciousness is established within all beings.
When that radiance is set to rest, one becomes the Fourth (turya) and does not grieve for beings.
By whomsoever it is illumined by the intellect, she [the radiance] emerges in his own essential form.

He who is illuminated by the intellect, yet is himself awakened and possesses great power, dissolves into the intellect through the intellect; from the awakened one, the intellect is born. The entire universe is awakened by the intellect, and the support of the intellect exists [within itself].
One whose intellect has turned away from the cage of the eight elements toward the peace found in desires [is liberated];
when the intellect is dissolved in non-dual supreme bliss, it does not perceive [objects].
Difficult to be understood by all forms of cognition, he is the awakener through the intellect.
Having awakened to the Self by means of the self through my intellect, I am blameless;
I stand firm and unshakable, while all other beings remain in error.
The self-awakened light of the supreme non-dual *mā* is both transcendent and immanent;
like the sun, it is the illuminator in the world, having arisen from the midst of the sun. And from that very sun, the radiance has emerged, which illumines the entire universe.
Having drawn up the nectar of the sun, Soma should satisfy the elements;
having drawn up the nectar of the elements, Soma should satisfy the sun. The nectar-ray of the sun is the imperishable source of all beings.

Possessing an unsetting essence and capable of attracting the world, the channel (nāḍī) called Arkavatī vibrates; it melts the moving and the unmoving. She is indeed the imperishable form of Bhairavī, who causes the waning of the moon.
Just as the self is the dissolution of all beings through its very observation,
so too, by the mere vibration of power (*śakti*), one should assume a body; born of men, satisfied with the individual soul (*jīva*), such a speaker is for the gratification of Bhairava.
Though free from desire and knowing all desires, she is intent on being expelled;
she is the true form, distressed by the diverse elements, merged and protected by Bhairava.
When the elements have become abundant, they are born; merged, they reside in that state of consciousness.
When Śānti is [established] and Bhairava is well-established, one attains peace.
One regards the Self as vibration and perceives it everywhere as the Real.
By means of the Self, one likewise conceives of the Uncreated, the Immutable Dharma, and Immortality.

The eyeless is declared to be the all-seeing, the streamless state of the Supreme Self. Though without thought, it conceives the universe; though without intellect, it is always awakened. It is the source of all desires, yet it is forever free from longing for worldly phenomena.
The Lord, who originates from volition, transcends both truth and falsehood;
he is effortless, non-dual light, devoid of vibration and bliss. (116a)
Free from the manifestation of the mind, I am consciousness, unconstructed,
in that non-dual state which is devoid of the effort of universal festivity and free from conceptualization;
for it is beyond the senses, without appearance, and is the very nature of consciousness itself.
Within the lotus of the Sūtra, the bee of the Sūtra wanders at all times.
The supreme state of bliss is called *paramānanda*.
Exhausted, one sleeps fearlessly, fully satiated by the honey of bliss.
When that bliss which is liberated from all states arises—
bliss born of the Supreme, originating in the vital breath (prāṇa) within all consciousness—
and when one attains stability therein once again, that is traditionally known as prāṇāyāma.

In the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the supreme *prāṇa*, the life-force drawn in by living beings. For meditation (*dhyāna*) is the Self, inconceivable through the self; by means of the *prāṇa*, one reaches the Supreme Self.
When the *prāṇa* is equalized, one attains that Lord, the *prāṇa* who is equal within the *prāṇa*.
And when that channel is reached and established under my influence, it shall be proclaimed:
having drawn the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings— the vital breath (prāṇa) which is delighted by its own bliss—
into the downward breath (apāna), one should enter into the very interior of the prāṇa.
Upon the rising of the vital breath (prāṇa), its universal form (vaiśvarūpya) is attained;
from that embodied being, innumerable forms issue forth.
It is swallowed by the tip of the moon’s foot, and it is swallowed by the sun at the peak of the dust (rajas).

It is the eternal light, whose nature is to burn away darkness and which abides in the state of *dharmasthāma*. When the mind, intellect, and ego are established within that light by means of its radiance (*dhāman*),
the vital breath (*prāṇa*) dissolves into it— that light of the Supreme Self.
That is the supreme rest of the mind, illuminating the rays of the essence of consciousness;
it is the awakening of the mind, abiding in the mind, consisting of consciousness, yet devoid of the mind. It is free from all undertakings, that state in which the mind becomes perfectly steady.
(116b) Embracing nothing and appearing as nothing, Brahman alone is the ultimate reality.
The mind, unattached to desires, is inhabited by the consciousness of the Puruṣa.
The supreme *haṃsa* is well-established as Brahman alone from the perspective of ultimate reality.
When the mind, which comprises all things, becomes independent and rests upon Brahman,
attaining repose in ineffable bliss, it is not born again.
O Mother, in the beginning, beings were born as mind alone, free from desire;
thereafter, all phenomena born of conceptualization came into existence in their manifold variety.
Indeed, it is the mind itself that is always born in every state of being.
When one wanders through transmigratory existence by means of the intellect while not perceiving the Self,
as long as the seed of this tree of saṃsāra is not destroyed, so long does one— overwhelmed by the fruits of karma— die and take birth again.
At that time, Cūḍa’s wife gave birth to a large tree with fine grains (*dhānakā*).
As long as the grains were not cast into the fire, it remained standing as "Āva.
Indeed, when the mind, which has the nature of grain, is offered into the fire of consciousness, [it is consumed].
In this vast cycle of existence, birth does not arise again.
This nature of saṃsāra persists only so long as the mind is manifold;
when the mind is firmly established in its own state, that itself is the supreme state.
For one who is deluded by manifold thoughts, the true nature of the mind does not manifest.
When there is an internal abundance of bliss, that is designated as "mind.
That mind arises from wisdom; it belongs to no one, nowhere, at any time.
One who has set out upon the path of desire falls into dependence on another.
Just as a spider, once born, fashions snares for itself from its own body and thereby binds itself,
so does the silkworm bind itself with its own threads.
Joined with the yoga of practice, ever-disciplined and possessing great fortitude, content with the instructions of the teacher, they strive for the perfection of their own self-nature. (117a)
He was virtuous through his exclusive adherence to moral conduct and granted fearlessness to all living beings;
having restrained all his senses and fixed his mind within the heart,
he likewise [subdued] the mind, intellect, ego, and the asceticism of his own self.
Then one should cause all beings to enter into that very [Self].
From it the creation proceeds; into it alone it returns.
The internal intellect consists of bliss and is the imperishable light of consciousness.

The Self is the essence of the entire world; yet that state is here excluded. As long as one does not find or perceive the Self within oneself, existence is conceptualized as being permeated by the nature of all states.
When the Self, which consists of all things, abides as one within the self,
then one sees the Self by means of the self, like the sun obscured by clouds;
then, with delusion destroyed, free from attachment, and with an inner self devoid of desire.
Others, having established their consciousnesses in Brahman, the Supreme Self— in whom all bonds are severed— find that all sufferings have entirely ceased.
For the sake of destroying all dualities, he bestows liberation within the inner self.

"The eye is the sun, the universal self; Brahman alone becomes the immortal self. Those who thus perceive this manifestation of their own essence without interruption—non-dual, supreme bliss, unshakable, and firmly established—[attain liberation].
I do not see that which is not mine, nor do I see that which is not myself.
I alone am arisen, peaceful, omniscient, the Lord who performs all deeds;
I am the creator and sustainer of the world, the Father and the Grandfather.
I am the all-pervading vital breath, yet devoid of breath; I am the supreme Lord.
There exists nothing other than me, the Supreme Self, who delights in my own nature. Through both unity and multiplicity, I alone am the waveless ocean.
I am the Supreme, of perfect form, whose nature is the sustenance of the three worlds; I am Bhairava, free from all affliction, expanded in supreme bliss.
O you who are honored by the heroes, this consciousness is known as being free from waves;
it is liberated from both meditation and the object of meditation, and here it is devoid of desire.
All of this, along with the wonderful secret, has been fully explained, O beloved.
One should cause the earrings of Anantābhā to be given to the devotee;
O beautiful one, she should be bestowed here upon those devoted to the Tantras of the Goddess.
Thus [ends] the third Ṣaṭka in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great Tantra, within the *Śiraccheda* of the Vidyāpīṭha, in the hymn to Bhairava.
The Fifteenth Chapter on the Ritual of Kuṇḍaleśvarī.
988. The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, [tell me of] that best of gods whose crest is marked by the moon.

O God, [I have heard of] the Hero, the Lord of Heroes, Bhairava of radiant countenance, who is attainable through yoga, the Sovereign of the Gods, whose body is the Vidyā, and who is free from all ailment. O highly fortunate one, I have heard of the Vidyā Kālarātrī, who possesses great power.
Mahāmārī, Mahāghorā, Sarvapratyaṅgirā— the dyad;
the goddess Matacakreśvarī, as well as the other, Kuṇḍaleśvarī—
[these are found] in this Jayadratha, the great sovereign king of tantras, the supreme Yāmala.
O Mahāvidyeśvarī, O Ghorā, [you have taught] the compendium of the essence of the Vidyās.
Even now I have a doubt for the benefit of practitioners:
how is it that the Goddess Ekākṣarā is supreme as Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī?
Or how, O God, does that which arises from speech reside within the spokes of the wheel of knowledge?
O Maheśāna, tell me all this, if you are pleased with me.
Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom, Jñānagarbhā, my beloved!
To Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, to Soma, Sūrya, Agni, and Māruta—to no one has this been made known by me;
that I shall now declare to you, O blameless one."
The single-syllable great vidyā is the supreme performer of fierce deeds;
she is the illustrious Mistress of Vāgbhava, most formidable and not to be revealed.
Ninety-eight lakhs and seventy-seven crores—these are my most formidable vidyās that have issued from the mouth of Bhairava.
O Sovereign of the Gods, all of them are joined with their own lord; this vidyā belongs to him.
Indeed, this speech of the Mistress of Vāc is never equal even to a ten-millionth part of that which is the peaceful,
unborn God, beyond the sphere of causes,
the perfectly full Bhairava, who abides in the delight of the inconceivable consciousness.
Her supreme will is that power (śakti), the exalted Manonmanī.
Her eightfold [manifestation] is declared to be supreme; it is the great cause from which speech becomes manifest: the Yoni, Uṣyā, as well as Nakva, the hexagon, and the lineage of Kuṇḍalī.
Māyā, Nārāyaṇa, Haṃsa, Aṣṭaka, and Vāgbhava are remembered [as the five limbs]. In the supreme abode whose nature is consciousness, which is filled with the compassion of the Supreme Power—
that light which illuminates everything and manifests as speech in its fourfold transformation.

She is eternal, innate, subtle, and the manifestor of the eight families; she is beyond action within the Kula and illuminates both ritual action and gnosis. She is proclaimed as Vidyeśvarī and is likewise remembered as Vāgbhaveśī.
I shall declare its extraction; listen, O Bhairavabhāminī!
There, upon the stone slab in the ancestral abode, O Bhairavī, the eight groups of letters are situated according to the division of each class.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Tāpa, Vidya, Vidyeshvari, and Kalā.
Then, one should extract the goddess whose form is Mahābhairava;
having placed the end of the "sa" (sānta) at the beginning, one should extract the twenty-sixth [letter].
Below and above, constricted by fire, joined at the head and the secret place,
and pierced by the letter *ta* from the sixth group— this is remembered as the single-syllable goddess.
The Supreme Power (Parāśakti), who is to be accomplished through recitation (*japa*), is directed along the path of sound;
she has ascended to the station of the Temple of Speech and stands behind the form of Bhairavī.
Then one should remember the Great Vidyā, situated in the center of the wheels of Will (*icchā*) and Knowledge (*vidyā*).
Having recited [the mantra] twenty-seven hundred thousand times, one indeed attains success.
In a most formidable place such as a cremation ground, or at a site where bodies fall,
eating sparingly and joined with meditation, adorned in black garments—
One should meditate upon her who is fierce, most terrifying, red and black, and fearsome;
whose limbs are black, who is mounted upon a corpse, naked, and has a distorted face;
who wears a crown of skulls and has tawny-colored hair.
She was obstructed by the swinging of the hungry ghosts, with earrings hanging down to her ears;
she held a skull in her hand, was deformed, and was intent upon wine filled with blood;
she was adorned with ornaments of snakes and wore a sacred thread made of serpents.

One should meditate upon the form of the Goddess as being entirely of this nature: fierce, with eighteen arms, five faces, and three eyes; bearing all weapons, and bestowing the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation. Thus one should contemplate the complete form of the Goddess.
The partless [state] has already been described; now hear something more by way of brief indication.
That Goddess, whose form is sound (*nāda*), travels upward through the *piṅgalā* and reaches its end.
Resembling smokeless embers, she is established at the crown of the head.
Subtle, shaped like the flame of a lamp, consisting of the nature of awakening, and free from the three impurities;
firmly rooted at the end of the state of deep sleep, arising from the splendor of Śiva;
mounted upon the machine of sound (nāda), auspicious, and performing divine actions.

That digit (kalā), which devours time, is firmly rooted in the syllable Vāgbhava. When one remains established in that [state], having consumed what has entered there, one becomes the Lord of Speech (Vāgeśvara). She is the source, the Mistress of Expansion, the Sovereign of Power, possessing a threefold nature.
(119a) In another tradition, she is said to be the form of the bliss of the triangle;
that is the first [syllable], Vāgbhava, wherein resides the expanding Speech.
The goddess of gods is proclaimed to be within the path of the *ūṣman* vowels;
by means of the coiling of the earring, the second *vāgbhava* is remembered.
This is the manifestation of the first letter when the practitioner is established in expansion.
O Goddess, the third [syllable] is Vāgbhava, which is unchanging by nature.
O Goddess, between the navel and the penis is the six-cornered [center] named Kanda.
Through the contraction of the three seats, O Goddess, there then arises the great expansion of speech.
In the supreme void (paravyoman), that fourth Vāgbhava is revealed;
likewise, Kuṇḍalī Śakti resides in the foundation (ādhāra) and in the palace of the heart. In the station of Śakti she is called Parā, the abode of Vāgbhava.
O lady of beautiful hips, through its universal form, its expansion, and its contraction;
O fortunate one, through the eclipse of the moon, the fifth [syllable] is known as Vāgbhava.
It is the very nature of mantra, the form of consciousness, whose abode is the supreme sky.
That sixth [syllable], the supreme Vāgbhava, is a dense thicket of illusion;
when it exists in the form of expansion, it is devoid of bindu and nāda.
When the emission (visarga) and the rest have completely subsided, its essential nature is that of the vowels.

Then, O Goddess, that seventh [syllable] is Vāgbhava, whose essence is Bhairava; it is garlanded with a network of thirty-eight kalās and abides in the three states of movement. O Dear One, the eighth Vāgbhava consists of the aggregate of the three abodes.

Thus, O Supreme Goddess, the eightfold Vāgbhava has been proclaimed. O Goddess, the supreme Bhairavī-kalā residing within this wheel is celebrated as the Goddess Vidyāvidyeśvarī, the Mistress of Speech (Vāgbhaveśī).
Or rather, from this very state of existence, the supreme eightfold sovereignty of speech is born. One should remember that as its body; therefore, one should always meditate upon it there.
Then the speech of the chief practitioner shall become unimpeded;
by mere recollection, the state of knowing the meaning of all scriptures arises.
Having attained such a yoga, one may perform whatever action is desired.

Otherwise, O Bhairavī, it must not be performed at all until this is known by the lord of practitioners and the hero who follows the conduct (*vīrācāra*). By means of this yoga, O Bhairavī, one accomplishes all rites.
O Goddess of the gods, in the animal sacrifice (paśu) there are five [vowels], O Yoginī, six, and seven.
With five, with six, and with seven, O Mistress of the fifth,
the knower of mantras, mounted upon Śakti, should enter the portion of nectar.
One should crush its lotus— the previously mentioned *kulākula*—
and then repeatedly extract it with the trident of terrible form.
O virtuous lady, having consumed the divine [essence] in the Kali age, one assumes a lean form.
Having taken a portion of the nectar, one should enter one's own body.
By doing so, O lady of excellent hips, one may even summon the gods;
for that best of practitioners becomes free from old age, immortal, and devoid of sorrow.
Having enjoyed the sovereignty of the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest, one shall go to the city of Śiva.
Having meditated with the supreme nectar-like syllables,
[one sees] Hari seated upon the trident, mounted on the wheel of the *khecarī*.
Through the subtle yoga, one may destroy all beings when [the breath] arises from the void (nila).

For the purpose of subjugation, one should meditate on her as red, with a luster like a mountain of vermilion, accompanied by gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rakṣasas, and great serpents (mahoragas).
O Goddess, what need is there to speak of men and women?
Whether it be the Lord of Gods, the one born from the lotus-womb, or even the god Indra—
if one applies [this practice] at the three junctions of the day, he will kill [the target] without a doubt.
One should remember the Goddess as pigeon-colored for [the rite of] pacification; for subjugation, she is red and black;
for causing dissension, the Goddess is green; and for expulsion, she resembles glowing embers.

She is said to be yellow for the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), and reddish-yellow for the rite of paralyzing (*stobhana*). She has the luster of the moon’s orb for the rite of pacification (*śāntika*), and is white and red for the rite of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*).
Thus the Goddess, who performs various actions, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I shall now describe her mudrā, which strikes fear into all beings.
At the beginning of the recitation, one should contemplate the terrible [form], and at the end of the recitation, one should contemplate it again.
Seated on a high seat, the practitioner of mantra, with body erect and neck held straight, [should perform it].
With a face clearly enraged, Koṭarākṣa, who is most terrifying,
should act just as the hands were positioned when drawn together by the strings of entrails;
he should likewise tear open his lips at the corners of the mouth.
Moving the tongue repeatedly, one should dry up the body through forceful *uṣṇīṣa*;
one should utter a terrible cry of "Hā! Hā!"—this is the Mudrā of the distorted face.
If properly employed, it angrily shatters the apertures.

O Bhairavī, by means of the utterance of this Vidyā, there shall be the accomplishment of all things— attraction, expulsion, inciting enmity, killing, driving away, and nourishment. O Goddess, it has no heart, nor indeed does it have a head or a crest-lock.
O Goddess of gods, O lady of excellent vows, there is no need for armor, nor for ear-rings, nor for protection by means of the weapon-mantra;
for it is this very Goddess who brings forth the accomplishment of all tasks.
Having correctly learned from the mouth of the Guru the mantra that accomplishes all aims—
The great mantras beginning with Bhairava bestow liberation at the end of the body.
Whatever karma—whether seen or unseen—the supreme practitioner may attain, such as cruel acts, eye-salves, incense, and the concealments of sorcery like Indra-jāla; [all these are accomplished].
Subtle, gross, and likewise long—having experienced these, one shall go to the city of Śiva.
This has been fully explained to you as the definitive determination regarding the Mistress of Vāgbhava.
"What else shall I speak? Tell me, O daughter of the Lord of Mountains!

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, concerning the procedure for Vāgbhavā, in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of the *Śiraccheda* within the *Vidyāpīṭha* of the *Bhairavastrotaḥ*.
Having thus heard this great expansion of the Vāgbhava mantra from Girijā,
the Queen of the Gods, desiring to hear more and overcome by further doubt,
prostrated herself and spoke as follows, seeking the welfare of Jayadratha.
The Goddess said:
"O portion of the universe, I am satiated by listening to the multitude of scriptures;
now I desire to hear the most wonderful secret."
O Destroyer of Tripura, that which was not told to anyone by you—
the two-fold Vidyā consisting of the thousand-syllable garland, both peaceful-fierce and fierce—
has been heard by me, O Lord, as the terrible Karaṅkiṇī.
Now, O Lord of the Gods, this most terrible garland of a thousand syllables is indeed known as the Name; it is more secret than the secret itself,
by the mere remembrance of which the destruction of all sins occurs.
That which attains the knowledge of mindfulness established within the mouth of the Yoginī,
by which all the previously mentioned accomplishments (*siddhis*) come to be perfectly realized—
O Parameśvara, it is indeed called *Nāmā* through the grace of Sureśāna.
Having heard this, the God of gods, the destroyer of worldly existence, spoke.
Bhairava said:
"Listen, I shall tell you this wonderful secret."
O Goddess, that [mantra] of a thousand syllables, whose nature is both terrible and most terrible—
its incomparable ritual procedure has been guarded by the Kulakaula;
it was concealed by me, O Beloved, out of fear for the destruction of the world.
(121a) By the mere conversation of this [goddess], even the Fire of Time would be reduced to ashes.
O Goddess, who could possibly recite the praises of her who effects the dissolution of the universe?
May there be well-being for all the worlds; may no calamity befall us. By the grace of the God of gods and the Goddess, may there be complete protection for us.
Having gone to the fearsome cremation ground or even to the house of our preceptor—
There, having cleansed that altar, which is smeared with the five jewels,
rubbed with human bone, made into earth, and anointed with red [pigment],
one should spread there the *mātrikā* consisting of all speech.
Endowed with the eight groups [of consonants], one should worship according to one's means;
having worshipped with supreme devotion, one should then extract the Vidyā.
First, one should extract the goddess Kuleśvarī, who is immeasurable.
One should again extract Krodheśvara twice; then one should extract the first [syllable] from the heart of Sadāśiva, obstructed by Bhīma and Śaṅku. This six-syllabled word is proclaimed as the first.

With this king of mantras, one should accomplish whatever is desired by the mind; one should meditate upon the Goddess of Mantra, who possesses a universal form and performs all rites. Indeed, O Mistress of Gods, there is nothing that is not successfully accomplished by means of this.
Furthermore, O Goddess worshipped by the best of gods, Krodheśvara should be given [as the first part] in two ways.
[Then] Kāla joined with Dāraṇā, and Vahni adorned with three vowels—
this four-syllabled [mantra] is indeed extracted as the second word.

By this, one may slay this entire universe, both moving and unmoving. One should meditate here upon the Great Goddess, the Mistress of Gods, who resembles a hundred fires of cosmic destruction, who effects the annihilation of enemies, and who holds a sword and a torch.

One should contemplate that [energy] falling upon the head like a flash of lightning, together with the [letter] *sa*. One should likewise contemplate Ananta, established in fire and adorned by the circle of the bindu;
and likewise Bhairava and the others, with Bhairava seated upon the *haṃsa*.
With earrings, mounted on fire, and adorned with the Bindu;
one should bestow Krodheśvara in two ways, and then extract the Amṛta once more.
Having placed [the syllable] *ca* at the beginning, with the seat formed by the fire of time (*kālānala*);
then Śakra marked by the abode of fire (*vahnikṣaya*), followed by the nectar (*amṛta*) situated in the sixth position;
then Ananta established in time, adorned with the house of fire (*vahnigeha*).
Nārāyaṇa in his essential form, Varuṇa established in Vāyu,
preceded by the womb (the letter *y*), the fifth [consonant] (*pa*) with the first [vowel] (*a*), and likewise the abode of fire (*ra*) alone;
this twelve-syllabled mantra is indeed the third supreme word.

O Goddess, that knowledge which has come forth in three ways— gross, subtle, and known as the supreme— will become manifest within six months through its worship. This king of words is proclaimed to be the performer of all actions.
One should contemplate the God and Goddess here in whatever form is desired.
One should again extract the first [syllable] of the Veda, then the Vidyā, and then that again;
Sadāśiva should then be assigned, constrained by the Bhīma-śaṅku.
The end of Varuṇa mounted upon Kāla, and the end of Varuṇa together with the goad;
the pure Niṣedha should be given, and likewise the pure [seed] beginning with Kāla;
Amṛta mounted upon Kāla, conjoined with the bow in the sixth position.
O Bhairavī, having extracted the *soma* alone, which is adorned with *agni*, place that marked [syllable]— the first of the fifth [vowel] situated in *vahni*.
The first of the fifth [vowel], accompanied by the goad (*aṅkuśa*), should be placed within the knot of Gaṇendra.
The third [syllable] is the head of the vowel *u* (Ū), and the *haṃsa* (HA) situated in the seventh position;
then the first of the bow (DĀ) alone, followed again by the wind (YA) marked by the end of fire (RA).
This fourteenth word consists of eighteen syllables.

O Goddess, one should contemplate the Melāpakaraṇa, which has the form of a fierce fire, is surrounded by hundreds of flames, and bestows all siddhis. It consists of the first of the third [group] marked by the third digit, and the first of the fifth [group] marked by that same [digit].
One should visualize [the deity] standing upon Varuṇa, trampling upon a double-tongued serpent and a goad,
adorned by that very prohibition.
One should give only the nectar (amṛta) and again only Varuṇa;
[this consists of] the sixth vowel and so forth, mounted upon the seventh consonant and adorned by the seventh.
This is the excellent fifth word, consisting of thirteen syllables.
For the sake of accomplishing the *haḍamelāpa*, that which bestows success is said to be [attained] from a thousand [repetitions].
*Mahāmāṃsa* is worshipped by all goddesses and grants all accomplishments.
Having extracted *Kālakevala*, one should join it with *Haṃsa* and the two vowels.
One should place Varuṇa and Kāla, adorned with the second vowel (ū),
followed by the negation alone and then Varuṇa with the goad.
In the third [position], one should place Amṛta joined with the vowel and the negator.
One should likewise arrange the fire preceded by the womb (Yoni) in the fifth position.
Having formed this two-word phrase, [one places] the Nectar (Amṛta) together with the Goad (Aṅkuśa),
the Prohibition (Niṣedha) firmly established in one's own self, and conjoined with the destruction of fire (Vahnikṣaya).
The bow should be visualized as situated in the wind (vāyu), endowed with the garment of the digits (kalā).
This is declared to be the unsurpassed sixth pada, consisting of fifteen syllables.
By the mere remembrance of this, the Goddess comes into one's presence.
She shall become the accomplisher of all rites for the high-souled practitioner.
Having again extracted Kālādya, then Gaṇeśa,
then Varuṇa alone, and then the fifth [syllable] preceded by three Suns;
Preceded by the Yoni and marked with the Sāṅkuśa, one should extract Śakra;
likewise Gaṇeśa with the Niṣedha, struck on the head by the three Suns.

The fire [letter *ra*] with the fifth [vowel *u*], the bow [letter *ca*] preceded by fire [letter *ra*] situated in fire [letter *ra*], the end of compassion [letter *ha*] alone, the fifth [vowel *u*] preceded by the first [vowel *a*] alone,
the bow [letter *ca*] preceded by the first [vowel *a*] alone again, and the wind [letter *ya*] marked by three suns [the letter *ma*].
The first of the five is the variegated womb; then the King of Wrath (Krodharāja) in two parts.

Then Mohinī is to be given in two parts, followed by the earring situated in fire (the letter *ra*), endowed with the drop (*bindu*), fire (*ra*), and destruction (*kṣa*), and obstructed by the terrible spike (*śa*).
This seventh word, adorned with twenty syllables,

should be known as the state of all accomplishments (sarvasiddhipada), situated within the cavity of the fire of time (kālāgni). Therein resides that supreme radiance, infinite and consisting of the nature of consciousness.
That Great Goddess arises through the power of this pada.
Again, having extracted the *kāla*, together with the *haṃsa* that pierces the mouth,
it should be preceded by the *yoni* and consist solely of what is called the nectar (*amṛta*).
To this, one should again give the preceding [syllable] and extract only the arm;
ending with the trident, situated before the womb, it is struck on the head by the triple-sun.
Then, marked by that horse, one should again extract only the swan.
[One should visualize] the vital points (marmas) attached to one's own body, together with the arms and clothing;
again, the vital point situated within oneself from the previous [state];
again, the channels (śirās) overcome by the goad (aṅkuśa); and again, the wind (vāyu) along with the fifth element.
One should extract the bow together with the house of fire (Ra), and Soma alone (Sa).
Likewise, the arm situated in Varuṇa (Va) and the fifth [syllable] following the bow (Ca).
Then Varuṇa (Va) mounted upon a skull (Kha), and Niṣedha (Ma) marked by three vowels (Ā, I, U).
O Goddess, one should extract the Soma [syllable] together with Kālāgnirudra;
then again, the Kevala [syllable] preceded by Cāpa (the bow), marked with three vowels,
and firmly restrained by Bhīma and Śaṅku— thus the eighth pada is extracted.
In twenty-one cycles, he becomes the voracious devourer of the cosmic egg;
indeed, roused by the fire of time, he effortlessly brings about destruction.
It shines at the crown, at the head of the wheel of causes (*kāraṇa-svaracakra*).
It should be known as the performer of all rites; it is proclaimed to be situated there.
Again, make it mount upon Vahni-Bhairava and reside within the *kuṇḍala*.
Again, one should place the syllable *vahni* (ra), adorned with the *mohanī* bindu (the nasal dot).
One should then place the *haṃsa* (ha) mounted on the fifth vowel (*u*), and again place the *indra* (la) situated therein.
This word should be formed in this manner, and then one should give the *yoni* (the letter *e*) first once more.
Again, O Mistress of the Gods, fashion this mantra as follows:
take the syllable *va* (Varuṇa) thrice, conjoined with *ra* (the Earth), preceded by the Yoni (*e*), and followed by the seventh vowel (*u*).
Then extract the fifth letter from the beginning (*ka*), which is solitary, and the Fire (*ra*) conjoined with the Goad (*i*).
One should extract Varuṇa (va) conjoined with Yoni (e), and then Kāla (ma) alone.
O Goddess Haṃsā, one should likewise extract [the letter] joined with Mukhadāraṇā (au).
Then [one should extract] Kāla (ma) preceded by Mohanī (i), and again Kāla (ma) alone.
Furthermore, its first [syllable] is to be given; then Soma and the others alone;
then the horse joined with Mohanī, adorned with the Yoni, the double-tongued one (the serpent) trampled by the goad, situated above Varuṇa.
Śakra is joined with the goad, and Kāla is adorned by him alone;
Dvijihva is stepped upon by the goad and stands above Varuṇa;
Śakra is joined with the goad, and Kāla is adorned by him alone.
