Caṇḍālī, Kālikā, and likewise Mahāsaṃkarṣaṇī;
Ḍāmareśī and another, as well as Jñeyaprabhāparā;
another by the name Bhagavatī, and likewise Yaṃtrapramāthinī.
Mahāmāyā, the mother of the three worlds, has departed from me;
likewise there is Māhāmātrīśvarī, and another, Bhairaveśī;
and Caṇḍā, and Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, and another, Citānandā.
Another is Ānandabharitā, and another is the supreme Harahuṃkāriṇī; another is Viśvarāviṇikā, and likewise another is Mahāmāyā; another is Jñānaśakti, and another is Jñeyaprabhā.
The one who feeds the Great Puruṣa, likewise the ender of sins;
the one who possesses great wisdom (Ānandanyā), the supreme Mistress of the Yoga of the Moon;
the one who feeds the Great Puruṣa, the mother of the Great Garuḍa.
Another is Nārāyaṇabalā, and another is Caṇḍakātyāyanī;
likewise there is Rudrapadā, and another is Viśvagrāsinikā.
She has the form of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, and Svar, and she is everywhere devoted to the Mother.
The supreme Goddess is of the nature of the world; another is Huṇḍā, the supreme sovereign.
She is the mistress of the great Bhairava-lords, as well as the beloved of the wise and the people.
Another is Jīvanirdalakarī, and likewise another is Prāṇagrāsā; Khādanī, Viccā, and another is Caṇḍakālikā;
Kālarātrī, Jambhanī, Rāvinī, and likewise Drāviṇī.
Another is Vidrāvaṇī, and another is Vasiṣṭhapriyakā;
there is Varākulā, Bhīṣaṇī, and Doṣanirdalanā; another is Jīvasammardanī, and another is Ānandajananī.
The utterances of *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ* are likewise the deliverer of the living soul;
[there are] Mahāmārī, Brahmamārī, Kālarātri, and Karṣaṇī;
and another, Kālamekhalikā, as well as Jambhanī and Mohanī.
Bhaṃ Bhoṃthā, Devadeveśī, Yogeśī, and Mahābalā;
Kharaheṣā, and likewise another, Dhāṃjhārī, and yet another;
the goddess Ḍhaṇḍhā is thus proclaimed, as well as Rudrarājeśvarī.
The goddess Karaṅkamukhikā, as well as Haṭṭakhalūpikā;
Bhairaveśvarī, Phekkārī, and likewise Vidyārājeśvarī;
and also Haṭṭabharūdrī, and another, Rākṣaseśvarikā.
The supreme among all is Mahāmāyā, Vāgīśī, and Viśvakarmaṇī;
likewise Viśvarūpā, Huṇḍamukhī, and Somarājeśvarī;
as well as Cāmuṇḍā and another, Cintāmaṇikalānankī.
Kularājeśvarī, likewise Jīvacakkreśvarī,
Viśvalakṣmī, Viśvaśakti, and the supreme Citprakṛti; Caṇḍeśī, Paramāviccā, and the supreme progenitress of the three wheels.
She who sustains the earth of the six chakras as the foundation, the Mother, the leader Bhairavī; likewise, she who dwells in the supreme abode, who carries the syllable *huṃ* within her,
the Mistress of the Wheel of the Great King of Weapons, the Yoginī Jālaśamvara.
(143a) Kālavaktrā, Tadeśānī, and likewise Kālavimocanī;
another is Rudrasya Dayitā, as well as Caṇḍāmuṇḍā and Huṇḍikā.
Kālī, Paramā, and Aghorā are remembered as the others;
likewise there is another called Paramaghorā, and yet another known as Viśvodarī. Mahābhogyā, Vasānā, and another Kālī are also proclaimed.
Mahākālī, Haraṇī, and likewise Duḥkhavināśanī;
Caṇḍālī, Karālī, Kālikā, and likewise Mālinī—
she who is renowned as the destroyer of all fevers and who brings joy to Brahmāṇī and the others.
The Western Supreme Goddess is to be known as the bestower of great bliss;
thus the Goddess herself is the Wet One (Klinnā), garlanded with a thousand syllables. She is always to be worshipped and adored by the deity under various names.
Indeed, there are as many excellent divisions of the God and Goddess;
for it is taught that by one established in his own station, the worship of all [the goddesses] is performed.
O Beloved, she who performs those respective rites should be known as the fivefold potency (*pañcavīrya*).
Thus, O King, there are always thousands of these [circles] due to the arrangement of the preceding enclosures, as they are described as six, eight, twelve,
sixteen, twenty-four, and thirty-two in their respective sectors here.
At the end of the sixty-four spokes, according to the divisions of their own faces and coverings,
forty-one words are proclaimed;
through the conjunction with the covering of the channels (*nāḍī*), their divisions are infinite.
In this way, the one Great Sovereign (Maheśānī) may be differentiated through various distinct divisions.

She should be worshipped and served according to the ritual procedure for the Solitary Heroine (Ekavīrā), and then her mantra should be recited. Alternatively, each individual word [of the mantra] should always be recited and cultivated by the wise.
There is never any distinction in mantra for one who is always honored by the best of gods;
thus it is for one whose mind is non-dual and whose body is forever that of an Avadhūta.
O fortunate one, for one who is free from conventional conduct, that which is meditated upon indeed attains fulfillment.
This "pervasion of the path" has been declared for practitioners at the beginning of worship and other rites.
Now, O slender-waisted lady, what more shall I say?
Thus, in the Bhairava-stream, in the Vidyāpīṭha, in the Śiraccheda, in the Jayadrathayāmala Mahātatra, in the third Ṣaṭka, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work,
in the Ghoraghoratarācakra, [this is the chapter] titled "The Pervasion of the Deities of the Feet. The Goddess said:
Now, O Maheśvara, I wish to hear about her meditation:
how is Mahāmātrī to be meditated upon as she arises in the sequence of the gross and the subtle;
and [how] the garland of a thousand syllables, through its division into one and many?
O Blessed One, explain this along with its secret, which bestows great benefit;
by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner shall become worthy of all accomplishments and shall indeed become a perfected master who performs all rites.
O Lord of the Gods, it must indeed be explained in such a way that one may become free from doubt.
Bhairava said:
Listen attentively, O best of gods; I shall proclaim the secret to you.
That which stands between the states of consciousness and unconsciousness is that unsurpassed form:
characterized by radiance, subtle, self-perceived, free from affliction,
filled with its own bliss, tranquil, containing all, and the source of all activity.
The Śākta [power] is the fire-drill for all mantras, situated in the midst of light and bliss;

it is designated as manifestation (vibhūti), maintenance (dhṛti), tranquility (saṃśānti), and absorption in one's own radiance (svollāsalaya). Furthermore, it is called cessation (vicchitti), flow (pravāha), and movement (cāra).
O Goddess, the ninth, called Janma, is manifest through the divisions of Kaula.
When that Śākta energy, consisting of nine limbs, is sequentially condensed,
it should then be known as the tenth, augmented by all energies.
Each [of these] further divides into a hundredfold varieties according to the distinctions of syllables and mantras; thus,
the manifestation of power becomes clearly evident in its accomplishment, slowly unfolding through the radiance of creative energy.
The abode that is the source of all mantras, the lineage-sequence of Mahākālī, manifested with the expansion of a thousand-fold shimmering splendor of color;
it has become terrible and most terrible, destroying the world as it exists.
Then the goddess became even more massive, garlanded with a thousand syllables;
she stood upon seventeen steps, bearing the hand-ornament of the heroic Aghora,
possessing a thousand faces and eyes, and radiant with a thousand arms.
She has a thousand bellies and necks, she is covered with a thousand feet;
she is intent upon a thousand weapons, and she releases a thousand blows.
She acts for a thousand ages, and she is the devourer of a thousand Yamas.
Indeed, she resembles the autumnal sky with its flocks of crows, cuckoos, and bees;
one should meditate upon her as terrifyingly formidable in her swallowing of the entire universe's splendor,
resounding with fierce *bhāṃkāra*, *huṃkāra*, and *ṭāṃkāra* cries.
We vomited forth [the earth] which possessed the sound of the clashing of masses of roaring doomsday clouds,
which was swallowed by the fierce fire of the kalpa that consumed the moon, sun, and stars,
and which was instantly being devoured with flames by powerful and terrifying beings.
Scattering thousands of meteors that tore the hollows of the earth’s slopes,
she was like the fire of the cosmic dissolution due to the friction of her teeth against her hips;
most terrifying, with eyes like wells whose depths were as vast as the interior of the universe.
For a moment, her single tuft of hair— tawny like the fierce fire at the end of an aeon— was tossed about with a clanging sound, scattering the pavilion of the universe;
it was brilliantly adorned with a garland fashioned from the lotus-like heads of the lords of the worlds.
She who has made a crest-ornament of the skull of Tārkṣya with its great wings;
she who is resplendent with a crown overflowing with the heads of a hundred Rudras;
she who wears the stalk of Brahmā as a dark ornament; she whose hands bear auspicious scars.
She is made singular by the multitude of severed heads of the lords of causes, radiant with offerings;
her body is smeared with blood from the unrestrained crushing of the universe.
With a roar of laughter as terrifying as the thunderbolt of a vajra,
she shattered the pavilion of the Brahmāṇḍa with the impact of her broad footsteps;
her thighs and hips were encircled by a magnificent garland of hundreds of thousands of cosmic eggs.
[She is] Sadāśiva’s great and terrible girdle of skeletons,
whose touch is like a diamond needle and whose voice is resonant; she is radiant with folds [of skin], a forest of ten [types of trees], and the destroyer of the trees of worldly existence.
She whose hair has the touch of a fierce donkey’s bristle like a vajra-awl,
who wears a formidable sacred thread made from the crest-jewel of a great serpent-king,
who is consecrated by the immediate sacrifice of universal destruction, and who possesses a terrifying countenance.
She whose naked form is set ablaze by a torrent of fire issuing from her deeds,
adorned with hands holding a vajra, a bell, a sword, a trident, and a fierce khaṭvāṅga;
she who bears an axe, a bow, an arrow, a horn, a spear, and a javelin.
She who terrifies all beings with the unrestrained sound of her great ḍamaru drum;
whose hands are adorned with a garland of skulls, severed heads, and lotuses;
and who raises a terrible vīṇā, a bhindipāla missile, an axe, and a club.
Fierce with the great weapons held by the haughty warriors of the great *haṭṭa* clans; delighted by the death-cries of the Time of Universal Destruction;
and adorned by the soles of her feet, which are as terrible as the flood of time at the end of the *Kālāgnirudra*.
O Nābhi, you who have been sprinkled by the flood of the water of all attained reality;
you who have destroyed the entire succession of paths with the fierce and terrifying roar of Bhairava;
you who have made the crest-ornament of Nṛsiṃhabhairava into your ear-jewel.
Her hair is adorned by a multitude of severed heads numbering a hundred thousand like suns;
her body is resplendent with the excellent elephant hide stripped off by Mahāmataṅga.
Her body was terrifying and formidable, consisting of dry entrails and sinews devoid of flesh;
her foul mouth was filled with a great garland of severed entrails, produced by the violent friction and collision of the entire mass of their splendors.
She whose breasts have the faces of a lion, a boar, a rhinoceros, a serpent, and a tiger;
she whose mouths are those of a bear, a jackal, an excellent lion, a horse, and a boar;
and she who is radiant with the faces of a hawk, an owl, a great vulture, and a cat.

One should meditate upon her who possesses the form of the universe, who consists of the universe, and who is the splendor of the universe— she whose mouth is a sacrificial pit from which fierce flames burst forth, consuming all the principles (tattvas), and who is filled with emerging sparks of fire possessing the brilliance of millions of towering Meru mountains.
One should meditate upon the supreme Kālī, who bestows the fruits of all desires, possessing whatever form is desired and whatever vehicle is desired—
whether as a solitary heroine (ekavīrā), exceedingly fierce, or according to her specific color and nature.
Or else, by means of the division of words, or according to the lineage of the deity—
whether it be one or many— that which bestows the fruit of the desired object;
thus has the excellent meditation been described, distinguished as gross and subtle.
The best of men obtains all desires from this Vyāna.
All this has been fully explained; what else do you wish to ask?
Thus [ends] the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraccheda* of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavasrotas*.
The method of meditation for the most terrible wheel (*ghorataracakra*) in the third hexad.
Having heard this, the Mistress of the Gods, having prostrated herself with a heart filled with joy yet possessed by doubt, spoke again to Śaṅkara.
The Goddess said:

"O Lord of the Gods, O Maheśvara, regarding those various types of initiation (dīkṣā) that have been described by you, how should they be performed? Please explain them according to their distinct divisions."
I have not understood through your analysis the supreme determination regarding initiation and knowledge.

Tell me: how, by what manner, for whom, and by whom should these rites be performed? What is the pervasion (*vyāpti*), what is the tradition (*samāmnāya*), and what is the procedure (*vidhi*)? Please explain this to me.
O Maheśāna, speak now that which is accompanied by its secret, concealed within all tantras,
the most essential of essences, which was previously only indicated.
Having heard this, Bhairava, the destroyer of worldly existence,
suddenly spoke again to that Goddess whose lotus-eyes were now fully awakened.
Bhairava said:
Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! Since I have now been questioned by you,
I shall explain this secret to you, even though it is not to be told—
this incomparable collection of initiations hidden throughout all the tantras.
Indeed, initiation must always be performed by a Guru who knows the meaning of all scriptures, who is perfected in both theoretical knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*),
and whose minds are solely intent upon Śiva for those terrified by the fear of cyclic existence.

Initiation must certainly be performed by a Guru who knows the reality for those who are pure, devoted to their teacher, and who possess the descent of power (śaktipāta). [It should also be performed] for the elderly, those afflicted by various diseases, children, the simple-minded, and those addicted to worldly enjoyments.
O beloved, for women, animals, deer, and the like, as well as for stationary beings,
and likewise for those who have gone to the next world— even for elephants and horses—
this [rite] is always beneficial even when they have been killed by beasts of prey, thieves, lions, and so forth.

For those whose funeral offerings of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), water, and so forth have been omitted, the wise preceptor who has mastered the meaning of the Tantras should properly perform the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*) to truly uplift the deceased. Whatever living being or material object exists in this world, whether moving or stationary, [is pervaded by Maya].
O Goddess, with a mind permeated by compassion,
the Guru, whose self is Bhairava, should initiate each [disciple] with a non-conceptual mind,
uplifting the entire universe through the sequences of yoga, knowledge, and action.
O Goddess of gods, through the various sequences of initiation always proclaimed by Śiva,
I shall now explain in brief the wonderful determination of initiation (*dīkṣā-nirṇaya*),
which has not been told to anyone and contains its secret, O Daughter of the Mountain.
(146a) Now,
the nectar of initiation into reality is taught as it truly is:
first, Śiva, who is infinite, perfectly complete, and free from ailment.
It has the form of an unbroken circle, is self-cognizable, and is infinite.
O Great Goddess, its power, known as Parā, is inherent;
she should be understood as Bhairavī, who possesses that nature, like the edge of a sword.
Just as fluidity belongs to water, heat to fire, and radiance to the sun,
so too does his body consisting of power (śakti) exist in the form of potency (vīrya).
For it is from that which consists of the forms of will, knowledge, and action that Sadāśiva becomes manifest.
The fifth is the Lord of the Mantra-tattva, the leader who stands above all paths.
Following that is the principle known as Īśvara-tattva, which is beyond compare for its wonder;
having brought this entire world, both moving and unmoving, under his control.

Then there would be the piercing of the *vidyā*; [this] reality (*tattva*) is eternal and beyond reproach. Thus, this group of four realities, which is perfectly pure and belongs to the Supreme Lord, was previously proclaimed by me in the first hexad, having analyzed it in great detail.
For the purpose of binding the intellect and for the uprooting of saṃsāra,
that one great all-pervading *māyā-tattva*— which is the source of the doctrine of ignorance—
is the deluder within the aggregate of atoms and the cause of the sprout of saṃsāra.
Then the principle named Kāla is remembered as that which causes the awakening of Nāda;
it is the entity consisting of action and knowledge, manifesting the individual soul (yauktika).
Then, within Kāla, that threefold, manifest, and irreproachable principle [is established].
Intent on the threefold reckoning of the future, the past, and the present,
it should be known as eighteen-fold when analyzed according to its pairs and so forth.
Beyond that is the principle named Niyāmaka, which is designated as Niyati (Restriction).
It restrains itself as if by force, and likewise its own acquisitions;
it is the knower of knowledge, the reality that discerns action,
and the manifest experiencer of the effects of accumulated deeds.
(146b) Therefore, the reality below consists of passion; it is supreme because of its coloring. It indeed colors the individual (pudgala) amidst both pure and impure enjoyments.
Thus, the knower of reality should be known as abiding in the interval between existence and non-existence.
This sixfold reality—beginning with Māyā and ending with Rāga—is to be known;
when united within the Self and dissolved therein, this Māyā is called Bharga.
Therefore, O slender-waisted one, he shall be known as Prādhānika.
Between these two, the Puruṣa exists, solely intent upon enjoyment;
yet he does not know himself, nor his auspicious origin.
Therefore, the Pradhāna should be understood as having the nature of the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas).
It is designated as "profound," the root known as the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas—these are declared to be the three qualities.
One [quality] is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*), which is great and brings about existence and lightness; the other is of the nature of activity (*pravṛtti*), which always indicates motion;
and the third is indeed supportive (*upastambhaka*), which causes the destruction of specific light (*viśeṣāloka*).

Beyond this, the third is proclaimed as the regulator, which is attached to the Guru, non-excessive, and the support of one's own nature. O Mistress, these [qualities] are indeed mutual producers and are characterized by mutual subjugation.
The pairs should be understood as functioning mutually with one another;
indeed, because of distinctions such as non-luminosity and so forth, their cognition is considered secondary (gauṇī).
That [nature] consisting of the three guṇas is to be known as eightfold, according to the distinctions of the qualities such as dharma and the rest.
From that, the ego (ahaṃkāra) arises, consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa) and endowed with its threefold divisions.
It is traditionally known as the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the other, the *bhūtādi*.
From the *taijasa* [ego] the mind (*manas*) is produced, and it has the nature of volition (*saṃkalpa*).
From the *vaikārika* ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the ten faculties were born; O Goddess of the gods, listen now as I shall describe them to you.
The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and likewise the nose—
these are the organs of perception, engaged in their respective functions;
they manifest the power of consciousness residing within the Puruṣa.

The organs of speech, the hands, the feet, and the anus as the fifth are traditionally held to manifest the power of action (kriyā-śakti) which is always presided over by the Puruṣa. Engaged in their own respective functions, these are designated as being of the nature of the organs of action (karmendriya).
From the *bhūtādi* [tattva] as well, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) emerge;
these are traditionally known as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
They are called *tanmātras* because they possess no specific qualities other than their own particular effects. Thus they are so designated.
From those, the elements were produced in succession, each possessing its own specific quality:
space has sound as its sole quality; wind possesses both sound and touch;
likewise, fire is held to possess the three qualities of sound, touch, and form.
The element of fire arises from three qualities, and water from four;
those four likewise [possess] smell, while earth consists of five qualities.
Thus, by means of these thirty-six principles, the wonderful universe is formed in its three divisions.
The Manifested [world] has arisen through the various divisions and subdivisions known as gross and subtle;
it consists of the three abysses of creation called Śiva, Māyā, and Pradhāna.
There is nothing higher than this within the interior of the universe.
Thus has the classification of the principles been correctly proclaimed.

Everything situated within the fire-pit (agni-kuṇḍa) should be worshipped according to its hair-like [minute] parts. Having gathered the consciousness of the disciple through the coming and going of the noose and the goad, [one should proceed].
Through union with the *viloma-tattva* (the principle of reversal), Vāgeśī resides within the cavern of the womb.
Birth, authority, dissolution, enjoyment, expiation, and grace—
these are to be performed by the Sovereign of the States (*padarāja*), according to whichever [function] he chooses.
O Dear One, the disciple should always be joined by the Guru, in due order, to the principle of Śiva— whether it be the Sakala or the Niṣkala— until [the goal is reached]. (147b)

Thus, O Goddess, the procedure for initiation into the principles (*tattvadīkṣā*) has been explained by me at length in the first hexad; here, it is proclaimed in brief. The First [Chapter]: The Procedure for Initiation into the Principles.
Now I shall explain the initiation of the *kalās* in brief:
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and the fifth, Śāntyatītā; these five have been correctly proclaimed.

Indeed, this entire collection of principles from Ābhūti up to Pradhāna is to be known as the sphere of Nivṛtti, for it is withdrawn from the process of emanation. Beyond that, the principle of Pratiṣṭhā pervades and abides throughout the path ending with Māyā.
Then, O fair-faced one, as far as that Īśvara-tattva extends, [the power] pervades it;
likewise, the Śāntā pervades up to the Sādāśiva and Śākta levels.
It is taught that the Śāntātītā leads [the soul] directly to the Śiva-tattva.

The Guru must perform the fivefold act beginning with birth, through the contemplation of the paths and the pervasion of the *kalās*, exactly as enjoined by the scriptures. The ritual of union (*yojana*) should be performed as before, in accordance with the disciple’s wealth.
In brief, this *kalādīkṣā* has been fully explained to you.
[End of] the second chapter, the Ritual of *Kalādīkṣā*.
Therefore, O Pārvatī, listen now to the other initiation, that of the worlds (*bhuvanadīkṣā*), according to its true nature.

O beautiful lady, although I have previously explained this entire group of six in its entirety, I shall nevertheless describe it to you here in brief, O fair-waisted one; for indeed, that multitude of principles which was taught by me to you [previously]— [Note: The final line of the source text appears to be a fragment or a repetition of the preceding thought regarding the "multitude of principles" (*tattvavrāta*). The translation provided reflects the intent of the preceding verse.]
O beautiful goddess, these worlds situated there between should be understood in their proper sequence, each positioned higher than the last,
together with their respective lords and presided over by their powers.
Endowed with the weight of many enjoyments, possessed of manifold splendors,
fashioned with various arrangements, and inlaid with diverse precious gems.
Endowed with various mothers and adorned with diverse garlands, perfumes, and unguents—
now hear their classification, O you who are praised by the lords of heroes.
Within the pavilion of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍamaṇḍapa), one should purify the worlds.
The world of Ādāna, Anantabhuvana, Kauṣmāṇḍa, Hāṭakeśvara,
the great Kālāgnibhuvana following Anantabhuvana,
as well as the worlds of Śarva, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the supreme world of Rudra.
Within the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), these eight are indeed proclaimed.
Thereafter, O beloved, hear of the worlds of the hundred Rudras,
which are always situated in the ten directions beginning with Indra, in their respective order.
They are established in their respective order; now hear them by name:
Kapālīśa, Aja, Budhnya, Vajradeha, Pramardaka, Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākī, and Tridaśādhipa.
Ādya, Agni, Rudra, Hutabhuk,
Piṅgala, Khādaka, Hara, Jvalana, Udahana, Vabhrū, Bhasmakṣaya, Anta, Yāmya, Mṛtyu, and Hari.
The Ordainer and the Non-Ordainer, the Maker and the Binder, the Impeller;
likewise Dharmā, Adharmā, Caru, Nairṛta, and Māraṇa;
the Slayer, the One of Cruel Gaze, and another, Bhayāntaka.
Ūrdhvaliṅga, Rūpākṣa, and Dhūmra are remembered as the others;
likewise, the one named Lohitadaṃṣṭra is known as Rudra, and Bala; likewise, there is another called Atibala, who is of great strength and holds a noose in his hand.
Śveta, Japabhadra, Dīrghabāhu, Jalāntaka, Meghanāda, Sunāda, Śīghra,
Laghutara, Vāyuvega, Sūkṣma, Tīkṣṇa, and Kṣayāntaka.
Pañcāntaka, Pañcacūḍa, and another known as Kapardin;
Meghavāha, Nidhīśa, and Rūpabāndhaya; Savyeśa, Jaṭādhārī, Lakṣmībhṛt, and likewise Ratnabhṛt.
Kāmī, Prasādana by name, and likewise another, Prabhāsaka; Vidyādhipa, O Sarvajña, Jñānabhuja, and Vedapāraga.
Sureśa, Śarva, Jyeṣṭha, [another] Ulūka,
Balipriya, Vṛṣa, another Vṛṣadhara,
Ananta, Krodhana, and likewise another Mārutāśana.
Grasana is proclaimed as another, and Dumbareśa is yet another;
Phaṇīndra, Vajradaṃṣṭra, Śambhu, and the all-pervading Vibhu; Dhanādhyakṣa and Tryakṣaka, and likewise another, Tridaśeśvara.
Saṃvāha, Vivāha, and the three-eyed Lord desiring to grasp the sky—
O fair-faced one, these constitute one hundred and eight worlds.
Within the earthly principle (pārthiva-tattva), compassion must be purified by the knower of the Tantra.

Beyond this, O Goddess, after the water element (aptattva), there are the worlds of the Mūla-paścimā; they are to be known as five groups of eight. Understand them from me, O Mistress of the Gods: listen now to their division into fifty-six.
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, Tripuṣkara,
Diṇḍyāṣāḍhī, Bhārabhūti, and likewise Anākuleśvara—
this is declared to be the group of eight secret [shrines]. Now hear the group of eight most secret [shrines].
Śrīśaila, Hariścandra, Jalpaka, and likewise Agnika; Āmrātika, Mahākāla, and Kedārabhairava in the center;
Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Nākhala, and likewise Amara.
Likewise, Kaṇakhala and others—Aṭṭasāsa, Maheṃdraka, and Bhīmeśvara—are proclaimed; this is the secret beyond secrets.
[Also] Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Mahābala, and Vimuktaka.
Rudrakarṇa, Gokarṇa, Sthāṇu, and Svarṇākṣa, as well as Śūnya— O Goddess, these are renowned as the supreme and most sacred group of eight. Also Chagalāṇḍa, Durāṇḍa, Mākoṭī, and Maṇḍaleśvara.
Kālañjara, Śaṅkukarṇa, and likewise Sthūla and Sthūleśvara—
this is declared to be Sthāṇvaṇḍaka, O beloved, up to the limit of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Because he exercises agency over the tanmātras, he is not mentioned separately from them.
Karāla, Sunanda, the handsome Subhadra,
Vibhūti, Amṛtākṣa, and another, Prajeśvara— these are they.
Another is named Pitāmaha; these are remembered as the eight classes of divine origins (*devayoni*).
Residing within the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), they are to be purified by a teacher who knows the principles.
Thereafter, O Goddess, hear separately about the eightfold yoga in the *Guṇasāra*.

O God, the Bhairava, Brāhma, Vaiṣṇava, Kaumāra, Sauma, and Śrīkaṇṭha worlds have thus been proclaimed. Furthermore, those who are the lords of the worlds here, beginning with Ādya and ending with Avamāyā—

Listen to that, O highly fortunate one, as I shall explain it to you exactly as it is. Long ago, O Goddess, within the *Agasaṃpuṭa*, there were Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Trimūrti, and likewise Ekanetra.
Śrīkaṇṭha, Ekarudra, and likewise the one named Śikhaṇḍaka;
[then] Kalā, Vidyā, Puṭa, and those worlds situated therein—listen:
Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, Raudra, Kāla, and another.
And Kalavikaraṇa, as well as Balavikaraṇa;
another is Balapramathana, and likewise Sarvabhūtadama;
and another is Manonmana—these, O Goddess, are proclaimed [as your attendants].
Now listen to how that which is to be purified is likewise [purified] at the fixed time:
Śuddha, Buddha, Prabuddha, Śāntadhvaja, Bhavodbhava, and Śarva—
O Supreme Goddess, these must always be thoroughly purified by the Guru.
Understand that above Māyā, below it, and in its very center,
there is Viśvagopa, and likewise another, the Jagannidhi. O Goddess,
listen now to that which must be purified, beginning with Vidyā.
Brahmavetālikā does not exist; another is remembered as Triguṇā.
Likewise [there are] Ambikā, Sthānumatī, Nandinī, and Mandinī.

And likewise Jvālinī— these others have been proclaimed. Those who were previously mentioned as the nine Vidyā-Īśvaras are indeed present there in the principle of Bindu (bindutattva), intent upon enjoyment, as well as Dharma, Jñāna, and the other [powers].
O Maheśvarī, the cities known as Icchā (Will), Jñāna (Knowledge), and Kriyā (Action) are also [there].
Rudra, Oṃkāra, and Īśvara are proclaimed as fifteen;
beyond that is the Sādāśiva-tattva, surrounded by eighteen [cities].
In this system, the division of Śiva should always be regarded by the teachers as tenfold;
the division of Rudra is likewise declared to be tenfold, along with the one hundred and eight [forms].
Now, learn from me as I speak of the Lords of the Śakti-tattva here.
Beyond Śāntyatītā is Sadāśiva, who is indeed subtle here.
O lady of beautiful hips, the five kalās— Idhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, Mocikā, and Urdhvagā— are proclaimed as belonging to the region of Nāda.
Suṣumna, Iṣamada, Ūrdhva, Brahmeśvara, and therefore Prabhu;
likewise Vyomātman, Ananta, Vyāpin, and Bhuvaneśvara;
Anātha, Anāśrita, Śiva, and so forth—these are the names.
Thus has the multitude of worlds been described, O lady of excellent complexion.
These are to be purified in due order by the Guru who knows the principles (tattvas).
Thus ends the third [chapter], the procedure for initiation into the worlds, in the Jayadrathayāmala.
Henceforth, O fair-faced one, the steps (padas) herein must be known;
those forty steps arising from the Vidyā have been proclaimed, O beloved,
each of which effects its own result according to the gross and subtle sequence.
Thus, eighty [principles] are to be understood, for that which is one is indeed partless.
O slender-waisted lady, these eighty-one categories are to be known according to the arrangement of the earthly principle into its gross and subtle forms.
The first ten words should consist of two each up to the end of *pradhāna*;

in the *puruṣa* [tattva], there should be exactly sixteen; it is held that up to the end of *māyā*, there are two [words] each. One should correctly apply them in three ways according to the progression of the three parts.
In the remainder, one should know each step indeed until the end of Śiva.
Thus, O fortunate one, in this sequence, there is a series of eighty-one steps.
The Guru, who has reached the further shore of the meaning of the Tantras, should initiate the person after having prepared him;
O Bhairavī, he may do so by means of even a single word previously spoken,
or he may perform this initiation in whatever way pleases the Guru.
The five births [of the disciple] should be performed in the common manner according to the rule, O lady of excellent hips, following the sequence of the previous sixfold [rite].
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Rule for the Initiation of the Foot, in the Ghoratarācakra of the Jayadrathayāmala.
Therefore, O Goddess, I shall describe to you the initiation consisting of phonemes (*varṇamayī dīkṣā*).
This great multitude of phonemes begins with *a* and ends with *kṣ*.
Here, those who perceive reality should see it divided into nine groups.

The *a*-group, the *ka*-group, the *ca*-group, and the *ṭa*-group; likewise, the *ta*-group and the *pa*-group are to be known, as well as the subsequent *ya*-group and *śa*-group. The *kṣa*-group alone constitutes the indicator of the blending of phonemes (*varṇasaṃkara*).
O slender-waisted lady, the nine principles (tattvas) are to be understood here in their proper sequence:
Śivatattva, Sādākhya, and thereafter that which is known as Aiśvara;
then those called Vidyā and Māyā, as well as Kāla and Niyati.

Through the sequential cultivation of pervasion (*vyāpti*)— namely, the human and the elemental— the entire process of birth and so forth, which is to be performed according to the divisions of the classes (*varṇa*), occurs. O Goddess, in this way initiation (*dīkṣā*) becomes that which is called "the letters" (*varṇākhyā*), the Supreme Sovereign.
In Jayadratha, there is the initiation of color (*varṇa-dīkṣā*).
O daughter of the Mountain, hear now the initiation of mantra (*mantra-dīkṣā*) which has come down through the lineage;
it consists of a thousand syllables, O Goddess, and forty-four words.
All that has been described with one syllable more is contained within that slender body;
whether by uttering each word individually or by uttering many words as a single unit,
Kālacakra, having uttered [the mantra], proceeds by way of the path of Suṣumnā.
There, having brought the disciple near, O slender-waisted one, by means of the separation from the nooses and the hook,
he should be planted within the circle of mantras through his own utterance.
One should direct the disciple as far as the station of the three-fold fuel (the three worlds).
There, O beautiful one, one should indeed unite him either with the manifest (sakala) or [with the unmanifest],
by means of offering a single oblation, through the state of pervading the entire path.
"O fortunate one, by a single utterance one may initiate even immobile beings.
This mantra-initiation (*māntrī dīkṣā*) has been declared to you by me with its secret, O beloved.
Thus ends the sixth [chapter], the procedure for mantra-initiation, in the Ghoratarācakra of the Jayadrathayāmala.

O Goddess of gods, this initiation, which consists of six types and is very extensive in the Purāṣaṭka, has been proclaimed to you; here it is presented in brief. Now, the sequence of the Śaktidīkṣā, which has arrived [in due order], is being proclaimed.
Having gone to the beautiful sacrificial hall, gladdened by the joy of wine,
well-perfumed with incense, having chewed betel, and adorned with garlands and wreaths of flowers—
the Guru, standing there, [should properly [unify] the disciple and himself along with the Śakti].
One should cause [the disciple] to grasp this very goad within the fierce union of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*).
The power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) and the power of vital breath (*prāṇaśakti*), auspiciously strengthened by one another,
having been joined together according to the distinction between the pure and the impure.

When the rite is impure, one should employ the pure [mantra]; when the rite is pure, the very pure [mantra]. Beginning from the *mūlādhāra* up to the limit of the crest (*śikhā*), one should then unite the disciple with either the *sakala* (with parts) or the *niṣkala* (partless) [form of the deity].
Thus, the disciple who has been so united shall indeed become Śiva himself.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Procedure for the Initiation by Power (*śaktidīkṣā*), in the *Jayadratha*.
Hereafter, O Dear One, listen to the initiation by the Bindu (*bindudīkṣā*) which follows in due order.
The Bindu is the deity Sādāśiva, who rests upon the union of Śiva and Śakti;
he possesses four kalās and five kalās, and resides within the cavity of the three wheels (cakras).
These are Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti, as well as the other [Śāntyatītā].
O Goddess of the Five Devas, the five Lords— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, Īśvara, and Śiva— are established here in sequence, with Śāntyatītā as the fifth.
O fortunate one, understand from me the five principles ending with Sadāśiva:
earth, water, fire, air, and space, O beautiful goddess;
thus, by this very sequence of five, the Lord Bindu is established.

O slender-waisted Goddess of the gods, the Guru should contemplate [the center] as being fivefold, situated from the forehead up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), having the form of a kadamba flower and radiant with shimmering rays.

O beautiful one, with his eyes closed, the Guru should, by means of the Kālikā-weapon and through the application of the goad (*aṅkuśa*), unite the disciple’s self [with the supreme reality]. Through this union, he becomes initiated and a vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And one gains authority over all mantras; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the eighth [chapter], the ritual for the initiation of the Point (*bindu-dīkṣā-vidhi*), in the *Jayadrathayāmala*.
Now I shall explain another initiation, which indeed arises from the Sound (*nāda*).
At the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] is the Great Moon, whose form is composed of digits (*kalā*),
blazing with shimmering rays, auspicious and possessing sixteen parts. From that, as far as the space within the lotus of the heart, is proclaimed to be *nāda*.
There, one should cause the disciple’s self to rest within that Wheel of Puruṣa,
proceeding by means of re-entrance as far as the twelfth station.
Having thus joined the consciousness of the disciple, O Dear One, it becomes absolute (kevala).
When one joins the disciple with the sound (*nāda*) arising from the resonance (*nāda*), then the practitioner shall become a lord of enjoyment; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus ends the ninth [chapter], the procedure for the initiation of sound (*nādadīkṣā-vidhi*), in the *Jayadrathayāmala*.
Beyond this, O God and Goddess, the initiation of the vital breath (prāṇadīkṣā) has come down through the lineage.
Listen, for I shall explain it correctly, in due order and according to the truth:
the vital breath consists of the individual soul (jīva), and the individual soul consists of the vital breaths—both prāṇa and apāna—along with the deities.
It is remembered as having the nature of both creation and dissolution, consisting of the moon and the sun.
Between those two, the great fire stands in the station known as the Three Abodes (tridhāman).
It resides in the dwelling of the heart-lotus through its union with the goad of dissolution.
Having drawn forth the consciousness of the disciple as far as one's own cranial abode,
and having placed it within the center of the three abodes, it should then be impelled upward once more.
Having pierced the five voids with the thread of breath (*prāṇasūtra*) during the great heat (*mahātapa*),

one should lead the consciousness of the disciple through that very central path (*madhyamārga*) to the seventh conjunction (*melaya*). Then, [one should place it] again in the differentiated and undifferentiated states.

Then the disciple, having been initiated by the Guru, certainly becomes liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra; of this there is no doubt. Thus has the secret initiation consisting of the vital breath (prāṇamaya) been explained to you.
In the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the tenth [chapter] is the procedure for the initiation of the living (*prāṇadīkṣā*).
O Bhairavī, hear now in truth the initiation of the living that has come down through the lineage:
the aggregate (*piṇḍa*) consisting of Man, Power, and Śiva is designated as the "living" (*jīva*).
O highly fortunate one, having contracted by means of the yoga of expansion that [light] residing within the cavity of the heart-lotus— which consists of fire, sun, and nectar—
until it reaches the supreme cave of the heart,
one should repeatedly join the disciple’s self to that path.
Being thus disciplined and having attained a state of equanimity, he becomes one whose tree of worldly enjoyment has grown into liberation.
From that moment on, O highly fortunate lady, this disciple becomes truly perfected and equal to Śiva,
due to the purity of his very life.

O Goddess, the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of that one whose body is enveloped by the living digit (*jīvakalā*) consisting of Agni and Soma has been explained to you according to its true meaning. Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the procedure for the initiation of the living, in the *Jayadrathayāmala*.
O Daughter of the Mountain, I shall now explain the initiation of the movement [of breath] (cāradīkṣā) as it has come down through the lineage;
listen to how the Guru should properly perform it for the disciple.
O slender-waisted one, it is based upon that which is the root of the movement of the vital breath (prāṇacāra).

Having turned oneself toward the disciple, through the union of the left and right [nostrils] by means of the application of the *vāyu-tāra* [mantra], one should withdraw the consciousness of that [disciple]. O Dear One, the Guru should then unite the withdrawn [consciousness] with the *tattva* of the supreme disciple.
(152a) "O Goddess, one who is thus engaged shall possess the factors conducive to liberation; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus ends the twelfth [chapter], the Initiation of the Spy, in the Jayadrathayāmala.
Now listen, O you who are worshipped by the lords of heroes, to the initiation involving touch (*sparśavatī-dīkṣā*).
I shall explain it correctly, just as it is to be performed by the best of gurus.
Having projected the thousand-syllabled Goddess (*sahasrārṇā*) upon his own body, the most excellent of gurus—
O Goddess, having performed the practice of ascending and descending in forward and reverse order,
and having made the internal organ firm, one should form the Karaṅkiṇī mudrā;
then, having laughed eight times, O Beloved, one should subsequently touch the [target] with the tongue.
O Goddess, one should initiate each [disciple] through the practice of a firm embrace;
O Goddess, he leads them to union with Śakti—of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, having performed the sequence of sounds (rāvakrama), one whose speech is thus inspired should lead them.

"O Bhairavabhāminī, you have been properly initiated by me. O Goddess Bhairavī, he shall be led to union with Brahman by mere speech. Thus, O Goddess, the initiation by speech (*vāgdīkṣā*) and the initiation by touch (*sparśadīkṣā*) have been revealed to you.
Thus ends the procedure for initiation by touch and the procedure for initiation by word within the most terrible wheel (*ghoraghoratara-cakra*) of the *Jayadrathayāmala*.
O Maheśvarī, I shall now proclaim the initiation by piercing (*vedhadīkṣā*), which has come down through the lineage.
O Maheśvarī, the sixfold piercing was previously taught in the *Kāliṣaṭka*.
That very [process] must be awakened here at the time of initiation by the most excellent gurus.
O Goddess, the first is the piercing of the mantra (*mantravedha*), the second is the piercing of the thunderbolt (*śāṅka*),
the third is the supreme piercing (*paravedha*), and the fourth is the serpent-piercing (*bhujaṅgavedha*).
The fifth is of the nature of sound (nāda), and the sixth is held to be called "sound" (nādākhya).
Their essential nature has already been established through a prior analysis; therefore, it should be understood from that very source, and no further distinction is prescribed here.
"O slender-waisted one, six initiations beginning with piercing have been proclaimed for you.
Thus ends the sixth [chapter], on the initiation of piercing, in the Ghorataracakrā of the Jayadrathayāmala.
O Daughter of the Mountain, listen to the initiation consisting of the balance (dhaṭa-dīkṣā).
Having worshipped the Supreme Goddess according to the sequence to be described,
one should perform the fire-rite there and duly install the balance.
The staff should be three and a half cubits long, and the scale itself one cubit in measure.
The pillar should be four cubits high, and one should suspend the scale from it at a height of three cubits.
Having thus established the balance, making it very firm with strong ropes:
Then, having worshipped her there with the garland of a thousand syllables,
one should place [the two] vessels upon both thighs by means of the playful swinging of the swing.
In the middle, one should place the Śārvī of the staff-measure, possessing the form of being embraced by Śakti.
Having thus arranged [the ritual objects] and performed worship, one should subsequently cause the disciple to enter.
At first, even without having sprinkled [him with water], one should place him upon the back of the balance.
Then, after leveling them, that many stones should likewise be placed [on the other side].
Having brought [the disciple] down, one should sprinkle him and strike him while reciting the mantra.
Mounted upon the Śakti, Muṇḍā, and Kula, through the application of intense thunderous force,
one should burn the disciple from the very roots by means of the fivefold practice.
Afterwards, O best of men, one should place the fire-vessel upon the balance.
Thereafter, no doubt arises that there is an increase in the weight of the stones.
Having lowered [the vessel], O Goddess, one should again perform the striking, sprinkling, and other rites.
Having performed [the preliminary rites], one should again perform the grasping of the consciousness (cid-grahaṇa) once;
by means of the application of the noose and the goad, place it within the cavity of the heart.
Having joined it with the Vidyā in the hollow, one should then plant it upon the scale.

O Goddess of the lords of gods, when a hundred *amā* remain by weight and measure, one should then take another *amā* from that [total] in *palas*. O Goddess, that consciousness should be grasped as before and placed within the *saṃpuṭa*.
O Goddess, having joined [the breath] in the auspicious abode of the three abodes, one should impel it slowly;
one should unite the Kula with the Śākta until it reaches the state of Kālī-yoga.
O Bhairavī, having relied upon the Great Pervasion (mahāvyāpti) through the bond of stability,
the most excellent Guru, having utterly consumed the extremely fierce series of causes,
should unite the initiated disciple, whose bonds of worldly existence have been burnt away.
Then the initiated disciple becomes equal to space;
indeed, he becomes like Bhairava himself, with the bonds of worldly existence burnt away.
Afterwards, one should offer the scales, having cast aside the stones.

One should offer a garland made of twenty-seven flowers. When the practitioner becomes equal to that [deity] and is freed from all veils, he is united with the state of Śiva and becomes liberated; not otherwise.
O deer-eyed one, for those whose minds are filled with doubt and who are terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, the initiation known as the *dhaṭa* should be performed; thereafter,
the teacher should withdraw everything that has been deposited within their body.
Thus has this secret been declared to you according to its true meaning.
Thus ends the ritual for the six initiations (*ṣaḍdīkṣāvidhi*) in the *Jayadrathayāmala*.
Following this is the initiation consisting of clothing (*vastrātmikā dīkṣā*), which purifies all sins.
O Goddess of gods, I shall speak to you; listen now as it truly is.
Having procured a hero’s garment, one should then dye it black.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship the Goddess of gods with great magnificence.
Having caused the disciple to enter there, veiled in black cloth,
bowing low with eyes fixed upon the consecrated image and palms joined in *añjali*,
one should afterwards cause the moon to dissolve into the hollow of the fire of time (*kālāgni*) within the Lord.
Then, having raised her up, Ghoreśī— whose garments are ablaze with fire—
should kindle the great seven-flamed [fire] and blow forth the multitude of flame-wreaths.
By means of the union of their falling together, she should purify the body of the disciple.
Or, having arrived from a distance of a thousand [yojanas] through the application of that consciousness-impact (*cidghāta*),
the supreme guru should behold that painted cloth for the sake of providing conviction.
Then he should initiate the disciples, even those burdened with great sins.
(153b) This initiation with a cloth (*paṭadīkṣā*) is proclaimed in the *Jayadratha*, the king of tantras.
Thus ends the procedure for the initiation with a cloth in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*.
Now, therefore, O fair-faced one, I shall fully explain in due order the initiation by the jar (*ghaṭadīkṣā*) in brief; listen, O Pārvatī, according to the truth.
Having first worshipped the Goddess of the gods, who is adorned with the thousand-syllable mantra, as before—
Then, O Maheśvarī, having brought a jar with a hundred eyes,
one should place within it a single measure (prastha) of grain;
then, beholding the supreme wheel called Rāva, which belongs to the lineage of Rāvinī.
Having contracted the *kaumbhakī* wheel, one should withdraw the disciple’s self;
tenfold and fivefold, like the earth and the flow of the earth.
One should join the disciple’s self to the sun, which is the *kuṃbha* held in that hand.
Having forcibly joined the disciple’s self with the tip of the *śakti*,
he then praises that jar together with the disciple's two hands;
thereafter, it floats up as far as the head, accompanied by the two hands.
If that excellent water-pot should bend even slightly when it has been filled for only a moment and the vessel standing before it has become completely full, then the bath is accomplished.

Then that initiation called the "Jar" (ghaṭadīkṣā) is accomplished for the practitioner; by means of this, that lord among practitioners attains union with Śiva. Thus ends the procedure for the Jar Initiation in the third Ṣaṭka of the Jayadrathayāmala.
Therefore, O blessed one, even more than this, for one whose sins have been exhausted—or likewise for one who is sinful, O fortunate one; or for one who is diseased, O dear one;
or even for an elderly person—the auspicious *sadyonirvāṇikā* rite should be performed immediately.
Listen to the initiation in brief, exactly as it is, in the middle [mandala].
O fortunate one, having worshipped the goddesses in the common abodes and so forth.
Then, through the accumulation of great wealth and by means of the sequence of rites to be described,
one should [worship] the Mother of the World who has arisen from the support of the fire of time (kālānala),
who is intense and resembles a blazing, most terrible, and destructive conflagration.
One should contemplate the Mother Mantra, consisting of a thousand syllables and terrifying in nature. Having established the disciple before oneself,
one should project him into her form through the application of the Great Vidyā, continuing until a thousand [projections] have occurred.
O beautiful one, one should visualize the body of the disciple to be purified;
and that consciousness, O beloved, being thoroughly cleansed according to its own nature,
diligently nourishes the perfection of its true form, O dear one.
That power indeed burns away the infinite net of bonds;
at that very moment, the body, having experienced its enjoyments, falls away.
When it is considered to be all-pervasive, that which is eternal and indivisible arises within whatever is born.
Thus has the initiation that bestows immediate liberation been fully revealed by you.
Thus ends the procedure for the initiation that bestows immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*) in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*.
Now, I shall describe the initiation transmitted through the lineage, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Having thus worshipped the God and Goddess Kṛṣodarī in the vessel of liquor,
the consciousness of the disciple— enclosed within the *pada* and the *mantra*—
should be embraced by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which consists of the nature of both knowing and acting.
By that very same path of ritual procedure, bring [the disciple] into the support of his own time.
Then, having pierced through the six wheels and being united with the consciousness of the disciple,
one should go to that Kula of yours and contemplate it as dissolved therein.
When the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) has arisen, then one becomes a partaker of *nirvāṇa*.
Freed from the conduct of conventional observances (*samayācāra*), one attains the stainless state.
This initiation leading to *nirvāṇa* has been revealed to you today.
Thus ends the ritual for the initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*) in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*.
Now, I shall explain another [ritual] correctly and in due order.

O Goddess, this sequence of initiation has been declared by me with effort, both briefly and in detail, as it is most secret and extremely formidable; never before has it been told. Now, O Knower, I shall explain to you another method of initiation known as the Half-Moon.

O Maheśvarī, these twelve [energies], ending with the Half-Moon at the end of the Pole Star (dhruva), are the entire essence of the categories of objects of knowledge; they are situated one above the other in sequential order.
By the very process of ascending, they arise from the Kula as a birth of flames.
Having pierced through as far as Ālaṃvikā, one reaches the lineage of the Bindu and the Half-moon;
there, one should ascend the subtle twelve-fold [center] by means of the activity of the mind.
I shall describe these to you in sequence according to the practice of the Great Pervasion (mahāvyāpti).
The Half-Moon, the Obstructive, the Sound, and the Pervasive;
likewise the Equalizing, the Intoxicated, and the Mouth of the Guru;
then the Equinox known as the Unborn Touch, the Tranquil, and that which is born of Emission.

O Maheśvarī, initiation should take place twelve times, up until the limit of the *dhruvadhāman*. In whichever great sacred site the Guru has become one with the same flavor (*samarasī*) as the consciousness of the disciple, in each of those places [initiation is performed].
Divine initiation arises, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Each of those families should be thoroughly known as the most excellent among all abodes.
In this manner, the procedure for all initiations is supreme in its sequence.
It should be understood, O illustrious one, that no distinction is prescribed;
this has been declared nowhere else except in relation to this excellent body.
Thus ends the twelfth rule on initiation in the third Ṣaṭka of the Jayadrathayāmala.

Henceforth, O slender-waisted one, I shall explain the initiation of illumination (*ālokadīkṣā*), O fortunate lady, for which there is no equal. Having indeed deposited the Goddess residing within one's own body by means of the sequence of movement and utterance (*cāroccāra*).
Thereafter, one should extract the Vidyā through the distinction of emanation and withdrawal.
Mounted upon the lineage of Mahākālī, radiant with a mass of shimmering rays,
O Goddess, whomever he gazes upon, him he leads to the eternal state.
O Goddess of the gods, one should initiate even immobile beings by means of this sequence.
This initiation, which is to be given to the utmost degree, is devoid of the sacrificial pit and the mandala.
Thus ends the procedure for the initiation of illumination (*ālokadīkṣā*) in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*.
O slender-waisted one, listen to the initiation conjoined with knowledge and realization (*jñāna-vijñāna*). I shall consider the path of the sixfold way, or whatever is pleasing to your mind.

Therein, he who is the observer should investigate in due order; that [observer] becomes either the primordial one through the differentiation of states, or the individual soul, or else [the supreme].
By him, the entire world is filled with the nature of consciousness.
By that very one, who is the subtle essence of consciousness, the universe is pervaded.
[I bow to] Śiva, whose form is supreme, who is the thread woven through all beings,
the Lord whose nature is self-luminous light, and the abode of qualities such as omniscience.
The Sugata abides as the six paths in the form of the presiding deity;
by the thorough knowledge of his true nature, one who stands therein attains identity with him.
Through that realization, one awakens the consciousness of the disciple with the rays of the words of awakening.
O beautiful goddess, one who has awakened never again falls into the state of a bound soul (paśutā).
Thus, the initiation of knowledge (jñāna-dīkṣā) is defined; now hear from me that which is called the initiation of higher realization (vijñāna).
When one restrains the pair of the moon and the sun by means of this knowledge, [that is it].

By means of the practice of expansion through the play of Mahābhairava, one should enter that armor of the disciple; thus he indeed becomes initiated. This very initiation of higher knowledge has been described here in brief.
O Goddess worshipped by the best of gods, the initiation for these two is the same as for the others;
however, in this mandala, the goddess Karaṅkiṇī is not to be worshipped,
nor is there any fire-ritual here, nor meditation, nor concentration.
Established solely in his own essential nature, he may initiate even immobile beings,
provided he fashions [the initiation] for those whose impurities have been ripened and who are spiritually prepared.
Thus ends the procedure for initiation through knowledge and realization in the third hexad of the Jayadrathayāmala.
(155b) Now, therefore, O lady of beautiful waist, I shall fully explain the most excellent initiation known as the "Gate," which has come down through the traditional sequence. Listen!
For those whose funeral offerings have been stolen by one who has no protector, as well as for those killed by infants,
for those who died through ill fortune, and for those who have passed away, this initiation shall be the nectar of immortality.
I shall proclaim this in secret, which has never been told by me anywhere before.

Having fully worshipped the Supreme Goddess, who is fierce and triumphant over the three worlds, one should perform the fire-rite (*agnikarman*) with whatever abundance of materials is available. For that purpose, a hearth (*aṭṭaka*) made of clay or wood should be prepared.
Having accepted [the invitation], he should perform the ritual according to the correct method.
Having entered the Great Abode known as Viśva through the application of the *pada*,
[he enters] that wherein the universe is woven together and wherein all that is moving and unmoving is dissolved.
In that [state] wherein all this, beginning with the vital breath, indeed reaches its dissolution;
from which it arises again and again, characterized by light and bliss;
which is consciousness, the supreme, subtle, and the cause even of causes.

One should bring forth the consciousness of the dead by means of the vision of all things through that supreme deity Śiva, who is adorned by his own power, and by the expansion of its manifestation known as the "Great Net."
Having thus seized [the soul] by the throat with wrath, one should establish it within its own nature (prakṛti).
By the application of the noose and the goad, the bound soul (paśu), wherever it may be situated,
is moved from that state through the employment of the process of ascension (rūḍhi) into that [nature].

In that regard, the binding (grathana) should be performed, preceded by the secret knowledge (gūḍhavidyā). That which consists of consciousness is the unfolding (unmeṣa), for that unfolding is indeed an activity.
And that activity is the movement (cāra), which is established as fourfold.

By means of the form of power (*śakti*), there is attraction; by that which is designated as the living soul (*jīva*), there is grasping. By means of the lamp of the *saudhavana* [channel], there is illumination; by that called the *haṃsa*, there is purification.
Having resorted to the state of the *khecarī* through the practice of the *khecarīmudrā*.
The Guru should respectfully perform the rite of initiation into the consciousness of the deceased;
having performed the rites for birth and so forth, he should now act for one who resides therein. (156a)
Afterwards, having grasped the mouth of the Kālāgni fire,
they are led very slowly through the path of the channels (*nāḍī*) from the interior of the navel into the supreme abode.
O fortunate one, the Guru, resting in the effort according to the sequence of practice, [leads them there].
One should offer that [oblation] into the fire by means of the ritual of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

Having united the life-force of the deceased in the supreme abode, which is consciousness beyond the mind, it becomes pure and of the very nature of Śiva; this is indeed so, and there is nothing marvelous in it.
This incomparable procedure for initiation, as far as it exists, has been declared as a secret in this *Pārameśvara-tantra*, O Dear One.
And this, O Goddess, must never be given to those who lack devotion.
Apart from this severing of the head, it has not been deliberated upon elsewhere. This matter must be kept strictly secret by you; it must not be told to anyone.
This incomparable ritual bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The great [cycle] consisting of forty-four [deities] is called Dīkṣā;
within the Cakra, it is proclaimed along with its secret [teachings] as Ghoraghoratarā.
Thus has this most profound secret been fully and correctly proclaimed, O you who are worshipped by all the Siddhas and the lords of the gods.
Now hear of another form of worship, which is the essence, which grants success everywhere, and which is delightful with infinite qualities.

Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for initiation in the forty-fourth [chapter] of the Ghoraghoratara-cakra, within the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the *Śiraścheda* in the Vidyāpīṭha of the Bhairava-stream.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed worship of the Goddess. Having gone to a terrifying cremation ground, or to a mountain peak,
or to a beautiful shore of the ocean, or wherever the mind finds delight.
There, accompanied by his disciples, he should perform the purification of the ground,
[smearing it] with the crushed remains of a great skeleton and anointed with great blood.
Alternatively, [the site] should be adorned with the five jewels, smeared with sandalwood and agallochum,

filled with incense and abundant fragrance, and beautified by a canopy. One whose consciousness is intoxicated with the joy of wine, and who is languid with the delight of fine incense, [should perform the rite].
There, one should delineate a most beautiful maṇḍala with nine channels,
endowed with nine lotuses and well-adorned with eight doors;
each [lotus] possesses eight petals, is furnished with filaments and a pericarp.
With red pigment, one should prepare an unsurpassed [diagram] measuring nine cubits,
according to one's desired proportions and endowed with all beauties;
its dimensions and characteristics have been revealed here in the previous six chapters.
There, having gathered the requisites and performed the preliminary consecration as before,
one should worship the slender-waisted goddess of a thousand syllables residing within the central lotus;
having meditated upon her according to the previously stated rule, one should place her within the interior of the lotus.
By means of the yoga of the higher and lower (parāpara), one should place [the letters] one by one upon each petal;
furthermore, one should install Bhairavī in the lotuses of the directions with those very feet.
Thus, there are always forty-six [deities] according to the division of the higher and lower.
O Goddess of the gods, there are eighty [squares]; one should designate each one individually.

Having thus deposited [the mantras] in sequence, O Goddess, starting from the east up to the northeast corner, O lady of excellent hips, this is the arrangement of the eighty-one squares according to the order of the lotus.
Furthermore, by means of the yoga of joining the rays, they should all be situated in the center.
Having thus performed the ritual placement, O fortunate one, one should satisfy the nine [deities] with wealth.
Taking a great vessel filled with the nectar of the left [hand], |||
With that, one should cause the offering of water for honor (*argha*) to be given to the Goddess, as well as water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*).
One should likewise cause various kinds of flowers and great incense (*mahādhūpa*) to be presented.
Great lamps should be offered, along with manifold sacrificial gifts (*upahāra*).
One should likewise cause to be given large game, small game, and the meat of goats and sheep;
as well as the flesh of wild animals, fish, and birds.
Various kinds of meats should be offered here according to the prescribed rule. One should likewise offer liquor, *surā*, *śīdhu*, and various types of *āsava*.
*Śaṣkulī* cakes and *modaka* sweets made with jaggery and sugar-candy should also be given.
Likewise, one who is free from stinginess regarding wealth should offer a crown belonging to Maheśa as a pleasing gift to the Goddess of the Gods; he should fill its front for her,
having first worshipped the former gurus, Vāgeśī, and the lineage of the Siddhas.
One should worship Gaṇeśa in the direction of Vāyu (the northwest), and Kṣetranāyaka in the Rākṣasa (southeast) direction.
One should worship Kālī, Jayā, Gaṅgā, and Vārāhī as they stand at the door.
Having worshipped the seat located upon the pedestal, one should worship [the deities] beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Śiva.

Having thus worshipped the goddess of gods, the slender-waisted Subhagā, he should then cause the disciple— who has his eyes bound and his hands joined in *añjali*— to enter. Having performed the ritual procedures such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), he should make him prostrate like a staff.
Having worshipped the Supreme Goddess, he should lead [the disciple] in due order to the site of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

There, he should perform initiation for him according to the previously stated procedure. Then, once [the disciple] has been seated upon the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha), the consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed.
In this manner, O slender-waisted goddess, the initiation of the disciple should be performed.
From that time forth, O Goddess, he shall become a fit candidate for the secret practice (*sādhana*).
One should worship according to this application of ritual, either individually or collectively.
One should always worship the Sole Heroine, who consists of a thousand syllables, within a single lotus;
or one may worship the Supreme Goddess by dividing her into individual syllables.
In this practice, there is no fixed visualization; one may arrange it according to one's own preference.
This most beautiful sacrifice of the Goddess has been declared as a secret.
What else shall I tell you? Speak, O lotus-petal-eyed one, O momentary one!

Thus ends the chapter on the Sacrifice of the Most Terrible and Terriblest [Goddess] in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraccheda* of the Vidyāpīṭha in the Bhairava-stream.
The Goddess said:
Now I wish to hear the supreme sādhana of the Goddess.
"How is it to be accomplished, O Mahādeva? Therefore, tell me in brief.
Bhairava said:
"Listen, O woman of excellent complexion; I shall now describe the means of accomplishment."
Just as that goddess is accomplished for the high-souled practitioner:
having gone to a garden on a preeminent mountain, the practitioner, equipped with the necessary means of accomplishment,
should there fully accomplish the goddess and recite the supreme mantra ten thousand times.

The practitioner of mantras should offer a thousand oblations; through the recitation of the mantra and other rites, she who resides within the fire at the conclusion of the *homa* becomes manifest to the foremost of adepts and grants whatever he desires.
Having granted the practitioner his desired boon according to his wish,
she then departs for her own abode together with him;
this, O Goddess, is proclaimed as your supreme accomplishment (siddhi).

Having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times, the practitioner, firm in his vows, should perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number; thereafter, the mantrin should proceed to the entrance of the cave.
There, at night, the oblation must indeed be performed by the practitioner.
O Goddess, if one offers a hundred oblations of mustard seeds mixed with great *kaduka* and derived from meat,
the earth trembles;
then, maidens with eyes rolling from intoxication emerge from it.
Moving with the gait of elephants in rut, with full and elevated breasts, those beautiful women, characterized by the quality of *tamas*, took up intoxicating drinks and then entreated him:
"Save us! Save us, O best of men!"
"Accept this incomparable honor, which is difficult for those of unrefined self to attain.
Having heard this from them, he should not speak a word in reply;
remaining silent, he should offer there fifty oblations.
Then, O fortunate one, the best of royal maidens arrive, O Goddess of gods;
taking the rājasa drink, they bow as before.
Remaining silent, O Goddess of gods, one should not address them with words.
Furthermore, the practitioner, with a firm focus, should offer one hundred oblations;
thus equipped with the previous meditation, he shall burn those who dwell in the netherworld.
Then everything blazes up as far as the realm of Brahmā.
Afflicted, the maidens let out a most terrible cry of "Alas! Alas!
All the noble women, brought under the sway of the arrows of desire, flee forth.

Moving with the gait of intoxicated elephants, beautiful and in the prime of youth—their form, O Goddess of the Gods, is not capable of being fully described by me. They are declared to be of the *sattva* nature; their drinking is the most excellent *sāttvika* drink.
They bestow [the fruits] upon the practitioner, bowing down again and again.
Thus, at that time, accompanied by them and his retinue,
the hero should enter the illustrious mouth, crushing all obstacles.

There, having first worshipped the Lord of Gods, the great sovereign Hāṭakeśa, who bestows divine vision, one should then take up the drink. This supreme, sattvic drink should be offered to the Guru and drunk by oneself.
To those of the *rājasa* nature, one should give female companions and excellent women;
to those of the *tāmasa* nature, one should give low-born women and women of the lowest class.
Having thus distinguished them for a very long time, he lives through a great kalpa.
"O beautiful goddess of the gods, the entry into the netherworld (pātāla) by means of forceful effort (haṭha) has been described. The Goddess said:
O Lord, how many types of entries are there therein, and how many kinds of drinks?"
How many types of women have been declared? Tell me, how many kinds of cities are there?
O God, how many kinds of yantras are there, and how many kinds of *vilāsas* are remembered?
O Maheśāna, tell me all of this for the benefit of living beings.
Bhairava said:
Listen, for I shall tell you this supreme procedure for Pātāla,
by the thorough mastery of which all perfections (siddhis) will be attained in secret.
In this regard, understand that entry is threefold in brief:
the first is the forceful entry (*haṭhapraveśa*), which is primary and born from the perfection of mantra;
the second, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, is called the ordinary entry (*sāmānyapraveśa*).
Indeed, this mantra is to be accomplished through yogic ointments (*yogāñjana*), for it then attains the state of being fit for oblation (*huta*).
O Goddess of Gods, the third [stage], the entry into the ritual procedure (*vidhipraveśa*), is thus recited.
Now listen as I describe their classification in due order.

Through the grace of the Great Mantra, the most excellent practitioner, having attained perfect accomplishment and being disciplined by austerity, vows, and recitation, shall achieve the practice of forceful means (*haṭhasādhana*).
O slender-waisted one, having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for the mantra,
and subsequently having accomplished the applications of collyrium (*añjana*), the heroic practitioner— the best of men—
will undoubtedly achieve the common accomplishment (*sāmānyasādhana*).
In this regard, O moon-faced one, I shall proclaim an auspicious collyrium; listen.
Having collected the *stotāñjana*, one should consecrate it once with mantras, combined with the blood of a monitor lizard and the juice of *brāhmī*.

Recited one hundred times while standing in a cremation ground within the *mahānaraka-sampuṭa*, a man whose eyes are anointed with this [ointment] becomes one who captivates the hearts of others. He stands fearlessly at the summit of all the *yantras* in the underworld (*pātāla*).
Its movement cannot be obstructed by any kind of mechanical device.
O Goddess of Gods, the collyrium of this type is to be accomplished; furthermore, one should collect that which comes from the stream from the left ear of a boar itself.
Then, O Goddess of the gods, by rubbing that red [substance] upon a stone with mantras, one shall conquer again;
having entered the very core of the eyes,
he enters all cavities, and his movement cannot be obstructed.
At the end of enjoying the pleasures of the netherworld (pātāla), one shall go to the state of Maheśvara.
Now, having extracted the heart of a tortoise and combined it with collyrium,
one should encase it in three metals and consecrate it by reciting the mantra one hundred times.
Having placed this pill in one's mouth, one becomes the lord of Pātāla;
having entered the hearts of all beings, one may wander wherever one pleases.
Even when entering the middle of the ocean, one is not afflicted by the water there.
One sees all the jewels and is born among those who possess them.
One is not harmed by any of the fierce beings dwelling in the waters.
Thus, through the application of these two types of ointment, the subterranean realm (pātāla) is mastered by men.
O slender-waisted one, I shall now explain to you the entry into the ritual procedure.
Having first performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), the lord of practitioners should enter the *vilam*.
O Goddess of gods, during the festival of lamps, when the sky is cloudless,
one should perform the fire-ritual at midnight and enter [the ritual space] without collyrium.
Then, even from the most intense darkness, women will come of their own accord.
And here I shall describe the lamp that shatters the machine of darkness:
having taken a stalk, O fortunate one, combined with lac and guggulu,
along with śrīvāsaka, sarjarasa, oil, and the product of jyotiṣmatī.
Having taken it, O Dear One, one should smear the shaft and then consecrate it with mantras;
one should then ignite it with fire arising from a cremation ground, O Bhairavī.
This is that terrible *dīpikā* [lamp-weapon], which destroys all yantras.
This cannot be extinguished even by the most forceful winds.
I shall now describe a foot-ointment that destroys the diamond-paste (*vajrakardama*),
pacifies heaps of glowing coals, acts as water, and destroys the sun.

Having gathered apāmārga [plant] together with elephant dung, one should smear it on both feet; then, free from fear, one may enter. One shall paralyze all mechanical devices, whether they be peaceful or fierce.
A paste of poison prepared by mixing curd, ghee, and honey,
when applied as an ointment to the feet, prevents one's movement from being obstructed even in the netherworld (Pātāla).
Then, on the day [of the ritual], one who lacks other means should enter among the others.
O Maheśvarī, on the new moon day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, when Jupiter is in the constellation Svāti,
there indeed arise the weapon-less voids (vivara-āstras) in the southern asterism on that full moon day of that same month.
Indeed, all the openings here become unobstructed.
In whichever month the Guru [Jupiter] is in the constellation of Ikṣa (Punarvasu), and on whatever day of the Guru,
on that day all the subterranean apertures on the surface of the earth are opened by Hari.
The openings indeed become unobstructed during the transits [of the planets] and on the festival days (parvan);
at the time of a planetary eclipse, however, the aperture becomes entirely free from obstruction.
O Goddess of gods, by such means as these, that which is the entry of the breaths occurs.
This has been declared as the ritual procedure for practitioners, bringing them happiness.
Now, listen indeed to the various types of drinking that are about to be described. (159b)
When the nectar had first emerged from the excellent ocean of milk, Kṣīroda,
during that great agitation caused by the battle between the gods and the Dānavas,
there was a yoginī named Uśanas, who was the mother of Śukra.

By her, the gods beginning with Nārāyaṇa and headed by Śakra were utterly deluded, and half [of the kingdom] was seized from that very Kamaṇḍalu. Then, having taken refuge in Pātāla, she gave it back to Śukra.
At that time, she set aside a certain portion of nectar for his drink;
however, she also placed another thing there which was purely *sāttvika*.
With that as the primary cause, the remainder was joined with other flavors.
That liquor known as *rājasa* is declared to be mixed with nectar (*amṛta*).
It is remembered that for an ordinary [liquor], half a part of another essence is used;
for the best, it is one-tenth. That is indeed described as *tāmasa*.
That which is established there by the most excellent yoga of a hundredth part is declared to be common;
it remains there imperishable due to my boon of granting boons. Thus, the fourfold potency has been described; now the supreme potency is being told.
By drinking the *sāttvika* [elixir], one becomes equal in luster to Viṣṇu,
skilled in the meaning of all scriptures, and a master of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas.
One shall reside in the city of Mahākalpa, becoming an expert in both discipline and warfare.
He is the lord of all the netherworlds (pātālas), just like the god Janārdana;
he may traverse the fourteen worlds wherever he pleases,
and ten million excellent women of virtuous nature always desire him.
