The Lord of Yoga may divide Himself into millions of forms;
however many Yoga scriptures there may be, endowed with great knowledge,
they all come into existence here, O Goddess of gods, within the sphere of the earth beginning from Śiva.
By means of the application of the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣa-lakṣaṇa*), one comes to know all things;

in the end, one attains *nirvāṇa*, which is difficult to reach for those who have not disciplined themselves. O Lord, by drinking the Rājasa [nectar], one may oneself assume a body of desire (*kāma-vapuḥ*).
One shall live for three *manvantaras*, languid with the weight of great enjoyments,
skilled in the meaning of all scriptures, and having reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅgas*).
Endowed with such superior strength, he desires a hundred thousand women; O highly fortunate one, he attains all classes of women belonging to the *rājasī* [nature].
Having enjoyed these pleasures, he returns and is born as a Great Lord (*maheśvara*).
It dissolves into the supreme Śiva up to the seventh mekhala-line.
By drinking [the nectar] for one month, he becomes immortal; possessing the form of a god, he shall live for seven human kalpas and always desire a thousand [years].
Surrounded by excellent women of a *tāmasa* nature and endowed with various enjoyments,
he who always knows himself only slightly and possesses a perpetually unsubdued mind becomes,
at the end, a sovereign ruler of a province, the best among men.
There, by performing the Yajñavarāha sacrifice, one attains again that which is desired.
By drinking [the water] in common with the Lord, this best of men, assuming a divine form,
remains in a state of equality for one hundred million years.
He constantly desires a hundred ordinary celestial women,
yet even when reminded, O Daughter of the Mountain, he does not recognize his own self.
With his head severed by a discus, he is reborn as a sovereign of a province.
Thus, O beautiful one, the procedure for drinking has been declared to you in its divisions.
Now, O Bhairavī, I shall tell you about the origin of women.
Formerly, when all the gods and asuras had prepared the nectar of immortality (amṛta), [the following occurred].
At that time, women indeed arose who were born of nectar—
thirty thousand crores and three hundred crores of them.
All of them, O beloved, were produced by the Daityas from their own limbs.
And they were established in the netherworld (pātāla), well-guarded by formidable machines.
The origin of these machines is threefold: consisting of karma, māyā, and darkness (tamas).
There were thirty-two thousand of them, and they were most terrible.
Among them, the most excellent and formidable group consisted of one thousand and thirty.
By these, all those supreme and desirable women were guarded.
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, there are no such women to be found within the belly of the world whose fingernail-tips possess a luster equal to the moon;
by the mere touch of whom a hundred thousand couples are restored to life.

O beloved daughter of the mountain, the essence of the entire world—its beauty and sovereignty—is yours; yet you are not equal even to a hundredth part of them. Therefore, I am not capable of describing their beauty and virtues.
Their residence is within the inner sanctum of the womb, radiant with all forms of prosperity;
yet even the gods, led by Nārāyaṇa, though desiring to attain the status of their husbands,
O Queen of the Gods, do not obtain it, being tormented by the fear of my will.
Due to their lack of discipline toward Nārāyaṇa, those gods became vessels for his curse;
yet, by virtue of your own granting of boons, human beings there became the vessels [of grace].
Those who are my devotees, devoted to the Tantras, O Goddess, and firm in their vows—[they too shall be so].
The desire for this arises only in those for whom this is their final birth;
these tigers among men have indeed been gazed upon by the power of Śiva.
For those who possess the desire to obtain the mantra worshipped by the best of gods, [it shall be attained].

O Bhairavī, those embodied beings there who are Rudras and practitioners are surely born from a subtle digit of nectar; they are the stationary women of the King [of the Night]. Their female servants should be known as the principal wives of the [other] lords.
O slender-waisted one, I do not see in the entire universe any women equal to them in beauty—
those women who, standing bashfully after lovemaking, felt ashamed even of Lakṣmī herself.
O beautiful one, how can I describe their physical excellence?
These cities, situated upon the filaments of those lotuses, should be known as the foremost among lotus-cities.
Therefore, O daughter of the mountain, hear the origin of the tāmasas. Long ago, when the gods were engaged in austerities for a hundred thousand years,
the god Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, was propitiated by them.
"O Lord of Gods, grant such excellent wives whose beauty, virtue, and splendor are truly peerless among the fourteen worlds. Having heard this, Brahmā, the creator of the world, then [responded].
Having gathered the essence of the three worlds, that which exists as beauty,
he fashioned hundreds of thousands and even millions of women;
go now to those most excellent Daityas, who are equal to them.
I am not capable of describing their form or splendor.
These attendants stand before the Kesara [Purī];
O Goddess of the Gods, within their petals indeed reside the very cities themselves.
Now, O beloved, I shall describe the classification of all the common [beings],
specifically those women who are the most excellent among all the gods,
as well as those of the Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and Bhogins— even among human beings.
Furthermore, O Goddess, the daughters and wives of the yakṣas who were proud of their beauty,
as well as all the apsarases and others, were seized by the immensely powerful asuras— who were arrogant due to the boon they had received— and established in their own city.
O Goddess of gods, the jewels among women are indeed the very essence of the world;
yet, O slender-waisted one, those jewels among women may become common here.
O Goddess of gods, their cities are indeed situated upon the spokes of the wheel.
These are the attendants of the altar situated in front;
thus, O Goddess of gods, the forms of the Āsuras should always be understood by the foremost of practitioners in this successive order, each being more excellent than the last.
In ancient times, they were indeed proclaimed to be like the spokes and hub of a wheel;
they are said to be within the center of the wheel, inside the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
Their city is situated in its interior, clothed in garments with a radiance equal to ten million suns.
The inner apartment, made of great jewels, brilliant and unobstructed by any gems,
is said to be a hundred times more delightful than heaven, situated amidst the filaments.
The city situated on the petals is to be known as ten times superior to heaven;
it is strewn with hundreds of various jewels and grants the fulfillment of all desires and aims.
On the spokes of the wheel is the secondary city (*kupura*), which likewise grants the fulfillment of all desires and aims.
Made of gold and strewn with hundreds of jewels, it is remembered as being three times greater than heaven;
O Goddess of the Gods, that which is the most excellent among the fourteen worlds was fashioned by the Lotus-born One and situated within the depths of the netherworlds (pātāla).
And because of the granting of boons, everything remains forever inexhaustible. Thus has been described the division of the Viras; now the Vilas are being discussed.
The Śrīmukha is to be known as the most excellent, filled with many inner chambers.
The middle one shall be known as *Vila*, endowed with hundreds of inner apartments;
it is declared to have a common opening and to be surrounded by hundreds of perfected substances.
Thus is the division of the *Vilas* established; now the [distribution] among the regions is described.
At Prayāga and Gayā, at Śrīśaila and Maṇḍaleśvara;
at Hariścandra and the Narmadā, as well as on Mount Kāliñjara;
at Śūlabheda in Kaśmīra, and the most excellent Rota-pūrṇa-vila.
At Vijaya, at Varāha, at Jyeṣṭha, and at Uttaramānasa;
near Tuṅgasvāmin, likewise on Mount Mahādeva;
at Pātramūla, at Padmasaras, and likewise at Mahāmāyūraka.
In such regions as these, they are proclaimed as Śrīmukhas.
Three crores of cavities are declared in the middle world;
two crores are remembered in the earthly realm (Bhūloka), and one crore is held to be in the sky (Ākāśa).
In Jambudvīpa it is remembered as such, and in the ocean it is remembered as double that;
thus they are proclaimed according to the progressive measurement in each successive island.
In this way, the entire circle of the earth should be known as being filled with auspicious openings (vilas).
And within the three realms, they are to be fully known as superior, inferior, and middling.
Thus, the entire essence of the netherworld has been recounted to you in brief.
What else shall I tell you? Speak, O Pārvatī; do not delay.

Thus ends the chapter on the attainment of the netherworld (*pātālasiddhi*) within the practice of the most terrible among the terrible (*ghoraghoratara*), in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the *Śiraccheda* in the *Vidyāpīṭha* of the *Bhairavasrotas*.
The Goddess said:
Now I wish to hear the various means of accomplishment (sādhana) individually.
"Now, please tell me about that which is common and intermediate.
Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Pārameśvarī; I shall explain the practice in brief."
The meaning of the individual words has already been stated and is not elaborated upon here;
however, I shall now briefly state something regarding the collective sense by way of summary:
having gone to a terrifying cremation ground and having taken hold of a corpse that is wounded.
Having placed [the corpse] in the center of the altar, the practitioners should recite on its back the thousand-syllable garland, adopting a fierce mode of practice. Then, by force, the corpse,
dripping with blood, should be made to stand upon its own feet.
Then, having cut off the throbbing flesh with a sword, one should eat it;
one should scatter it in all directions and release a terrifying roar.
Thereupon, the Yoginīs who are established in the three faces will arrive.
They say to the practitioner thus: "O Lord of Heroes, give us some portion of the consecrated liquor.
Having heard this from them, he indeed gives that which arises from his left side.
Afterwards, O Bhairavī, having cut off that flesh, it should be given;
the Yoginīs then dance upon the wheel after devouring it.
Dancing together with Nābhi, they leap through the midst of the sky.
The practitioner there shall become like Bhairava; of this there is no doubt.
By such a procedure as this, O Goddess, one should accomplish the Vetāla on the mountain. As long as he perspires, so long do obstacles arise.
Having let out a very loud, boisterous laugh, he says to the practitioner:
"I am accomplished for you, O Lord of Heroes; what shall I do for you? I stand here at your service. Upon hearing this from him, the practitioner should say:
(163a) "O Vetāla, great being, do not lead me to the temple of the deity where the Blessed Goddess Kālī, together with Karṣaṇī, resides in person."
Having heard this, that Vetāla did not indeed fall upon the practitioner;
for he reached that place, Sādhakeśvara, where Mahākālī herself is present.
Having arrived there, O Goddess, that lord of practitioners no longer grieves.
Now, if one should desire to become invisible, then one should perform this rite:
having taken great oil and placed it upon a perfectly pure leaf of the *naraka* plant,
one should prepare a wick made of dead oil and place it before the priest during the conjunction of the flowers.
Having prepared it, one situated in a cremation ground should accomplish this supreme collyrium.
Having taken it while placed in a skull-cup, one should cause it to be consecrated by reciting the mantra a hundred times.
A man whose eyes are anointed with this shall become invisible.

The practitioner shall indeed live for ten thousand years, always endowed with youth, possessing the strength of ten elephants, and remaining young. When it begins to smoke due to the application of the collyrium, this is the characteristic sign that occurs.
O Lord, O Sovereign of the Goddesses, when [the fire] has blazed, one becomes a Dhareśvara through the Vidyā.
Then, having taken wood produced from a trident, fashion a pair of sandals.
Having resorted to a cremation ground, one should then recite [the mantra] a thousand times correctly.
O Goddess, one should offer human excrement as an oblation while the sandals are indeed blazing.
Then, O slender-waisted lady, she should be known as perfected by her characteristic signs;
having covered the feet with that [substance], one becomes a Lord of Vidyās.
Having traversed fourteen worlds and endowed with sovereignty over the three realms,
he indeed brought the previously mentioned wood, which had its neck severed;
from that, a trident fifty fingers high should be fashioned.
O slender-waisted one, having established that trident on the mountain peak—
smeared with the pollen of flowering *mrija* flowers and anointed with the blood of heroes—
the preeminent practitioner should perform three thousand recitations.
O beloved, it gradually becomes warm, then smokes,
and thereafter it blazes forth; one should examine that [state] by its characteristics.
O Queen of the Gods, by the first [mantra], one becomes the lord of the seven continents for a thousand years of life, endowed with great strength and prowess;
by the second, O illustrious lady, one gains the power of flight for ten yojanas.
By the third [initiation], O Goddess, one becomes a lord of the Vidyādharas of the trident.
Having enjoyed the pleasures of that Mahākalpa according to the Tantra, he shall go to the city of Śiva.
Now I shall further explain the great means of accomplishment for the Bhūtas.
Having gone to the cremation ground, O Hero, one should worship Śivā in the center of the sacrificial altar.
Having smeared his body with that ash and subsisting on alms, he should perform recitation (*japa*).
There, O Goddess, naked as the directions, he should recite this *daṇḍaka* at night.
One should not interrupt anyone’s speech while wandering for alms.
With a voice of full resonance, one should recite the *daṇḍaka*:
*Oṃ ho he mahākula bhairava auṃ | ṇadūihiṃḍaimajhriṭhiauṃ | mahikhaṃdhicadāvi asattisā |*

Ghorī, the mistress of the cremation ground; she who possesses a mouth like a great, roaring, gaping maw; she who emits a terrifying, loud, and piercing shriek; she who casts forth a mass of flames that are fearsome with their tongues of fire; she who causes the multitude of spirits to leap up; she who is formidable with her matted hair standing erect; she who utters cries of "Hā! Hā! and "Alas!"; she who has seized the heart of Mahādeva; she who has become the very embodiment of the sacrificial fire.
Having thus uttered the staff-mantra and gathered alms,
the practitioner should eat whatever is obtained from wherever it may be found.
Afterwards, having returned to one's own place, one should recite the mantra while joined with the *bhūtas*:
"May all *bhūtas* come here, their pride in their knowledge destroyed. Thus the word should be in the middle; then one should utter the Goddess (*tamaḥ*).
Having thus consecrated himself for one month in this manner, he shall observe the vow beloved by Bhairava.
Then all those beings will surely come quickly—
rākṣasas, piśācas, yakṣas, and likewise kumbhāṇḍakas.
The Vetālas, Kiṃkaras, Bhūtas, and whatever others have been proclaimed—
indeed, all of them become subject to that practitioner as his servants;
there is no doubt that they always perform every task for him.
These [beings] pulverize the mountains and even dry up the oceans;
they drink up all the rivers and even devour the nāgas;
they pierce through the netherworlds as far as the abode of the fire of time (kālāgni).
Indra and the other world-protectors forcibly draw them away;
these kings crush them, and they entice the great mountain ranges.
Wherever they are impelled, they perform those very acts without hesitation.
Thus, the accomplishment of the Bhūtas and other spirits has been proclaimed to you in this tantra.
Now, O beautiful lady, I shall describe to you the accomplishment of the Yakṣiṇīs.
Having identified the Yakṣiṇī by her name, one should write it upon a cloth from a corpse.
Having installed her according to the prescribed rite beneath the banyan tree,

one should then recite [the mantra] a thousand times, O Mistress of the God of Gods; thereafter, striking with flowers produced from a corpse should be performed while knowing the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and uttering the [mantra].
O slender-waisted one, one should strike the wife’s family from the region of the vulva;
the mother’s family from the soles of the feet; and the friend from the heart.
These families previously mentioned by me to you were designated within the six Kali periods.
In this manner, one should strike her violently for as long as seven days;
then that yakṣī will arrive, terrified and utterly distraught.
This [practice] grants all aims, just as previously described when first taught.
Now, I shall further explain the sādhana of the *ceṭakas*:
Vappila, Kampila, Puṣpahāsa, and Madotkaṭa.
And their names, encased within this very vidyā,
should be recited three thousand times with devotion while standing upon a mountain peak.
Then, deluded by the pride of their own magical power, they will quickly arrive.
Established as the jewel of servants (kiṅkara-ratna), they act according to their will;
they dry up all rivers and even grind mountains to powder.
They cause flowers and fruits to bear fruit out of season, yielding their produce in an instant.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, they bend down the trees here, drag away my flesh,
and even hurl the mountains into the sky;
all the gods, Indra and the rest, draw them [the mountains] back in an instant.
"O Goddess of the lords of gods, whatever is pleasing to him, all that they shall always do for you when they are set in motion by the command of the practitioner. Thus,
O Daughter of the Mountain, the perfection of the *ceṭaka* has been described to you."
Now I shall tell you of the extraction of substances, known as withdrawal (saṃhāra). O Goddess, one should paint the Goddess on a cloth exactly as she was visualized in the previous meditation—
residing upon a cloth from a corpse, O Goddess, and adorned with all her limbs.
Having installed that Goddess of the Gods in the Jyeṣṭhā-sthāna, O Maheśvarī,
one should install ten vessels before her,
O beloved: a vessel for liquor, a vessel for milk, and likewise a vessel for ghee.
O woman of excellent complexion, one should install three vessels for oil, three for cooked rice, and likewise three for condiments;
then, in brief, two vessels for grain, crops, and so forth.
Having installed all these [vessels] according to the prescribed rite, they should be dedicated to Ucchuṣma.
The ritual implements should always be provided with small holes;
thereafter, one should worship the Goddess with substances purchased from heroic persons.
Having likewise brought those substances, one should fill the vessels with them.
The practitioner, with a firm mind, should thus recite for one month;
the Mistress of the Gods should always be visualized as attracting all substances. (165a)
One should perform such a vow continuously for a day and night.
At the end of each month, one should always offer all the ritual substances to the deity.
One should offer oneself as the equivalent of a thousand [units] and present various kinds of enjoyments.

Thus has this great method of attracting the *vyañjana* been fully explained; having obtained it, a man shall quickly accomplish whatever he desires in his mind. Now I shall proclaim the auspicious ritual for the *prāsanika*.
By means of which one understands everything established within the three worlds.
O Dear One, having recited it one hundred times during the rite of preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*),
[one perceives] in a sword, a mirror, a conch, water, the moon, and the sky.
O Goddess, when the lamp, the thumb, the ash-vessel, and likewise the eyes of the maiden are seen with flowers by the auspicious mantrins themselves,
having worshipped [the deity] with ritual materials and extensive offerings according to one's means; ||| 12 ||
If one burns incense continuously, then everything becomes visible:
the past, the present, the future, and whatever time is current—
all that is seen truly by the mantra-practitioner, whether through a virgin or otherwise.

By performing a thousand-fold service, one sees the verses written down and hears the sound within; there, O Goddess, there is no loss. Thus has Prasena been described; now the possession of those who are healthy is being told.
Having brought a beautiful maiden endowed with auspicious marks,
he should reside there and worship the Goddess with the thousand-syllable mantra,
along with various garlands, offerings, excellent incense, and pure flowers.
Having anointed her face with lac, one should begin the recitation of the mantra.
One should burn incense continuously and offer various foods to the fire.
O Maheśvarī, many vessels of liquor should be placed there.
Then he quickly enters that goddess Kṛṣodarī who resides there;
she stands in the sky at a distance of one cubit, appearing most terrifying.
There he performs his rites; he drinks wine and blood.
Then, O Goddess, he proclaims everything that exists within the belly of the universe—past and future; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Bowing down, one should indeed worship her with many offerings of flowers.
Having thus asked the goddess for forgiveness, one should then dismiss her.
Through the descent of the deity into one's own self, there shall be a dream; this is what is called the "human speech" [of the deity].
Having taken recourse to a bright bed, one should worship Śivā at the head of it.
Having consecrated white mustard seeds with the Niṣpanna mantra, one should place them in the mouth;
one should scatter other [seeds] upon the bed and then lie down on one's back.
Whatever has been, is, or will be, and whatever has come within the range of the mind—all that the best of practitioners perceives as true in the dream state.
Thus the procedure for dreams has been declared; now the possession by the *khorikā* is described.
Having fashioned a beautiful bronze vessel, a bowl filled with mercury,
one should worship there the auspicious Goddess, who is mounted upon the wheel of wind—
trembling, most terrible, and devouring the three worlds.
One should worship Kṛṣodarī with great accumulations of wealth;
one should burn incense continuously and repeat the mantra.
Then, O woman of excellent complexion, the Khorikā will quickly appear.

O Goddess Maheśvarī, where wealth is established through the force of arrows and umbrellas, where there is elixir, rejuvenation, and the auspicious face that grants excellent success— there is no other kṣetrapāla for you there.
In this way, one should accomplish all things, including the attainment of treasures and elixirs.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed agitation of the city (*purakṣobha*). Having reached the house of Mātṛkā and having worshipped the Supreme Goddess, [one should proceed].
Remaining there, the supreme practitioner should contemplate the Power (śakti) arisen from the hollow interior of the fire of time (kālāgni),
possessing the brilliance of ten million times ten thousand flashes of lightning.
Resembling a mass of vermilion and like the flower of the pomegranate tree,
issuing forth from every path and crowded with many sparks,
she covered the entire world like a cloud.
One should remember her raining down a flood of intoxicating liquor upon a city or a town;
or, O highly fortunate one, one should indeed remember her everywhere upon the earth.
Through the yoga of returning again and again, let her pervade the entire range of the worlds.
The best of practitioners should remember her as she enters his own path;
O Goddess of the Gods, that supreme among men should remain without interruption for even half a month,
and for as long as he maintains meditation, he shall cause the city [of the body] to tremble.
O Goddess of the Gods, as many women there as there are men,
as well as children, the elderly, and the animals— all those inhabitants of the maṇḍala—
come from every direction, deluded by the pride of their own knowledge.
And by their very wealth, they always fall into servitude.
Those who are circle-leaders (maṇḍalīkas) or kings [fall] through the play of various dice-casts.
Thus, the agitation of the earth has been described in brief.
O highly fortunate one, by meditating for one month, the *bhūcarīs* come under control;
they bestow their own supernatural knowledge upon the great-souled practitioner.
O Goddess of the gods, after two months, the *khecarīs* come under control.
Those who reside within the interior of the cosmic egg and dwell in the proximity of the hundred Rudras undoubtedly bestow their own realization upon the practitioner;
thus is described the agitation that effects the attraction of realization.
Now I shall further explain the auspicious rite for subjugation and attraction.

When, by means of the *saṃpuṭa* application, one recites this Great Goddess within the interior of the heart-cave, with the letters of the name of the person to be accomplished situated between [the mantra syllables].
Within seven days, O God, O Mistress of the Gods, he shall bring under his control all that is moving and unmoving;
by the application of the noose and the goad, O Goddess, there is no doubt in this matter.

By means of such a rite, through the union with the heart-lotus and the application of the Great Noose, one may draw forth even the lords of the gods. There is nothing in this world that it cannot forcibly attract.
Now, for the purpose of inciting hatred, one should meditate on her as smoky-colored and making a terrible sound;
by joining the feet [in this posture], one should recite this mantra, and then the world will become hostile.
[The practitioners] stand in the sky with averted faces, each holding a thunderbolt in their hand, [directed] against one another.
Striking one another without support and turning away from each other—
by such application of meditation, he should cause both the moving and the unmoving to be consumed by hatred.
Now, O slender-waisted lady, I shall describe another rite, that of eradication.
The practitioner should write the Vidyā on a black cloth with the blood of a goat;
he should write Ghoreśī together with the name of the target using a crow’s wing-feather. She should be depicted as hanging down from the back of a Piśāca tree.
O Goddess of the Gods, it can even uproot the Himālaya itself.
I shall now fully explain the rite of killing (māraṇa) by which it is performed against enemies:
one should write the name [of the enemy] upon a cloth used for the dead, using poison, charcoal, and excrement.
O Goddess, [one should write] the *vidyā* encapsulated and joined with its own words, "māraya" (kill).
Having written it thus, one should then bury it at the foot of a tree in a cremation ground.
Then, having kindled a fire on one's back, one should offer oblations of the poison-demoness (*viṣamāsurī*).
O Goddess, he could slay even Śatru-puraṃdara (Indra) in a single day.
Now listen, O you who are worshipped by the lords of heroes, to this most fierce rite of immobilization (*staṃbhanam*).
One should draw [the diagram] with one's own hand and recite [the mantra] to the Goddess using yellow substances, and it must not be seen by anyone.
Joined with the syllables of the name of the one to be accomplished and accompanied by the *śma* [syllable], one should cast it downward;
O Goddess of the gods, it shall paralyze an army, as well as the womb and movement.
It paralyzes all speech and sciences, and whatever else a man may desire.
Thus has the *stava* been fully explained; now hear, O Bhairavī, the *stobhana*.
Having consecrated the net once with the mantra, the practitioner strikes it.
O Goddess, one should strike [the victim] with each [mantra]; what need is there to mention those possessed by spirits?
O Goddess, Viśavinī destroys them, or otherwise through striking the deities. One should destroy possession by planets, spirits, fever, and scabies simply by sprinkling [water).
One may destroy clouds, winds, and thunderbolts through meditation alone.
Now, O beloved, I shall tell you of the destruction of the epilepsy-graha:
having worshipped the Goddess as she proceeds along the single path, then—

Free from the afflictions caused by the great accumulation of worldly possessions, one should then cause the person afflicted by the planets to enter there; however, O Goddess, the two-eyed [initiate] should not be made to enter.
Then, as previously described, one should manifest the initiation for him.
"O fair-hipped one, by initiation alone that terrible planet is quickly subdued;
by means of consecration, O lady of beautiful thighs, it shall not afflict him again.
Thus, my dear, did Vasiṣṭha formerly [act] for Nara and Nārāyaṇa."
That terrible planet, which is a great source of evil and remains formidable,
is indeed destroyed by this method; O Supreme Goddess, those ailments here that are difficult to cure perish by this rite— of this there is no doubt.
Thus has the treatment for epilepsy been explained to you.
By means of this *kumbhaka* alone, through the scattering of dust, the Great Goddess can paralyze carts,
boats, machines, and even the most excellent of women.
A man may effortlessly bind a non-venomous snake at the entrance of its hole.
Then, having gone to the abode of the serpents, the mantra-practitioner, holding a trident, should with reverence [invoke] Ananta and the others there, accompanied by the names of the snakes.
One should recite the Vidyā joined with one's own name in a loud voice;
O Goddess of the gods, within seven days, by the power of this great mantra, one shall dry up even a lake as vast as the ocean— of this there is no doubt.
This nāga, terrified and with eyes full of dread,
came toward me while accompanied by his retinue, crying out, "Save me! [I took] the elixirs, the rejuvenators, the jewels, and whatever perfected substances there were.
They will undoubtedly bestow these upon that practitioner;
or else, they should be properly consumed in his house according to his desire.
The bull among men should dispatch that elephant wherever he may please.
Thus has the ritual concerning elephants been explained to you in full detail.
Now, therefore, I shall proclaim this supreme secret.
That which brings benefit to practitioners and has not been revealed anywhere—
by means of which the summoning of the Great Beast (Mahāpaśu) is accomplished with ease—
having reached a solitary place, there [resides] the goddess Kṛṣodarī.
Having worshipped before her, one should prepare the collyrium (añjana),
having taken it from two human corpses as well as from the vomit of a cat;
having collected these according to their respective divisions, distinguishing between the left and the right.
Having brought cow’s ghee combined with a great quantity of oil, O Goddess,
one should treat these eyes of this best of men by applying it;
by turning the *kṣepāla* [instrument] once properly, success is achieved.

Then the Goddess should request: "O Mistress of the Gods, by your grace, the collyrium has been perfected for me, by which I shall indeed be free from doubt. Now, O Mistress of the Gods, I shall also offer you the auspicious *caru*."
"If the Veda does not strike down its own foremost [portion] when it is offended, then,
having spoken thus, at dawn, as soon as the birds have awakened,
he should go out from his house and reflect with eyes anointed [with collyrium]."
Whichever man or woman endowed with auspicious marks is seen here,
having gathered the dust from his or her feet seven times, then,
by means of the application of the mudrā-bindu and the application of the Great Net (mahājāla), [one attains the desired result].
Then, O Goddess, having performed the mudrā, one should collect the dust in this manner.
O Goddess, while established in the pinnacle of meditation within the *ucchūṣma* casket, one should cast it [into the fire].
Having obtained the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), O Goddess, one should let out a roar before the Goddess.
I shall now fully describe that mudrā known as Śivārāvā, which is difficult to master:
having sat down there in front [of the deity], one should place the right knee-cap [on the ground]. (168a)
Having slightly extended and contracted the left heel, one should thrust it into the anus.
Turn the left hand back and place the tip of the left leg upon it.
O fortunate lady, then let the right [heel] touch the ground and the other be raised high.
With distorted eyes, his face turned upward and most terrifying,
he should drink from the hollow of the heart-cakra and let out a roar difficult to restrain. By laughing seven times, he will surely agitate the host of yoginīs.

Having bound this most formidable mudrā, the best of practitioners attains union with the Goddess once; the Goddess, being pleased, becomes gracious. Afterwards, the man should seal the opening located at the junction of the head.

Then, O beloved, one who delights in meditation should remain there with a large stake or a small peg; being undisturbed, that is what is called "meditation" here. Having drawn [the victim] by means of the noose (*pāśa*), one should hang him after striking him with the goad (*aṅkuśa*).
One should visualize the form of the sacrificial animal pierced by the trident, streaming [blood],
as it is led away head-first by means of playful swinging, sport, the throbbing of its life-breath, and nooses.
Its entire essence of food and vigor is thus rendered accessible.
Thus, for one who delights in meditation, after three days it becomes a *kalala*;
after seven days it becomes fragrant and supremely bliss-inducing;
and after the period of fourteen days, bees arise there in great abundance.
After three weeks, heat will arise; then one should declare success.
O fortunate lady, listen now to the procedure that I shall describe in due order.
Then, having worshipped the Goddess with all his wealth, the practitioner—
Having offered [the meat], one should afterwards consume it, having performed the ritual identification of one's own body (*sakalīkṛtavigraha*).
O Dear One, by thus consuming the seven types of animals, one becomes immortal;
one floats through the expanse of the sky where the goddess Kṛṣodarī resides.
Alternatively, taking the sacrificial pap (caru), intent on wandering at night,
one should go to the foremost cremation ground and worship the Goddess there.
Holding the *caru* in his hand, he should bind the previous mudrā.
Then the Khecarīs, filled with great bliss and intoxicated, arrive;
O Goddess, they request the *caru* from the high-souled practitioner.
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, their desired object must be sought among them—
whether it be the eightfold powers beginning with *aṇiman*, or the supreme state of moving through the sky (*khecarī*),
or even the netherworld (*pātāla*), O Goddess, according to his own preference.
They speak thus of that practitioner; there is no doubt regarding this.
Then, having personally received the sacrificial oblation (caru) from the wheel, the practitioner shall indeed attain his desired goal, O Goddess; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus do those goddesses rejoice— the Yoginīs and the Ḍāmarās, as well as the Ḍāginīs, the Lāmās, and Mahācchuṣmā; and the Nara women,
some of whom breathe upward and others who breathe downward.
Likewise, there is Nakracūṣyā and the other Yoginīs who have been proclaimed;
as many as were previously taught at great length in the Śaṃvara Tantra in its ten- and twelve-thousand-verse versions, so many are his foremost attendants.
O Supreme Goddess, these become perfectly accomplished for the practitioner alone.
This is declared to be the accomplishment of the *caru*, which bestows perfect success upon practitioners.
Thus, O Goddess, the wheel of Ghoreśvarī has been described to you.
"Now speak what has come to mind in your heart, O son; and I shall declare it.

Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the Ghoraghoratara-cakra in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra of Twenty-four Thousand [Verses], within the third Ṣaṭka, in the *Śiraccheda* of the Vidyāpīṭha in the Bhairava-stream.
The Goddess said:
O Supreme Lord, that which was previously spoken in the Śaṃvara Tantra has been understood by me, O God, in detail from that secret tantra.
O Lord, how did that formidable and mighty body come to reside within you?
How do the goddesses worship it, and how many of their lineages (kulas) are traditionally remembered?
"O Lord, how is their sequence, and how is their movement so deeply secret?
How is the accomplishment of the *caru* for them? Tell me this in detail.
Having heard these words falling from the lotus-face of the Mistress of the Gods, [he replied:]
Mahādeva spoke these words once more to Vavomṛta.
Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one, you who are a vessel for the meaning of all knowledge!"
I shall explain in brief the incomparable great secret, the supreme movement of the Yoginīs; listen with a one-pointed mind.
It is endowed with the three secret wheels and accompanied by the three great sacrifices.
Endowed with many accomplishments and crowded with numerous secrets,
it is that which exists as the perfected state of the Fish-Wheel (Mīnacakra) of Kāśyapa;
therein the attainment of the sixfold yoga is eternally established.
It is crowded with the mandalas of the five fierce secret Mothers;
it is filled with the hosts of Gaṇas and Dūtīs and the families of A-raṃ-ta-ka;
it is a receptacle for the weight of many yogas and is agitated by hundreds of great wonders.
Endowed with the words of perfected mantras, adorned with the mantras of the [spiritual] family,
fully accomplished through the conduct of the observance (samaya), and adorned by the signs of the directions;
it is liberated from [the need for] recitation and vows, bestowing success and granting the perfection of yoga.
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the ritual practice along with its secret [instruction].
Formerly, when Yajñamitras was properly initiated, that was imparted to him;
nevertheless, O Goddess of Gods, the secret therein was not revealed.
Since the movement of the *yoginīs* is most strictly secret,
listen now to that which is correctly desired regarding this supreme tantra. That God who is both supreme and non-supreme is renowned as the "Transcendent" (*paramottara*).
He is all-pervasive, the Adhyaya, the Ordainer, complete, and the supreme consciousness;
he who is traditionally celebrated as Śiva, the omnipresent one whose form is the possessor of power.
Whatever undivided power and potency reside within that aggregate,
all mantras of great strength are born from a portion of that splendor.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, you are indeed formless and devoid of any shape.
How did these mantras arise for you? Tell me that, O Maheśvara.
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, because it is of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*), its state as the form of pure awareness (*cidrūpa*) remains unbroken;
and that great radiance truly attains manifestation.
Furthermore, the activity directed toward the phonemes (*varṇa*) takes hold of that very [radiance].
Having taken recourse to a body consisting of the Great Sound (Mahānāda), that Supreme Lord,
the Sovereign Himself, attains the state of Mantra and Tantra.
Manifest as the Lord of gods and demons, He is the Master of both restraint and grace.
The Goddess said:
If the Lord Bhairava performs both restraint and grace,
then he would possess duality and attachment, just as a person does.
Bhairava said:
"O fortunate one, neither passion nor aversion is attributed to him;
just as the sun, O fortunate one, effects the blossoming of a cluster of lotuses."
The radiance of his voice performs [its work] and brings some to full maturation;
yet, O Bhairavī, there is neither passion nor aversion in that god.
O Goddess, for those by whom impurity has been gradually destroyed, their state is perfectly stainless.

O Supreme Goddess, that mind accomplishes [its goal] like Śiva; it restrains the flood of fetters, impurity, and karma, and [attains] steadfastness toward worldly existence. Bhairava, the destroyer of worldly existence, is declared to be the one who effects their restraint.
She bestows grace through the manifestation of her own essential nature.
O Goddess, thus have both restraint and grace been fully revealed as yours alone.
She who is the source of the phonemes and the measures (mātrās) is remembered as the fire-drill for mantras.
And that Kuṇḍalinī energy is to be known as the supreme digit (kalā);
from her, the mantras and the various Kulas have arisen individually.
O Goddess of the gods, O Sovereign of the Suras, those tantras were previously proclaimed by me in great detail in the first hexad;
here, O you who are praised by the lords of heroes, I shall proclaim them concisely— listen!
The Root Tantra, Kubjikā, the Yoginījālaśambara,
Adūśasvaranāga, Hahūdhūli, and another;
the Calākṣara Mahātantra, which is the descent for universal play.
The Mahāmāyontara, likewise the Sarvavīramata,
the great tantra Alaṃgrāsa, the Kruñcikodghāṭa, the Siddhacakra, the Prakāśa, the Paṭa, and the Tūra, as well as others.
The Siddhakaula, the Mahājāla, as well as the Bhairavagahvara; that which is named Kulagahvara, the Kulaḍāmarabhairava;
the extremely fierce Jhāṃkārakula, and likewise the auspicious Siddhāmata.
There is another [tantra] called Kāñcana, as well as that known as Kusumālika;
likewise the Siddhayogeśvarī-tantra, the Trikasārottara,
the Picu-tantra, the Mahāraudra, and that designated as Vimalocchuṣma.
The tantra named Khaḍgarāvaṇa, as well as another called Ṭakamaṇḍana; the Karoṭī, the one known as Muṇḍamālā, the Śiraccheda, and the terrifying Bhayānaka;
the Hāhārava, the Antara-tantra, and the Krodha-unmattabhairava.
The extremely fierce Ruruyāmala, as well as another Rudrayāmala;
another Umāyāmala and also a Gaurīyāmala;
another Skandayāmala, and likewise a Bhairavayāmala.
There is indeed the Viṣṇuyāmala, as well as the Nandiyāmala;
there is another, the Śukrayāmala, and also the Kkrayāmala.
The *Kapālīśamata*, likewise the *Meghanādīśvara*,
the one named *Haṃsayāmala*, *Caṇḍogra*, *Hāṭakeśvara*,
the *Mahāvāmeśvarī-tantra*, and the excellent *Laṅkeśīmata*.
The Laṃpaṭādya, the Haḍḍāṣata, and another,
the Durvāsamatam— these and many others such as these are proclaimed as the supreme tantras, saluted by the circle of Yoginīs.
In these very supreme tantras, their movement and deliberation have been analyzed;
however, this secret concerning the nature of the deities has not been spoken of in these [others],
nor has it been revealed today in the *Mahātantra Śiraccheda*.
O Goddess of gods, as far as their investigation extends, so is the established order of the Yoginīs;
indeed, just like the *saṃvaras*, their movement and manifestation are exactly as they are,
according to the diversity of their various modes of conduct.
Just as there is the examination of the sacrificial animal and the transformation of form and so forth,
and just as there is the sealing (*mudraṇa*) here, as well as delusion (*moha*) and union (*melaka*),
all that has been described by me here skillfully, O Mistress of the Gods.
Thus the power of this All-pervasive Lord has issued forth as Bhairaveśvarī. Just as the manifestation of this gross deity is [described] through the Śāmbara system,
so too is its manifestation in the [divine] abodes explained according to the sequence and differentiation of its limbs.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, listen attentively as I shall correctly explain the station of that Bhairava, who is more divine than the gods and endowed with such splendor;
for from a portion of his brilliance all the mantras of great power have arisen.
During that terrible great dissolution, two [flames] issued from his forehead;
O Goddess, the eyebrows were beautiful with the Tilaka, Arka, and Vicai;
and the five crests of hair, O Goddess Caṇḍā, were enveloped by the wind.
Bhṛkuṭī, Bhagamālā, Lokavāmā, Sukeśinī, Tārā, Kṣitijayā, Rūpā, Śauṇḍī, Nandinī, Gominī,
Tṛguṇī, Satyā, as well as Dākṣāyaṇī and Satī.
Umāhvayā, Mahākālā, Caṇḍālā, Jayā, Śriyā,
Bhadrakālī, Sumedhā, Arkīṇī, and likewise Subhagā.
Tārakā, Bharaṇī, and Raudrī are crowded with garlands of flames. Emerging from her hair are fierce goddesses who bring fear to all beings;
they have variegated tilakas on their foreheads and are enchanting to all creatures.
From the tongue issued blazing flames filling every direction;
likewise, Vāgeśvarī was present, firmly holding a golden staff.
Also present were Mahāgaurī, Mahāmāyā, and Mahāvetālī.
The world-sustainers (*lokadhātrī*), who can assume any form at will and possess great power, have emerged,
surrounded by ten thousand Mahāmātrīs and Netrots.
Also present are Nādakrodha, Kūhāśa, and the mighty Krodhīśa.
Mahogrāsa was born from the two tusks, surrounded by ten koṭis;
Gaṇḍava was born from Bhairava, and the terrifying Kālarātri from him as well.
And Caṇḍahāsā was born from the laughter, while Kulinī likewise emerged from the chin.
Likewise, Śrīsampuṭā emerged from the two eyes, while Kaṅkārudra and Vāriṇī were born from the ears; Sāvitrī was produced from the service [of the mouth],
and Sarvatobhadrā and Mahāvidyā were brought forth from the nose.
From his two arms emerged thousands of Śūlapatras and Piṅgalas,
as well as all the Kāpālikas and the highly powerful Guardians of the Quarters (Dikpālas).
From his fingers arose the great-bodied ones and the mighty hosts beginning with Kāla.
Emerging from the region of the chest are the Rudras who strike with the discus;
they should be known as the Gaṇas, the Hālāhalas, and likewise the Hālāhālas. Furthermore, there is the great Ākarmaka.
By means of their breasts, which are the objects of knowledge and thought, they bestow happiness upon all sentient beings;
Jayā and Vijayā likewise reside on the two sides of the shanks.
From the region of the back emerged the Virūpiṇīs and the Mahākālis;
from the secret region [the organ] emerged Guhyaka and Guhya, while Tripuraghna became the phallus.
From the testicles came the two most excellent Gaṇas, Mahālaya and Kala.
Likewise, the Ucchuṣmas and Caṇḍālas are in the region of the thighs; the Karṇapravāhas are in the ears; the Lohapāśas and Vajrajaṅghas are everywhere in the shanks;
and the Vādhākālocanas, Dārakas, and Vijanas are likewise [located there].
The Śaviras, as well as the Caṇḍas and Mātaṅgas who grant all desires, were produced from the pores of his body; Kāma, born of the senses, was also produced,
and Vīrabhadra was likewise fashioned from them.
From his perspiration emerged Bhīma, the god who destroys the bodies of desire.
Thus, from that splendor, all the mantras of great power issued forth;
through the application of their own heroism and strength, they are all possessed of omniscient wisdom.
They are the creators of all progeny, all-pervading, and powerful;
they are the givers of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), existing both outside and within it.
Having gathered their splendor together with Śiva, the Supreme Self—
For this Blessed One is an emanation who brings all sentient beings under his control. He is proclaimed by the wise as having three morae and four feet. At the end of his first mora, Aghora is born.
The Lord Mahāghora, who brings about the dissolution of those [beings] born from the second measure (mātrā),
is the performer of cruel and most cruel deeds.
From the third measure, he becomes Mṛta, whose nature is the destruction and withdrawal of that [world].
Aghorā has arisen as the triad of Yogīśvarīs within the Raudra [tattva].
Aghorā, Ambikā, and Jyeṣṭhā are endowed with the power of yoga;
they are the source-forms of the mantras of the great-souled ones who have become abundant.
The three families of Śākinīs have arisen from the Great Terrible;
the group of four belongs to the Cūmbikās, while that of the Mūṣikās consists of five.
There are eight families of *patralehyas*, fourteen of *ucchusmas*,
ten of *nakracūṣīs*, three of *ūrddhaniśvāsikas*,
and thousands of *adho-niśvāsikas* along with *sakapūtanās*.
The entire world is pervaded by noble ones belonging to the *kula*s and *upakula*s.
Those who are most terrible and even more terrible have given birth to the Mothers (*mātṛ*s),
who are distinguished by sixty-three *kula*s and accompanied by female messengers (*dūtī*s) and servants (*kiṅkara*s).
Mahāmāyā, along with the ninefold group of Saṃbhinnā and others, is established in nine ways;
there, this all-pervading Lord is the leader, who is most fierce, terrifying, and wrathful.
Likewise, O fair-faced one, the group of six has arisen, divided into six.
"By means of the six petals and leaves perfectly established, [there arise] the yoginīs of great splendor.
Thus has the rule of yoga been declared in the *Yoginījālasaṃcara*. Now listen to the "beyond-yoga" (*niryoga*) as it was taught according to its origin.
Thus, in the Bhairava-stream, in the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), in the *Śiraccheda*, in the *Jayadrathayāmala* Great Tantra of twenty-four thousand verses,
in the third hexad, [this is] the chapter titled "The Arising of the Vowels from the Lord of the Yoginī-cakra.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, for those whose forms have been determined, what are the mantras and what is the other ritual procedure?
How are they to be propitiated, and what kind of fruit will there be?
Likewise, [what are] the general forms and the heart-mantras of Maheśvara?"
How many different forms do they assume as practiced by yogins?
What is the nature of the recitation of the mantras, or their power?
What is the yoga of those [mantras], and what are their commitments (samayas)?
O Lord, what is the nature of conduct (*caryā*) and what is the nature of behavior (*ācāra*)?
O Maheśvara, how many distinct divisions of *kula* are there?
O Blessed One, you ought to explain all of this according to its true reality.
Bhairava said:
[I shall explain] the arrangement of the secret wheel and the application of the origin of the mantras.
O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall describe various deeds;
O beloved, the third characteristic of that school is that which is touched by the *bindu* and the *kalā* at the beginning— that [is what constitutes] the world of moving and non-moving beings.
Nāda, Sphoṭa, and likewise Śānta; from Śāntā arises Bindu. Then Ghaṇṭā, Ciñcinī, and after that Ghoṣiṇī. This creation consists of Nāda; now hear about the form of Bindu.
Just as syllable, tone, color, word, sound, and likewise resonance;
the *kūṭa*, the *visarga*, the *rañjikā*, and that which arises from the *bindu*—these manifest forms to one another;
this is their mutual manifestation.
These lords of sages create the twenty-fifth principle by means of the [lower] puruṣas—
that by which this entire world, possessing universal form, is pervaded from Brahmā down to the Avīci hell. Now, hear of its form.
He who is of the nature of Māyā abides in bodies that consist of Māyā;

he who abides in Vidyā resides in those whose nature is Vidyā; he who is of the form of Śakti resides in Śakti. He who is with parts (sakala) resides in that which has parts, and he who is without parts (niṣkala) resides in that which is without parts.
O Goddess, the accomplisher of mantras is established in the secret wheel.
O lady of excellent vows, I shall tell you how the god [resides] among the yoginīs,
as well as the twenty-four principles according to their directional divisions.
Having placed the Puruṣa in the center, accompanied by the groups of elements and the classes [of letters],
it is then surrounded externally by the solar wheel and the digits of the moon;
[and further surrounded by] the unmanifest, earth, water, space, wind, and fire.
One should arrange the [elements] in direct and reverse order, starting from the East and the Southeast.
The nose, the tongue, the ears, and the feet are the middle [positions].
O Goddess, one should join the twenty principles (tattvas) in the Purifier and the North.
Sound, touch, form,
as well as the dispersed ego-sense (ahaṃmanas)— having placed these in reverse order here on the northern and northeastern petals.
Having thus arranged three [syllables] on each petal in due order, O Goddess, one should fill them with the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *bha*. [The petals are occupied by:
Marīcī, Jvālinī, Dhūmrā, Tapanī, and likewise Tāpanī.
Pāvakī, Havyavāhā, and likewise Tejovatī; Śatadhāmā, Dhāmā, and Padmaprabodhanī;
and Tamopahā—these indeed are the channels (nāḍīs) of the Sun.

Having placed the vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *visarga*, excluding the neuter ones, upon the tips of the petals; and having placed the [syllables] beginning with *māyā* (hrīm), along with the *vukas* and *saras*; one should arrange the *saṃhāra* (reversal) conjoined with *kāla* (kṣ) in the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
Māyā, Kalā, as well as Kāla, Niyati, Vidyā, and Īśvara; O Goddess, Sādāśiva and Śiva, and again Utkāla—
these one should place within the middle of the Kuśeśaya with the letters of the *ya*-group.
Having thus arranged the wheel, one should then extract the mantras:
[the syllable] pervaded by the mind-seed (manobīja) and split by the fire-god (havyavāha), O Goddess, is the Heart of the Yoginī; it is the common extraction of the Mātṛs.
Jvālinī, Jvalat, and Haṃsa joined with Puruṣa constitute the second heart, which is considered the supreme cruel [mantra] of the Mothers.
That same [mantra], with Sa-iva, Haṃsa, and joined with Kalā, is the Dhāmamālā, which destroys all impurities.
The third among the Nikāyas is thus proclaimed.
Ni-yati is enveloped by Dhūmra; Havyavāha adorns the sky.
Guru is the heart of Mātrī, the delight of the sixty-three Kulas.
Jvālinī is afflicted by the anus; the unmanifest is pierced by Dhūmra.
Sparśa is heated by Tapanī; the fifth is the auspicious heart. (173b)
The name of the Śākinīs, the Dūtīs, and the Kiṅkarīs is Suvrata;
Patralekhā is remembered as the performer of all rites for the Kulas.
Furthermore, Ādhūpita belongs to Dhūmrā, and likewise Śabdavyoma.
The Vidyā blazes in the center; O Dear One, the sixth is the Heart.
It belongs to the Cumbikās and Cūṣikās, to the Pūtanās along with the Guhyakas, to the Ucchuṣmās and Nakracūṣīs, and to those who live on breath and upward-spewing [substances].
O Goddess, the nose is slightly smoky and adorned with a veil that destroys darkness;
it is remembered as the common heart of all the bodies of the Yoginīs.
O Goddess of gods, Sadāśiva is the heart of the human Yoginīs.
Adorned with a garland of lotuses hanging from his left [hand],
he is the abode of wisdom, O Goddess; he whose body is radiant like a blooming lotus is remembered as the leader of all yoginīs, the possessor of all perfections.
The second, O Goddess, is partless (*niṣkala*), the leader of those who are partless.
Śiva is conjoined with Puruṣa; the Lord is the one who has been purified by the *snāpinī* [power].
Śiva resides within *kalā*, O Mistress of the Gods, adorned with a garland of flames.
He is the all-pervading leader of all the *mālās* and *śākinīs*.
Released from the *kalā-jvālā*, he is endowed with the dispelling of darkness.
He is remembered as the sovereign lord of all the *cakras* of the women of the earth (*kāśyapī*).
But the general *hṛdayas*, O Goddess, rich in asceticism, have been described; now hear the specific ones, O lady of good vows:
Vidyālaya, Śiva, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
The first is conjoined with Jvālinī; the other is endowed with a hundred rays.
These two, which dispel darkness during the transition through darkness, are known as the "Great Four" at the end of Bhairava’s blazing [mantra], performing all ritual actions.
On the other hand, the Śākinīs are in Sampredya, and likewise the Rudrāṇīs in Kausala;
they are all at crossroads, in Raktā, and in the abodes of heroes.
The seed-syllables of all ritual actions are those very ones in the vow of the Śākinīs.
Māyā, whose form is essence (rasa), with the upper and lower [syllables] pressed together,
struck by the destroyer of darkness (Tamo-ghna), and illuminated, constitutes the two Unmanīs beginning with Tāraka.
Endowed with the faces of knowledge, honored by the people of Kāśyapī,
O Goddess, you bring about the presence of those who move through the sky and the limbs of space.
This is the radiant fivefold power (pañcakala) of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
The supreme heart-mantra is accomplished; it sets in motion secret activities.
O Goddess of good vows, all those Yoginīs who are unnameable and those who are named remain under one's control like servants simply by being remembered.
When two men fall, blazing and inflamed with hatred, one should,
at the second step, employ the "smoky" (*dhūmrā*) and "cruel" (*krūra*) positions,
joined with Bhairava and the others.
This is established in the heart as the ritual procedure for the group of six beginning with Jaya;
indeed, when performed, even inconceivable deeds are accomplished through mere remembrance.
The letter ŪṢMĀ (Ṣ) is pierced by a digit (kalā), conjoined with TAPANI (R) and the bindu.
O Goddess, having placed the supreme Tārakā in the first step,
[one should place] Avyaktavidhi, Īśānā, who is situated within the tongue,
joined with the power (kalā) of Rudra, awakened by the lotus, and adorned.
Smiling, O Maheśānī, you bestow the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
These are the seed-syllables (bījas) of the six powers beginning with Jvālā, O one of great ascetic heat;
through the ritual of placement (nyāsa) and meditation, they are unfailing and possess formidable prowess.
The bearer of oblations, moving within the fire, possesses a hundred abodes;
Tejovatī, possessing a hundred abodes, is divided by the northern digit.
Mounted upon a man at the end of a palm tree, he performs the rites of Rudra and others; O fair-complexioned one, she who has attained perfection through yoga brings her presence.
First there was the weeping of the Mothers, accompanied by the fire.

Then Tejas was the third; he was the bearer of Time for the purpose of heating. He was endowed with a portion of the Unmanifest (avyakta), adorned with a hundred lights, and joined with the Puruṣa of the Mātrirodana garland.
The skin is conjoined with the heart; the supreme essence (rasottama) is mounted upon the digit (kalā).
Then, mounted upon the crest (śikhā), it is adorned by the garland of speech (vācāmālā).
This [essence] is to be given, residing within the enclosure of the digits (kalāsaṃpuṭa), situated in the state of "Cī."

O Goddess, this [mantra] in the heart, consisting of the mere space [syllables] with the bindu, performs all rites; it is radiant and free from the requirement of sacrificial vows. When conjoined with the Heart [mantra], it is a male [mantra]; when disjoined, it is female.
O Goddess of gods, having deposited the unmanifest, there follows the weeping of Mātrī.
Īśāna, heated by the Tāpanī [fire], performs the manifest rite again with scents.
[He worships] Bhairava of terrifying prowess, conjoined with the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*.
The heart is that of those who possess only skulls; it is the source of all ritual actions.
First, O Lord Sadāśiva, is the one adorned with a hundred abodes.
Then follows the fifth, and thereafter the sixth, which is the Earth accompanied by the atom of dust.
The second and the fourth should be performed as the weeping of Mātrī;
the third, O Goddess, is adorned by the fire (Havyavāha).
This is the secret heart of the Mātṛs, born from the Heart.
O Goddess, this is more secret than the secret; it must be guarded with great effort.
By means of this, O Mistress of the Gods, Nandīśa and the other leaders of the Siddhas, as well as Mahākāla, attained the state of Vīreśa among the Yogīs.
The mantra beginning with "carmamuṇḍā" followed by the word "kāpālini"—
one should extract that vidyā from its position, devoid of the seed-syllables.
Abiding in the station of Mahocchuṣma, he [subdues] the family of Caṇḍa and the others,
beginning with Tārā and ending with Dāna, including all those who bestow [blessings].
Then indeed comes Āmardaka, and thereafter Agnipiṅgalākṣa.

Mahākālī and Kālī, as well as other Bhūtamātṛs, all the lords of the cremation grounds, and the Siddhas and Vidyās— O auspicious one, O lady of virtuous vows, I shall now fully explain their common [mantras] to you.
The utterances of the seed-syllables of the heart, which abide according to the Kula tradition,
should be performed beginning with the Leader (Nāyaka) and ending with the seed-syllable of the Servant (Kiṅkara).
Through the differentiation of these mantras of the Mothers, all goals are accomplished.
Otherwise, for the family mantras, [the name] should be adorned with the sacred syllables (*pavitrapada*),
and at the end, it should be illuminated by the heart-seed-syllable (*hṛdbīja*) and differentiated by the name.
It should be differentiated by the three principles (*tritattva*), and the lord of the seed-syllables (*bījeśa*) should be illuminated at the end.
He who dwells in the lineage that has neither end nor middle, the Purifier, whose vehicle is the ram, the Lord,
the leader of all powers, the Yoginīs, and Mahodara;
he who is the burner, the scorcher, the sound, the resonance, the letter *Va*, adorned with the Bindu.
The nose is indeed unmanifest, and the hairs are inverted by their very nature.
Having given a blazing form, then the hands of the digits (*kalā*) in succession,
emitting smoke and enveloping [the body], the nose is endowed with the coloring [of the breath].
This is indeed the seed-syllable of Kiṅkarī, which bestows supreme accomplishment upon the great ones.
O you of restless heart, the Praṇava at the end of the Vidyā and those two syllables [OṂ and HRĪM] are the "Vīra" and "Kula-mantra" respectively; such is the utterance of the mantras.
Thus, in the Bhairava-stream, in the Seat of Knowledge (Vidyāpīṭha), in the Śiraccheda section of the Jayadrathayāmala Mahātantra, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work, in the third Ṣaṭka.
The Extraction of the General Heart-Mantra for the Circle of Yoginīs.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, you have spoken of that Tantra which is devoted to yoga and meditation."
Bound by the practice of restrictive observances, it is difficult for all embodied beings to accomplish.
The three gods possess little strength, being devoid of restrictive vows and observances.
Meditation and reflection have fallen away from them; indeed, it is difficult for those of small intelligence to maintain [the practice].
Devoid of the mantras of the Gaṇas, may they always be subject to the highest end. For their very benefit, you ought to speak with favor.
Previously, you have described for the benefit of all sentient beings the two-fold accomplishment of mantra, distinguished as gross and subtle:
the gross consists of the tantra and the mantra, while the subtle belongs to the Lord.
"O Lord, how can thoughts, which are by nature mobile, be established in the heart?
O Lord of Gods, even the path of mantra has been defiled by the Vināyakas with various kinds of cruel [obstacles], and the path of yoga is difficult to traverse."
Interspersed with portions of ritual action and its constituent parts, and joined with deities and guests,
these [mantras] are mounted upon the consciousness of those whose minds are fixed on the cosmic order (kalpa), in accordance with their specific knowledge.
Those mantras which, by mere recollection, set all ritual actions in motion.
"O Lord, tell those mantras for those engaged in the secret conduct.
Bhairava said:
"O fair-faced one, the wheel of knowledge (vidyācakra) belongs to the God of the Vidyālaya."

Out of affection for you, I shall tell you this which is endowed with the words of perfected mantras. O Goddess, this must not be revealed even in the slightest degree to those who mock the conduct, movements, and observances of the deities.
Success is quickly attained by them; thus it is revealed in the Tantra.
Indeed, for those who possess power within their home, their field, and their body, having understood this through diligent effort, they become destroyers of birth and death.
When one is endowed with the [proper] characteristics, then one should reveal this knowledge.

It must not be given even to one's own son who possesses the aforementioned faults; however, it should be given to one who is attentive, tranquil, devoted to the guru, and capable of bearing the burden.
Otherwise, it must never be given even if one were to sacrifice one's life.
[This concerns] the rites of the secret wheel, the arising of mantras, and their application.
Having become pure, listen now with a one-pointed mind.
One who has mastered the mantra should draw the previously described wheel and extract [the syllables].
Even though it is consumed by mercury, it is not scorched; it possesses a digit accompanied by fire.
The first syllable is joined with the second at that very time by the letter *dhūmra*;
at the end, it is conjoined with the radiant letter *ka* and its *kalā*, which bestows all accomplishments.
Sound (*śabda*) is mounted upon the *kalās*, while the nose is the end of the consonants (*sparśa*).
Furthermore, the verbal [form] consists of the sense organs, and those are adorned by the fire-carriers (the breaths).
This third step is indeed a transformation of form:
it is unmanifest, distinct from the purifier (fire), and endowed with the void and the digits of the void.
From Dhūmrārcis comes Kāla, and likewise Kalopa;
at the end is Havyavāha, and at the end is the Unmanifest (Avyakta), which bestows all accomplishments.
The fourth word is secret, the essence, worshipped by the people of Sāraṅga.
But in the fifth pada, O Goddess, Bhairava himself is stationed;
he bestows affection upon all the powers and is beneficial for the extraction of nectar.
Dhṛti, Tapani, Santānā, Dhūmrā, and that which is divided before the city.
The *dhūmrāpama* [mantra] is always situated at the end of the seventh [syllable].
It should be employed for the protection of living beings and for the satiation of those who are emaciated;
it is beneficial for the destruction of all the wicked and for the extraction of nectar (*amṛta*).
When this is being remembered, the Rākṣasas, Rakṣasas, and Guhyakas,
as well as obstacles of various forms, flee to the ten directions.
It is joined with the word "Vāc," followed by "adhaḥ," "pāvakī," "yuktā," "anantā," "kāma," and "asragāḥ."
And *sparśa* is joined with a digit (*kalā*), while *tapanī* is adorned at the feet;
from that comes *sphoṭa*, which is established in its own nature at the end of the skin and the two [channels] that cannot be led away.
The eighth step is declared to always bestow the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
It is beneficial for killing, paralyzing, and constant transference.
O Goddess of gods, O lady of excellent vows, at the beginning are the mudrās ending with the syllable *chiḥ*.
One should extract the infallible words of all the powers (*sarvaśakti*):
the ninth [syllable] of Sadāśiva, followed by two, then the end, and finally the end—these are the six syllables.
O Goddess, I have already previously declared this as the *viśeṣahṛdaya*.
By means of this [mudrā], one should perform all rites, whether they are achievable or unachievable.
For a mantra-practitioner who follows the prescribed ritual, these succeed through mere recollection. Thus have these powers, esteemed as secret, arisen.
I shall declare the measure of the mantra and its ritual application; listen to that.
O Goddess, the first power consists of three syllables and is situated on the eastern petal;
the second consists of four syllables and is located in the southeast.
Likewise, another six-syllable [mantra] is situated on the southern petal;
the fourth is exactly the same, though it resides on a different petal.
There is a two-syllable [mantra] in the western direction and a three-syllable [mantra] in the northwestern direction.
The four-syllable mantra, which is gentle, is located on the petal in the northeast direction;
the six-syllable mantra in the center has already been described by me.
The first [syllable] draws forth blood, while the second indeed draws forth fat.
The third is Mahāśakti; she is beneficial for the supreme pacification of passion (rajas).
The fourth is declared to be Majjahā, and the fifth is remembered as Snehadā. The sixth, Mahātapa, is the paralyzer of all living beings.
The seventh, however, is Mahāśakti, who is always beneficial for nourishment;
O beloved, the eighth causes the transformation of form.
And she alone, O lady of virtuous vows, performs all ritual actions.
Nevertheless, I have declared to you this commandment which is exceedingly difficult to attain:
one should perform the *moṅkāra-kaṇa* of the five [elements] at that very moment.
Having applied the second mudrā for the purposes of terrifying,
piercing, deluding, sealing, seizing the bound soul (paśu), and liberating it—
this third [mudrā], O Lord of Gods, is the sovereign that performs all rites.
O Maheśānī, he performs the drying up of oceans as well as the stopping of rivers;
likewise, by means of speech or even the mind, he effects the seizing of all living beings,
for he is a master of the accomplishment of actions according to his will.
O Great Lord, one should employ the first [mantra] through recitation and fire-oblation, and the second through the mind.
One should employ the fourth for the transformation of form and so forth;
those desiring liberation should employ the fifth, while the sixth is for cruel rites.
One should employ these mantras for the purpose of creating diversity, for delusion, for the falling of fruits,
and for burning and drying;
such is the application of place, of which I have spoken only by way of illustration.
But I shall explain the practice preceded by yoga above.
First is the placement of the wheels (*cakranyāsa*).
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the second [practice], which is exceedingly difficult to attain.

O fair-faced one, I shall declare to you the extraction (*uddhāra*) of the mantras of immeasurable power, which are joined with the wheels (*cakra*), the perfected syllables (*siddhapada*), and the powers (*śakti*). By the mere recollection of these, the people of the earth tremble.
The fiftieth [letter] and the twenty-fifth [letter], situated above the twenty-seventh;
the twenty-sixth, however, should be joined with the letter of fire (ra) below.
It has a lofty crest formed by the upper *nāda* and is adorned with the *bindu* at its peak.
This Bhairava has indeed been described as the leader of this wheel.
Accompanied by him, these Śaktis stationed within the wheel perform all rites, O lady of good vows, even those that are unfailing.
O Goddess, O lady of excellent vows, I shall now declare to you the extraction (*uddhāra*) of all the powers (*śaktis*) together with Vīreśa; listen to them in their proper order.
[The syllable] *ta* (the dispeller of darkness), followed by *pa*, surrounded by *ri*, then *kṣi*, *ta*, *ā*, *paḥ*, *krū*, and ending with *ra*.
(177b) In the center, Bhairava is blazing; he is the Lord of Heroes, the Leader of the Gaṇas.
O Goddess, at the outset one should establish Dhṛti, who is accompanied by Havyavāha.
Slightly smoky in color, they are adorned by Bhairava in the middle of the nose.
This is declared to be the first Śakti; Aindrī arises from the eastern group.
O Goddess, it is endowed with the aspect of the eye and adorned by the Praṇava (Om).
Vārāhī is designated as the power (śakti), ignited within the preceding power;
joined with fire and space, she is endowed with the skin that carries the radiance.
One should establish the remainder as before; this power is known as Māheśvarī.
The Guru is the burner (*tāpanī*) and the colorer (*rañjikā*), together with the *bindu*. O Goddess, the pervasive Haṃsa is indeed composed of fire and the carrier of speech (*vāhā*);
he is declared to be the Vaiṣṇavī Śakti, residing in the northern direction.
The intellect (mati) is blazing and radiant; it is situated below and endowed with a digit (kalā).
It is struck by the smoke-handed Puruṣa and adorned with the weeping of the Mātṛs. In the Bhairava [cakra], Kaumārī is to be known on the petal of fire.
O Goddess, Māyā is endowed with Kalā and united with the Śiva-tattva;
she is completely covered by Bindu and restrained by the syllables *huṃ phaṭ* at the end.
She is designated as the power Brahmāṇī, residing in the western direction.

O Goddess, the leader of the Śaktis, the Lord of the Gaṇas of Īśāna, should be performed [as the mantra]. The word differentiated by the letter *i*, further differentiated by the bindu and nāda, has the form of the nose as it is declared, O Goddess; its form is blazing, O Beloved.
Kalā, Hasta, Samūsrā, Savisarga, Caṣaṭ, and Paṭa—
these are declared to be the Bhairavī Śaktis residing in the southwestern direction (Nairṛtī).
O fair-faced one, the host of spirits has been raised to eminence by these friends.
This supreme group of four consists of the letter with the bindu, joined with the fire-letter (ra), adorned with the bindu;
it should be known as the seventh group of the dūtīs.
The *ka*-group is the group of elements (*bhūta-varga*); the subtle [elements] are in the second;

the sense organs (*indriya*) are in the third; and the objects of the senses (*indriya-gocara*) are in the fourth. Furthermore, the mind (*manas*), ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the person (*puruṣa*) [are in the fifth].
O fair-faced one, the five principles (pañcatattva) have been described in the fifth [chapter].
Thus, O Goddess, the group of Śaktis rests upon the second wheel.
I shall now explain their application in due order.
O lady of excellent complexion, various rites such as *jaya* and others become successful for practitioners seeking fruits,
provided they perform the appropriate yoga while reciting [the mantra] with great power.
The Aindrī [mudrā] brings about nourishment, health, and supreme strength; furthermore,
it grants victory in battles, the immobilization of enemy armies,
the power of traveling through the sky, and the transformation of one's physical form.
For one reciting the Kaumārī mantra, her splendor indeed increases;
he becomes possessed of great speed, great heroism, and great strength and prowess. He is likewise invincible, incapable of being slain, and of immeasurable power.
She crushes the enemy armies and can indeed cause even the gods to fall.
For one who recites the Vārāhī mantra, the fulfillment of all desires arises.
By her word she slays instantly, and by her word she brings the dead back to life.
By means of speech one may attract trees; by means of speech one may paralyze an animal.
By muttering [the mantra] upon marrow or a collection of bones, one may mentally attract a vow.
One who mutters the Bhairavī [mantra] shall attain all ritual accomplishments.
Having mounted his chariot, he goes there to the tree beloved by its leaves;
having traveled a hundred yojanas, he returns swiftly,
invisible to all beings and invulnerable to Daityas and Dānavas.
When recited, Brahmāṇī brings about the mastery of speech and,
through her grace, generates the eightfold supernatural powers (aṣṭaguṇaiśvarya) for the practitioner. (178b)
The Vaiṣṇavī [mudrā] performs whatever action is intended by the mind: the illusions of a great magician’s trickery, the immobilization of armies,
the destruction of enemies, and even the extraction of blood.
She performs invisibility and the transformation of form.
When recited even as a play, the Great Goddess, the Great Power,
brings the three worlds under her control or destroys the enemies.
The practitioner may cause the best of mountains to fall, and he may even solidify the oceans;
having flown up himself, he may go where he is unseen.
He may cause a great rain to fall, and he may also ward off that which is falling.
She performs great conduct and restrains that which has been set in motion;
she herself makes all actions terrible.
O highly fortunate one, the group of nine is not [bound] by action according to the prescribed rite.
The second wheel has been described; now hear the third.
In the center is the *rasa* (taste) mounted upon *māyā*, and *gandha* (smell) is within it, followed by *jvālinī*.
O Goddess, the first is *vācādi* (the beginning of speech), and the second is the station of *karālī*.
The first power has been described as being in the third wheel, O Goddess;
it is conjoined with Anantajvālinī, and the digits (kalās) ending with Māyā are illumined by it.
But those beginning with Bhairava, O Mistress of the Gods, are remembered as the second Yoginī.
Endowed with the seventh digit (kalā), adorned with a clearly manifest vulva,
and joined with the face of Niyati, she is the third, most excellent Śakti.
O Goddess of the Gods, her feet are like water, and she is adorned with a hundred abodes.
In the middle is the smoke-colored [letter] at the end; after that is the touch (sparśa).
The fourth power is declared to be Amoghā, of terrible prowess.
O Goddess of all gods, the fifth bestows happiness upon all beings.
The fire-carriers are joined together, bestowing the state of Ugreśa;
having first established the seed-syllable *re*, they are thoroughly ignited by the *tāpanī*.
Buddhi, endowed with its parts (kalās), stands in the middle; by her they are adorned. The sixth is declared to be Śakti, the accomplisher of fierce deeds.
Niyati and Kālā stand at the end, endowed with the quality of rajas.
O fair-faced one, the sixth is indeed the *rañjitā* and the *ṣaṭpada*;
the seventh power is declared to be the bestower of invisibility.
At the beginning, [the deity] is mounted upon the *śabdakalā*, and the Vidyā exists in its own essential form.
Sadāśiva, the devotee of Speech, resides within the *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* in the center.
Joined with the seventh vowel, it is proclaimed as the eighth [syllable].
O Goddess of the Gods, having understood the ninth, she is the Mistress in the center of the wheel.
One should extract all mantras beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) at their beginning and end.
Now hear the application of the powers (*śakti*) of this wheel:
the goddess whose name is *Viccā* is indeed beneficial for attraction.
Whether it be a woman or a man, she quickly draws in wine, meat, and blood; she is the activator of all rites.
She is indeed for the sealing of mudrās, as well as for deluding and paralyzing.
Joined with the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*, she is remembered as the performer of all rites.
Just as that Goddess who dwells within the body of Kāmāri [is present] in every movement,
one should take secret yellow pigment (*rocanā*) smeared with blood and mixed with realgar (*śilā*).
Having thus anointed oneself from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head,
one becomes invisible, O Goddess, and is freed from all dualities;
[one remains unharmed] amidst fire, weapons, water, serpents, thieves, kings, and their retinues.
