No fear arises for him, and he is victorious in all debates.
As for the goddess named Mārayā, who dwells within the body of Vārāhī—
whether from a good path, a village, or even from very far away from a city.
Having learned whether there is news from heaven or the underworld,
one should recite mantras over flowers and cast them at the city gate.
Among those who are Śākinīs there, whatever they may do,
there is the lore named Varadā, which effects the immobilization of water and fire;
Gominī [grants] a form made of cow-dung and the power of traveling through the sky.
Having recited the mantra over yellow pigment (rocanā) a hundred times and meditated upon Śiva while facing the north,
one who applies a tilaka mark goes at that very moment through the sky.
And as for the goddess who dwells within all beings, she is Aindrī, residing in the body.
This most powerful Vaiṣṇavī goddess, when employed at the root of a *śapastambha* and constantly applied to the binding of the mouth,
shall quickly draw forth the blood of the unfortunate, provided one is endowed with the meditation on Śiva.

The goddess Mayādevī, Cāmuṇḍā, who possesses great power, when sealed, shall perform the summoning of those who are protected according to one's desire. The syllable *Sroṃ* shall effect the summoning of even the five [elements] at that very moment.
Likewise, there is transference, as well as the state of being visible at will and the accomplishment of fruits.
The goddess of this wheel, who performs all actions, is called Amoghā; she is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the Yoginī, and the bestower of the perfection of yoga.

The Third Wheel. Thus, in the Bhairava Stream, in the Seat of Knowledge (Vidyāpīṭha), in the Śiraccheda, in the Jayadrathayāmala Mahātantra, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work, in the third hexad, in the Yoginīsaṃcāra, [this concludes] the section titled "The Extraction of the Three Wheels."
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the mandala of the accomplishment of mantras,
by which practitioners here attain the eightfold sovereign powers (aṣṭaguṇamaiśvarya). Having gone to the region of the cremation ground, how is the seizing of the field (kṣetra) performed?
First, being composed, one should purify the drink by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma),
either with the mantra of Bhairava or with that of the hexagon.
Having meditated upon Bhairava as one's own body, one should perform the binding of the directions (*diśābandha*) with the net of weapons of the five elements and the weapon of Śaṅkara, O ascetic;
or with the Bhairava-weapon against the cruel ones, or with the heart-mantra of Nārīśa.

One should first purify the hands; one should not [purify] the hearts of the Mothers at the outset. One should place [the fingers] starting from the left hand's index finger down to the little finger;
the right hand should be exactly the same. Thus, there are five [on each], making eight [fingers] in total, each separately.
One should place those beginning with Aindra on the left and those beginning with Vāruṇa on the right.
By that same sequential method, one should place the six [syllables] on the two thumbs;
then, O Goddess of the Gods, one should arrange them upon the joints of the body.
One should arrange the twenty-five principles within the body.
First, one should place the five gross elements, beginning with earth, in the feet;
the five subtle elements in the two calves; and the sense organs in the two thighs.
Then, within the body that is to be grasped, one should again duly place the organs of action;
likewise the mind, intellect, ego, the unmanifest, and the Puruṣa.
Having thus performed the placement according to the rule, one should then place the group of Śaktis.
The first [touch] is from the knees to the feet; the second is from the knees to the hips; the third is at the secret organ; and the fourth is at the navel-circle.
[This is done] with the left and right sides, using the right hand on the left side.
The fifth [syllable] should be placed at the end of the knees, and the sixth above that;
the seventh from the navel upward, and the eighth at the heart one should place.
O Goddess, having formed the heart-wheel with the left hand, one should place the six seed-syllables.
Above that, however, is its very same placement; this bestows the perfection of yoga.
Then, the entire body is the mass of the syllables of Bhairava.
Above that, one should apply the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) according to their respective locations.
Having thus installed Bhairava, the Lord of Beings, whose form consists of the seed-syllables,
one should then, O Goddess, install the groups of Mothers situated within the mandala.
One should place the third [syllable] at the navel-cakra and the second at the heart.
Having first placed the *prasāda*, one should then fashion the faces;
in the fourfold sequence, one should fashion that northern face.
One should place the messenger-deities (dūtīs) upon the branches; then one should place the goddesses of the sciences (vidyās).
One should place the five kalās situated in the region of the wheel beginning with Tāra.
From the center of the wheel, it is surrounded by six syllables that dispel darkness.
One should join the vowels *ai*, *e*, *au*, and *o* with those beginning with *vāruṇa* (the letter *va*).
Having thus assigned the faces and meditated upon the Mother Bhairavī in her form,
one should then draw the excellent mandala using fierce ashes.
O Goddess, having first corded it with a rope made from the hair of a corpse’s head,
one should draw three lines using colors such as white and red;
[the mandala] shall have one cubit [in size], four gates, and be adorned with a lotus in its center.
There should be an auspicious eight-petaled lotus adorned with a pericarp (*karṇikā*).
Therein, the pericarp should be fashioned, decorated with six petals.
Having thus prepared this excellent mandala, one should then perform the worship.
First, one should place the principles (tattvas) on all six petals according to the previously mentioned division and through the proper application of the southern tradition.
O Goddess of gods, the group of elements (bhūtavarga), however, is the fourth, distinguished by the variations of the vowels.
One should join [the elements] to those located in the northwest, southeast, southwest, and northeast.
One should place the pentad of gross elements (bhūta-pañcaka) in the vessels starting from the east and southeast;
one should deposit the five subtle elements (sūkṣma-pañcaka) in the vessels of the south and southwest.
In the western vessel, one should place the five sense organs (buddhīndriyas) belonging to Varuṇa and Vāyu;

likewise, in the northern and northeastern vessels, one should place the organs of action (karmendriyas). Furthermore, one should place the mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), the unmanifest (avyakta), and the person (puruṣa).
One should place these very five principles upon the pericarp;
here, on the petals in the northeast, southeast, southwest, northwest, and so forth.

Then, one should place the four neuter [syllables] within oneself; all of them should be joined in due order upon the petals beginning with the eastern one (apūrva). Starting from the eastern petal and so forth, they should be applied in sequence according to their established position.
O Goddess, one should place the channels (nāḍīs) in pairs, situated in a joined enclosure (saṃpuṭa).
Having placed them, the practitioner of mantra should worship them according to their positions in the previous wheel,
starting from the eastern petal up to the petal in the northeast direction.
O Goddess, in the center of the six-syllable mantra, one should place Bhairava in its middle.
There, the wise one should arrange the previously mentioned syllables of the words;
he should make it complete with the faces and limbs, situated upon the yoga-pīṭha.
O Goddess, one should place the Mothers at the end;
Aindrī should be joined in the eastern petal, Vārāhī in the south,
Māheśī in the western petal, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī in the north.

One should install Kaumārī in the southeast, Bhairavī on the southwestern petal, Brahmāṇī in the northwest, and Vāyavī in the northeast; one should place the Leader (Nāyaka) in the northeast. Then, in the third enclosure, one should install the Kālamātṛs.

Just as one would slay, O Goddess, [the guardians] from the human direction to the netherworld in due order, so too one should place four [deities] upon the petals starting from the east and ending at the southwest (nairṛta).
O Goddess who grants boons, you are praised; O unfortunate one, you are the source of happiness!
One should place the words in reverse order upon the petals in the directions of Varuṇa and Īśāna.
Having thus placed the three wheels, one should then place the Lord of Beings (Bhūtapati) in the intermediate and cardinal directions, O Lord of Gods, according to the sequence of the name-mantras.
Nandikaṇḍa, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgirīṭī, Haravyaya, Āmardaka, Agni, and then Piṅgalākṣa; furthermore,
Mahākālī is to be known as the eighth among the Bhūtas and Mātṛs.
Having likewise performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the world-protectors, Indra and the others, and their mantras elsewhere,
one should then arrange the worship after having completed the entire placement in this manner.
One should perform the entire ritual procedure for worship using one's own mantras alone,
with perfumes, flowers, incense, and well-prepared offerings,
as well as various kinds of fish and meat, and honey, rum, wine, and spirits.

One should display the Bhairavī-mudrā, characterized by the *lālikā* formed with the syllable *haṃ*. Having pressed the little finger of the left hand with the thumb, the other three fingers should be extended; this is the mudrā honored by yogins.
One should worship daily with this [mantra] and cause perfumes and other offerings to be presented.
Indeed, one should perform all ritual actions with this alone.
Perform everything, O Lord of Gods; for through this, the siddhis previously mentioned are attained.
One should cause the *argha*, *ācamanīya*, and other offerings to be presented with the great conch.
With his body adorned by the *mātrās* and surrounded by the *Śaktis*,
he is constantly worshipped as the yellow-clad one (*pītāmbara*), purified by the vow of sixty-three [days].

Having thus worshipped according to the ritual procedure, the wise practitioner should then accomplish the rite; he should attract that which arises from the great sacrificial animal (mahāpaśu). O Goddess, having taken the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) according to the sequence of the Kula tradition, he should proceed.
Having prepared a well-consecrated *caru* that bestows great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*),
one should then, after having accomplished it, offer it to the deities.
If one has gone to the sacrificial ground (*yāgabhūmi*), one should then cast the *bali* offering there.

The hero should offer the *bali* oblation, accompanied by liquor and meat, in due order to the *lāmās*, the *cuṃbikās*, the *cūṣikā*, and likewise the *pūtanās*, as well as to the *bhūtas*, all conjoined with the great nectar (*mahāmṛta*).

One should prepare incense and lamps with great oil and great meat. Or, while reciting the mantra, the *kaṭakaṭas* bring about their presence. Having worshipped according to the rules and subsequently offered the *arghya*, one should remain composed.
Standing facing north, he should then request permission;
thereafter, being composed, he should recite his own mantra or one belonging to his family lineage.

One should pass the night with dance, song, and instrumental music, as well as with laughter, joy, and weeping; and by means of recitation, worship, fire-rituals, and meditation. Afterwards, O beloved, one should offer oneself to the God for his benefit.

O Goddess, one should worship Śakti with the *kalaputraka* mantras established upon the *kavarga*; thereafter, one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*) within one's own body by means of inhalation (*pūraka*),
and the invocation (*āvāhana*) from one's own body by means of exhalation (*recaka*).
Mounted upon the three wheels of the six cakras, that messenger has attained union.
He who is a hero among heroes, adorned with the great enjoyment and the mudrās of the Krama, attains the perfection of the Yoginī; thus one should proceed by means of the two Kālikās.

"I am the one authorized for his yoga, and I alone am the bestower of its fruit. Thus ends the fifth chapter, "The Siddha-Yoga," within the *Yoginī-saṃcāra*, the third hexad of the *Jayadratha-yāmala*, a great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the *Śiraścheda* division of the *Vidyā-pīṭha* in the *Bhairava-srotas*.
The Goddess said:
"O God, those varieties previously mentioned by you which arise from the seven families—
namely Pūṣanā, Cuṃbikā, and likewise others among the Mūṣikās— "
The Lāmās, the Śākinīs, the Yoginīs, and likewise the Mothers—
their respective divisions and characteristics have been declared to me. These others, numbering seventy-eight, are those who wander through various births.
O Lord of Gods, they too are not unproclaimed, even if [described] merely by name.
Rūpikā, Piṅgalā, Bhīmā, Aparāvṛttā, Bālikā, Ativṛttā, Hṛdvedhinī, and Kālikā have attained perfection.
The lord of gods said: "In that [state], there is yogic perfection (*siddhi*) born from the fettered beings (*paśu*).
What kind of perfection is Kālikā’s, by which those [others] become perfected?
Bhairava replied:
Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret which has not been told to anyone by me;
it is the sixfold secret of the Yoga Tantra that bestows accomplishment.

The ritual procedure for one who has been initiated, consecrated, and authorized— which is unexamined by Śakra and esteemed by the people of Kāśyapī— is as follows: having duly honored the Guru who has undertaken the Śākinī vow.
One who is endowed with that tradition and knows the mantras should perform the placement (nyāsa). Practice is said to be of two kinds: the yogic and the ritual (kalaka).
The yogic [practice] consists of five yogas; the attainment of the sequence is indeed yogic.

The practitioner of yoga, having consecrated the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), should accomplish it. Likewise, from the "living" (jīva) caru or other [types], success arises; it is not otherwise. Furthermore, effort is said to be of two kinds: that which is scriptural and that which is based on practice.
The study of the scriptures is generally for the sake of practice, and one practices again through repeated application.
Time is said to be of three kinds: constant (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and specific (kāmya).
Constant [time] bestows fruit upon one who is ever-yoked and has ascended to yogic perfection.

Likewise, there is the Kāmikī accomplishment, which is inferior, middling, and superior. O Dear One, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, it is said to be inferior or middling; however, during the northern solstice, it is declared to be superior—now listen.

O observer of excellent vows, on the fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika, those who have not yet attained success are proclaimed to be honored with the highest qualities at the time of sacrifice. Through three or four recitations of the sound, accomplishment arises here.
The power to attract blood from others arises after one year;
however, O Lord of Gods, for the five nectars (*amṛta*),
minor accomplishments (*kṣudrasiddhi*) arise respectively after six months or even a year.
O Goddess, with twelve syllables, one who has undertaken the vow of the Śākinī, being intent on the Abhikālikī [mantra], should address the Jīva residing within the sacrificial oblation. (183a)
O Goddess of the Gods, one who has completely abandoned the mass of greed and is free from attachment and aversion quickly attains the secondary supernatural powers (siddhis).
One should not practice any ritual action, such as the primary life-force or the breath, without first [attaining this].
Then, due to a lack of excellence, obstacles indeed arise in the city of Adyar. Consequently, those Śākinīs who perform rites there create hindrances everywhere and proclaim their own deficiencies.
They constantly bestow the oral tradition upon one who is devoted to the guru;
otherwise, a violation of their covenant occurs for them.
O lady of excellent vows, for twelve years the mantra-practice does not reach fruition.
For one who has cast off doubt, mantras become effective through service at the feet of the Guru,
O Goddess of Gods, and ritual action proceeds therein.
Even one who lacks vows and is devoid of purity succeeds if he serves the feet of the Guru.
Constantly devoted to Śiva and a protector of the *samayas*,
having accomplished these rites, one shall obtain the great *caru*.
Thus indeed, O sinless one, has the accomplishment pertaining to Kālī been described by me.
Or even the Yoginī, O Mistress of the Gods—what else shall I tell you?
This is the supreme secret, O Goddess, which must be guarded with great effort.
It has not been disclosed to anyone here, due to the specific faults observed [in others].

O Goddess of the Gods, this should be given correctly to one who is devoted to the Guru and has been thoroughly tested; it must also be guarded with great effort by the practitioner. In this way, accomplishment proceeds; otherwise, there is danger to one's life.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, the *Kulajā* is known as the supreme accomplishment for attracting women;
the *Ugreśā* consists primarily of movement; and the *Yogikī* bestows knowledge."
But as for other rites, how do they become defiled?
It is through the greatness of the form, as well as its various modalities:
namely, paralyzing, bewildering, killing, and likewise withering.
The immobilization of fire, weapons, and water; the practice of the five arrows;
the thorough knowledge of time; and the entry into another's body.
A doubt has arisen in me: which of the two types of accomplishment does he rely upon? O Lord of Gods, therefore [tell me] the practice that brings about accomplishment for the Master.
Bhairava said:

Knowledge, action, and likewise meditation are declared to be the three aggregates (*skandha*). Within the Bhairava system, however, which possesses many aggregates, these three aggregates are perfectly pure.
The first is the creation consisting of mantra, which is the defining characteristic of the Yoginīs.

The gradual preservation of the conduct and activities of the observance (samaya) is to be known as the "aggregate of knowledge" (jñānaskandha), which involves the acceptance of the arising of inquiry. The application of various powers with diverse intentions is the "aggregate of action" (kriyāskandha).
In the sacrifice, there is the conceptualization of protection and the elaborate worship of the *arghya* with power;

in meditation (*dhyāna*), however, there is the knowledge of the conjunction of the channels (*nāḍī*) and seed-syllables (*bīja*). Furthermore, there are meditations on light, conceptualizations, and likewise the rules concerning the postures (*āsana*).
These three sections concerning the welfare of others have been proclaimed by the gods.
O Goddess of the Gods, having understood this, one shall quickly attain success.
I shall now explain these three sections, which possess various forms and bring great prosperity.
Merely by attracting the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), the fruit of all actions shall be attained;
for in this [system], the accomplishment of action is preceded by the attraction of mercury. Furthermore, the satiation of the deities is for the sake of the successful fulfillment of that action.
Therefore, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the application of the nectar.
First, O Mistress of the Gods, one should install the entire form of Bhairava,
endowed with the three fierce wheels, which bestows all accomplishments.
Having diligently sacrificed the animal, one should then commence the ritual action.
Having consecrated a triple-knotted wooden stick, a clod of earth,
and even the hand with nine mantra-words, it is correctly said that [the animal] has been properly bound behind the back.
Then, O illustrious one, why did he not take water as his refuge today?
[He knows] the various secret deeds and the secret powers [of the gods].
The arising of the wheel of channels follows the arising of the solar wheel.
The arising within the channels occurs sequentially for two and a half *ghaṭikās*.
A *ghaṭikā* consists of three hundred and sixty breaths (*prāṇas*).
That should be known as the Kālacakra, difficult to attain for those of left-handed practice.
One should visualize it in the center of the petals and arrange it like a sacrificial offering upon kusa grass.
There, in the center of the lotus, one should place the twenty-five [deities].

One should place the intellect (*manas*), the mind (*buddhi*), and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) below that; above that, one should likewise place the god Bhairava with his limbs (*sāṅga*). Then, one should fashion the eight petals in order, starting from the east.
Divided according to the channels of reality through the application of the sequence previously described,
one should first perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), Earth, and Water within the initial mantra.
O Goddess, in the center of that, one should place that which is established at the end of the syllable *huṃ*.
The Bhairava [seed-syllable],
joined with the letter *jña* and illuminated by the *bindu* attached below the back [the letter *m*],
should be used; having performed the *kumbhaka*, one should then effect the binding of the directions.

In the second [rite] as well, it should be done in this very same way; having performed the breath-retention according to the rule, one should first strike the vessel and then commence the ritual action. Having meditated on the object of attainment (sādhya) in front and the Vidyā upon the head, the practitioner [should proceed].
Then, by means of the *phaṭ*-syllable in the state of retention (*guṇi*), one should join it with the *soṃ*-syllable.
One should draw in the black [wind] in the form of a void, like nectar from the mouth. It is taught that one should draw in the *soṃ*-syllable by means of a red inhalation (*pūraka*).

Having reflected upon the words regarding the vessel, the one of great power becomes wind; joined to the upper channels, he brings [the object] by means of the yoga of breath. O God, having filled his mouth, he should then gaze at the vessel.
By this very procedure, the wise one should perform the summoning of even the five [elements] at that moment through the application of the activity of his own channel;
or he should cause them to fall into the vessel, or press them with the mudrā.
Having pressed down with the thumb of the left hand upon the middle finger,
the remaining fingers should likewise be bent; this mudrā is beneficial for pressing.

Through *anaya* one should afflict everything, or kill [the enemy] when endowed with *aruṣa*. Having performed *kuṃbhaka*, O Goddess of the Gods, one makes the target [subject] at the head like a trembling reed, or even causes blood to vomit.
For a moment, by means of the application of speech, he consoles her again.
If there is a corruption, however, one should cast [the remedy] upon it through the grace of the eight measures;
one should employ the supreme [mantras] that bestow nectar, which cause joy and are free from affliction.
Having understood this, O Goddess of the Gods, one should accomplish the ritual action according to one's desire.
By the power of this very [mantra], the rites are performed; listen, O lady of excellent vows, to the mantra.
One should write the name of the person to be acted upon in red ink together with *rocanā*.
One should place the hands and fingers of the Goddess, together with Bhairava,
beginning with all the Śaktis, within the hollow of the palms. Then, by means of recitation (*jāpa*), one should [worship] one's own wheel (*cakra*) one hundred and eight times.
Through this action, one’s connection goes to destruction at that very moment;
one who is capable, when released by the pacified and burnt [element], certainly dies.
When the soul, joined with Indra, reaches the end of the letter *ka*, it departs.
Then, O Goddess of Rites, O sinless one, even those rites not explicitly mentioned for practitioners will be accomplished. On the second day, I shall explain them to you:
one should place fire, wind, and space in the southeastern petal of the diagram.
In the second [state], she is situated between the knees, awakened by the seventh [vowel];
struck on the crown by the twenty-second [consonant], she is established within the center of the channels.
One should quickly draw forth the metal, awakened by its own seed-syllable.
Accompanied by the recitation of mantras and joined with all the yogas for the sake of the sacrificial animals,
one should take a stake made of khadira wood measuring twelve finger-breadths;
having consecrated it with its own mantra, one should cause the ground to be dug with it.
Having collected buffalo urine, the wise one should stir it with that [substance] and cast it in,
while mentally reciting the name of the person to be accomplished one hundred times. (185a)
Then, he will certainly see the shadow of that animal situated there;
at night, while reciting the vidyā, he should cut that shadow with a sharp weapon.
Thereupon, that person to be subdued (sādhya) falls down wherever he may be stationed.

The wise practitioner should have an image made on birch bark using red sandalwood powder mixed with his own blood, marked with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). On the second mantra, he should write the power (*śakti*) in the form of syllables.
There, having applied the bile of a cow upon that [substance], one should cause it to tremble;
having placed it in a pit and kindled a fire of *khadira* wood,
blowing upon it, the person to be acted upon is burned, rendered unconscious, and is even deprived of life.
And she [is used] with water mixed with milk for rites of pacification (*śāntika*). Now listen as I proclaim the third [nāḍī], which performs the work of power (*śaktikarman*):
it is the channel carrying the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the channel carrying the essence (*rasa*), and the eye, respectively.
One should place [the letter] situated upon the syllable *ukāra* on the southern petal;
it is constricted at the beginning and end by the syllable *oṃ*, awakened by the letter *ka*,
struck with the seven measures (*mātrā*), and filled by that very same [sound].
One should place there the deity residing in the twenty-five elements.
By means of the application of the eastern channel, one should instantly draw out the skin;
having pressed it, one should dry it, and when it has burst open, it perishes.

Having prepared a mark (tilaka) on the forehead, the heart, the throat, as well as the two arms, the two sides, the two thighs, the two knees, and the joints of the two ankles— using yellow pigment (rocanā) mixed with ashes and red ochre, consecrated with the seven purifications (saptasaṃskṛta).
Having placed Bhairava upon his body, he should then place the deity of the city.
Having done this, he should emerge from the city onto the ground;
there he beholds the deities, and having seen them, they converse with him.
They grant him success, and he becomes equal to Kāśyapa.
Now hear about the fourth [mudrā], Amoghā, which accomplishes all powers and actions.
One should place the ear, the skin, and the two feet upon the petal of the direction of Nairṛta (the southwest).
Then, having placed the channel (nāḍī), one should place the sixth deity with the fourth [vowel],
ending with the syllable *phaṭ* as previously mentioned.

Having opened the openings of the channels (*nāḍī*) by that very [method], one should fill them. By [the breath] passing through the mouth, one produces the pain of cholera; by [the breath] being obstructed, one becomes mute and blind.
Having crossed the hands, the churning of the channels is performed with the seed-syllables.
One should place the deity [of the hands] on the two hands;
the anus and the generative organ belong to Varuṇa and should be placed on the petals of the directions.
There, the fifth deity is seated upon the throne of the vowel *ai*.
The knower of yoga, having drawn in the vital breath with the internal seed-syllable, should fill it;
then, having exhaled himself, he should fill his mouth with the syllable *ha*.
By the prior recollection of the mantra, this is the supreme means for attracting the blood.
Then, having been liberated by the *anuloma* [mantras], one should accomplish the rite for piercing the pain.
Having written the name with the mantra, one should then obtain it by means of the *śaktis*.
One should cause it to flow away into a great river; this is the supreme procedure for eradication (*uccāṭana*).
One should place speech, the sense organ, supreme fragrance, and taste, along with the subtle elements.
In the northwestern direction, upon the path of the channels (*nāḍīmārga*), one should place *raudrī* together with *kala*.
Therein, one should place the sixth deity, who is established between the syllables *phaṭ* and others.
Having filled [the breath] with the *kumbha* [vessel], the excellent practitioner, while muttering [the mantra], should exhale again; thus he makes everything invisible.
One whose self is joined with time (*kāla*) should again draw in [the breath] through the *jānta*.
A pain in the heart shall arise for him; your life will be at great risk.
Having touched the tree-cart, the practitioner should mount it there, having placed the previously described wheel surrounded by the Śaktis.
One should recite the six-syllable deity-mantra; then one will certainly fly up.
Having gone to the desired place, one returns again in an instant.
The knowledge known as "Vāyava" is illuminated by the mantra beginning with *sa oṃ*.
If one desires to go [to a certain place], one should cause oneself to be seized by that [mantra];
having brought forth and drawn toward oneself the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
One should place form, touch, and sound in the subtle [elements] from the northward.

Then, having given the letter *e*, the wise one should place the seventh [element]. By means of the application of the eastern channel, he should establish the internal channel within the resonance (*nāda*).
One should recite and fill [the breath], illuminating it with the syllable *Oṃ* at the beginning and end;
by quickly casting the five nectars (*amṛta*), one swiftly attracts the target. Having performed the *kuṃbhaka* (retention), one should fill [the vessel] with one's own mantra.
It renders the practitioner mute, or it swiftly carries him away.
One should place the mind, intellect, and ego on the eighth petal;
one should place the eighth deity, constrained by the letters beginning with *U* and ending with [the final letter], at the end.
O Goddess of the Gods, having opened the channel, one should fill it with the wind-mantra;
this instantly produces the pain of cholera in the victim within a moment.
Indeed, the Lord performs all these sixfold actions.
The mind, intellect, ego, and the unmanifest are fully honored.
O God, stationed in the center of the wheel, you blaze forth with faces turned toward all the channels (nāḍīs). Whichever channel the Lord enters and traverses, he becomes awakened therein.
For that very person, the Lord, the Sovereign, performs actions;
O God, He should deposit and restrain them for the purification of dharma and adharma.
O Amogha-devī, this is the secret rite worshipped by the Yoginīs.
I shall tell you that which was declared to Yantaka with affection:
having meditated upon the Great Wheel (mahācakra) within the heart, white and adorned with a pericarp (karṇikā),
the Lord (Īśa) resides in the pericarp, presiding over it.
The principle of *kalā* should be known as difficult to attain for those of sinful karma;
one should assign the twenty-four principles and so forth to the petals.

O Goddess, O lady of excellent vows, one should arrange the nine thousand channels on each petal of the Āṇḍa [cakra] in their proper order by means of the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*;
indeed, one should fashion each individual *cakra* by means of three thousand [channels] each.
Having thus established the Unmanifest and so forth, there is a channel (nāḍikā) in each wheel (cakra).
Indeed, when a wheel accompanied by the seed-syllable of the Void (śūnyabīja) is set in motion,
that channel in his heart always accomplishes the ritual action.
The ninth seed-syllable of the three groups of six is situated above the mobile seed-syllable;
by means of the channel and through the sequential yoga, it accomplishes all rites.
It abides in the wheel throughout the past, the present, and the future.

Wherever the self moves within the body, impelled by the power of the mind, there one should know the emergence of the powers in all actions. That which is past is known when [the self] resides in the navel; that which is present is known when it is situated in the heart.
The Lord of Yogins, stationed within the corners of the eyes, perceives everything from all sides.
By this sequential yoga, there are twenty-four channels;
through the differentiation of the channels and sub-channels, he is established in a thousandfold arising.
O fair-faced one, those very seventy-two thousand [channels] are indeed provided with three seed-syllables of action and endowed with the three channels,
by means of which the yoginīs who follow the path of yoga perform their activity.
O observer of good vows, when twelve and eleven [breaths] meet through the seed-syllable of mobility (*calabīja*),
all the channels at the mouth of the *ghaṭṭana* channel proceed along the path of the *udāna*.
O ascetic, having meditated upon the channel of the wind mounted on the peak in the northeast, [one attains success].
Then, O Goddess of gods, he flies up and goes wherever he desires.
When the practitioner of mantra stands in the past [sound] while the vowel is situated in the future, his self becomes opposed to all the channels; then he shall enter the body of another.
When one who possesses desire becomes intent upon his wish, he indeed unifies the future sound within the body of another with the past sound within himself.
Sixty breath-moments (prāṇakalās) are said to constitute one day and night.
In that regard, O Goddess, there is increase and decrease; from that [process] comes the destruction of all things.
Rising is the dawn, increase is midday, and then there is decline, followed by increase and then decline again.
One should perform acts of increase during a period of decline, but during an increase, one should resort to acts of decline.
During both decline and increase, however, one should perform neutral actions.
O Goddess, having understood the mutual relationship between friends and enemies, [one should act accordingly].

And when there is mutual contradiction, one should perform the ritual as desired. O Goddess of gods, those whose karma is exhausted are established in the *ārmaṇya* arts; they are common and reside in the common state.
For one whose [vitality] is diminished, a remedial rite should be performed; for those who are living and well-nourished, it is common.
O Goddess, having repeatedly drawn [the breath], one should satisfy [the deity].
Thus, having understood both of these as well as the movement of the channels (nāḍī).
O Lord of Gods, one should perform the rites with the powers (śaktis) that have attained the path of perfection.
[The mantra] should be employed for sealing through placement (nyāsa) by means of the yoga of breath-retention (kuṃbhaka).
And it should be applied to the channels (nāḍīs), becoming present through breath-retention alone.

In the case of *unmudraṇa*, it should be employed with *recaka* (exhalation); for producing variety in the heart, and likewise for the practice of the postures (*āsana*) and the piercing (*bhedana*), it should be joined with the vital air (*vāyu*).
Its specific application in the process of utterance (*uccāraṇa*) is to be learned from the mouth of the Guru.
By means of that, the placement of the clod of earth occurs through the conjunction of the third channel;
it performs the pinning and the piercing, as well as all ritual actions—
by means of a specific pronunciation, this is done without a doubt.
The Lord also performs everything according to the division of the channels of life.
Joined with various words, whatever is intended by the mind—
beginning with the fourth [vowel] followed by the first of the fifth [consonants], and joined with the beginning of the sixth word.
It effects the withdrawal of form as desired by the mind;
it is impelled by the exhalation (*recaka*) of the five *prayoginīs*.
By means of the application of *rañjikānta*, he leads [the breath] to the collection of nectar;
likewise, he effects liberation from all karmas right here.
Through the yoga of the sixth praise, he brings about great disease.
With *phaṭ* and *kāma* joined at the end, it is struck by the armor (*kaṅkaṭa*).
With *oṃ* joined at the beginning, assuming the form of fire and wind,
it indeed performs every rite, even those such as the *tapanīya*.

Thus, having thoroughly ascertained the reality of mantra through the application of mantra and having understood it from the mouth of the guru, one should perform the ritual according to one's desire. O Goddess, there is nothing in the three worlds that cannot be accomplished by this means.
"Indeed, by the grace of the Guru alone one enters [the state]; for here the Guru is the deity.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Movement of the Yoginīs," in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, a great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses belonging to the *Śiraccheda* within the *Vidyāpīṭha* of the *Bhairava-srotas*.
The Goddess said:
When yoga is not attained, or when a guru is not found,
or when the lineage tradition is interrupted due to negligence on the part of the seeker of yoga—
Then, O Lord of Gods, how do those who are eager for liberation attain success?
Or how, O God, do they know that the time of death has arrived? And how, O Lord of Gods, do they recognize the omens of untimely death for those who have fallen under its power?

O Lord of the Gods of gods, how many animals (paśus) are remembered as bestowers of success? Which ones lead to the failure of success, and which ones grant the supreme bliss? How many Mothers seize the animal through the yoga of meditation?
Bhairava said:
When yoga is not attained, nor the Guru who has mastered the planets,
then [one must rely on] the seven divisions here as taught by the high-souled Kālīśa.
O Goddess, the mantra that has been explained is the bestower of its own specific accomplishment for those previously mentioned.
Their characteristics have not yet been stated; therefore, listen now to those distinctions.
Kulajā is to be known as Pūtanā; Najñā is remembered as Cuṃbikā.
Mūṣikā is mounted upon three feet, surrounded by the eight Lāmās and their commitments (samaya).
Śākinī resides in the Kālacakra, situated within the middle wheel of time.
O Goddess, those Yoginīs who have attained the eightfold sovereignty (aṣṭaguṇamaiśvarya) and are worshipped move at their own will; they are the agents of creation and destruction,
ageless, immortal, formidable, and are proclaimed as the Mothers (Mātaraḥ).
O Goddess of the gods, they seize this human being who has descended from heaven, born of a distinguished lineage and having accumulated [karma] over seven lifetimes—
[seizing him] with the six circles of Mantrins and with a hundred Yogeśvaras.
One who has been a beast for seven births is never released from life until its end; yet,
when even a single hair of that person is offered into the fire,
it grants the desired fruit to seven generations of their lineage.
But when blood, fat, flesh, or even marrow, or oil, skin, or hair is obtained, then the Mothers play;
O Goddess, if his *caru* is prepared together with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
That which is attained [by this]— what need is there for any other mantra?
O Goddess, those who touch his limbs or converse with him,
having realized it through this very body, attain perfection at that very moment.
Even one who has fallen, been cast out, or is abandoned by his kin,
attains success upon touching the body of a seven-times-born animal (a Brahmin) at the very place where he dies and where he is reduced to ashes.
There the Mothers, whose forms are illusory, sport eternally.
There is nothing purer than this, nothing greater than this;
there is no accomplishment higher than this, and no fruit greater than this.
There is nothing more difficult for even the gods to obtain than this;
it remains ever-present on all sides, whether one is laughing or even while remaining still.
He indeed becomes a constant reciter of mantras, one who delights in his mother and maternal kin.
Born through the power of karma in the *kula-kṣetra* and among the *puliṃdra* people, as well as among the *jāta-jāma* people, he is likewise born in Ḍahala and Koṅkaṇa.

Even those situated at a distance, those in the vicinity, or those in a single village or a single house— freed from fear and distress, they attain success when the time arrives. Whether it be a father, or a brother, or a son, or a friend.
O lady of excellent vows, whether he be a child, an elder, or an ascetic, and whether he bestows truth or supernatural powers,
or even if he has been born only once— if such a person is obtained, O Ugreśa, he shall grant the mind its desired course.
I shall now describe those who bestow even minor accomplishments; listen to this.
Woman, man, camel, owl, cat, dog, jackal, vulture, and parrot—these are to be known as the eight celebrated animals.
O Siddhi, mistress of all yoginīs, listen here to me!
Having established the horse [mantra] and the *sarvanāsthā*, one should perceive the owl as the state of a *rākṣasa*.
The cat, the *jālaśākinī*, and the female jackal belong to the *paśu* class.
Speech, the ability to go at will, and the state of being the Lord of All from the parrot;
these, established in the seven *sāmans*, bestow minor accomplishments.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, how is it known that they have arisen from another birth?
And how, O All-pervading One, do these bound souls (paśus) become bestowers of minor supernatural powers (kṣudrasiddhis)?
Bhairava said:

O lady of excellent vows, I shall describe to you the characteristics arising from one birth and those arising from three births— both the manifest and the secret. One who is treacherous, malicious, prone to anger, devoid of shame, and arrogant for a moment [is characterized by these traits].
O fair-faced one, those who are seen to possess the characteristics of being envious, shameless, fearful, and tranquil in mind when encircled [by the thread],
they are to be examined with the mantra for the successful accomplishment of the rite, like a sacrificial animal.
O Goddess, the seed-syllable, completed with three measures and a half-measure at the end and adorned with five characteristics,
is placed within the mouth and belly like a sacrificial animal.
By means of the path of that blazing meditation, one causes [the deity] to enter at that very moment.
O Goddess, that which arises from a single birth is proclaimed as *sapaśu*.
That which arises from the wheel of power (*śakticakra*) is placed in the center, reaching the end of the six steps.
Having uttered "Soma" (the letter *sa*), one should lead the Bindu and Īśāna to the tip of the crest-lock (*śikhāgra*).
O fair-faced one, by that [mantra], one’s own three births reach a state of exhaustion.
O virtuous lady, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with the limbs upon Bhairava, who is mounted on the six limbs, one should proceed.
One should place the *rañjikā* in the middle of the eyebrows, the mind in the *bindu* and *nāda*,
and [the deity] mounted upon the *kalā* above the crest (*śikhā*), situated within the mouth of the *kalā* during the interval of the inhalation (*pūraka*).
Having thus projected [the mantra] onto the body of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), one should observe it at the time of the mixture (*miśrakāla*).

If one's limbs, tongue, teeth, nails, and likewise the hair on the body are seen to be joined with a dark, medium hue by the sight of one's own eyes, and saliva flows from the mouth everywhere upon the limbs; [this is a sign of death].

O fair-faced one, he whose mind does not find delight even in the vow of the best of all tantras— though he may possess cattle and seven sons, and though he be free from physical deformity— is truly one who has reached the end [of his spiritual purpose].
O Goddess, the characteristics of those animals that are common are now being stated.

Whichever form of the [deity’s] eye was previously described by me, that [eye] is not seen among the stars (tārā) due to the placement (nyāsa); I shall explain it clearly above the mixed and unmixed [lines].
A *paśu* (bound soul) should be known as being of such a nature that it accomplishes the fruits of its own karma.
O Goddess, this has been declared for you as the mere definition of the *paśu*.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the mantra that accomplishes all aims.
O Goddess, O Guru, for one who has turned away from the sacrificial offerings of animal victims (paśu-caru),
since practitioners achieve perfection through repeated practice and worship,
I shall describe to you, O sinless one, its application as the Great Vessel (mahāpota).
O Goddess of gods, by the mere remembrance of whom even those deluded by sense objects— though devoid of proper conduct— attain equanimity as *khecarīs*.
Listen, O goddess of great wisdom, as I tell you this knowledge concerning women in particular and men of disciplined mind;
for they do not perform that action which possesses the luster of coral.
In that [place], O Goddess, Sadāśiva dwells eternally, peaceful;
indeed, he is subject to the sixth vowel. His two measures (mātrās), by virtue of their short and long forms, follow him alone.
O Goddess, those two powers of that God have been thus described:
the *suṣumṇā* is indeed the finger that always moves upward;
the *iḍā*, shaped like a staff, should be known as extending down to the seven netherworlds.
The upward movement of the face, which is impelled by whichever wind [is active],
causes one to be led upward from there by that [wind]; thus, the Supreme Lord,
having pervaded his own form situated at the crown of the head and the quarters of the sky, [leads him up].
O fair-faced one, with his self purified by *prāṇāyāma*, he should meditate constantly;
having thus united [the elements], the lord of yogis should then practice yoga.
O fair-faced one, beneath that deity is a wheel (*cakra*) ending with the letter *sa*.
One should contemplate the form of Vāyu, joined with the syllable *soṃ* at the beginning and end;

by means of the mantra to be described, one should fill the openings of the channels and the centers (*cakras*) with the breath through the technique of retention (*kumbhaka*), illuminating the end of each word.
One should meditate upon oneself as being at the center of the heart-cakra, possessing a radiance equal to Śiva.
Having visualized the seed-syllable *Bi*, one should place the unborn *Bindu*, which is peaceful and quiescent, at the tip of the *Bindu*.
Then, piercing through the *Iḍā* and the *Suṣumṇā*, one should fill [the central channel] with the *Udāna* breath.
The knower of mantras, having opened the mouth of the channel by means of the syllable *E* alone,
then pierces that mass of darkness with a radiance equal to lightning.
Upon uttering the syllable *soṃ*, he went to the hermitage where the Mothers of Space reside;
there, like an ordinary person from the land of Kāśyapī, he stood upon the station of the eight heroes (*vīrāṣṭaka*).
From that time forward, the Lord of Yoga wandered the earth according to his will.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, as it has been explained regarding how one attains oneness with the Self through His grace, tell me:
what is the nature of the heart of that God of gods?"
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, listen to the six-syllabled mantra of the God of gods within his heart;
O fair-faced one, it has the middle seed-syllable of the eye preceded by the *praṇava*.
Then, having placed the letter *ha*, which is unmanifest and joined with the fire-seed (*ra*),
and having established *māyā* there, one is adorned by a mass of splendor.
O Goddess, this is the supreme Śakti, consisting of six parts, the bestower of all accomplishments.

By means of this [mantra] being recited, even a human being in any state whatsoever becomes dear to the goddesses; he shall not touch the earth with his feet. [This is accomplished] by the second of the twelve [syllables], standing at the end of the seventh.
"Those vital breaths of yours have ceased; he is the one who accomplishes the body of the temple.
Having fashioned the temple as a physical form, he adorns it once again.
Indeed, in no long time at all, he becomes the very embodiment of grace."
Impelled by this king of mantras,
the mantras embodied as Śakti grant immediate success when employed for each respective rite,
such as the attainment of the Cakras or the summoning of bound souls (paśus).
Likewise, in the purification of the bound soul (paśu) through the procedure of piercing (vedha) and friction (ghaṭṭa),

that which is joined with the seed-syllable at the beginning and end by means of a powerful word is called "the drop" (bindu); it is conjoined with the initial word of the application of sound (visvaniyoga).
One should employ the friction [of the breath] endowed with the seed-mantra syllables.
Yogis should understand that "friction" (ghaṭṭana) is the protection of one's own mantra.
Likewise, when protection has been established, one should perform piercing (vedha) and splitting (viddha).
One who knows the methods of piercing and striking becomes a practitioner in this way:
one should draw a four-cubit wheel upon a cremation ground.
Having placed the principles (tattvas) and the goddesses there in their proper order,
and having meditated upon himself as Bhairava, the knower of mantras, having ascended the wheel,
goes through the sky with concentrated mind according to the previously stated procedure.
The knower of sacrifice, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for each individual accomplishment, [should employ] the substances and the elements;
having placed the syllable *soṃ* and its support upon the tip of the tongue,
and having enclosed it between the syllables *soṃ* at the beginning and end, one should offer perfumes and other offerings to oneself.

Endowed with the previous meditations, the practitioner endowed with the mantra moves through the air without doubt; likewise, by partaking of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), the mantra-master attains the speed of mind and wind, [traveling] upon trees, sandals, litters, vehicles, and seats.
Whether accepting gifts or engaging in conversation for the sake of making a living,
he is not stained at all, just as the sky is not defiled by mud.
Moving according to his own will, he goes wherever he desires.
There Vīreśa sports, just as the god Maheśvara does;
O Queen of the Gods, the wise one should draw the world with white mustard seeds.
Having placed the wheel in the cardinal directions, surrounded by the Śaktis.
Having performed worship according to one's ability, one should recite the mantras in their proper sequence.
Having meditated upon Śiva, who is the end of the *cuṃbaka* [vowel], surrounded by his powers (*śakti*s), He becomes manifest in an instant to the mind of that person from the end of the *nāda*.
The world was divine, made of gold, auspicious, and blazing with various jewels;
it was adorned with divine pillars made of gems and decorated with networks of tinkling bells,
and filled with wonderful, magnificent palaces crowded with celestial women.
For the sake of fulfilling all desires, a palace arises for one in an instant.
Indeed, this is known as the nocturnal sport of the inhabitants of the earth;
having taken clay by name from seven anthills.
Even for one who has entered the womb, one should fashion a male form by means of that [mantra].
O Goddess, the mantra consists of two words beginning with "tattva" and joined internally with the syllable *oṃ*.
O fair-faced one, having performed the ninth complete nyāsa upon Vīreśa,
one should meditate on the bindu and recite the mantras with the consciousness absorbed in the nāda.
By means of pūraka according to the prescribed rule, one may attract the object of practice (sādhya) in an instant.
One should perform the purification of that [substance] which has been brought forth with mantras well-consecrated,
arising from one's own channel and ending with the syllable *phaṭ*.
Then, O fair-faced one, one should pierce it at the crown with the weapon-mantra of destruction (*naidhanāstra*).
Alternatively, having caused [the breath] to go to the ether, or remaining on the surface of the earth,
one should purify the deceased by means of Bhairava in the form of fire.
The auspicious descent is cast down from the sky, returning through the navel.
One should prepare the *caru* well-consecrated with that *praṇava*,
joined with the five deities (or groups), and protected by the spreading *mātrā*. Having obtained that, O lady of excellent limbs, one proceeds like the seven winds.
With death conquered by his will and endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers (aṣṭāṅga-aiśvarya),
he becomes a consumer of whatever he desires at will;
thus, one who knows the methods of piercing (vedha) performs actions effortlessly.
Whether in forward or reverse order, or even from reverse to forward,
the knower of mantra should indeed perform piercing (*vedhana*) or friction (*ghaṭṭana*).
This most secret of secrets has been declared by the Guru as the *bhaga*.
Having attained that initiation, one should lead people [to liberation], like one standing on a mountain peak looking down upon those on the ground.
This [teaching] should be proclaimed to the initiate (*samayin*) and made known to the devoted lord of heroes (*vīreśa*).
It must be explained to one's own disciple; otherwise, there is ruin and hell.
The Goddess said:
"Those who grant success like that of animal sacrifices have been specifically proclaimed.
Those in whom no obstructors are mentioned, not even the slightest,
do not encounter obstacles; even one established in the Śākinī vow, or one born of a noble family, O Maheśvara, does not fail to attain supreme accomplishment due to those obstructing impediments.
"O best of gods, tell her how practitioners achieve success through knowledge,
so that people of the land of Kāśyapī may indeed become esteemed.
Bhairava said:

O fair-faced goddess, the procedure for the animal-sacrifices (*paśu*) that was previously indicated grants you success when followed correctly; however, O Goddess, when performed in reverse, they become obstacles.
When joined with the state of being a "female animal" (*strīpaśutva*), they destroy great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*).
Likewise, O Goddess, one should not bestow [the teaching] elsewhere, except for that which arises from the body;
for without the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*),
even by the gift of great gold, your awakening has been brought about [only through such means].
O fair-faced goddess, whatever is protected by mantras belonging to other systems, one should take that by force; O Goddess, the remainder causes the destruction of accomplishment.
O lady of excellent limbs, that which has died of its own accord is born of the sixty-three families.
Or even a great sacrificial animal (*mahāmṛtapaśu*), which otherwise obstructs the fruit;
O fair-faced one, that which dies within eight days—
one should take it with its own mantras, for otherwise it does not bestow the fruit.

O Goddess, those who are deluded by the darkness of ignorance and are hostile toward the Māsādi [deity] employ others in the state of a beast; their success remains close at hand. O fair-faced one, it is said that for another who is already endowed with the fruit of his own accomplishment, [the result is immediate].
O Goddess of gods, once he has fallen, he quickly causes suffering. He afflicts the child with disease, or makes him crippled and afflicted by wind-disorders;
O Goddess of gods, having made him impotent or a mere beast, he does not attain success.
O Goddess, for those supreme men who, having drunk the nectar of greed and delusion,
perform even the worship of Siddhas and Vīras, that [worship] becomes an obstacle to their spiritual attainment (siddhi).
Just as [the fire] near the deity [is affected], O Goddess, so are the Śaktis [affected] by agallochum (agaru).
(192a) Departing from that [place] elsewhere immediately destroys the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of men;
this applies even more so to those possessing powers (*śakti*) who are established in the *cakra*.
Even malice toward [the teacher] through speech or mind is an obstacle to spiritual accomplishment.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, you have stated that one perishes within eight days."
If the breath exceeds [the limit] by one *nāḍikā*, it grants success; if it is subtracted, it grants the attainment of what is to be accomplished.
O God, how does that arise as the supreme cause of accomplishment?
How does the knowledge of the lifespan become deluded, whether regarding oneself or another?
Bhairava said:
Above the navel is that which is called Śagā, which is joined with all supernatural powers (siddhis) in every respect;
O fair-faced one, it vibrates and throbs again and again.
When three seasons have passed and his time has reached its ultimate end,
then, departing from the joints, it roars with a gurgling sound in the chest;
at that time, one no longer hears the sounds situated within both ears.

Foul-smelling, black blood, devoid of its natural luster like oil, arises from the pressure; and when the fourth lunar mansion (Turya) is seen, one does not see [the moon]. There is a piercing pain at the base of the tongue and in the skin of the hair.
Even for those who undergo emaciation, there is an increase in vitality according to the teachings on the vital points (*marman*) of the body.
Now, the characteristics of one whose death is imminent within six months are as follows:
when the breath has reached the eighth station of death and is situated in the *abhira* [channel], [death occurs].
The supreme wind called apāna remains pervading its own junction.
When the two feet are then touched, they become soundless and devoid of blood;
however, the semen becomes accompanied by blood, as does the heat of that mountain.
If one enters the openings of the channels at night, one becomes as if scorched by a conflagration of the quarters;
even while awake, one would then see what is described as being like a dream. When [the breath] remains for six months—equivalent to a year—this is the sign of death within six months.
This Brahman is not known; learn the means for its realization:
the seed-syllable of Fire situated within its own city in the midst of the circle of Wind.
One should place the letter *dh* (flaming) in three locations and the six vowels (*a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*) in the six parts [of the hands].
[The wise] should place them on the palms, at the bases of the thumbs, on one's own faces, and between the breasts—
by means of the six deities beginning with *A* and accompanied by the nasal bindu, as understood by those of dull intellect.
Having restrained [the breath], one should place the seed-syllable and the mandala consisting of fire;
one should gather the blazing [syllable] ending in *dh* (i.e., *dhūṃ*), which emits dense sparks.
By this practice, one shall see death standing near at hand.
I shall now proclaim another practice; listen, O observer of excellent vows!
Having performed the arrangement of the three wheels in half, half, and half [of the body], the practitioner should thereafter place the supreme, all-pervading Prāsāda mantra upon the body.
Having placed the sun behind one's back, one should examine the remainder of one’s lifespan.
When one can no longer see the two ears, one perishes after twelve years;
however, if [the hands are not visible], it is after seven years, and if the hands [are not visible], it is after ten years.

One who does not see with eight fingers' breadth, nor with three on the side, has a lifespan of two years; for some, it is certainly one year. He whose head one does not see will perish within six months.
If one cannot see for one month when [the breath] is in the neck, or for half a month when it is in the chin; or for nine, ten, or eleven days when the eyes do not see;
or if one sees a hole in the heart, one will perish in seven days.
He who perceives two bodies perishes instantly.
Time alone recognizes that [destruction] has arrived for itself.
What is the use of saying more here? Sound (*nāda*) is likewise a portion of Viṣṇu.

O lady of excellent hips, when one no longer perceives through the ears, the eyes, or the apertures of the mouth, at that very moment one goes to the abode of Yama. Now listen as I explain what it is that one perceives of another.

Having sipped water and become pure, one who is awakened by the three principles (*tritattva*) should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the hand and the body with the Lord of the Texts (*granthīśvara*).
One should apply the garment to the moon situated in the middle of the right side of the sun;
on the forehead, one should place the kalā of the seed-syllable of Īśa, conjoined with the pervasive [mantra].
Having placed the splendor of Śiva in the heart, one should then rest upon the weapon of the world.
Having established the self within the self, one should then project the seed-syllable.
Having placed *kaṃ* upon the crest-lock, perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the object of attainment (*sādhya*).
Then, with the four [syllables] distinct from the seed-syllable, place the four [limbs] in sequence.
Having placed the [elements] beginning with Vāyu in their respective order of colors,
O lady of excellent hips, one should place them within the Akhajas by means of the Tāra-mantra in sequence.
Within the four-legged [structure], the elements are situated, while the Shadow (chāyā) is in the center of the Lakṣa.

O Goddess, one should place the supreme and most excellent seed-syllable on the forehead, with the letters *ṭa-ṭha-ḍa-ḍha-ṇa* and *ya-stha* following it, as well as in the houses and temples of the deities. Now listen as I describe the application of the special placement (*viśeṣanyāsa*).
I shall describe to you the reversal of the placement of the seeds for mobile and immobile beings— beasts, birds, and reptiles— as they correspond to their respective seeds:
one should place the seed of Vāyu at the tip of the crest-lock (śikhā) and the seed of Agni on the head.
The seed-syllable of space (haṃ) is to be placed at the navel; this placement is applied everywhere.
One should place the seed-syllable of Mahendra (laṃ) on the face, and the seed-syllable of Varuṇa (vaṃ) one should place at the heart.
The seed-syllable of space (haṃ) is to be placed at the navel; this placement is applied everywhere.

O lady of virtuous vows, having become pure and consecrated one's own eyes with these mantras, one should, at the time of mixing, gaze upon the shadow of the animal situated in the midst of the marks of the horse (chāgralakṣaṇa), which indicates the auspicious and inauspicious.
"Sṛjaya" is the first word; "śūlapāṇe" is the second;
"harahara" is the third; "dahadaha" is the fourth;
and "darśayasvarūpam" followed by "hūṃ phaṭ" at the end is the fifth.
Combined with the seed-syllable of Paśu, the sixth is declared to be Ṣaḍa;
O fair-faced one, the first mantra is preceded by the syllable Oṃ.
Having uttered "To Rudra with matted hair," one should place the steps in reverse order:
"Turu suru" as before, followed by "Huṃ Hrīṃ" twice, and likewise "Ha.
Then, showing one's own form, [the mantra] ends with "Duritāni huṃ phaṭ."
Having placed the shadow of the *lakṣa* into ponds and wells, the practitioner,
having consecrated it seven times with these [mantras], should observe the shadow:
[one] three years old, lacking feet, and deprived of both shanks.
If [the breath] remains for one year in the knees, it lives for ten months in the thighs; if deprived of the waist, it certainly lives for eight or seven months;
if the abdomen is diminished, it survives for six or five months.
Indeed, three, two, one, and four [days] are for the neck in the case of gradual loss;
for the hands, one fortnight; and for one deprived of the arms, ten days.
For one deprived of a limb, it is a day and night; when the heart bursts, it is certainly certain.
O Goddess of the Gods, one who possesses four [of these] signs goes to the abode of Yama;
seeing his shadow fallen upon his head, he perishes within half a day.
He whose shadow is not seen perishes at that very moment.
Thus, O Goddess, one should examine the shadow for purity during the period of transition.
For by failing to examine it, one perceives [the truth] neither of oneself nor of another.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, I shall speak of the even more subtle knowledge of lifespan.

O lady of virtuous vows, that which has not been told to anyone else, I shall tell you out of affection for you. Even if one has gone to another country or is far away, they know [the truth] by the mere mention of their lineage; listen accordingly as it is at the proper time.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables from *a* to *ḥ* upon the left eye,
and having observed one's own reflection while remaining motionless, one should then gaze into the empty space.
In that state, O dear one, whichever limb is lost from the field of vision, that very limb perishes.
If there were error regarding what was seen once, one might conceptualize it as "it is thus"; yet if it were likewise seen again, it would necessarily be exactly so.
Whether he is wearing armor, observing a vow, or even sleeping on the ground, when [the breath] reaches the *lakṣa*, one should then predict his impending death (*ariṣṭa*).
In the first watch of the night, it lasts for six seasons; in the second watch, for eight months.
In the third [month], one should know there are twenty-four [days]; in the fourth, one should calculate only one [day].
In the fifth, it is with fifteen [days]; in the sixth, the remainder of the season [is calculated].
O lady of excellent hips, in the seventh, it is proclaimed to be exactly one month.
One should investigate this very process according to the sequential application of the Yāmas,
by a reduction of five-fifths (one) until five remain.
Then, indeed, by the reduction of days, it continues until only one day remains at the end.
Having determined the movement during the day and night, one should thus investigate the lifespan;
one should observe that [lifespan] down to the end of three years and even to the single day.
Then, having examined the specific time, one should remain established during the periods of the twilights (saṃdhyā).

The four [periods] should be known according to the rules by means of the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*): white, red, yellow, and black, respectively from the east. Having discerned the time, one should take [the substance], and the ritual involving the animal (*paśukarma*) will be successful.
Thus, having drawn the tree and the mountain at the junctions of the *prasāda* [sections],
this most excellent knowledge of time spoken by Śiva should be applied with all its characteristics.
O Goddess, no knowledge of time superior to this proceeds forth.
This has been explained to you in detail; what more shall I tell you?

Thus ends the chapter on the knowledge of the time for the movement of the Yoginīs, in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraccheda* of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavasrotas*.
The Goddess said: O Lord,
that which has been described by you— the Time agitated by the rising of Time,
the movement through the fine apertures of the channels, and the multitude of meditation-mandalas— [is this so?]
"How will these women of small intelligence perform their work? Or how can there be success for those whose thoughts are so fickle? (194b)
"O Lord, tell me about the *bhacakraka* (the circle of eating), by the mere remembrance of which Śaṅkara causes all women to perform every rite with ease.
Bhairava said:
I shall describe to you the wheel of knowledge (vidyācakra) of the Lord, the Sovereign of Knowledge.
Having meditated upon the great wheel in the heart, one should either draw it on auspicious ground;
there, in the pericarp, one should place Śiva, endowed with his five kalās.
Having visualized that divine one of golden luster, possessing the form of Mahābhairava,
and having arranged the moon and sun [within the maṇḍala], one should perform worship there;
situated in the center of the infinite petals, his body consists of all the letters ending with the final phoneme.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, having gathered [the energies], one should place the pervasive heart-mantra. One should establish the hundred intermediate portions of Māyā on the right arm.
The eighteen other auspicious matrices (yoni) are Rañjikā and Arañjikā.
One should place Śānta behind, joined with the fifth [letter];
O lady of excellent hips, it should pervade that [mantra] whose head is stepped upon by Ananta.
Above and below, the digit of Māyā, situated within the letter Rañjī, is adorned.
Or, in the course of a month, one should cause the nineteen-fold source to enter [the womb],
having placed the entire body ending with the final phoneme at the head of the Vidyā.
Having thus become intent upon Śiva, one should then perform the worship.
Except for constant recitation, [the mantra] ending in *krāṃ* is beneficial for attraction;
that ending in *bhairava* is for inciting enmity; the auspicious one ending in *uṃ* is for subjugation;
it should be joined with *ṣaṭ* at the end for causing death; and for expulsion, it ends in *sphaṭ*.
One should first employ [the first] kalā for the sovereignty of the kings of kings;
O Goddess of the gods, one should place the second kalā among the royalty;
and the third is indeed for addressing others and for one's own rites of pacification.
O Goddess of gods, whatever the practitioner intends while reciting the *śiva* mantra,
this [mantra] performs that very action through the ritual application (*nyāsa*) and worship according to the prescribed rule. (195a)

The first *kalā* is surrounded by the *tavarga*; the second is on the northern petal, likewise accompanied by the *tavarga*. The third is on the southern petal, O Goddess, and the fourth is accompanied by the *cavarga*, just as is Śiva.
The fifth [vowel] is on the western petal, surrounded by the *ṭa*-group;
O Goddess, one should place Nārīśa in the pericarp according to the sequence.
The Rudras are to be joined on the fire-petal (southeast), and Suprabhā on the petal in the direction of Īśa (northeast).
One should assign Bhīmārudrā to the northwest and likewise Bhīmatī to the southwest;
one should assign Bhadrakālī at the base of the pericarp in the south,
and the yogin should assign Bhīmā in the northern portion of the pericarp.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rule with perfumes, flowers, and various kinds of food offerings, one should then commence the ritual action.
One should employ Śiva, endowed with the five kalās, for all ritual activities.

For the sake of the complete accomplishment of all rites, one should constantly recite and worship [the mantra]. O Goddess of the gods, the first digit (kalā), beginning with the *praṇava* (OM), is beneficial for traveling through the sky; the second belongs to him who resides in the previously mentioned wheel.
The third and the fourth [syllables], auspicious for making oneself invisible,
should be joined as before, illuminated by his "word of utterance" (uccārapada).
The fourth and the fifth are others that cause the attraction of blood.
In the previous ritual arrangement, however, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) of Śiva are beneficial for the vessels.
By the recitation (japa) of all mantras in their proper sequence, whether in the right place or not,
a person undoubtedly attains divinity and immortality through this recitation.

O lady of excellent vows, listen to the many deeds of this very God of gods, who is united with yoga and endowed with grace. Having performed the arrangement of the body as before, illuminated by his power—
Then perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the hand with the six-syllabled wheel.
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
The non-disclosure of anyone’s deed, even the concealment of a secret;
the desire for the welfare of others, contentment, satisfaction, and likewise fortitude;
immortality, the state of being unshakeable, and the auspiciousness of the lunar day—these are the functions of the goddess Mīti.
Śaśinī, Jvalinī, Chāyā, Sampūrṇamaṇḍalā—
these are indeed the fifteen digits (kalās), while the sixteenth is known as Amṛtā.
Through these, ritual actions are accomplished in accordance with the influence of the arising of time.
These perform all rites for one established in Śivā.
Indeed, these lunar days among the luminaries are the supreme Jayā of the Yoginīs.
O Goddess, in the Moon, the digits of the Moon are established as the three forms.
They perform all rites when joined with the complete ritual procedure;
however, one should employ that rite when [the power] is diminished by being reversed.
One should satisfy [the deities] during the waning phases of the previous [periods], and increase [the practice] when it has waned during the full [phases].
If one should employ the ritual action when the consumed portion has been exhausted,
one should thoroughly join it with the seeds of the goal and the seeds of the seed-mantras.
O Goddess, having observed increase and decrease, Indra should cause the planting of the seed.

Having placed the twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa, in the center of the wheel by means of the letters beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga*, situated as they naturally are within its own wheel,
one should accomplish his ritual action through the *karanyāsa*, O Goddess of Gods.

One should apply Śiva conjoined with the Moon (Śa) to the thumb; likewise, one should apply the Sun (Ra) conjoined with the Full Mandala (Ū) to the index finger. O Goddess, one should place [the letter] conjoined with Chāyā (E) on the middle finger, and indeed [the letter] conjoined with Anāmikā (I) on the ring finger.
One should place *pūrṇāyukta* on the little finger, *mṛtāyuta* in the middle of the hand,
*yaśāyukta* at the wrist, and *prītisaṃyuta* during the encircling.
Then, one should apply the group of *mātṛkās* in the center of both hands.
The thumb is the seed-vessel of Varuṇa; the index finger is situated in the east;
the ring finger is in the north; and the middle finger is in the southern direction.

O Goddess, one should install the groups of spirits (bhūtavarga) in due order, corresponding respectively to the northwest, southeast, southwest, and northeast. Having thus performed the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), one should then accomplish the ritual action.
One who is well-versed in mantra should join the hundred [offerings] with the seed-syllable of the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*) once it has been produced;
whatever substance is present, when consecrated by meditation, it brings about [the desired result].
At the end of the *jā* [syllable], one should always join that which is joined with the seed-syllable of the index finger (*tarjanī*).
Success will be within one's grasp and the state of Ugreśa will arise.
If one constantly recites while joined with the six syllables in the first seed-syllable,
one will before long behold the Yoginīs and likewise the Mothers face to face.
They attend upon him in his ritual acts and provide what is beneficial for him;
they show him the sacrificial animal and grant him the success of his rites.
Within six months, they bestow upon him the sovereignty of the supernatural powers, such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
In activities intended to overcome enemies, in battle, and during great austerities,
victory comes from all sides for one who recites and offers oblations.
Furthermore, by means of the *śikhā*, one shall proceed and attain the state of the Lord.

O Goddess, that which is endowed with joy, empty, and conjoined with time, declared by Nārīśa as the Heart that bestows the perfection of yoga— this supreme piercing of the channels consists of the syllables within the center of the wheel.
It is employed for the drying up and the cutting down of enemies.
By touching it with the hand, he [the enemy] is paralyzed, without a doubt.
O Goddess, even one who is without splendor trembles at the mere sight of it.
Having touched trees, lords, ropes, and so forth, as well as men, women, and carts,
the yogin should proceed at his ease with his hand placed [upon them].
He should apply the seed-syllable to the right side of the wheel for the purpose of sealing.
For its sealing, one should employ the Varuṇa seed-syllable, accompanied by meditation and recitation;
it should be joined with the ashes of the funeral pyre. Who indeed would subject the hero to great heat?
For the destruction of the eyes and for the destruction of trees,
one should place the western [syllable] on the head, the southern on the heart,
the eastern at the navel, and the northern on the feet.
O Goddess of the gods, for the constant placement upon the one purified by mudrā during the seizing of the target,
the eastern and northern [directions] should indeed be reversed;
he who performs these peaceful [placements] effects an attraction through mudrā in an instant.
O Goddess, the complete maṇḍala, joined with the shadow (chāyā) and multiplied by three,
beginning with the Praṇava and ending with the word for giving (dāna), becomes the Mudrā when it is sealed.
With the middle fingers placed [together], this is proclaimed as the Seal of Sealing (mudraṇa).
This Gāyatrī, stationed on the index finger, performs the unsealing (unmudraṇa).
O Goddess, in the word "kusuma," it is supreme for attracting the red [element].
Sāvitrī, however, begins with the Praṇava and is endowed with three *uṃ* syllables.
And the supreme mantra-warden is situated in both hands.
O Goddess, that word "vict" (vic), preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with "dāna," constantly bestows accomplishment upon the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
The first yoga of placement for the wheel has been told to you.
O sinless one, I shall now tell you the third, the placement of the wheels.
O Goddess, one should place Śiva at the end of the station of Kalā, and Tuṃburu [at the end] of Viniyoga.
For the sake of accomplishing all rites, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the mantra and the body:
with *yaśā* in the heart, *pūṣan* in the head;
*aṃśumālin* in the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and *śaśinī* as the armor (*kavaca*).
The weapon-mantra (*astra*) is joined with the *mahāmṛta* [syllables]; the placement of the wheel (*cakra-nyāsa*), however, is as before.
