The seed-syllable (*bīja*) which is in the center of the wheel, arising from the openings of all the channels (*nāḍī*), is placed upon the mouth of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), excluding the vowels, and likewise upon oneself.
One should place the *kalās* of Paśurāla in the center of the navel of the person situated to the east.
This practice for the extraction of nectar (*amṛtākarṣaṇa*) is declared to be of formidable power.
In the sealing of kings, one should place the presiding lord of the first letter;
but in the sealing of animals, by means of the differentiation of the second vowel,
the mantra situated on the ring finger is differentiated by the principle of Vidyā-tattva.

One may paralyze all beings or, in an instant, attract them; once attracted and brought under control, they indeed become givers of wealth. [He is] adorned with a great crown in the Sadāśivāṃśumālinī [mudrā].
The *utkrāmaṇī* [mantra] should be employed for the funeral pyre and likewise for the ashes;
joined with the *kalā* and the *praṇava*, it is remembered as bestowing great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*).
Recited three times over those of low birth, it effects their death through the method of *vidarbhaṇa*.
O virtuous lady, the wheel is sealed by the western seed-syllable accompanied by the syllable *phaṭ*;
it becomes unsealed even by Bhairava himself through its own internal seed-syllable joined with the shadow.
Invisibility has been proclaimed, as well as the power of moving through the sky at will.
O lady of virtuous vows, by means of the right-hand seed-syllable of the wheel together with the *anusvāra*,
one may perform the immobilization of water and fire, and the warding off of mechanical devices.

The *praṇava* (Om) is practiced four times, adorned by the word "Ananta" (Endless), and joined with the "unstruck" (*anāhata*) pillar; this is remembered as the state ascended upon the wish-fulfilling tree (*cintārūḍha*). Having performed the consecration seven times over the fire, its name is to be interlaced (*vidarbhitam*).
O Goddess, one should cast [the substance] into water; this is the supreme rite for a corpse-pillar (śavastambha).
O Goddess, Śiva mounted upon Kalā and adorned by the end of Amṛta—the auspicious Heart-mantra of Āsannaka—is the performer of all rites.

O beautiful woman, the animal clan (paśugotra) is pierced at the heart by the Mother; it is bound on all sides by the essence of the syllable *tok* and gazed upon with a cruel glance. It is brought to life, and together with its flesh, it draws forth the blood of women.
O Goddess, the digit (kalā) is pervaded by Shadow (chāyā) and adorned by the end of Māyā;
she abides through the worship of the lineage (gotra) for the sake of the liberation from this devouring (grāsa). (197b)
Having placed [the fingers] on the thumb, the middle finger, and the third from the little finger,
one should quickly utter the first [syllable] ending with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*).
Then, O Goddess, one should press that person's shadow with the fist.
O lady of excellent hips, having accomplished the objective, one is said to be intent on binding the gaze.
Having rendered Śaśinī deluded, she is adorned with the beloved Rañjikā.
And just as it was obstructed by the Mothers, beginning with the Praṇava and ending with the six [syllables].
O Goddess, when the syllable *oṃ* is joined with ten thousand and a fraction of its own differentiated parts,
weapons [become effective] through mantrification; they cut away brilliance and shadow,
and for men, that which is distant moves and accomplishes the goal in an instant.
Taking buffalo dung and liquefying it with cow urine,
one should perform this practice according to the previously mentioned procedure while endowed with meditation on Śiva.
O Goddess of the God of Gods, this application is unfailing and possesses terrifying power.

Having performed the subjugation by means of the syllable *ukāra* preceded by the *praṇava*, and having struck [the target] with darbha grass consecrated by mantra, the suppression of the Śākinīs is beneficial. By means of the Heart-mantra on the petal, the Nāda is unfailing; thus it was spoken by Śiva.

Sadāśiva is perfectly endowed with vastness and possessed of steadfastness; he is pervaded by Ananta and adorned by the Pratyakṣa and other deities. The mantra praised as the space and the firmament is the consecration of trees and other such things.
One hundred and eight times, according to the number of all the substances employed;
each [mantra] is joined with the supreme [deity], O Goddess, mounted upon a *kalā* and ending with "namaḥ.
In the center, conjoined with Nārīśa, it serves for the transformation of form.

Any mantra that begins with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) is for beings possessing bones; others are for those without bones. One should plant [the seeds] upon the heads of those living beings that possess bones—such as cats, jackals, bears, wolves, donkeys, camels, and goats.
Having bound yellow mustard seeds moistened with red water in one's hand, and having formed the *kuru* mudrā, one becomes identical in form [to that deity] in an instant.
O fair-faced one, having enclosed the syllable *uṃ* within the seed-syllable of Bala,
one should consecrate the ashes with it; touched by that, [the spirit] dances, goes elsewhere,
or departs to another region when employed with five recitations.
The *Aṅkuśa* (Goad) mantra, situated within *Bhairava*, preceded by the *Praṇava* (*Oṃ*) and ending with the directions (*Diśāntaga*),
effects the binding of the quarters and likewise the blinding of the eyes of living beings.
Having placed the *Praṇava* on the head, one's own mantra in the heart, and the *Vastu* mantra in the navel.
O Goddess, one should contemplate the school (vidyālaya) as pervading the body,
joined with the complete maṇḍala, and at its end, the Lord Sadāśiva.
Contemplated thus, it brings about the single transition of the mode of existence into the body.
Having been empowered by Śiva through the second [mantra] arisen from reality (tattva), which is joined to reality according to reality, she proceeds as she desires. The goad,
beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ), is peaceful and beneficial for the act of drawing [the soul].
O lady of excellent hips, for those who are sealed, there is no other [means] than the *yonimudrā*.
When joined with the *śaṅkhapatra*, it brings the three worlds under control;
when joined with the *kapāla* and *pāśa* mudrās, it is the means for the practitioner of wealth.
That very Kuśa, having colored the *rañjikā* within the *puruṣa*,
and having drawn a weapon at the end of the middle [section], should write [the name] to paralyze the vow.
With the powder of charcoal from a cremation ground, whatever one desires in the mind [should be written].
The supreme Śiva is joined with Amṛtā, beginning with Kṣurikā, above the Kalā.
It consists of the Praṇava and so forth for the severing of the bonds of those who have not yet attained stability.
Combined with the ashes of the cremation ground, it is consecrated by mantra along with Gorocanā.
Whatever the world touches through her, all that shall come under one's control.
O lady of excellent hips, the Heart-mantra begins with the *praṇava* and ends with the weeping of the Mother.
Having joined it with four *oṃkāras* and adorned it with the *puruṣa*,
and having performed seven consecrations (*abhimantraṇa*) with both hands ending in the *visarga*,
there is indeed the sealing (*mudraṇa*) of those who cause harm and of those who are harmful by means of the sound "Lāmā."
"O you who possess lightning like a serpent, O great wind, O great flame, bring about cessation!"—
this is considered the supreme method for the immobilization (*stambhana*) of those who consume stones.
Endowed with the utterance of two *kalās*, she is established in the body and reaches the end of death.
The third [mantra] is Rañjikāntasthā, standing alone and preceded by the Praṇava;
wherever it is worshipped, O Goddess, it generates disease for the bound souls (paśus),
yet there and everywhere it is indeed unfailing (amoghā) due to its connection with the lineage (gotra).
I shall now declare the great secret, the supreme quartet of mantras.
It is surrounded by divine thorns that grant immediate accomplishment.
The first word is "atattve," preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ).
Established in the vow, having worshipped the wheel on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) according to the rules while facing south, one who remains for seven nights should offer his own heart.
At night, while asleep, he perceives all that is auspicious and inauspicious in a dream.
Established in samādhi, he perceives the self of reality through this word "pada" as before; whatever pleases his mind,
he knows by consecrating his left hand and touching it to that [person's] head.

O Goddess of the gods, one should seal that [state] with the *dakṣiṇonmudraṇa* (the rightward unsealing), which is beneficial. The word ending in the letter *cha*, consisting of the nature of *bhava* and adorned with the *tāraka* (the Savior),—
by means of that, one who has merely crossed over childhood beholds the Lord Bindu.
Having placed the divine syllable in the heart, one discerns the auspicious and the inauspicious;
whether it concerns another or oneself, if one becomes deluded through yoga,
there shall be four *phaṭ* sounds at the end of the first *pada*.
The four stars [of the constellation] are likewise [the letters] *kṛ*, *ka*, *cchṛ*, and *kā*;
one should then apply the words that have arisen from those [syllables] to the invocation (*āhāva*).
The syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) is at the end; beyond that is the supreme ether (*paraṃ vyoma*), and after that, the pervasive one (*vyāpinī*).
With the word *svāhā* at the end, the body—from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head—is [purified].
By means of the letter *kha*, one goes [to the goal] without doubt through the yoga of the previously mentioned wheel.
O fair-faced one, the word *nirañjanā* comes first, followed by *bhairavādyam*.
O Queen of the Gods, the phrase *vidmahe* follows the word *nirākāśāya*.
Likewise, having uttered *dhīmahi*, one says *tannaḥ sūkṣmapracodayāt*.
O Goddess, one should recite [the mantra] ending with *prasāda* to destroy disease and death. Having placed the *bhāvapadā* on the two feet, when the self has departed, this is the supreme rite:
*thaṃ thaṃ thaṃ*.

One should apply these [mantras] in reverse order for the subjugation of cattle; by means of the practice of the fourfold repetition, one should apply them with the immobilization of *kṛcchra*. And in the reversal of the form of the mantra ending in *phaṭ*, [the same applies].
Druk, kaṃcaka, likewise druk, sruk, kṣyuk, jruk, hruk, and then in sequence hrut—
this is the supreme heart-mantra of the eight Mothers for the performance of the eight rites.
By reciting this, they bestow the fruits upon the practitioner.
O Goddess, they become mothers and bestow the sacred tradition (saṃpradāya) upon those who constantly remember them with bonds, O Lord of the Earth.
O Goddess, [the mantra] consists of the syllables of the name of the sacrificial animal (paśu), mixed with certain other syllables.
Closing one's mouth while reciting is the supreme method for attracting a woman with passion.
Whatever rites have been taught in the *Yoginījālaśamvara*,
by reciting [the mantra] ten thousand times, one indeed accomplishes them all with ease.
O Goddess, she brings about rain during drought and likewise the cessation of rain as easily as play; whatever else is desired, she accomplishes.
When enraged, she slays all beings, and at all times she grants them life.
Wherever the falling of a thunderbolt occurs within the radiant sphere,
one should apply those various rites that are heard of or seen upon the surface of the earth, or even those that are spoken of, to those desired objects.

(199b) Thus ends the chapter on the procedure for the Supreme Wheel (*paramacakra*) within the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*, the third hexad, in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, belonging to the *Śiraccheda* of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the stream of Bhairava (*Bhairavasrotas*).
The Goddess said:
"O God of gods, the procedure for the distinguished sacrifices has been told;
now I wish to hear about the general great sacrifice."
O Lord of the gods of gods, O slayer of the bound, O ascetic, by the mere sight of him, even those powers of terrible prowess become like fettered beasts. Bhairava said:
In mountain caves and secret places, or on the shores of the great ocean,
or in cremation grounds established from the beginning, one should draw an auspicious maṇḍala.
[One should prepare the ground] with auspicious cow dung mixed with the ashes of a cremation ground.
One should smear the ground with that mixture, including blood-water.
Having collected cremation-ground ashes, one should draw an auspicious eight-petaled lotus in the cremation ground using the charcoal powder from the cremation ground,
forming a mandala with three lines.
The master of the line should mark out [the mandala] with a corpse-thread soaked in blood, measuring one cubit, two cubits, or likewise four or eight cubits.
The preceptor should be wrathful toward [obstacles], pure, skillful, and one who has reached the further shore of knowledge.
Adorned with a garland of skulls and smeared with fierce ashes,
he bears the vow of the five mudrās and is embellished by the limbs of Bhairava;
he is completely enveloped by a net of great elements.
One should draw the excellent maṇḍala that bestows formidable accomplishments:
square, with four doors, and adorned in the center by a lotus;
that auspicious lotus has eight petals and is presided over by the pericarp.
In its center, O Goddess, one should place Bhairavī of terrifying prowess,
facing south, blazing, of fearsome form, and inspiring dread.

Then, one should place the goddess Aghorā standing before him, possessing a fierce form and enraged, facing Bhairava due to her formidable prowess. Then, one should place Karṇamoḍhī in the west and the auspicious Umā in the north.
One should worship Nandi and Gaṇapati with a water-pot and a shield in the east; Ghoravacanā in the southeast; Krodhamūrtijā in the southwest;
the one named Krodharaudrā in the northwest; and Yogasaṃbhavā in the northeast.
One should place the twenty-four Yoginīs upon the tips of the filaments;
the Pretas, Rākṣasas, and Bhūtas shall constitute the second enclosure.
Having placed the [eight] directions in the third, one should place the goddesses in the fourth.
In the fifth [section], one should assign all the gods; in the sixth, the sixty Śākinīs and Guhyakas;
in the seventh, having assigned the planets (graha), and likewise the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) in the eighth;
in the ninth, having assigned the oceans, one should worship them according to one's capacity.
With perfumes, flowers, incense, and well-prepared foods and drinks;
with arched gateways adorned with banners and resounding with the tinkling of bells and small bells;
filled with the clamor of hand-drums and the tumultuous sound of ghaṭahikās.
Having fully worshipped the excellent mandala, he should then cause the disciple to enter. Having fasted and purified herself, she should be made to worship while facing north.
Touching her head with a skull-cup, he should place his joined palms upon her heart.
One should touch all the limbs of the son with the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga).
One should cause a bell, a large drum (paṭaha), and likewise a hand-drum (ḍamaru) to be sounded in front.
O Goddess, his face should be covered with cloth, and he should likewise hold an excellent handful of flowers.
Having circumambulated [the deity] and taken refuge in the Puradakṣiṇāmūrtti,
the disciple (putraka) should then cause a flower to be cast upon the Lord.
Whichever [deity] that flower falls upon, one should designate that as his lineage (kula).
One should apply [the ointment] to the forehead and other parts with [a substance] consecrated by the recitation of the heart-mantra;
having uncovered his face, one should show him the maṇḍala.
One should show him all that belongs to his deity and his station. Having caused him to hear the *samaya* and having prostrated before the Guru,
one should, according to the previous rule, cause him to hear the perfected [teaching] desired by the spiritual sons (*putraka*).
Having worshipped the Guru according to the prescribed rites, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth,
and having received the mantras born of the Kula lineage, as well as the vows and the commitments (samayas),
one should then propitiate the Yoginīs, the Mothers, and the Guru, O Goddess.

O Goddess, [the path] is purified by the sixty-three sacrificial oblations (caru) through the sequence of non-ascension (aroṣaṇā), reaching the end of the vows and the duties toward one's mother in due order;
it consists of the worlds of Bhairavī, surrounded by the Śaktis.
O sinless one, this excellent maṇḍala called Māyā has been described to you.
Now, for the sake of accomplishing the second vow, I shall describe the maṇḍala to you:
it is one cubit in size, with four doors, and adorned in the center with a lotus.
O Goddess, one should place Aghorā, who originates from Rudra, upon the pericarp.
Having placed the Yoginīs on the petals according to the previously mentioned sequence,
one should place the twenty-four [Yoginīs] previously described within the inner maṇḍala.
One should place the goddess Vāgbhavā in the east, Manobhavā in the southeast,
Yogajā in the south, and Pūtanā in the west;
likewise, one should place Ākāśajā in the southwest and Diṅmātṛ in the north.
O Goddess, the Mother of Pātāla is stationed in the northeast corner.
O Goddess, in the center is a golden pitcher filled with water,
joined with fruits and unbroken rice grains, and its neck encircled by a thread.

One who desires supreme accomplishment should perform consecration with a water-pot over which the *upahṛda* of the Goddess has been recited one thousand times. Having received permission and being thus consecrated, he shall be honored by the people of the earth.
Then one should perform the excellent vow originating from the sixty-three families;
likewise, the Bhairava-vow on the left side and the Cāmuṇḍā-vow.
One should always wear black garments and be anointed with black perfumes.
Wearing a black garland and adorned with earrings,
he was endowed with bracelets and ornaments and graced by the sound of anklets.
Clad in red garments and with red feet, assuming the form of a celestial woman,
silent and secluded in a solitary place, one should observe the vow of the vidyā.
For one month, or twelve months, the practitioner of mantra should perform this great vow.
Within a month, however, the great yogin beholds the Yoginī according to his desire.
Surrounded by them and having prepared the *caru* oblation, he may traverse the three worlds in an instant.
He becomes omniscient, the creator of all, and the agent of emanation and reabsorption.
O Goddess, by the power of the Yoginīs, one becomes both the destroyer and the creator.
Now I shall describe the second vow, belonging to the one who has the form of the terrible Kāpālika:
he wears a crown of skulls upon his head and is adorned with a garland of heads.
Adorning his hands, ears, and feet with ornaments made of bones,
he should carry a skull-cup in his left hand and a khaṭvāṅga staff in his right hand;
observing silence, he should wander through the cremation ground for sixty-three days.
At the conclusion of the vow, O lady of beautiful hips, the Mothers certainly enter the body,
O Goddess of the lords of gods, and bestow supreme perfection. They become ageless and immortal, capable of both cursing and granting grace.
He becomes the supreme practitioner even for all the three worlds. The Goddess said:
[The place] is a great and terrifying abode of spirits, crowded with hosts of *bhūtas* and *saṃhagas*.
O Lord, how can beings of little merit attain the state of Śiva’s consort there?
At night, the Kula-born Śaktis and the great ascetic Parāvīras are present;
yet, O All-pervading One, you have not taught the Yoga associated with their presence.
The powers of the Essence of the Siddhas— namely *siddhā*, *susiddhā*, and *bhūta*—
manifest their presence wherever the Lord is present,
just as they become perceptible in the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) within the form of the mantra.
"O Śaṅkara, tell me likewise of the divine mudrās, conducts, and observances.
Bhairava said:
"O lady of excellent countenance, the ash is fierce, the great incense, and the great lamp."
(201b) O Goddess, wherever Bhairavī is present, there she dwells;
she is Mahāmudrā, Karodyā, Kālī, and Alāsthiśṛṅkhalā.
Vikaṭā, Karaṅkiṇī, Kabandhā, and Kroṣṭrakī,
as well as Kapāla, are declared to be the supreme bodies of Bhairava;
where these, O Goddess, are bound together, there the Lord of Beings (Bhūtapati) himself resides.
Wherever the powers (śaktis) are seen, adorned with the five mudrās, their faces filled with the syllable *pheṃ*, and who are the lords of spirits (*bhūteśas*),
there indeed is the offering (*upahāra*) of the deceased established within the great conch.
Facing south, one should personally worship the assembly of Mothers there;
O fair-faced one, at the time of sacrifice, that hymn which issues from the mouths of the Bhairavīs with a roar as great as Mahābhairava is sung there.
O lady of excellent complexion, the Yoginīs, Mātṛs, Lāmās, Śākinīs, and likewise the Guhyakas,
manifest their presence here and there;
wherever the clans of Svadharmapūtanā and others are seen.
Vīreśa’s seat of authority is there; success is not far off.
Where even the Kaṅka, Rudra, and Mahātapa remain in writing, how much more so when the cremation ground is actually present? What need is there for further recitation?
Śarabhā, Suvīrā, Vajribhārā, Asabhā, Cakravartinī, Pauṇḍrī, Khaḍgakarṇā,
Mahātapā, Cakravegā, Mahāyāmyā, Subhadrā, and Gajakarṇikā.
Carā, Somadevī, Gavākṣī, Vāyuvegagā,
Airāvatī, Mahānāsā, Daṃṣṭrālī, Sukarkaśā, Vedhanī,
Bhaṭṭā, Droṇā, and likewise Kākenakā.

O Great Ascetic, wherever the names of the yogis are uttered, there the cremation grounds themselves come into presence at that very moment. Now listen, O Goddess, to the arrangement of the cremation grounds within the yoga.
O fair-faced one, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in yoga according to the path taught by Śiva—
whether in groups of six, four, seven, or nine— then,
O highly fortunate lady, perform it in the abode of the cremation ground.
O Goddess, one should then place the Lord of the Cremation Ground, who is strewn with fierce ashes and consecrated with the *kālakaṣaṭka* mantra, in a counter-clockwise direction.
One should place Mahākāla in the south and likewise in the southeast;
having placed Parvateśa on the throne, one should place Nandin in the petal of the northeast direction.
One should place Bhairava in the north and likewise Marmaka in the northwest.
One should install Kṣetrapāla in the southeast, and the terrifying Bhayāvaha in the west.
One should always place Aṭṭahāsa in the southwest,
along with Betāla, Chagala, the pot-colored [deity], Hetuka, and Mahābala.
Piṅgala, Gajakarṇa, Dantika, Bhṛkuṭīmukha, Kailāsa, Nāḍijaṅgha, Gokarṇa, Kapālin,
Dantika, Lohajaṅgha, Ūrdhvakeśa, and Mahāmukha.
One should install Mahodara, Bhūteśa, Bhṛṅgin, Gaṇanāyaka, Jvālāmukha, and Droṇa with their respective name-mantras. Likewise,
one should install Aiti-vṛkṣāṅka, Karaja, Paṭa, and Aśvattha.
There is a tree that is both barren and dark, the *tamāla* and the *dhāribhadraka*.
One should draw trees in the directions starting from the south and ending with the southwest (*naiṛta*).
[One should also depict] a place covered by a multitude of people, crowded with herons and vultures.
One should place a *karavīra* flower upon the petal in the south-eastern direction, which is surrounded on all sides by blazing flames;
O Goddess of the Gods, it should be crowded with hosts of *vetālas* by means of the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*.

Having established [the deity] upon the eastern petal with Śiva accompanied by the *visarga*, the yogi should place the great lineage of Yoga, O Goddess, along with the seed-syllable of fire (*raḥ*). One should then install the seed-syllable of wind (*yaḥ*) upon the northern petal, that of Vāyu.
O Goddess of good vows, one should establish the son of Kaśyapa with the seed-syllable *cala* (ca) in the western quarter,
and at its end, with the syllable *bhairava*.
Below that is the fierce cremation ground, surrounded by millions of spirits.
Yamaghaṇṭā, Karālā, Mahāvaktrā, Bhayānakā, Bhīmakī,
Kroṣṭrakī, and Ghaṇṭā with her blazing face.
Bhṛkuṭī, Vidyujjihvā, Gokarṇī, Kumbhakarṇikā, Viḍālī, Pūtanā, Kramaṇī, Krāmaṇī,
Garjanī, Bhadrakālī, Vāyuvegā, and Patadbalā.
Bhīmā, Kroṣṭakī, Sumanā, and Devakī,
as well as Manovegā, Mahārāvā, Bhīmakī, and Citrakānanā—
these [goddesses] adorned with garlands, wreaths, and strings of flowers, stood here surrounding the circle.
Drinking much blood from skull-cups filled with blood—
thus, O lady of excellent complexion, the arrangement of the cremation ground may be performed either by means of mantras or through meditation,
or by means of one [mantra] for the six limbs.
When the seed-mantra of the Upahr̥t is offered, it becomes effective in an instant.
The Goddess said:
"O sinless Lord, you have not previously spoken to me of the perfected mantras."
"O Lord of Gods, tell me now that by the mere remembrance of which sovereignty, yoga, and enjoyment arise.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to these mantra-words issued from the limbs of Aghorī;
sovereignty arises, O Goddess, even from their mere recollection.
Endowed with fortitude, established in the Kula, and preceded by the syllable Om, [it is] Śiva.
Ghoreśvarī begins with the letter *A* and consists of the *kalās*; likewise, there is Pūrvaśiva.
When pronounced twice in reverse order, it is joined with the same [sequence] of utterances:
*haha hūṃ*, *dahaha hūṃ*, and the syllables ending in *phaṭ*.
O Śaṅkarī, this mantra of twenty-four syllables, when recited one hundred thousand times,
makes the practitioner a master of all mantras taught for yogis.
Preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *rañjikā*, it is indeed that very [mantra].
The letter *ha* is uttered twice, followed by the cruel word *aṃde*.
This supreme eight-syllable mantra of the Goddess is the Amogha-hṛdaya;
with its heart-constituent syllables, it is the supreme performer of all rites.
O fair-faced one, [the mantra] consists of Śiva repeated twice, ending with Bhairava;
then the letter *ha* ending in Amṛta, followed again by a double utterance.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *tāraka* ending in *phaṭ* upon the head, O fair-faced one, with the excellent mantras according to the previously mentioned division, it is unfailing and performs all rites.
First is the word *haṃ he ha ha*; second is *hūṃ hrīṃ hūṃ haḥ*.
The third word is remembered as being joined with *ha ha phaṭ* at the end.
O lady of beautiful countenance, this Śikhā-mantra, consisting of eleven syllables, has been described;
it performs manifold rites most effectively.
O Goddess of excellent complexion, the word for the spleen (*plīha*) ends with the letter *na*;
O highly fortunate one, it is remembered as the eye of the Goddess, performing all rites.
When the letter *la*, which possesses four qualities, is deprived of its [original] state and adorned by the void (*kha*), [it becomes the seed-syllable].
At the end, Bhairava and the Preceptor are struck twice;
joined with that very [seed-syllable] "saivahai," this nine-syllabled armor (kavaca) should be employed everywhere in the ritual of protection, O lady of excellent vows.
First, the word "hara" preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *hrīḥ*;
immediately thereafter, one should utter the second word ending in the accusative case along with its optional variations.
Then follows "ha ha hūṃ phaṭ," and fourthly, the word "krūra" accompanied by *hrīḥ*.
O Goddess, this mantra of the weapon (*astra*), ending with the word *krūra*, is the means for its accomplishment.
That supreme weapon of the Goddess, spoken by Śiva,
consists of twenty-one divine syllables and sets all ritual actions in motion.
Uṃ hūṃ, make difficult to sustain; jrūṃ drū kuṃ dhrūkkari sirjini jihi ha haḥ; the heart-mantra for the goddess of the feet, which performs all rites.
These mantras, O Great Goddess, are unfailing and possess terrifying prowess.
Since they have been spoken by you, O Sovereign of the Gods of Gods, what more do you wish to ask?

Thus ends the Chapter on General and Particular [Matters] in the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*, within the third hexad of the twenty-four thousand verse *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra concerning the Severing of the Head, in the Vidyāpīṭha of the Bhairava Current.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, you have been enjoined to the observance of the rules of conduct;
for in the practice of the yogins, supreme perfection arises."
"O Lord, what is the nature of the *samaya* (vows), and what is the nature of the conduct?
What indeed should be the activity? You ought to explain this.
Bhairava said:
I shall now declare the limits of the *samaya*, which are difficult to find in those tantras:

"O Goddess, he who is devoted to Śiva and the *āpana* [practice] is indeed the preceptor (*ācārya*). O high-minded Goddess, those who are gurus in the tantra for the sake of practitioners (*sādhaka*)..."

Those scriptures, the perfected ones, and the yoginīs who have ascended to heaven—these should not be reviled nor should they be disparaged; rather, one should worship them constantly. Having established the threefold division, one should learn these three words.
One should not allow attachment to another deity even by way of jest;
one should speak of the Guru as taught in the Tantra, or else cause [the disciple] to enter through various means.
Those who remain greedy for sense objects abide in a river that flows away from the goal.
He should always remain indifferent toward the conduct and activities of the *samaya*.
Pervaded by non-duality, he should perceive the Self everywhere.
Restraint arising from the practice of the "woman" (*nārīcaryā*) constitutes the observance of the vow.

On each lunar day (tithi), one should perform [the practice] adorned with the observances (niyamas). Through one's own discernment, one proceeds according to the tradition of the *lāmās*. Furthermore, while the [mantra] moves through the ears, one should always remain free from anger.

Thus, O Great Goddess, the eight pledges (*samaya*) of the *lāmā* class, which bestow accomplishment, have been declared. Now hear the pledges of the *śākinīs*. One should avoid revealing my mantras and should completely shun the tantra.
Constantly reciting mantras and established in meditative absorption, one should perform the sacrifice; one who delights in Śiva and feeds on blood should always remember the Sound (nāda).
During the period of the sun’s southern course, one must not transgress the rules of conduct (samaya).
One should perform the blameless rite concerning animals when it is purified by mantras. Furthermore, one should not allow the mind to feel agitation even when its own species is being harmed.
One should protect one’s own family with effort, guarding against the confusion that arises from the improper transmission of the lineage.
O illustrious lady, even a minister who occupies his position must exert himself to perform his duties correctly among those who have transgressed the traditional order,
and he must conduct himself with propriety in public squares.
One should not harbor resentment upon seeing the fierce conduct [of others], whether within one's own family or in another lineage; one should always remain peaceful in mind.
[This applies] toward the group of women of the Kāśyapa clan through the actions of speech, mind, and body.
One should offer a welcome, water for the feet, and the arghya offering, and cause the progeny to perform [these rites] everywhere.
One should eat together with the yogis that which is the delight of the sixty-three families;
as for the most excellent food offering (naivedya), one should especially cause that to be given.
O lady of excellent hips, one should cause Bhairavī to be given even within one's own circle with effort;
otherwise, it should not be given elsewhere except to one who possesses formidable excellence.
O Goddess, a mixture [of recipients] regarding the food offering (*naivedya*) gives rise to the obstruction of great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*).

Therefore, those who desire the fruits [of their practice] and have taken refuge in the vow of the Śākinīs should protect [this teaching] with effort. They should not kill living beings in vain, nor should they offer sacrifices and the like in vain, or otherwise cause harm to living beings.
Or, one who is appointed to the task of a messenger, having reached the earth through yoga,
certainly falls by transgressing her out of greed for the gift;
such are the rules, O Goddess, regarding the six Kālīs in the great heat.
O Mistress of Beings, I have now declared the Śākinīs who have been installed;
I shall now fully explain those who bestow the perfection of yoga upon yogins.
Having risen daily at dawn and having carefully performed ritual ablution, one should proceed with diligence.

Having paid homage to the venerable Guru, perform your worship elsewhere thereafter; O lady of excellent vows, even when the Supreme Wheel is out of sight, meditate upon it and worship it. Whatever actions one performs, they shall indeed be accomplished for that person.
O fair-faced one, since Śiva, the Lord of Beings, bestows knowledge by resorting to the body of the teacher, therefore one should always worship him.
Even brothers are always to be honored, as were the Cakravartins in former times;
one should cause this to be done for all others according to family custom.
This applies to sisters who reside in their own lineage as well as those who reside in another lineage.
Even in times of adversity, one should never abandon these; always maintain your own proper conduct.
For those who remain steadfast in adversity as they do in prosperity, one should be equal in both suffering and happiness under all circumstances.

In this world, O lady of beautiful countenance, he who is always hostile toward his own kin and he who flees from them— what kind of friend is such a person? O illustrious one, worthy of constant salutation, Śaṅkhapūṣa is not a destroyer of vows.
In the sixty-third chapter, their own vow is the cessation [of those practices]:
one should not revile liquor or meat, nor should one offer oblations at crossroads.
[This applies to] those who are intoxicated, insane, naked, negligent, or of deluded mind.
O lady of excellent hips, one should honor the traveler on the path with the Vajragupta [mudrā].
One should offer hospitality to those who have sons from battle and to those observing vows.
O highly fortunate one, such is hospitality; others are merely plunderers of remaining goods.
O Goddess, the practitioner should always perform the obligatory and occasional rites, as well as the concluding rituals, even while on the most formidable terrains.
O Mistress of the Gods, even within the interior of his own home, whether waking, standing, sleeping, or moving about, he should remain steadfast.
Having visualized [her] with the cremation ground, one should proceed in all rites.
O Goddess, Mahākālī, who destroys flaws and is connected to the self, is well-guarded;
she always assumes the form of the universe and consists of Nāda and Bindu.
O illustrious lady, although he perceives himself as the foremost among all yogis, nevertheless,
apart from the Śaiva [tradition],
his mantra, secret vows, conduct, and the manifestation of his own power remain hidden.
One should not disclose it during a dispute, nor should one cause the meaning of the Tantra to be performed [in such a way].
One who is naked [in spirit] should perform the worship of the deity together with Śakti.
If one should become agitated through negligence, then one should remember the Brahman.
One should worship the owls of Śiva and not hate those who live by night.
With a joyful soul, one should always salute all the Kātakas.
O lady of excellent vows, one must not violate the vow except in the case of [one's own] lineage.
Even if there is a conflict with a great attraction for those established in the teaching of the Goddesses,
it arises from the sight of a single word of Śiva regarding the occurrence of a great sin.
O you of excellent vows, one should proceed in all rites with the conduct of a Vāmācārin, by transgressing the conventions of the Ācāryas and their customary behavior. Likewise,
one should act through the offering of wine to the deity and at the gathering of garlands.
I have declared to you those who abide by the commitments (*samaya*) of those whose wheels (*cakra*) are mounted upon the Middle Way (*madhyamā*).

Now I shall describe to you the conduct of the lineages (*gotra*) and the activities of the families (*kula*). O Great Goddess, in the great yoga during the gathering of all lineages, [this is taught].
One should not cause any deficiency in ritual actions through conversation.
A lapse in conduct or action is purified by the gift of a *paśu*;
a lapse in speech is purified by the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) for the great yogi.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, effort must always be made regarding speech;
and, O illustrious lady, it should be practiced by practitioners who desire success. The seven spheres of the great lords of yoga have been proclaimed.
Brahmā, Rudrakumāra, Viṣṇu, and likewise the Lord of the Pretas;
the Lord of Indra and the Creator of the host of Mātṛs—
[their respective weapons are] the water-pot, the trident, the discus, and likewise the spear.
The staff, the thunderbolt, and the skull are proclaimed as the family mudrās (gotramudrā).
O Great Goddess, these are the mudrās for the union with the Lord of Heroes (Vīreśa).
O high-minded one, [the birds] are the swan, the vulture, the peacock, and the king of the yakṣas.
The buffalo, the lion of the family, and these born of the Mothers—
O fair-faced one, these are the thirty-two families of the Yoginīs here.
Among them, O lady of excellent complexion, seven are the principal and great ones.
The lotus, the charming one, the salutation, and the red-dyed one;
likewise the skull-bowl, the khaṭvāṅga staff, the trident, and the staff.
For the yogi, this constitutes the eight mudrās of all the families (kula).
Indeed, the yogi enumerates the families by means of those very [mudrās] as the primary ones. Now hear separately the number of the ascetic families and their respective mudrās.
The conch, discus, mace, trident, sword, and noose, followed by the knife,
chain, spear, thunderbolt, shield, and tomara—
these are proclaimed as the family mudrās of those belonging to the Samīpa-gotra.
O highly fortunate one, now hear the family seals (kula-mudrās) of those who are mixed:
the hare, the nose, the spear, the banner,
the pitcher, the stone, the ear-ornament, the crest, the matted hair, and likewise the coiled earring.
O Goddess, while moving, the Karṇamudrā and the Saṃkīrṇakulanāyikā reveal these groups of clanswomen (*gotrajāṃ gaṇām*).
For one whose wheel is awakened, O Great Adept, there is a twofold division in each case.
The Mothers are proclaimed in their sequential order starting from the east and so forth.
One should perform the deposition of the wheels (cakranyāsa) with Vīreśa in the northeastern direction.
By this sequential method, one [establishes] both the Kulas and the Apakulas.
One should establish the mixed and distinct [deities] during the pressing of the womb.
One should place them within the pericarp of the wheel of Bhairaveśa.
Having understood the sequence, then perform the worship through yoga according to its majesty.
The navel-cakra is the heart of Kāla and of Madhyama;
the space between the eyebrows is that of Prasāda and likewise of Śrīkaṇṭha.
The place up to the end of the forehead is known as Sadāśiva on the path of the void.
In the center of the wheel of Tārā and the others, this Bhairavī is remembered as supreme.
Above that of the god Mahābhairava is the attainment of yoga;
it is the abode of all the siddhis of Brahmā and the other lords of the gods, O Mistress of the Suras.
(206a) The arrangement of the family circle and likewise the sons of the lineage; O illustrious one, they speak of the sixfold divisions of the lineage by means of the six [groups].
O highly fortunate one, they declare that for those who have not reached the navel, supreme accomplishment arises from contact;
likewise, the lower limb is the lower lip.
When the limbs are restrained, there is the cessation of obstruction through the single-limb manifestation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
O Goddess, there is great enmity when there is equality of *sāman* in the upward and downward divisions; likewise,
one should indicate it through words born of the origins of wind and fire, as well as those of water and earth,
and similarly by those that are unfriendly and produced from the enclosure.

That which is unattended by those of long-standing practice, disconnected, devoid of meaning, or purposeless; that which is self-serving yet spoken by those who know only their own interests—by such means, nothing at all can be achieved even from afar. There is suffering through words that are merely smoky (ambiguous), but great danger through those that are ablaze (explicit).
And one should indeed draw them connected by means of their respective languages and gestures. For those [deities] who dance, one should prescribe the *namaskāra* ending in *svāhā*;
for those ending in *huṃ*, the word *bheda*; and for those ending in *phaṭ*, the rites of recollection (*smaraṇa*) and so forth.
One should indicate contentment, peace, and nourishment by means of the vowels from *tā* to *ra*.
Now listen to the indicators of the Yoginīs of the Earth, which reveal the arising of various types of questions and the sequence of words in the *Nirghaṭa*.
"O Rāma, the immovable mountains flow"—this is considered the first question;
"the union of the reclining [posture]" is proclaimed by me today as the second;
"this substance, in blue bile, at the measure of a sesame seed," is the third.

O virtuous lady, in the fourth introduction, during the terrifying movement, as the cave collapses, the sixth and seventh [stages] reach their end; Jambha desired to devour him. This fifth question, which must be broken through with effort, has been told to you.
These are proclaimed as the "climbing" (prāsāruha) and the "sitting" (aniṣadya) [yogas]. Thus, the seventh is the supreme union of the "nail-growing" (kīlaruha).
These are the "disease-sleep" (vyādhiprasupti) and the "foam-like" (phenamena), which are considered the two-fold measure.
O Goddess, in the eighth [chapter], the question is difficult to penetrate even for the lords of yoga.
(206b) *Timīdivitalāṅgāni vīvimīnamīnalā.*

"Gamana" is the great question, the ninth, difficult to traverse and supreme. "Kini" is Mahāsunī, the great Nārāsinī, who repeatedly devours men. Karākṣariṇī is the tenth, and likewise among the Mātrīs.
This great question is difficult to penetrate:
"In what place, amidst the remaining trees and waters, does the birth [occur]? Just so, the tenth great question is difficult to understand.
Desiring the path in the great terror, one should utter the refined Paiśāca [language].
O fair-faced one, this is the first division, even though it has been carried forward today;
I have not yet stabilized it for the analysis of the second.
Today I drink the breaker of the trident, the piercer of the third;
O lady of good vows, the *lāmās* situated in the *avakāra* [syllable] are satisfied by these.
O Goddess of the gods, the piercing of the fourth is thus proclaimed.
"O fair-faced one, this modaka, which has been attached to me for seven lifetimes,
shall today come to my mouth;
it will leap up from the peak of the Prasāda in a mere moment, as if to be swallowed."
Intent upon that, he will arrive at a hundred thousand beautiful mantras.
Having gone through the sky by means of great austerity, he will reach the most formidable great accomplishment;
having ascended [the vehicle], he will arrive on the seventh day.
The life-force of the lord of men is said to be drunk today on the eighth;
on the ninth, one mounted upon a mountain in the abode of the gods smells fragrances.
On the hundredth [day], Mahānāsā moves about, and for him there is the *rocanā* [ointment].
"Taking that wood, let us go to another [place].
Such are the questions and the distinctions among the yoginīs at their gathering;
they have been told to you, O Goddess of Gods, as the supreme secrets more secret than the secret.
O Goddess, most secret one, listen to the conceptualization of speech:
"Abhivādana" means "enter," and "nārisīta" means "welcome.
*Lāsabhā* is known as mother; *bhāminī* is remembered as sister. *Duhinī* and *duhitā* are the names for daughter; *śvaśrū* and *samanī* are known as mother-in-law.
*Nīminī* is the name for brother’s wife, and likewise *sunayā* is for wife.
*mātṛjye* is said to mean maternal uncle (*mātula*); *pīḍimistha* likewise means father (*pitṛ*); *triminī* similarly means grandson (*naptṛ*); *vīlusī* means great-grandson (*pautra*);
*manāmahe* is spoken as maternal grandfather (*pitāmaha*); and *noniḥ* is proclaimed to mean mother (*mātṛ*).
The devotees of the Goddess attained prosperity; they were released from milk and curds.
Likewise, there was clarified butter, honey, and food in heaven.
This should be understood as the "Secret of the Tree" (Dumagūḍha), O Mistress, which brings success through recitation.

"I am drinking," "I have drunk," and "I have come"—[these are the forms]. "I am about to go" is called *nigāniṣye*; "I am sleeping" is called *supta*. The speech-forms *upta*, *vijyema*, *vinaka*, *bhāṣā*, and *nilīnī* are likewise [to be understood].
The body of the ocean is known as Anānī;
O Goddess, the mountains are the thighs, and likewise the seven rivers are the hips.
The gods are to be known as the breasts, and the thirty-three deities are recorded as the cities.
Piśitāla is likewise to be accomplished; Subhuja, Paśavara, Urdhvabhoja, Pakṣī, Ḍhiḍhila, Hastimat, Nukamjavā, and Aśva are likewise; they know Anīḍa to be Aja.
The donkey is said to be Khagara; cows are Srota and Javā;
O Goddess, the buffalo is Japā; the camel is Mīna and Dvira;
likewise, the tiger is Puranmāsa; and the Śīrakola is the deer.
O lady of beautiful hips, Sahinī, as well as the serpents and the remaining castes,
are recorded as those who collect materials for sacrifices among the performers of rites;
and there is great mutual conflict among these very groups, O sinless one.
Thousands indeed arise, following their own natures and modes of conduct:
Yoginī, Rūpiṇī, Lāmā, Śākinī, Hīṇālinī, and Khagī. (207b)
Cūlivilātrī, Khagagāpeśī, Dohinījalā, Revatī, Vedhanī, Lūkī, Paḍabhī, Raktinīhiṣā,
Karoṭī, Kāluśī, Bhadrā, Dundubhī, Mukharā, and Turā.
These are the twenty-four names used in the discourse concerning the *lāmās*:
"flesh," "succulent," "meat," "that which belongs to the dead," "food of the *rākṣasas*, "cruel," "pure," "the essence of all," "born of living beings," and "the water of the body."
The liquid, the slimy, the vital, the *jasauraja*, the mantra-born,
the black, the yellow, the white, and the tenth is known as blood;
then the wooden, the cursed, the dead, the sleeping, the unrefined, and that which is born from the funeral pyre.
One who has a hundred breaths, is nameless, and possesses the characteristics of a hungry ghost (preta);
who is empty, situated in the state of the vital air (samāna), and is an abode of moisture—such is the dead man.
[He cries out: "Eat! Eat! Devour! Drink! Consume! Devour! and "O you who have no heart!"
Prāṣya, voḍha— these are the ten names for consumption.
Pretālaya, mahāghora, śmaśāna, niśibhūṣaṇa, sarvojā,
śeṣaṇa, bhīṣa, and caṇḍarākṣasadhāmakam.
The Illumination, the Speech, the Darkness, and the Intense Darkness;
the Abode of Lāmā, the Great Siddhi, the Hundred Lights, and the Hundred Blazes— O Goddess of Gods, these are proclaimed as the cremation grounds that are the abodes of Śiva.
O Goddess, listen now to this which I consider more secret than the secret, the source of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). A woman who is not a eunuch, O Goddess—eat the book and consume it.
[With the mantra] *samātājīśvasma phet*, the wife [should eat] the flame surrounded by the hair-tuft.
One should make the *lasaṃtaplī*, the blood, the terrible flesh, and the *pheca* [into] a vessel.
Then the yoginī, whose form is that of the Nameless, should say:
"O Śākinī, go far away! Make the small hearth a great fire-pit!"
O Goddess, the syllable *kṣāṃ* is likewise to be known as the salutation;
these are the single-syllable utterances of the group of Mothers (*mātṛgaṇa*).
O lady of excellent vows, they are the forms of women who are destined to become curds.
(208a) Listen now with a one-pointed mind to those [women] whom I shall describe:
the woman who possesses the luster of a lotus stalk and whose face momentarily resembles a lotus petal.
She who always delights in white garments, who is fond of fresh sandalwood paste,
and who takes pleasure in the company of Śiva— she should be known as one born of the lineage of Śiva. She has a luster like molten gold and is fond of red and yellow garments.
That species which is rich in a sweet fragrance should be known as belonging to the sphere of Brahmā; and that which is dark like a blue lotus, fond of blue perfumes and garments,
and possesses the fragrance of a blue water-lily, is born of the lineage of Viṣṇu.
She who is the consort of the Moon, possessing a fair luster, whose form is like a plantain tree,
who constantly has the fragrance of a lotus stalk, and belongs to the Atri lineage— she is known as Gaurī.
As for the woman who is reddish-fair, wearing red garments, and endowed with beauty—
She who possesses the fragrance of jasmine and blue lotus is indeed born of the Kaumārī lineage;
she who is yellowish-dark in complexion and fond of auspicious colors and garments,
and who has the scent of the śirīṣa flower, is born of the Vārāhī lineage.

Āpītā has a yellowish complexion, she is fond of yellow-colored garments, and she always possesses the fragrance of camphor; for she is indeed Bhairavī, born of the lineage. These seven families of yoginīs have been described by me.
Now I shall fully explain how one is known as a *samayin*.
I shall speak of the piercing of speech (*vācavedha*), the description of one’s own mudrā and colors,
and the syllable of the *Kula-vidyā* which he practices through union.
He binds his own seal and utters the name of one born of his own clan.
He approaches women from the left, but for those on the left, he goes from the right.
He speaks with his left hand and gazes with a look from his left eye.

One who is joyful and contented with the samaya is called a *samayin*. One should speak somewhat with the *kula-bījas* to a *kulaputraka*, and one should not abandon one's own *kula-kriyā*; one should exert oneself in it.
One who recites the mantra of a woman of noble birth is a *samayin*, while one who kisses her is a *cumbaka*.
Or, having performed the salutation while mounted upon the left [leg], who would not bow to one who is truly humble?
At their meeting, all those birds remain well-settled and offer salutation.
Quickly digging in the left big toe, it draws lines for stability;
likewise, it scratches its head with the left hand while casting a sidelong glance.
Bound by the conventions of their conduct, those birds who remain with their essence intact communicate their own ignorance to one another through their respective dispositions.
O lady of excellent vows, [this occurs] either on the cheek, or on the chin, or even at the tip of the nose.
With teeth, fingers, and sidelong glances, they should observe the recitation and the mantra;
O Maheśānī, they communicate their true state to one another:
"Rare indeed is this earth among the classes of beings, nourished by the five nectars."
The Rūpikā, Cūmbikā, Lāmā, Parāvṛttā, Arthapālikā, Anivartā, and Hṛdvedhī— these arise from previous births;
yet at the time of union, they do not bestow supreme accomplishment.
First, she makes her presence known by a flush of red; then, breaking the silence, she speaks.
Having withdrawn her meaning and then taken it up again, she subsequently touches him.
Whether he is desired or not, whether he stands still or even engages in conversation, she kisses him.
She who kisses is to be known as Sānu; she is a Yoginī proud of her power.
With sidelong glances, a frowning face, and the knitting of her brows, she threatens as it were. By her terrifying sighs, one should designate her as Lāmā.
She indeed displays various gestures during union;
she feigns fear and turns away, yet is refined;
with eyes perpetually wide open, she is observed to be performing secret acts when looked upon.
One who has gone away and returns,
who behaves with apprehension, who is fickle and looks upward— such a woman one should designate as a "girl" (bālikā).
She may also be recognized by her mental gaze, her carrying of burdens, or her handling of clods of earth with her feet.
If she is seen by the Lord with a wooden staff at the edge of a cloth, she does not live;
one should know her to be irreversible, for she is declared incurable.
One should designate as a *vedhinī* that woman who, by means of another's disease arising from a foreign land, performs a sacrifice with the blood of a wicked person; she possesses the conduct,
observances, activities, and characteristics of the Lords of Yoga.
The secret has been told to you; now listen to the conduct of the Siddhas.
Meditating upon Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā, he is identical with the universal form.
Absorbed in the state beyond conduct, he abides in the body of an Avadhūta.
Eating the five products of the cow, he remained like one who is mute, deaf, and blind; with his self restrained, he was called Aniruddha; wearing a shaven head, he was known as Yāmalī;
and having taken up the *viḍālī* vow, he dwelt among all beings as a cat.
The support of the twenty-five principles, the six-footed one, whose eyes are the six stages;
endowed with all offerings, the beholder of the ten paths;
the observer of the sixty-three vows, who always has his abode in the mouth.

While [the world] sleeps, he remains awake; while he himself is awake, he is in the state of deep sleep; he is of the nature of both. Abiding within the Great Conqueror of Death, and without the powers of immortality, seeing the waking state everywhere, he perceives everything within the Self.

Everywhere he is the food and the eater, the illuminator at the end of every cycle; established in the state of awakening, he perceives the time of five kalās within the six divisions of deities and lunar days during the great heat.
In the domain of the unawakened, while tending the cattle of consciousness,

those who are not deluded regarding the withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) [perceive] the eyes as consisting of the primordial deity and the ears as eternally consisting of Rudra, within the nature of the channels (nāḍī), wheels (cakra), and so forth.
The mouth and belly are pervaded by *kalā*, and the body by the activity of the universe;
through *kalā* it bears the essence of splendor, eternally on the path of great austerity.
Even for one who has undertaken the greatest vow, the terrible Bhairava himself is the destroyer of the moon.
O Goddess of the Gods, he who consists of the act of attaining heaven, yet whose nature is knowledge for the destruction of that very heaven,
is Bhairava; established and concealed within [all things], he is the Leader.

O illustrious one, even though he is independent, that Vīreśa Sadāśiva performs auspicious and inauspicious acts by means of obstructing the powers (śaktis). He is fully endowed with knowledge and realization, yet he is deluded by Mahāmāyā.

That leader Śrīkaṇṭha does not know his own self; established solely in the form of the power Raudrī, he is the soul of destruction for the Great-Souled One. He destroys all darkness, and he is indeed within the heart of the three worlds.
He who is always under the control of the powers (*śakti*), relying upon the path of power (*śaktimārga*),
and performs his actions through the grace of power and so forth— he is the middling [practitioner].
But he who has taken refuge in a body within the splendor of that *tantra* during the divisions of time (*kālakalā*)— [he is the superior practitioner].
He who withdraws the vital breath even when the time has arrived is called "sakala" (with parts).
He who knows exclusively his own wheel, the peak, and the Kula conduct;
he who possesses devotion to me and is purified by the Kula—he is the teacher and the leader.
By means of mantras and powers (śaktis), the three [leaders] are at that time forcibly overcome.
In the absence of a leader, he becomes a "reborn leader" (punarbhū-nāyaka).
Proclaiming ignorance through the tantras, he conceals his secret conduct.
That teacher who follows the conduct of the Siddhas should praise the three paths;
he is well-concealed by the mudrā and the conch, surrounded by the eight [attendants].
That supreme follower of the conduct of the Siddhas should wander through the fierce lands.
The skull-bearer, the eye-gesture, the [wrathful] laugh, and the great asceticism;
the fangs, the matted locks, and likewise the face—these gestures are employed for protection.
The trident, the lotus, the discus, the spear, and likewise the thunderbolt.
The staff (daṇḍa), the trident (śūla), and the razor (kṣurī) are remembered as the group of messenger-mudrās (dūtīmudrā).
O Goddess, I shall now describe their characteristics according to their functions:
having formed the hand with half a finger [of space] between the index and middle fingers, O fair-faced one, this is the *nigvama* [mudrā].
For one who guards with one hand, those known as the *yāmala* [mantras] are two hands long;
they should be employed for the extraction of blood, as well as for paralyzing and killing.

The *pada-pracārikā* is indeed beneficial for traveling through the sky. When the hands are clenched into fists with the thumbs raised and facing downward, positioned at the forehead, these are proclaimed as the *netra-mudrās*.
By binding this [mudrā], the yogi becomes possessed of divine vision;
he who knows it shall bring all the siddhis under the control of yogis.
Indeed, when placed upon the regions of the limbs up to the crown of the head, it is that very [mudrā].
The mudrā originating from the khaṭvāṅga is always situated upon the half-thumb;
one should employ this for the immobilization of all beings,
as well as for the transformation of form, in yoga, and in the two fourfold vows.
When the two index fingers are placed at the tips of the fangs, bent and positioned at the mouth,
this is known as the *daṃṣṭrā-mudrā* (Fang Mudrā), which destroys all living beings—
including gods, dānavas, and humans— in the act of universal withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
And for the immobilization of armies, one should employ this [mudrā] during great austerity.
With the thumb joined to the index finger and all the others fingers contracted,
it is known as the Jaṭāmudrā, which should be placed upon one's own head.
If one who is inflamed with anger binds the *jaṭāmudrā*, he could destroy the entire three worlds; how much more so the humans on earth?
[In this mudrā,] the two index fingers and the two little fingers are joined at their tips.
Having withdrawn the hands and placed them upon the vessel, one should stir with the tongue.
Then, making the sound "hā hā" while the remaining fingers are held like the thumb,
this is declared to be the Vaktra-mudrā, which effects the great dissolution.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, the eight mudrās have been declared for the sake of protection; O Goddess, they exist within the characteristics [of the body] through awakening.
Having become as mobile as a staff, with both hands placed at the root of the ears—
The *śūla* [mudrā] consists of three *huṃ* sounds at the dissolution of the petals of the Rudra-form.
Having turned the hands toward each other and pressed the wrists together,
with all the fingers joined and their tips bent downward, it is called the *padma* [mudrā].
Having placed the left thumb upon the right hand,
when the index finger is extended during the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), it is called the "body wheel" (*śarīracakra*).
With the upper parts of the body, those two arms should be pressed against one another;
this is indeed proclaimed as the Śakti-mudrā, which removes all obstacles.
The little finger and the thumb of the two hands should be joined and established in the placement (nyāsa).
The joints located at the tips of the fingers and the diamond-peak (*vajramūrdha*) [mudrās] are supreme.
Placing the hands on the sides of the knees with the feet joined together,
one who holds the staff (*daṇḍa*)— characterized by shaking the head and snapping the mouth— is the sustainer of all rites.
Having firmly pressed the two hands together as a fist, with one hand released from the other,
and having likewise stepped upon it with the other foot,
O fair-faced one, the fingers should follow into the middle of the hand, and those very fingers [should be positioned] there.
Saṃhātavarjanī, Kṣura, Ghorīśvarī, and Priyā—
O highly fortunate one, these mudrās are eternally effective for the accomplishment of all goals.
O Goddess, O lady of great asceticism, they belong to the Śaktis through the binding mantra.
Thus, O Goddess of great austerity, this conduct of yours has been declared along with its secret ritual service (*upacāra*). What more shall I tell you?
Thus [ends] the third hexad in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraccheda* of the Vidyāpīṭha in the Bhairava-stream.
In the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*, this is the chapter on the ritual procedures for the conduct and activities of the *samaya*.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, you have explained the group of nine within the group of eight as being particularly distinguished.
And as for the group of eight, O Maheśāna, it is situated according to the sequence of the wheels.
O Lord of Gods, those six groups of Yoginīs which were spoken of by you have not been understood by me in their arising, maintenance, and dissolution.
O Lord of Gods, the seven Mothers, accompanied by the eight heroes and joined with the nine Bhairavas, were impelled in the primordial sūtra. (211a)

But as for these six Yoginīs who stand there, proud of their power— O Lord, what deities are praised among them, and of what nature are they? How were they born, how are they to be employed, what are their mantras, and what is the other ritual procedure?
Or how do the heroes perform their actions among them? Who would be the master over them?

How do they stand within the wheel during the piercing of the directions, and how are they situated at the rising of the channels? You ought to explain how these [channels] accomplish their functions.

Bhairava said: O Goddess, how the Dānavas were defeated by the gods in the battle between the Devas and Asuras, and how they were raised up by the Mothers— O Goddess, that was known to you previously.

O Goddess, that boon which was granted to them by Rudra in his terrifying form— by means of those slain great Asuras— is now manifest before your very eyes. Then, having killed the Asuras and being highly emboldened by the granting of the boon, they [acted].

Having disregarded her, O Goddess of gods, she prepared to kill Kumāra. Then, O lady of excellent complexion, having performed protection for the six-faced one— who had been appointed by me as a sacrificial victim— by means of the highly powerful limbs of the Vidyā;

But disregarding that protection, O Goddess of gods, Kārttikeya forcibly seized the *badara* fruits from those born of the Vidyā, Aṅga, and Kula lineages. O highly fortunate one, among the six sons, they were arrogant with strength at their mouths.
The six Yoginīs arose from the limbs of the lotus and entered the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra).
Then, having paralyzed that wheel of terrible form with those [mantras],
O highly fortunate one, all those Mothers were brought under control.
Then, by means of their strength, heroism, and prowess, they performed worship;
yet, their own power having been taken away, they sought refuge in me alone.
I then bestowed my grace upon those Mothers, placing it before them.
Whatever action you shall accomplish through my very presence,
all of that will always attain success for you.
From that time onwards, Vīreśa is in the eighth [cakra] and Aṣṭamī in the seventh;
Navamī is connected with the six Yoginīs, while Bhairava is in the center of the cakra.
Thus, O Goddess, the six Yoginīs of great power have arisen.
O lady of excellent vows, having eclipsed that collection of lunar digits— both fierce and gentle— which resides within the limbs of my six-limbed Kumāra,
they have set out to destroy the three worlds and the state known as Sadāśiva.
Then, by me, through those powers of the prince,
the ten powers of the god Mahābhairava were summoned.
Thereupon, they appeared, exceedingly gentle and possessing divine forms.
Holding lutes in their hands, highly fortunate, preceded by nooses and goads,
together with their servants and messengers, they bewilder that powerful circle of yoginīs with divine and sweet-sounding melodies.

O Maheśānī, having been addressed thus by the Yoginīs at that time, I was then brought under control by the four [deities] beginning with the Teacher (Śāstṛ), who are of the nature of bliss; and having been released by Kumāra, I was brought under his great influence. Thus, by the six [deities], I was completely subjugated. O Maheśānī, I was then spoken to in this manner by the Yoginīs.
He spoke now: "O Lord, there will be a report:
when you yourself, O Lord, remain obstructing the worlds, they will then come to you for refuge after withdrawing their heroic powers."
Then, O Goddess of great asceticism, the secret doctrines of those Yoginīs were taught to them in due order. The supreme Śaktis sport with the highest Śakti through the differentiation of power.
Lord Sadāśiva is eternally present within them in the form of knowledge and action;
he resides in the supreme wheel as the root of Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā.
That triple energy, whose nature is light, is my three eyes.
For those faces of yours, which are of great power through the energies such as Śānti and the rest,
are situated in the directions and their intermediate points and possess equal countenances.

The Lord of Knowledge (Vidyādhipa), the Head of Brahmā (Brahmaśiras), Rudrāṇī with Puruṣṭuta, the Great Pāśupata, and the Eye— these are the six limbs. The Wheel of Power (Śakticakra) has arisen, assuming the form of the syllables of withdrawal (saṃhāra).

Those who are my eight forms, the Mothers, both supreme and non-supreme, are all presided over by me alone; they sport according to their desire for the worlds. Through a state of progressive succession, there is indeed a higher and lower power.
Success is indeed of various forms, and powers reside only within actions.
"What need is there for another cause here? I alone am the cause in this matter.
Having thus incited them all with words full of pride, he—
Possessing the reality of knowledge of their own powers, they were assigned to their respective functions;
in this very manner, O one of great austerity, the six Yoginīs arose. Now hear the function of these [Yoginīs] according to the division of the network of channels (nāḍīcakra).

Thus ends the chapter on the origin of the Sixfold Wheel of Time (*kālacakra*) within the *Yoginīsaṃcāra*, the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*— the Great Tantra (*mahātantra*) of twenty-four thousand verses belonging to the *Śiraccheda* division of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavasrotas*.
[Now begins] the account of how the Mothers, worshipped by the gods, were born from a single limb.

O Lord of Gods, the six Yoginīs have been described as seated upon their thrones; they emerged from the mouths of Kārttikeya, as has been declared. O All-pervading One, these Mothers were born from the lords of the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
O Lord, worshipped by the gods, you have attained the perfection of the yoga of sovereignty, yet it is fickle.
How can you resolve my doubt regarding those Mothers—
how is it that they have emerged from the single syllable and become sixfold, O All-pervading One?
The mantras of those [goddesses] have arisen, as well as the channels (nāḍī) in their many varieties;
you should explain this regarding the directions numbered as eight.
Bhairava said:
My body is a mass of splendor, supreme and composed of the power of knowledge;
from that eternal one was born the mighty Kārttikeya.
O Goddess, when I too was protected by those who perform great penance,
these Yogamātṛs were born from the six limbs [of yoga],
and likewise, O lady of excellent complexion, they were born from the limbs of yoga.
Therefore, O Maheśānī, the six Yoginīs are proclaimed;
in the mere twinkling of an eye, these ones of great power sequentially pervade the fourteen worlds, divided both below and above.
Another application of the gift [of sound] occurs during the turning of the three channels and the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa), having emerged from the region of the throat;
the phonemes produced by that arise through the piercing of the cakras by those of great austerity.
I shall describe to you those [energies] cast forth according to the divisions of the directions as seeds:
the first is associated with the intellect (*buddhi*), the second is characterized by the diversity of the womb (*yoni*),
the third is endowed with the person (*puruṣa*), and the fourth is likewise.
The fifth is the union of *ai*, and the sixth is endowed with the three qualities (*triguṇa*).
Abiding in the nature of the principle of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-tattva*), these are the six Yoginīs of great power:
Subhadrā, Bhīmabhadrā, and Bhadrā as the third.
Listen now to how Bhīmabhīmavatī, Bhadrakālī, and Ṣaṣṭhikā were born from the mouths of Kārttikeya:
Subhadrā was born from the eastern mouth, while Bhīmabhadrā was from the southern.

Bhadrā is produced in the west, and Bhīmā indeed in the north; Bhadrakālī is in the southeast, and likewise Bhīmavatī in the northeast. They are produced according to their respective faces and should be joined in the same manner on the left.
O one of great asceticism, she who dwells eternally in the gentle wheel (saumyacakra) is to be worshipped.
O lady of excellent complexion, the gentle wheel is the arrangement established throughout the moving and unmoving worlds, divided into sixteen parts beginning with Pūṣan.
At the time of the collective sacrifice, however, it is distributed during the great heat of the ritual;
it has the luster of a conch, a Śūla, or an Indragopa insect, and is pure with the radiance of a pearl.
The channels originating from the mouth have the appearance of vomited gold.
Now hear concerning those that are distributed according to the sequence starting from the east:
they resemble Indra’s bow, are harsh, and are characterized by constant movement.

Resembling a blue lotus and possessing a radiance like a flickering fire, the visualization of the limbs [of the deity] proceeds from the northeast to the southeast. This has been told to you, O Great Goddess; now hear concerning the remaining [limbs].
White and red, with the luster of blood, and with great splendor blue and red;
having the radiance of blue pearls, and likewise exceedingly white;
yellow like jewels, situated within that, and another likewise white and yellow.
O Goddess, the supreme green [syllable] has thus been declared in due order as the deity of the sacrifice.
O Yogeshī, bestower of success in ritual action, the sequence of their colors has not been told;
likewise, O sinless one, I shall explain the procedure for the placement of the vowels within the wheel.

O illustrious one, having uttered those vowels which were produced from the mouth of the six-faced [Kārttikeya], one should place them in sequence, beginning with the eastern direction, O Śakra. Then, O highly fortunate one, one should place the remaining vowels and subsequently the *tattvas*.
At the tip of the forty petals, two channels are situated at the opening.
These are differentiated by the seed-syllables of the channels, beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*.
Then, a lord among yogis who has practiced yoga should accomplish his ritual activities.
The Goddess said:

O Lord of Gods, when mantras born from the syllables of withdrawal [Saṃhāra-kalā] are present under the command of the six-fold serpent-king, which mantras have been declared by you in their various forms?
Bhairava said:
Beyond those respective [levels] is the subtle Śiva, peaceful and free from affliction. From Him, Nāda (the primordial sound) was produced; from Nāda, Bindu (the point) was born.
The triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, has arisen from the Bindu;
therefore, O Vāyu, you are the sixteenth, and the Kalā is indeed the sixteenth.
The vowels are indeed sixteen, beginning with *a* and ending with the visarga (*ḥ*). [The channels are] Prapadā, Jvālinī, Dhūmrā, Kāmada, Vijayā, Amṛtā, Bahulā, Pakṣī, Ūrdhvabāhyā, and Alambuṣā.
The one that flows over the palate and tongue, as well as that which carries the *jīva*,
is known as the *jīvavāhā*, the *prāṇavāhā*, and the sixteenth, the *amṛtā*. These, O Goddess, are the Mothers, along with the gods through their emissions.
O Goddess, you abide as Kālā and Ekālā; listen now to that time.
You are Pūṣā, Yaśā, Sumanas, Prīti, Tuṣṭi, and Dhṛti;
likewise Dhṛti, Dhṛtikarī, Saumyā, Marīci, and Akṣṇamālinī.

Śaśinī, Jvālinī, Chāyā, Saṃpūrṇamaṇḍalā, and Amṛtā— O Goddess of Gods, these are established as the limbs of the arising of the Kalās. [The vital airs] Kṛkara, Devadatta, Pauṇḍarīka, and Dhanañjaya [are likewise established].
Trembling, dizziness, confusion, and even wandering;
Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna;
and Nāga, Kūrma, and Kṛkara—these are the sixteen great winds.
Jvālinī ending with Antaka, and Pūrvāntā joined with their respective vowels;
the entire body beginning with Kṛkara, along with the channels (nāḍī) and the digits of the vital breath (vāyukalā);
[all this] indeed emits space at the beginning, and therefore everything is composed of speech (vāṅmaya).
The letter *ā* is the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*), while the letter *i* is the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*).
The letter *u*, conjoined with a short vowel, is the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*).
The letter *e* is said to be passion (*rāga*), and *ai* is proclaimed as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
The letter *o* is to be known as the Puruṣa, and likewise the letter *au* as Prakṛti.
*Aṃ* is to be understood as the intellect (*buddhi*), and *aḥ* is said to be the ego (*ahaṃkāra*).
This group of four neuter vowels is established through the divisions of the intellect.
(214a) Through the differentiation of the division of colors, the form of the channels consists of vowels; however,
the channels, whose forms are the vowels of the sources, are situated in the mouth.
These [energies] generate the pervasive Lord, whose nature is the garland of yoga (yogamālā), as mantras.
Together with their own channels, they are the attendants of the Goddess within the mantras.
O Vīreśa, they are the pericarp, the stream, and all the radiant phonemes.

Situated in the middle of the infinite petals, he abides at the end of the sixty letters. One should extract these wheels of the initial, final, and intermediate channels, which rest upon a six-petaled lotus and delight the hosts of gods and goddesses.
There are many kinds of auspicious mantras joined with seed-syllables and matrices (*bīja-yoni*).

One should extract the letters in sequence, occupying sixteen parts of the channels (*nāḍī*). All [mantras] begin with the syllable *U* and end with the syllable *Kāra*, with the word *namaḥ* placed in the middle.

Huṃ phaṭ svāhā! She is clothed in fat, free from impurity, and the fulfiller of all desires. She is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the womb (*yoni*), the very nature of this [mantra]. There is nothing that cannot be accomplished for those practitioners who know her.
She should be understood as having a peaceful form by those who know the meaning of mantras and vidyās.
Wherever the mind finds favor among the eight forms of Śiva,
there one should worship the Self, established within the *cakra*, by means of meditation and other practices;
or else, according to the prescribed methods, with enjoyments that satisfy the desires of the mind.
And according to one's capacity, the self endowed with the *haṃsa* is worshipped in the gurus and the fires.
Thus, the practitioner who possesses the mantra, whose mind is fixed on the limbs of the Vidyā, and who is a deer-like seeker,
attains swift success as its employer in all rites.
I shall describe him who dwells within those extremities:
Kṛkara is enjoyed by Pramadā, while Devadatta is enjoyed by Jvālinī;
likewise, Puṇḍarīka is enjoyed by Dhūmrā, and Mañjana by Kāmadā.

Vijayā, Vepadhūḥ, Amṛtā, and likewise Saṃbhavā—these reside in the Bahulā [nāḍī]. O Goddess of the Gods, when the Prāṇa is supported by the upward-flowing [nāḍī], it experiences delusion (vibhrama). Indeed, Apāna is Pakṣī, and likewise Apāna is Laṃbusā.
Born from the power of Śiva, he assumes the form of the syllable of withdrawal;
those who are my eight forms, the Mothers, are both supreme and non-supreme.
Presided over by me alone, all those who abide in the worlds sport,
distinguished by their progressively superior portions of strength and power.
O you of great austerity, these six Yoginīs have arisen from my own limbs.
Through investigation of the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*), the supreme [attainments] are achieved for the sake of the *bindu*.

Indeed, the various forms of accomplishments (*siddhi*) and powers (*śakti*) are but the fruit of action (*karma*). What is there to be done here that yields such fruit? I alone am the cause in this matter.

Having thus exhorted all those women who are full of pride, he should employ them in their respective tasks according to the true nature of their own powers and knowledge. In this very manner, the six Yoginīs have arisen for the sake of the knowledge of the Self.
Then, O Goddess, it was fully proclaimed in the *Yoginījālaśamvara*:
by those such as Laṃpaṭa and Raktā, and especially by all the heroes,
in this supreme tantra, O auspicious one, which bestows auspicious accomplishments.
Thus has the movement been declared from the beginning in its proper sequence—
this great secret, incomparable, more essential than the essence itself, and auspicious.
Beyond this, O Goddess, tell me what else shall I do?
Thus, in the Bhairava-stream, in the Vidyāpīṭha, in the Śiraccheda, in the Jayadrathayāmala Mahātantra, in the third Ṣaṭka,
in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work, this is the chapter named "The Movement of the Yoginīs.
Having heard this, that Goddess, who is saluted by the best of heroes...
Approaching him with supreme contentment, she spoke again to Śaṅkara.
The Goddess said:
"O Supreme Lord, I am now satisfied by your grace."
