Furthermore, she vomits forth the wheel of consciousness, endowed with hundreds of great rays;
it is crowded with many hosts of mātrās and accompanied by the wheel of time (kālacakra).
Thus is Kālī, the creator of emanation, revealed through her threefold movement.
Then she remains unrestrained as the support of speech (*bhāsādhāra*).
By her, the entire universe has been emitted; she abides therein without differentiation. She is described as the Fulfiller, the Instrument, the Sustainer, and the very Form of Stability.
Thus the splendor of consciousness (cillakṣmī) flashes forth, arisen within the wheel of light (bhāsācakra).
Thus has the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama) been declared, from its full detail down to its summary.
It has come down through the succession of gurus and resides in the lotus-heart of the Yoginīs.
O Goddess of the gods, it must never be given away, even at the cost of one's life. That lowest of men who opens the fist incurs another transgression of the vow.
O Goddess, as much as has been correctly communicated, whether in a dream or otherwise—
"One should rest right here"—such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the procedure for the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) in the third hexad of the *Jayadratha*.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme sequence of Kālikā.
Having attained this, the power of the practitioner becomes great;
it is proclaimed that the lineage of gurus,
ending with the succession, is honored when the unsurpassed Śiva is fully realized as previously described.

Endowed with the sequence of speech and overflowing with the bliss of aesthetic rapture, she is the Kālī of manifestation who makes that [reality] manifest; she is the fire-drill for the multitude of rays of the manifestors.
Having previously cleansed all this, she whose belly is drawn in stands within that [space].
When that world-existence became intensely arrogant and exceedingly fierce,
then, at that very moment, from her own nature as Kālī,
she [manifested] while all those previously created beings had become entirely like ghosts.
The Mistress of Bhairava has ascended, expanding through the wheel of rays;
by them, this entire world of moving and unmoving beings is pervaded.
Hāṭakeśvara, Muṇḍasthā, and Kālī— the burner of the race of Time—
by their rays have brought forth Bhairavī, who experiences all states of being.
She is fashioned by the six rays in a sixfold manner, teeming with expanding virility.
The immensely powerful Kulakālī, exceedingly fierce,
yawns; then, mounted upon the great skull of Brahmā, that very Brahmakālī consumes the [victim] brought by its rays while stationed within the lineage of Viṣṇu.
Likewise, in the lineage of Rudreśvara, Kālī is intent upon devouring Time;
thus, situated within the circle of Bhairava, Kālikā is slow with her swallowing. And so, mounted upon the Vikula, she devours the universe as if in play.

Thus mounted upon the three fires, the Goddess of the gods, Paramānandabhairavī, having spontaneously drawn [the essence] by their power, enjoys it while remaining absorbed in bliss. In this way, she dwells even in the Mūlādhāra-cakra, which sustains the sixteen supports.
Having taken up the yoke of wisdom, he enjoys the wheel of nectar;
in this way, established within the wheels of sound and so forth, he devours them with ease.
All-knowing, he devours all this entire world by means of everything.
The Great Queen of the Family (Kuleśānī), beautiful with supreme bliss,
intent upon the dissolution of the sequence of the great wheel of flashing waves, she,
restless with her own play, thoroughly drinks up everything.
Thus is proclaimed the Vaktrāgama, conjoined with the third sequence.
This auspicious Mahāmātrī doctrine has come down through the succession of gurus.
O Samareśānī, it must not be told to a disciple who has not been properly tested.
The Chapter on the Kālakrama.
Hereafter I shall speak; listen, O Padmadalākṣaṇā!
This is an incomparable secret, which brings rest through the dissolution of all things.
(224a) You must act with the utmost secrecy; this must not be told to anyone.
There exists one's own power (*svadhā*) arising from the light of the *cakras*, manifested through the expansion of its own rays.
When she, impelling her own state of being, does not attain satisfaction,
then once more she becomes intensely agitated— the terrible Kālī, the great seeker of bliss.
She [resides] in the great wheel called Hāṭaka, endowed with all rays of light.
Resorting to a terrible mode of conduct, she then seized the entire head;
then that blazing,
fierce [power] once again seized the Brahma-wheel, which was enveloped by its own rays and was the destroyer of the universe.
When she was swallowed by that goddess, she blazed forth once more.
O beloved, when Viṣṇu’s discus with its own rays was again swallowed by her,
then Kālikā, the devourer of Kāla, became agitated and multiplied ten-millionfold.
By her, the wheel of Rudra, together with all its rays, was swallowed.
Thus that goddess of gods, Kṛṣodarī, blazed forth even more intensely.
Then the wheel of the Vidyeshvaras, joined with its own lord, was swallowed.
Again Mahākālī became agitated; she, the Mistress of the Gods, consumed the great body of the five mantras, which was surrounded by tens of millions of mantras.
Then, a hundred thousand times more agitated, making a great roar, she began to lick it.
With the sound "ṚG" alone, she swallowed the great host of Bhairavas.
Having thus devoured them, she became agitated once more and [swallowed] the wheel of the vowels with its rays of sound;
that [wheel], blazing and radiant as fire, was swallowed by Mahākālī.

Furthermore, O Dear One, having reached the thirteenth [cakra], the terrible Arkakālikā became agitated; she swallowed millions of great Mārtaṇḍas. Then, becoming even more terrible and agitated, she was the fall of the sixteenth cakra.
She, of terrifying speed, devours [all] and then blazes forth again with force.
Then the formidable Mahākālī becomes agitated, ten millionfold;
by her, the most terrible and fierce multitude of great fires is swallowed up.
Thus she is blazing, fierce, and the destroyer of seven generations;
Kālī, she who is black, she who is dark, she who is Kālī, she who agitates the darkness of the eon.
Sukālī, Kulakāpālī, Vikālī, and Kṣayakālikā—
agitated, with terrible faces, fierce eyes, and voracious with rage—
[saw] the Lord of the Wheel of Sound, whose body was seized by her in a horrific manner.
Joined with its own mothers and resplendent with its own rays,
the most terrible and agitated [power] then once again swallowed the entire family of Touch (sparśakula) all at once, just as before, as the destroyer of Death himself.
In the wheel of *rā* and the wheel of *rū*, conjoined with *ra-ri-rā-ri*,
there is the Lord of the Wheel (*cakra-nātha*), whose nature is terrible and who is greedy to devour the world.
United with his own mother’s rays, he devours [all] by means of his own *māyā*.

Then you were again agitated as Rūpakālī, the destroyer of the Kula. The Lord, whose body was swallowed by her, was joined with the six flavors, the necklace-circle, and the Lord of the Navel-sound, together with the rays of the vowels.
Then the most terrible goddess, agitated, fierce, and bearing bells,
rushed forward and ran about, devouring all that is moving and unmoving.
By her own playful power, she swallowed the Lord, the Master of the Wheel of Fragrance.
Furthermore, the wheel that had entered the mind,
consisting of egoism, great and accompanied by its own source,
was violently swallowed by that Goddess; it was swallowed by that Goddess of gods, the terrible Kālī, most formidable.
Then, the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa), who has ascended the path of the intellect and is joined with rays of light,
has his body completely swallowed by that enraged [power] according to its own essential nature.
In this way, he whose form is swallowed as a play, having integrated all the paths, [is absorbed].
When that Mahākālī, the Ender of Time, had been brought forth for the sake of destruction,
she swallowed up the entire terrible power of Time itself, which was destined for its own decay.
Then, having brought about a great dissolution, she—variegated by that dissolution—resides in her own abode.
By her, whose nature is self-luminous, all power is diminished within her own essential form;
yet, through the union with Pradhāna, everything is made manifest.
Then, through truth and detachment, within that great abode of dissolution,
the Radiance remains established there and manifests itself in various ways.
Having consumed this entire world, Kālī, the agent of the great dissolution, [remains].

Thus, O Gaurī, this supreme sequence of withdrawal has been fully explained by me, passed from mouth to mouth; it has not been known by anyone else in such a way. Indeed, by explaining it improperly, death would occur suddenly and prematurely.
Having died, one would ripen in the Avīci hell for eight years called *sādākhya*.
Knowing what is beneficial for oneself, one should do whatever is desired.
This [state] called *gaurīṭī* is never to be known through non-sequential means; one should not die anywhere [in vain].
This which has come down through such a lineage has been told to you by me today.
It must not be given to those with divided views, nor likewise to atheists.
After first worshipping the Goddess, one may then reveal this great secret.
For one who delights in the conduct of heroes, success is achieved in every state.
O high-minded one, the rays [of power] praise that practitioner as long as the supreme Goddess Śāṅkarī-Śakti has not descended.
O slender-waisted one, one should not attain this knowledge of the sequence until one has [studied] the Siddhānta,
the Gāruḍa, the Saura, the Bhūtatantra, the Kaṇṭaka, the Tantra, the Kula, as well as the Kaula and the Atimārga.
I have not revealed this Krama-knowledge, exactly as it exists, to anyone;
because it is most secret, O Goddess, I have kept it concealed. Yet, in this supreme Tantra, I have declared it to you along with its secret essence.
I shall explain in the sixth chapter on the determination of the *haḍḍā* (the wheel), that sequence of worship which is endowed with the sequence of wheels.
However, that which ought to be said there has not been investigated here.
Thus, O Goddess of the gods, I have declared to you this pure secret of the tradition from the excellent Jayadratha Tantra.
O Goddess, O fair-browed one, why do you speak again and again to me? I shall explain the essence of the transition that follows the Krama.
Thus, in the Bhairava-stream, in the Vidyāpīṭha, in the Śiraccheda, in the Jayadrathayāmala Mahātantra, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work, in the third Ṣaṭka.
The Chapter on the Array of the Gods.
While the Lord of Gods was speaking thus, showers of flowers fell;
shouts of "Śiva! arose, and the sky-dwellers clapped their hands in rhythm.
The entire world, along with the cosmic egg and the Hūhukas, trembled;
fragrant winds blew, and the universe became filled with joy.
The moon and sun, moving through the sky with blazing splendor, shone forth in a state of vibration.
Then the goddess, delighted and satisfied, prostrated before the bull-bannered Lord and pleased the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign of the Universe, with this hymn of praise. The Goddess said:
I am satisfied, O Śaṅkara; I am completely satisfied, I am fully fulfilled.
Today, O Maheśvara, my eyes have been opened wide.
By your grace, O Sarvajña Parameśvara, what more could there be?
Salutations to you, the three-eyed one, whose form is Mahābhairava;
salutations to you, the Lord of the Skull (Kapālīśa), who possesses a most fierce and terrible appearance.
Salutations to you, whose body is the sun (Mārttaṇḍa); salutations to you, the Lord of its digits.
Salutations to the one whose nature is speech, who assumes both conscious and unconscious forms;
salutations to you, the enemy of Tripura, who dwells within the infinite worlds, the cities, and the bodies,
and who is the Lord of that wheel situated within the Great Speech.
Salutations to the one whose form is throbbing vibration, who shines with the mark of the source of nectar;
salutations to the divine one who consumes the sun, who causes the destruction of fire;
salutations to the one whose body is intent upon striking the foundation of the fire of time.
(226a) Homage to you, O Lord who has dissolved Brahmā, who makes all things into your mouthful;
to the blazing lion of knowledge, O Lord of the Universe, who causes all things to dissolve away.
Salutations to the one who is tawny like gold, whose face is the Vasu, and who is the bountiful giver;
salutations to the one who resides within the vital breaths and who is the end of the Bindu and Nāda.
Salutations to the Lord of the sixteen and to him who is devoted to his seat.
Salutations to the one with six earrings, whose form is as terrible as the sun that devours the darkness.
Salutations to the supreme oblation, the matted-haired one, the wonder of the world.
You are the priest, you are the goal, you are the pure one; you are the *haṃsa*, you are both the transcendent and the immanent.

You are the remover of great delusion; you are the refuge of the entire world. You are the creator, you are the sustainer, you are all, and you are the supreme reality. You are the yogi, you are the Great Being, and you are the destroyer of great delusion.
"I have accomplished my purpose, O Blessed One, through your grace, O Maheśvara.
Now I wish to hear how the goddesses are situated,
and how their conduct is established, O Mahādeva."
How is their knowledge of the families [gotras], and what is their essential nature? How are the goddesses the meeting-places (melāpadas), and how do they destroy delusion?
O Blessed One, honored by the best of gods, I wish to hear this.
Having thus addressed her, the Blessed One, Maheśvara, whose moon-crest was quivering with joy, spoke these words with a loud laugh to the Goddess of gods. Bhairava said:
Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one, you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of hidden knowledge!
Listen, for I shall speak that which you have requested—
a supreme secret, incomparable, and vital to all the gods.
"O Goddess, listen as this great secret is being told:
those who reside in the *pīṭhas*, *kṣetras*, and *upapīṭhas*, as well as others in the *upakṣetras*,
and those established in the *saṃdohas* and *tamaḥ-saṃdohas*, are attained ones of great power."
(226b) O Dear One, these deities wander in a humble manner through forms such as the mind and so forth; they are of secret conduct, secret mantras, and secret vital power.

For who indeed knows their true conduct and behavior in that intermediate state? As long as [the practitioner] has not personally attained their grace, the essential rites and procedures for their activities remain unknown to him.
Whether for the sake of knowing the scriptures, or from the secret oral tradition of the Guru,
one should understand that these nine alone are the supreme sacrifices and possess the vital points [of the practice]. O deer-eyed one, they constantly perform their worship and salutation.
O Queen of the Gods, even at the end of their lives, they observe their commitments (samaya).
In certain places, they touch [the ground] with their feet during what is called a sacrifice.
When a disturbance arises in the land, they laugh and frolic.
At the time of a great plague, they weep and they laugh;
toward the diseased, the deformed, the terrified, the deceased, and the agitated;
toward the intoxicated, the lustful, and the untruthful—they are always exceedingly pure in their conduct.
The ever-present deities strike down the fool who reviles them and doubts the conduct of his guru;
they carry away his wealth and grain,
wither his body, and indeed take away his very life.
Constantly delighting in great sensual pleasure, all were greedy for material things;
devoted to serving their husbands, yet covered with hundreds of guiles and deceptions;
pitiless, devoid of heroism, and addicted to the forms of goddesses.

Always seeking out vulnerabilities, intent on poison, and radiant with the seizing of jewels; in quarrels, in the breaking of limbs, and in verbal disputes arising from childishness— the gods, who move at will, constantly take delight in such things.
Their principal lineages, numbering eight, have existed since ancient times;
having been described in detail previously, hear now a brief summary of them:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kārttikeyī, and Viṣṇujā.
Vārāhī, Śākrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and another,
Yogeśvarī as the eighth— these are the Kulamātṛs of great power. (227a)
From the Akula state, the Kula has arisen; that is Śākta, and it is fivefold.
Furthermore, it becomes eightfold, and again it reaches perfect infinity.
It is designated as the flow of dissolution and birth, and is known as the cessation of movement.
The sacrifice is declared to be fivefold, yet it is also of eight types.
The great mothers born of that lineage are the cause of the entire Kaula tradition;
all those who have arisen from their lineage are said to dwell within the interior of the universe.
The Ḍākinīs, the Ḍāmarikās and others, the Śākinīs, the Mothers (Mātṛs),
those born in specific regions, the Pīṭhakas,
and others who are intent on upward breathing; others who breathe out through the upper [nostril], and yet others who are "crocodile-suckers" (nakracūṣikā).
The Patralekhyas, the Parās, and the Jātahāriṇīs—
these and many others whose number is not known;
they possess complete forms and are endowed with specific marks and conventions.
Possessing many courses, manifold, endowed with hundreds of many illusions, having many forms and many languages, they are ever wondrous and marvelous;
the entire world-system of the cosmic egg is [perceived] by them as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.
O Goddess of the gods, they behold the past and what has passed away; they know everything that is present exactly as it is.
O Goddess, they perceive what resides in the hearts of others as clearly as a bilva fruit held in their own hands.
O beloved, neither a wall nor a mountain is an obstruction for them;
in an instant they pervade all regions, just as sunlight permeates water.
Whatever form you may desire, that very form they shall assume.
Indeed, they effortlessly manifest thousands of forms from a single form;
they never perish even when their vital breaths depart.
They always take delight in a cow-pen, worshiping cows and eating their dung.
The honoring of subjects, their affection, and the supreme vow of the Brahminic way—
Śiva, however, is always to be worshipped by me at the crossroads and in the cremation ground. (227b)
O auspicious lady, the observance of Māheśī consists always in consuming the water from Śiva’s feet,
being devoted to the worship of the book, and remaining constantly intent upon the child-form [of the deity].
The observance of Kaumārī should be known as being intent upon consuming the Brahman.
O Suramati, this pilgrimage, which is worshiped in battle, is always composed of illusion (māyā).

One should daily consume sandalwood paste, for it is remembered as being equal to [the worship of] Vaiṣṇavī. [The goddess] is capable of consuming excrement and wielding the thunderbolt, and she is intent upon beholding the earth.
One should always consume mixed [substances] during the Vārāhī observance;
one should constantly honor the manifestation, being intent upon the consumption of blood. Indeed, this is the observance of Aiṇḍī, who always consumes the three worlds.
Cāmuṇḍā, who is eternally dear to Vardhamāna, always remembers the *samaya*.
Carcikā is always devoted to worshipping the funeral garlands from the cremation ground;
she always eats the nine [offerings] as her constant *samaya*.
Thus has the blazing of the *samaya* been described; hear now, O beloved, their further classification.
Their form is pure and difficult to be discerned even by gods and asuras.
She who is fond of the Vedas, pure in conduct, and intent upon the procreation of offspring—
O Maheśvarī, she who has wide eyes, is well-bathed, has lips like the *bimba* fruit, and is beautiful to behold—
thus should she be known by the best of heroes in three ways.
She is lotus-fair, lotus-faced, virtuous, and a speaker of Brahman.
O one of divine mind, she who delights in the discourse of the three Vedas always rejoices in that [state].
She constantly draws a lotus in her home on every festival day.
Through laughter, she seizes life; she is attained through song—of this there is no doubt.
Born of the Brahma lineage, she is always equal-minded and fond of the staff posture;
she is beautiful, with limbs of yellowish-fair complexion, lotus-like eyes, and a lovely smile.
Constantly filled with joy, always intent on singing,
delighting in the great secret, devoted to great auspiciousness,
endowed with all ornaments, and ever engaged in playing the lute.

She who constantly draws a trident on her own body parts at home should be known as one born into the lineage of Māheśvarīs, yet she is addicted to everything. She is always capable of stealing fat, meat, and other such things.
Red-limbed and with red cows, she has exerted herself in the arts of learning;
she is eternally beloved by all birds and is intensely devoted to song and instrumental music.
She always draws the Śakti within her own dwelling in her home.
Greedy for the fragrance of flowers, she takes away life with her speech;
she is born of the Kula, known as Kaumārī, and is greedy for meat.
She possesses great illusion, delights in a hundred [enjoyments], is dark-complexioned, and has a beautiful smile.
Devoted to talk of great battles, she is beautiful-limbed and most enchanting;
always fond of drinking blood, she takes away life through her touch.
On her own festival day, she always has her wheel fixed within the house.
Her forehead perspires; she is indeed Vaiṣṇavī, of this there is no doubt.
She has a long face, thick cheeks, reddish-brown eyes, and is long-suffering in her wrath.
She is protruding-toothed, has coarse hair, is long-tempered, and possesses great strength.
She indeed brings [wealth] through various means such as diseases and other openings;
she always writes on leaves in a superior house.
Born of the Vārāhī lineage, she is always fond of the forest.
Fortunate, with a beautiful face, endowed with great fortune,
reddish-fair in complexion and red-eyed, she was intent on the commencement of her kingdom; indeed,
she always had a broad nose and was fond of battle.
She always draws a thunderbolt upon her own limb or in the house;
indeed, that cruel and pitiless woman steals the life-force through smelling. Born of the Aindra lineage, she is constantly addicted to meat.
Cruel, with a cruel disposition, terrifying, black, and hairy everywhere,
she indeed always delights in death, injury, and likewise in wounding.
Wherever she weeps, there she likewise displays her passion;
she is always attached to stories of death, and today she is fond of wine and the sword.
One should draw three lines on the forehead and a staff upon the joints.
That terrifying Yoginī, born from a portion of Yama’s lineage and possessed of great power, would take away the life of animals with a mere glance;
she has thick limbs, large cheeks, protruding lips, and a flat face.
Lambodarī has short arms, is red in color, and possesses great majesty;
she has tawny eyes and tawny hair, and she takes away life by kissing.
She is devoted to stories of great battles and is addicted to drinking blood.
She draws a skull on her dwelling and always laughs during the twilights;
she should be known as Cāmuṇḍā, born of the Kula and supreme among all families.
She has emaciated limbs, is tawny or black, has large cheeks, and a protruding belly.
Long-tongued and long-toothed, she is always agitated by anger;
though she has caused pain, she delights only in discourses on nectar.
Veiny and with a parched face, she is everywhere the delight of her family.
On the auspicious festival days, one should worship Dravakā intensely in her own abode.
O slender-waisted lady, when she has risen, she shall discharge urine and feces.
She who is endowed with such characteristics is Yogeshī, the delight of the Kula.
In this very way, O Kuleśvarī, there is the division of the five families (*pañcakula*).

O Goddess, when the lineage of the *Kula* is known, the practitioner becomes a participant in the assembly (*melāpin*), free from affliction. This indeed comes to pass; there is no doubt that he becomes beloved by all.
O Dear One, when there is a combination of various signs, the mixed portions arise.
Now hear the *chommakas* for the purpose of distinguishing their essential natures;
although they were previously indicated, I shall nevertheless explain them here.
(229a) Ā, ī, ū, ai, as well as o, ṛ, ṝ, and ra— these are the eight families,
O Goddess of the gods; they should indeed be understood in this sequence by the practitioner.
In the bright fortnight, during the movement of the moon, such is the rising remembered here;
the Lord of Sādhakas should proclaim it in sequence to those born of the Kula.
Then the Yoginīs will become pleased with the souls of the Sādhakas.
Thus has the white fortnight been described; now hear concerning the dark fortnight.
O Dear One, [the vowels] are A, I, U, likewise E, O, Ṛ, AU, and AṂ.
This group of eight is indeed always proclaimed for the dark fortnight;
at the time of sunrise, according to the sequence and the divisions of the Kula.
By this sequential distinction, the determination of speech is to be expressed.
In the family tradition of the deities, there is likewise a division into classes;

the sequence of these classes and the phonemes [of the mantras] are to be understood according to their respective order. Furthermore, one must know what is to be expressed for whom—whether for a woman or for a man.
That family of his is to be known, and his *ucchūṣmā* has been proclaimed.
Then he is pleased, O Goddess; hear now, my beloved, about the *aṅga-ucchūṣmā*:
the head, the face, the throat, the heart, the secret place, and the *liṅga*.
O fortunate one, the feet and hands are traditionally known as the eight *kulas* in sequence.
A man should display that which has been designated as her *kula*;
then, O Goddess, she becomes the *chusmakā* who pleases the practitioner.

Thus, for one who understands the distinction of sequence, there should be reflection on this matter. Here, the mental [states] are declared to be beneficial when they are free from agitation. That which is designated as "family" (kula) is so called because it is the cause of the mind's delight.
Those who know it know that very [reality] through the measurement of the conduct of their own family (kula).
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
mind, intellect, and ego—this is the eightfold family (kulāṣṭaka) in sequence.
Having thoroughly understood that mental [sign] through the sequence of gestures (*chommaka*),
one should likewise [understand] the words of the Goddess of Gods according to their eightfold divisions.
The sequence beginning with *chomma* should be known as threefold and consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*).
The practitioner should always practice it for the sake of attaining the desired union (*melāpa*).
Just as the accomplishment has infinite forms according to the division of its steps, so too is the practice.

Thus, O daughter of the mountain, the seventh [chapter] alone has been described to you here. Now, O Great Goddess, I shall explain to you correctly the ritual for the *melaka* (union) at Laṅkā, according to the division of the stages (*pada*).
O beloved, in former times Maheshani was propitiated by Ravana through the great sacrifices of the *melapa* rite, as well as by the wise Kumbhakarna,
by Vibhishana, and likewise by other heroic kings.
In that way, Mahāmāyā is to be propitiated by the foremost of practitioners who are free from defects—
those who are liberated from blemish, devoid of intoxication and delusion,
stainless, and resembling the sky; they are the vessels for the melāpa.

Those who have no suspicion regarding the body, no suspicion regarding caste, and no suspicion regarding material things— they are indeed the vessels for the assembly (*melāpa*). Indeed, among them there is no suspicion regarding mantra, no suspicion regarding place, and no suspicion regarding ritual action.

Those who are completely free from all suspicion are the vessels for the *melāpa*. O Goddess, those who are bold, pitiless, cruel, eternally intoxicated, agitated by passion, and have eyes like hollows (*koṭarākṣī*)— they indeed are the vessels for the *melāpa*.
Those who have studied the great tantra along with its secrets in full detail, and who are devoted to its sequential practice, are indeed fit vessels for the melāpa. For them,
wealth is like a blade of grass and worldly thought is like the weight of a mountain.
Those who delight in all forms of conduct are indeed vessels for the assembly (melāpa).
Those for whom there is constant coming and going during the union of the three abodes— indeed, throughout the watches of the night— they are truly vessels for the assembly.
Those who always consume the web of bindu, nāda,
and kalā— those great beings who eat all things— are indeed the vessels for the melāpa.
Those for whom the entire family of channels (*nāḍikula*) is spread out and situated like a path,
and who are intent upon experiencing that [reality], are indeed fit vessels for the *melāpa* (gathering).
Those by whom the entire family of the six causes (*ṣaṭkāraṇakula*) has been consumed through transgressive inversion (*vyutkrama*)...
Those whose nature of consciousness is uncontracted are indeed vessels for the *melāpa*. Those who are constantly free from duality upon the arising of the dissolution of the moon and sun,
and who are pervaded by the moon of *śakti*, are indeed vessels for the *melāpa*.
Those for whom one hundred thousand [drops] expand as they fall within three hundred thousand [beats],
with a mind free of conceptual construction, are indeed the vessels for the melāpa.
Those who are enriched by the play of their own power (*svaśakti*) and those who delight in that sexual union (*maithuna*).
Those who are devoted to feeding on those flowers are indeed vessels for the *melāpa*. Those whose power (*śakti*) is characterized by passion (*rajas*), whose girdles are reeling with intoxication,
and whose limbs and private parts tremble excessively— they are indeed vessels for the *melāpa*.

Those lustful men by whom the nectar has been drawn from the mouth of the Guru are ever-satisfied and full of joy; they are indeed the vessels for the *melāpa*. And those by whom the *dūtī* and the *kula* have been seen, and by whom that essence has been drunk.
Those who are always truly mighty are the vessels for the assembly (melāpa).
Those by whom the end-maker (Antaka) was brought from the abode of Brahmā,
and those by whom the reflection of the world (jagadbimba) was swallowed up— they indeed are the vessels for the assembly.
Those whose state is eternally manifest up to the limit of the sixteen supports (ādhāras),
and who are therefore of a nature in which darkness has subsided, are the vessels for the *melāpa*. Those whose full-formed nature has intensely emerged from their own essential being [are likewise].
Those Bhairavas who are heroic kings are indeed the recipients of the melāpa;
those who always move at their pleasure through the pathways of the nāḍīs,
and who have been gradually worn away by the Krama, are the recipients of the melāpa.
Delighting in morsels of the five nectars and intent on seizing the six flavors, those heroic kings of heroes are always worthy vessels for the melāpa.

Those who always drink Viṣṇu and always kiss Bhaga enjoy the three worlds; they are indeed the vessels for the *melāpa*. Those devoted to consuming the water of Brahmā are the *vuka*-eaters, and those who consume fire are the *hutāśana*s.
Those who are middling, superior, or supreme are the vessels for the melāpa;
for they partake of the oblation, the flower, and likewise that which arises from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
whether it be mixed or unmixed— they are indeed the vessels for the melāpa.
Those men who always delight in coming and going within the supreme void,
remaining there like the moon and the sun, are indeed the recipients of the *melāpa*.
They consume the *kalās*, they abide at the end of the *kalās*, they are beyond conceptualization, and they are free from time.
Those who are intoxicated by the *kṛkara* [sound] and the *bhṛgu* [wind], they are indeed vessels for the assembly (*melāpa*).
Those who possess great skeletons, those whose limbs are smeared with great ashes, those with matted hair, and those who wear the great sacred thread— they too are vessels for the assembly.
Those who destroy misfortune, those who remove it whether seen or unseen,
and those who maintain the glory of Kādyā— they are indeed the vessels for the melāpa.
Those who are destroyers of great delusion and who always observe the commitments (samaya).
Those who always uphold the Sūtras are indeed fit vessels for the assembly.
Those supreme among men who dwell in the empty wheel of the hand,
within the groves of awakened lotuses— they are indeed fit vessels for the assembly.
Those who constantly move back and forth within the wheel-family (cakrakula),
and those who have reached the pericarp (nābhi)— they are the vessels for the assembly (melāpa).
Those whose chewing is long-continued and greedy within the foundational wheels (ādhāracakra)...

But those who move within the family of awakening, who have abandoned coming and going, and who wander in the midst of the equinox— they are indeed the vessels for the melāpa. Furthermore, those whose minds move like chowries are the vessels for the melāpa.
Those who investigate the mantras, tantras, and the knowledge of what is to be known through wisdom,
and who are constantly skilled in that path— they are indeed fit vessels for the melāpa.

Those who delight in the wheel and the fierce one, those who abide in the center of the earring, and those who delight in the subtle vibration of consciousness— they are indeed the vessels for the *melāpa*.
Those who reside within the three states of speech, and those who are free from the three states of speech.
But those who have abandoned the great path are not vessels for the *melāpa*. Those for whom waking is like a dream, those for whom a dream is like deep sleep,
and those for whom everything becomes the fourth state (*turya*)— they alone are vessels for the *melāpa*.
Those who devour the sun and moon, those who drink the ocean,
and those who sport with the Fortune of the World— they are the recipients of the *melāpa*.
Those heroes who drink from the *bhaga* and lick the *liṅga*— they are the recipients of the *melāpa*.
Then, intoxicated by the essence of bliss, they become vessels for the *melāpa*.
From the arising of the flower until the end of the flower has arrived, as long as they remain within the play of the *bhaga*, they are indeed vessels for the *melāpa*.
Those who are constantly devoted to the *picu* (cotton) face, having entered the interior of the *picu* face,
and who have awakened to the inner essence of that movement— they are indeed the vessels for the *melāpa* (union).
They are eternally intent upon the worship of the feet [of the Guru] and are always greedy for the six flavors.
Those who are intent on drawing others [to themselves] are indeed vessels for the *melāpa*.
Those who live by means of the life-force (*jīva*) as if it were their own life, and who act like Śiva,
living with perpetual festivals, they are the vessels for the *melāpa*.
Those who abide at the conclusion of the Mahāyāna, those who always abide in arising,
and those who have entered the Krama-udara— these indeed are the vessels for the *melāpa*.
Thus has it been briefly explained, O slender-waisted one, after due reflection.
Thereafter, O Bhairavī, the rite of union (melāpaka) should be performed by the best of practitioners,
one by one in the sequence previously specified; otherwise, O lady of excellent complexion, one does not become a partaker of the union.
(231b) At the outset, for the sake of accomplishing the gathering (*melāpa*), one should observe this vow.
Then, O Goddess, having undertaken the *cīlla* vow, one should subsequently perform the gathering.
I shall proclaim this vow known by the name Kaṅkālabhāsura;
by performing it five times, the accomplishment of the *piṇḍa* shall belong to the great-souled practitioner.
Indeed, within the eight sections beginning with the letter *ka*, one should [visualize] a well-adorned garland of severed heads.
Having made that [skull] marked with handprints on every section, one should hold it upon the head.
The *khaṭvāṅga* is filled with apertures, adorned with a great fly-whisk (*cāmara*),
joined with strips of rags and small bells, possessing a fine handle, firm and without blemish.
One should carry [the skull] in the left hand, endowed with various beauties;
on both ears, auspicious rings made of human bone should be worn;
and around the neck, a garland made of bones, adorned with seven creepers.

A man [should visualize] him wearing a great hanging necklace, likewise holding in his right hand a skull-bowl filled with wine, liquor, and so forth; nor should a girdle made of bone fragments or adorned with severed heads be fashioned.

O lady with a vajra-like belly, it should be joined with small bells and provided with human hair; in its center, a human gem should be placed. The two anklets should be firmly fashioned, delicate, and variegated with small bells.
Smeared with the ashes of a hero, wearing the sacred thread, and composed in mind;
his consciousness filled with the bliss of wine, adorned with fragrant flowers;
his mouth full of betel, his eyes rolling with intoxication.
Wandering everywhere, I consume even human flesh;
I am a Kāpālika, a Kaṅkālī, and one greedy for the union of rays.
Though I devour all things, I am the fifty-eighth, the Lord of the Circle of Heroes.
One who speaks thus should always be a king among the wise and should constantly practice. Possessing great heroism, established in the *kalā*, and observing the conduct of Bhairava,
one who performs this for three months flies through the courtyard of the sky.
After six months, O King, he will become equal to the Goddess of the gods;
having observed this vow for one month, he shall become a vessel for the melāpa.
He indeed becomes a great hero, saluted by all who move through the sky.
O Goddess, this supreme vow is difficult to attain for those of unrefined self. Furthermore, one should perform the "Madman's" vow, which is most auspicious.
He would be a speaker of untruth and a deceiver by whatever means possible. Naked, with disheveled hair, eating everything yet free from greed;
he laughs one moment, sings the next, weeps the next, and shouts the next.
For a moment he may leap, for a moment he may dance, for a moment he may run, and for a moment he may frolic;
for a moment he may be peaceful, for a moment heroic, and for a moment terrified;
for a moment he may abide in the sentiment of wrath, and for a moment in the terrible.
O Goddess, for a moment he is full of passion, for a moment intent solely on laughter;
for a moment he is established in wonder, and for a moment he abides in compassion.
Thus, he is permeated by various aesthetic sentiments (rasas) and established in various mental states (bhāvas).
Endowed with various amorous sports and filled with the sounds of diverse songs,
he should constantly wear on his body discarded flower-garlands fallen from the street, or even the garlands of a corpse; and he should speak clearly in many languages.
At one moment it may sound like a jackal or a raven; at another, it is filled with the cries of a blue jay.
At one moment it may utter the neighing of a horse, and at another, the trumpeting of an elephant. At one moment it may cry out like a cat, and at another, it may warble like a crane.
For a moment he should utter a roar called *garva*, and for a moment he should sound the *kesara* note;
for a moment, with the fourfold *maṅga*, the man should neigh like a horse of the *valva* breed.
He should say, "I am a Kāpālika," and again, "I am a Caṇḍāla."
"I am tormented by passion, I am intoxicated, I am hungry;
I am lamenting"—one may speak such words, even though they are harsh.
Abiding within the throbbing *rāviṇīcakra*, one experiences the play of the *kalā* and *kula*.
Established in the supreme expanse of consciousness within the cavern of all sense-bases,
one should always practice this vow, endowed with its power.
Indeed, one should wander even at night for as long as a month in places such as cremation grounds;
then, within seven days, a vision of the goddesses will occur.
Appearing in various forms, both beautiful and ugly, they speak words that are appropriate or inappropriate.
Thereafter, they bestow those perfected substances which are:
a sword, a vessel, ash from a stone, yellow pigment (rocanā), and a sacred thread.
O Queen of the Gods, one should never touch these five nectars.
Using that very [substance], the great hero, the lord of practitioners, should rub his body and not discard even a little outside; he should practice in this manner for one month.
Then, indeed, he floats in the sky as far as the limit of Śakti.
She is worshipped at all times by the Lord Mahābhairava.
O Goddess, just as that Supreme Sovereign Kālikā is the Mistress Bhairavī, so too shall the practitioner become; what need is there for much more here?
Thus, O Goddess, this supreme vow is difficult to perform even for the Bhairavas; however,
it must be understood that the procedure for this vow is such that even those devoid of strength, the timid, and the lowest of men may worship it just as we do.
By honoring and venerating all the wheels of the Yoginīs, a man becomes worthy of respect.
As soon as he understands this vow, that man shall become a lord of Bhairava.
And whoever thus speaks daily, "I shall perform this supreme vow," [attains this state].
And he beholds the God and Goddess in just six months.
This most excellent and supreme vow has been proclaimed by you.
Thus, one should perform these two vows for a short while during the day.
Afterwards, one shall partake in the melāpa; otherwise, the ritual action is fruitless.
This has been explained in brief; what else shall I tell you?

Thus ends the chapter titled "The Rule for Vows" in the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the Great Tantra of the Severed Head within the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) of the Bhairava Current, in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work, in the third hexad.
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, it is exactly as you have told me;
O God, I have [received] your knowledge from the beginning in its proper sequence. In this regard, there is this great secret of mine, crowded with many mysteries."
"O Śaṅkara, best of gods, by your grace I am fully satisfied.
Now I wish to hear about the most wonderful easy method,
which is free from arduous practices and devoid of the performance of vows."
"O Mahādeva, O supreme compassionate one, tell me that rite for the assembly of the deities which bears the mark of the *vṛṣala*.
Having heard this, Hara, the lord of the gods, laughed for a long time.
He spoke at length on the procedure for the *melāpa* (union) with the Supreme Goddess—
[a rite] filled with many wheels (*cakras*), accompanied by secret teachings, and most wonderful.
Bhairava said:
Listen, for I shall speak as I am urged by you who are virtuous;
I shall describe that secret which has been taught in the sequence of the Kālīcakra.
Having received it from the mouth of the Guru and having practiced it, O slender-waisted one.
Having performed a brief recitation of the mantra, O Goddess, you should thereafter wander;
by means of the steps of the Wheel of Knowledge (*vidyācakra*), one should bring about the Great Assembly (*mahāmelāpa*).
When that person, whose body is smeared with vermilion, is possessed of the wealth of the bliss of wine, [then the assembly occurs].

One who is devoted to the great five nectars (pañcāmṛta) shall go to the family that protects the eon. Therefore, O Dear One, one should play with the wine from the vessel of liquor like a hero. One should not speak thus: "I am thirsty; give me this water to quench my thirst."
"For their satisfaction, let the Bhairavas be given to me from the vessel of wine,
by which the Mothers may be satiated with ten million portions of great bliss.
Having spoken thus, O Supreme Goddess, they offer the wine.
Having taken that and filled a jar with a *māḍhaka* measure plus a *smita*, he,
his eyes rolling with intoxication, satiated himself right there.
The practitioner of mantra should go to the house of a hero or else to an empty dwelling.
There, having filled his mouth [with breath], he should utter this single word: "Phūḥ.
As long as he continues to scatter it, the deities will arrive.
Assuming various forms such as those of dogs and cats, and intoxicated with passion,
they speak in many different languages before the practitioner; there is no doubt that he floats through the expanse of the sky together with them in accordance with reality.
Therefore, O Goddess of the gods, the practitioner becomes like Bhairava himself;
or rather, by drinking that very wine while remaining composed,
a gathering of Yoginīs occurs, known as *priyā*, which grants all desires.
Alternatively, one who has drunk wine may wander through many courtesans' quarters;
wherever the groups of women appear beautiful,
cry out, or dance, O fortunate lady, he should behave in that manner there.
Endowed with supreme vigor and possessing the highest vision,
as he acts in this manner there, O Dear One, the Yoginī who is his beloved quickly approaches him, filled with joy and full of affection.
Whatever secret belongs to that [tantra], she should proclaim it to the couple.
By means of that very knowledge, the discerning practitioner must not transgress her;
for there would arise an incomparable union, which is difficult even for the lords of the gods to obtain.
Then, seeking the *melāpa*, one should go from there to the house of an oil-presser.
Having gone there, O illustrious lady, the lord of practitioners (*sādhakeśvara*), first standing together with him,
mentally recites the lower mantras.
Mounted upon that wheel and established in the khecarī-bandha,
the yogi, absorbed in the bliss of his own true nature, should rotate [the wheel] a thousand times,
certainly for as long as seven days, until he attains the sovereignty of the state.
For that long, there occurs for him a great wandering like that of a wheel;
thereafter, that practitioner of great power enters the yogic sleep.
Then that hero of great intelligence, while in a state of sleep,
beheld an entire host of deities of various forms and many kinds;
together with them, he flew through the expanse of the sky for the duration of a month.
There he is worshipped by them as the leader Bhairava—
the omniscient, the creator of all, and the Lord of the Great Lords of Yoga.
Now I shall further describe another meeting-place (melāpa) that follows the vehicles (vāhana).
One should have a beautiful tripod (*dravaka*) made from *vīra* wood;
it should have three legs, with a circumference of eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and a mouth six finger-breadths wide.
O Lord, its length shall be thirty-six finger-breadths.
Its two base-pins made of wood should have silver feet,
O Goddess; having thus fashioned this excellent vehicle extending from east to west,
one should bathe it with honey and wine.
Again with the nectar of Vāmā, again indeed with the water of Śiva;
again with Candananātha, and again that with Brahmā;
again with the stalk and clarified butter, O Goddess, and again indeed with what?
The wife of the master of the house should bathe [the deity] with her excellent feet;
thereafter, the beautiful woman should bathe that supreme vehicle with flowers.
After that, O Supreme Goddess, he should be bathed with the three creations.

Thus, O Goddess, the body is the rite; it is a most beautiful place of accomplishment. Swayed by the great state through the wandering flow of the vital breath, the illustrious one situated in the wheel of space (khe-cakra) should worship the God and Goddess.
With divine fish-meat and spirits, as well as *surā* and *śīdhu*,
and with lamps made from fish oil and the like mixed with great oils,
he should worship the God and Goddess situated within the liquid in the center.
Indeed, for as long as seven days it smokes; then,
in due order, it becomes hot and thereafter it blazes forth.

Then one should know that the most excellent mount has been perfected. Listen, O fortunate one, as I shall describe in due order the characteristics of this very perfected [mount] while it is emitting smoke while situated in the cremation ground.
Established in the region of the anus, his movement through the sky extends for thirty *yojanas*.
Whatever place he contemplates, he reaches it in the interval of a single moment.
Taking whatever object is situated there, he returns with speed in an instant.

Whichever Yoginī resides there—whether she be a Bhūcarī or a Khecarī, a Ḍākinī or a Ḍāmarikā—she grants accomplishment (siddhi) to that person; of this there is no doubt. She bestows the knowledge of the Krama upon the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
Listen, O beloved, to what is emitted by that very heat:
situated within the house of the Great Hero, this practitioner travels through the sky for ten yojanas; he proceeds through the apertures of the *tintirī* tree—of this there is no doubt.
He shall partake in the union with the terrestrial *lāmās*,
by means of which the practitioner becomes all-knowing through that very union;
indeed, the practitioner becomes like Rudra himself— the destroyer and the creator.
O beloved, he always attains invisibility among human beings;
furthermore, the great Śambara-knowledge arises within his body.
Now listen as I shall explain this to you concerning him who is ablaze.
This means of accomplishment for Indra is even more difficult to obtain;
yet, having attained it while blazing there in his final birth,
he traverses the entire universe, and his movement comes to a complete halt.
By whichever great-souled practitioner that [deity] has been made into a vehicle,
he shall become Bhairava in person, worshipped by all the lords of yoga;
a hero who bestows both curses and favors, the lord of all melāpakas.
The protector of all, the refuge of all, possessed of great splendor and great strength,
he creates thousands of forms from a single form in an instant.
This one of great power is served by a hundred thousand yoginīs;
he constantly partakes of the great sacrificial pap (caru) and is eternally endowed with the fruits of spiritual accomplishment.
He becomes united with Śiva and Śakti; of this there is no doubt.
Thus has the accomplishment of Hara been truly explained to you.
Now, O Mistress, I shall describe to you the ritual for the union (*melaka*).
Previously, one who is satiated with wine, intoxicated, and possessed of great power—
Smeared with funeral ashes and anointed with great quantities of blood,
the Hero should proceed to the water-wheel, taking his steps as prescribed.
Mounted upon that very machine, he should bring about the complete cessation of worldly activity.
Then, within seven days alone, the practitioner shall obtain the *melaka*.
Having attained this, those best of men do not grieve again.
Now listen, O Goddess, to those nine sacrifices of the goddesses which were indeed performed in the past.
In the Sindhukhaṇḍa, I have described those [practices], by which the union (melāpa) is supreme:
having grown upon the surface of a grindstone, having bound the Karaṅkiṇī mudrā,
and previously reciting the mantra with joy for seven days while intoxicated with wine.

As long as the Hero remains present, so long does he participate in the *melāpa*. Indeed, by means of this very procedure, while firmly established in the state of *khaṇḍanī*, one should cause [the disciple] to carry it and bind the *mudrā*; then one shall attain *melāpa*.
O Goddess, there is no doubt that this should be done at the very same time previously mentioned; O Mistress of the Gods, one should perform the previously stated rite even at some other time.
Satiated by the previously mentioned liquor, one should firmly assume the divine mudrā.
Then, in just seven days, the hero shall partake in the *melāpa*.
Regarding the pestle (*musala*), one should perform only the ritual procedure for the mounts;
as before, the elixir of accomplishment (*siddhipāva*) is obtained, and no further distinction is prescribed.
I shall speak the sweet words of Mārjinī so that one may obtain the assembly exactly as it is:
having installed her before the Jyeṣṭhā [deity], one should worship the thousand-syllable mantra.
O Beloved, having first offered here whatever is desired, such as wine and so forth,
one should then compose a continuous stream of licks (lelihāna) following that.
Then, in just seven days, the practitioner shall obtain the union (melaka).
This very same procedure is to be known for the most supreme *culliyāga*.
There, one should first worship the bricks; within seven days, one will obtain the *melaka*.
Having brought a winnowing basket that is free of holes, one should worship it before the *Jyeṣṭhā* [deity].
Having prepared the sacrificial porridge for the Śrāvaka,
one should offer it; likewise, having first honored the ladle with great joy today,
one should proceed, O beloved, to the house of Mahāvīrya while holding [the vessel] in this manner.
Staying there, one should extract the Vidyā or that single word;
then, within two *ghaṭikās*, the practitioner shall partake in the *melāpa*.
Such is the procedure for the water-pitcher; this is the method for the *melaka*.

I shall explain how the union of the *melāpa* occurs in Vardhamāna. Having gone to the place called Vardhamāna, one should worship Saṃkarṣaṇī there with substances produced from the five jewels, and furthermore, through the binding of the *khecarī*.

The excellent hero who partakes in the *melāpa* becomes truly possessed of great power. A man whose purpose is the attainment of all desires and pleasures attains the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratā*). Fully perfected and endowed with supreme bliss, he attains liberation.
Thus was this supreme tantra learned by me; it was formerly studied by Vasiṣṭha and even by Nara and Nārāyaṇa. Furthermore, the mighty Śiraccheda was [studied] by Brahmā in my presence.
Today, this [teaching] of yours, crowded with a multitude of many mantras, has been revealed in such a way that it has not been known by anyone and has not been heard by anyone.
Likewise, the third excellent hexad, joined with the secret [teachings],
is proclaimed, O Goddess, to consist of six thousand verses. It should be known that through its recitation it bestows liberation, and through its retention it increases prosperity.
For then, O best of men, it should be known that this is one's final birth;
when this supreme *śiraccheda* tantra has come into one's hands,
true knowledge itself will arise within six months from its mastery.
Thus, I have declared this tantra of yours— the essence of all essences, the infinite secret, worthy of worship by the entire host of gods,
and the core of the various playful manifestations of the heroes.
I shall now speak of the Fourth State (*turya*), which has come down through the lineage and is even beyond that.

Thus ends the chapter on the Accomplishment of the Great Melāpa (*mahāmelāpasiddhipaṭala*) in the third hexad of the *Jayadrathayāmala*, the great tantra of twenty-four thousand verses, within the *Śiraccheda* section of the *Vidyāpīṭha* in the *Bhairavasrotas*.
Thus ends the third chapter of the Vāsiṣṭha. Oṃ, salutations to all the Siddhas and Yoginīs; salutations! Saṃvat 807, the bright fortnight of Māgha.
